<PB N=v>
<C>PREFACE</C>
<SHL>
<P><SC>Since</SC> these volumes, containing separate plays, are independent
of each other, it seems necessary that a statement of the plan on
which they are edited should accompany each issue. This state-
ment, however, in the present instance shall be as concise as pos-
sible; it is to be presumed that those who are interested in this
edition are, by this time, tolerably familiar with its scope.
<P>The attempt is here made to present, on the same page with the
text, all the various readings of the different editions of <I>King Lear</I>,
from the earliest Quarto to the latest critical edition of the play,
together with all the notes and comments thereon which the Edi-
tor has thought worthy of preservation, not only for the purpose of
elucidating the text, but at times as illustrations of the history of
Shakespearian criticism.
<P>In the <SC>Appendix</SC> will be found essays on <SC>The Text, The Date
of Composition, The Source of the Plot, Duration of the
Action, Insanity, Actors, Costume, Tate's Version</SC>, selections
from <SC>English</SC> and <SC>German Criticisms</SC>, a list of <SC>The Editions
Collated</SC>, with the abbreviations used to denote them, the <SC>Bibli-
ography</SC> of the Play, and an <SC>Index</SC>.
<P>We have two sources for the text of <I>Lear</I>, the Quartos and the
Folios, both from independent manuscripts. Although we may not
have in the Folio the very text, &lquo;absolute in its numbers,&rquo; as Shake-
speare &lquo;conceived it,&rquo; yet with all its defects it is much better than
that of the Quarto, which is evidently one of those &lquo;stolne and sur-
&lquo;reptitious&rquo; copies denounced by Heminge and Condell. Wherefore,
in this edition the text of the <SC>First Folio</SC> has been virtually fol-
<PB N=vi>
<HE>vi <I>PREFACE</I></HE>
<P>lowed, but without, it is to be trusted, an absolute surrender to that
&lquo;modern Manicheeism, the worship of the Printer's devil.&rquo; Where
the Folio is clearly defective the Quartos have been called in aid.
Moreover, since the Quartos, &lquo;maimed and deformed&rquo; though they
be &lquo;by the frauds and stealthes of injurious impostors,&rquo; do never-
theless contain lines, and even a whole scene, which do not appear
in the Folio, but are nevertheless Shakespeare's, it has not been
deemed fitting to omit these; they have been retained in the text
and their presence indicated by asterisks, a modification of the
Italic of the old editors, which is due to Dr <SC>Schmidt's</SC> admirable
edition.
<P>Happily, the day is fast declining when it is thought necessary
to modernise Shakespeare's text. Why should it be modernised?
We do not so treat <SC>Spenser</SC>. Is <SC>Shakespeare's</SC> text less sacred?
A step was made when &lquo;it&rquo; was boldly retained instead of modern-
ising the possessive case to <I>its.</I> In the present edition such words
as &lquo;moe,&rquo; &lquo;and&rquo; (when it is equivalent to <I>if</I>), &lquo;vilde,&rquo; &lquo;strook,&rquo;
and others, have been retained when found in the Folio. The ab-
breviated &lquo;th&rquo; has also been copied from the same edition. It is
a source of regret that it did not occur to the Editor, until too
late, that the modern substitution of &lquo;than,&rquo; for <I>then</I> of the Folio,
is equally uncalled for, a substitution which shall not occur in
future volumes of this edition.
<P>My thanks are gladly given to Mr <SC>Norris</SC> for the <SC>Bibliography</SC>
of English works; to my father, the Rev. Dr <SC>Furness</SC>, for his
translations of <SC>German Criticisms</SC>; and to one other, without
whose constant encouragement even this much of my long and
at times most weary task would not have been accomplished; to
her I am indebted for the <SC>Index</SC>.
<P>H. H. F.
<P><I>March, 1880.</I>

<CC><P><B>The Tragedy,</B> &amp;c.] &lquo;Of all Shakespeare's plays,&rquo; says <SC>Coleridge</SC>, &lquo;<I>Macbeth</I>
is the most rapid, <I>Hamlet</I> the slowest, in movement. <I>Lear</I> combines length with
rapidity,&mdash;like the hurricane and the whirlpool, absorbing while it advances. It
begins as a stormy day in summer, with brightness; but that brightness is lurid,
and anticipates the tempest.&rquo;
<P>1-6. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 13) would read these as seven lines of verse, ending
<I>th' duke . . . always . . . division . . . o' th' dukes . . . pois'd</I> [sic] . . . <I>choice
. . . moiety.</I> &lquo;After <I>moiety</I>,&rquo; he adds, &lquo;there is a short pause in the conversation,
which is resumed in prose. Yet <I>th' duke</I>, in this place, seems very unlike Sh.; and
<I>equalities</I> is perhaps more in place than &ldquo;qualities.&rdquo;&rquo;
<P>2. <B>Albany]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: Holinshed (<I>Chron.</I> i, $ol. 39 <I>b;</I> ed. 1577) gives the fol-
lowing account of the origin of this name: &lquo;The third and last part of the Island
he allotted vnto Albanacte hys youngest sonne. . . . This later parcel at the first,
toke the name of Albanactus, who called it Albania. But now a small portion
onely of the Region (beyng vnder the regiment of a Duke) reteyneth the sayd</CC>
<PB N=4>
<HE>4 <I>KING LEAR</I> [<SC>act i, sc.</SC> i.</HE>
<BO>division of the kingdom, it appears not which of the dukes<LB N=4></BO>
<AC><COL>4. <I>kingdom</I>] <I>kingdomes</I> Qq, Coll. i.</COL></AC>
<FHL>
<CC><P>denomination, the reast beyng called Scotlande, of certayne Scottes that came ouer
from Ireland to inhabite in those quarters. It is deuided from Loegres also by the
Humber, so that Albania as Brute left it, conteyned all the north part of the Island
that is to be found beyond the aforesayd streame, vnto the point of Cathenesse.&rquo;
<P>4. <B>division]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: There is something of obscurity or inaccuracy in this
preparatory scene. The king has already divided his kingdom, and yet when he
enters he examines his daughters, to discover in what proportion he should divide it.
Perhaps Kent and Gloster only were privy to his design, which he still kept in his
own hands, to be changed or performed as subsequent reasons should determine
him. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: It was not without $orethought, nor is it without its due signifi
cance, that the division of Lear's kingdom is in the first six lines of the play stated
as a thing already determined in all its particulars, previously to the trial of profes-
sions, as to the relative rewards of which the daughters were to be made to consider
their several portions. The strange, yet by no means unnatural, mixture of selfish-
ness, sensibility, and habit of feeling derived from, and fostered by, the particular
rank and usages of the individual;&mdash;the intense desire of being intensely beloved,&mdash;
selfish, and yet characteristic of the selfishness of a loving and kindly nature alone;&mdash;
the self-supportless leaning for all pleasure on another's breast;&mdash;the craving after
sympathy with a prodigal disinterestedness, frustrated by its own ostentation, and the
mode and nature of its claims;&mdash;the anxiety, the distrust, the jealousy, which more
or less accompany all selfish affections, and are amongst the surest contradistinctions
of mere fondness from true love, and which originate Lear's eager wish to enjoy his
daughters' violent professions, whilst the inveterate habits of sovereignty convert
the wish into claim and positive right, and an incompliance with it into crime and
treason;&mdash;these facts, these passions, these moral verities, on which the whole
tragedy is founded, are all prepared for, and will to the retrospect be found implied,
in these first four or five lines of the play. They let us know that the trial is but a
trick, and that the grossness of the old king's rage is in part the natural result of a
silly trick suddenly and most unexpectedly baffled and disappointed. It may here
be worthy of notice that <I>Lear</I> is the only serious performance of Shakespeare, the
interest and situations of which are derived from the assumption of a gross improba-
bility; whereas Beaumont and Fletcher's tragedies are, almost all of them, founded
on some out-of-the-way accident or exception to the general experience of mankind.
But observe the matchless judgement of our Shakespeare. First, improbable as the
conduct of Lear is in the first scene, yet it was an old story rooted in the popular
faith,&mdash;a thing taken for granted already, and consequently without any of the effects
of improbability. Secondly, it is merely the canvas for the characters and passions,&mdash;
a mere occasion for,&mdash;and not, in the manner of Beaumont and Fletcher, perpetually
recurring as the cause and <I>sine qua non</I> of,&mdash;the incidents and emotions. Let the
first scene of this play have been lost, and let it only be understood that a fond
father had been duped by hypocritical professions of love and duty on the part of
two daughters to disinherit the third, previously, and deservedly, more dear to him;
&mdash;and all the rest of the tragedy would retain its interest undiminished, and be per-
fectly intelligible. The accidental is nowhere the groundwork of the passions, but
that which is catholic, which in all ages has been, and ever will be, close and native</CC>

<CC><P>to the heart of man,&mdash;parental anguish from filial ingratitude, the genuineness of
worth, though coffined in bluntness, and the execrable vileness of a smooth iniquity.
Perhaps I ought to have added the <I>Merchant of Venice;</I> but here too the same
remarks apply. It was an old tale; and substitute any other danger than that of the
pound of flesh (the circumstance in which the improbability lies), yet all the situa-
tions and the emotions appertaining to them remain equally excellent and appropriate.
Whereas take away from the <I>Mad Lover</I> of Beaumont and Fletcher the fantastic
hypothesis of his engagement to cut out his own heart, and have it presented to his
mistress, and all the main scenes must go with it. <SC>Hudson</SC>: The opening thus
forecasts Lear's madness by indicating that dotage has already got the better of his
reason and judgment. <SC>Anon</SC> (cited by <SC>Halliwell</SC>) thinks Johnson's note is need-
less, because &lquo;it is clear that Lear's two councillors, Kent and Gloucester, are talking
of the division he has proposed in the secrecy of the council-board, and afterwards
he opens his hidden (&ldquo;darker&rdquo;) meaning to those whom it concerned (his sons and
daughters), before ignorant of it.&rquo;
<P>5. <B>qualities]</B> <SC>Capell</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, &amp;c., vol. i, part ii, p. 140): &lquo;Qualities&rquo; appears to
be a printer's corruption; both as suiting less with the context and as taking some-
thing from the passage's numerousness. [What this &lquo;numerousness&rquo; exactly means
I do not know. Capell does not print the passage as verse.] <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Zur Text-
kritik</I>, p. 12): <I>Equalities</I> cannot be right here; at best it can but be <I>equality.</I> Equal-
ity cannot be predicated of a part by itself, but only of the relationship of parts to
each other; it is therefore essentially a singular idea. We cannot say: &lquo;the equal-
ities of the three parts are perfect,&rquo; but only: &lquo;the equality,&rquo; &amp;c.
<P>5. <B>curiosity]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: &lquo;Curiosity&rquo; for <I>exactest scrutiny.</I> <SC>Steevens</SC>: That
is, <I>scrupulousness</I> or <I>captiousness.</I> [For the pronunciation, see I, ii, 4.]
<P>6. <B>moiety]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: The strict sense of this is <I>half, one of two equal parts</I>,
but Sh. commonly uses it for <I>any part</I> or <I>division.</I> Thus, 1 <I>Hen. IV:</I> III, i, 96:&mdash;
&lquo;Methinks my moiety north from Burton here In quantity equals not one of yours,&rquo;
and here the division was into three parts. <SC>Wright</SC>: It may be in the present pas-
sage the word is used in its literal sense, for it is not clear that Gloucester knew any-
thing of Lear's intention to include Cordelia in the distribution of the kingdom.
<P>7. <B>your son]</B> For <SC>Coleridge's</SC> fine remarks on Edmund, see Appendix, p. 419.
<P>9. <B>brazed]</B> Compare <I>Ham.</I> III, iv, 37.</CC>

<CC><P>p. 420.] <SC>Wright</SC>: Edmund has been seeking his fortune abroad, there being no
career for him at home in consequence of his illegitimate birth.
<P>32. <B>Burgundy]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> p. 240) says that the pronunciation <I>Burgogne</I>
(as it is spelled in the last scene, in F<SUB>1</SUB>, in <I>Hen. V</I>) would restore harmony to this
line. But <SC>Dyce</SC>, in a note on 2 <I>Hen. VI:</I> I, i, 7, says that Sh., like other early dram-
atists, considered himself at liberty occasionally to disregard the laws of metre in
the case of proper names; <I>e. g.</I> a blank-verse speech in <I>Rich. II:</I> II, i, 284, con-
tains the following formidable line: &lquo;Sir John Norberry, Sir Robert Waterton, and
Francis Quoint.&rquo; [It is spelled <I>Borgoyen</I> in <I>Paston Letters</I>, iii, 79, ed. Arber.]
<P>32. <B>Gloucester]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 236): In the Folio this name is printed <I>Glou-
cester</I>, or <I>Glocester</I>, in the stage-directions and titles of speeches; <I>Gloster</I>, sometimes
<I>Glouster</I>, in the text; in either case, with very few exceptions. I speak of all the
plays in which the name occurs; the distinction is least observed, perhaps, in <I>Lear.</I>
<P>33. <B>shall]</B> For instances of the use of &lquo;shall&rquo; in the sense of <I>I am bound to</I>
and <I>I am sure to</I>, and hence often used in the replies of inferiors to superiors, see
<SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect;315.
<P><B>darker]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: That is, <I>more secret;</I> not <I>indirect, oblique.</I> <SC>Johnson</SC>:
That is, we have already made known in some measure our desire of parting the
kingdom; we will now discover what has not been told before, the reasons by
which we shall regulate the partition. This interpretation will justify or palliate
the exordial dialogue.
<P>36. <B>fast]</B> <SC>Edwards</SC> (<I>Can. of Crit.</I> p. 91, ed. 1765): That is, <I>determined resolu-

ing <I>fixed, settled</I> intent, is, like &lquo;<I>darker</I> purpose&rquo; and &lquo;<I>constant</I> will,&rquo; peculiarly in
Shakespeare's manner.</CC>

<CC><P>Richardson), &lquo;God oftentymes by clere examples and bodely delyuerances <I>chalengeth</I>
to himself the glorye of his owne name.&rquo; In our own poet, too, cf. 3 <I>Hen. VI:</I>
III, iii, 86: &lquo;all her perfections <I>challenge</I> sovereignty;&rquo; IV, vi, 6: &lquo;Subjects may
<I>challenge</I> nothing of their sovereigns;&rquo; IV, viii, 48: &lquo;These graces <I>challenge</I> grace;&rquo;
and <I>Oth.</I> I, iii, 188: &lquo;So much I <I>challenge</I> that I may profess due to the Moor,
my lord&rquo;&mdash;<I>i. e. claim as my right.</I> Giving then this meaning to &lquo;challenge,&rquo; the
passage may be properly paraphrased, &lquo;where your natural relation to, and love for,
me <I>claim</I> my bounty, <I>by deserving it;</I> or, in other words, &lquo;that I may extend my
largest bounty where your natural affection <I>deservedly claims it as due.</I>&rquo; There is no
contention or challenge between &lquo;nature&rquo; and &lquo;merit,&rquo; in which the king's bounty is
to be the prize; he offers it solely to &lquo;nature,&rquo; <I>claiming</I> or demanding it on its own
deserts. <SC>Ulrici</SC> (p. 443): These words cannot possibly have been meant seriously;
for apart from the circumstance that they contradict the facts adduced, Lear himself
does not act in accordance with them, but does the very opposite. . . . Obviously,
therefore, the whole demand was but a freak of the imagination, which Lear did not
mean to take into serious consideration, but which it occurred to him to make mere-
ly to fill up the time till the return of Gloucester, who had been despatched to fetch
the duke of Burgundy and the king of France. The concealed motive of this freak,
and its execution, was probably Lear's wish,&mdash;by an open and public assurance of
his daughters' love and piety,&mdash;to convince himself that his abdication could be
of no danger to himself, and that doubts about its propriety were unfounded.
<SC>Bucknill</SC> (p. 174): That the trial is a mere trick is unquestionable; but is not
the significance of this fact greater than Coleridge suspected? Does it not lead
us to conclude that from the first the king's mind is off its balance; that the parti-
tion of his kingdom, involving inevitable feuds and wars, is the first act of his devel-
oping insanity; and that the manner of its partition, the mock-trial of his daughters'
affections, and its tragical d&eacute;nouement is the second, and but the second, act of his
madness.

in the <I>Holy Grail;</I> &lquo;reian&rquo; meaning in the Cornish &lquo;to give bounteously.&rquo;

<P>54. <B>word]</B> <SC>Knight</SC> and <SC>Delius</SC> (ed. 1) adopt <I>word</I> of Ff, and the latter justi-

<P>55. <B>space]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: The limits within which motion is possible. Compare <I>Ant.
and Cleop.</I> I, i. 34. &lquo;Rather,&rquo; says <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>ad loc.</I>), &lquo;is &ldquo;space,&rdquo; space in gen-
eral, the realm of external appearances, the world; &ldquo;eyesight&rdquo; is the capacity to
comprehend it; &ldquo;liberty&rdquo; the freedom to enjoy it. The lack of natural filial affec-
tion could not be more clearly manifested than in such exaggerations. Regan's
&ldquo;square of sense,&rdquo; line 73, affords a commentary on these words of Goneril.&rquo;
<P>60. <B>so much]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Beyond all assignable quantity; I love you beyond limits,
and cannot say it is <I>so much</I>, for how much soever I should name, it would yet be
more. <SC>Wright</SC>: Beyond all these comparisons by which Goneril sought to measure
her love. <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>ad loc.</I>) thinks the phrase would have been clear at once had
the old editions only used quotation-marks: &lquo;beyond all manner of &ldquo;so much&rdquo; I
love you.&rquo;
<P>61. <B>speak]</B> Apart from authority, the choice of readings here seems to me to
depend on whether we take &lquo;Love&rquo; and &lquo;be silent&rquo; as infinitives or imperatives.
If they are infinitives, we should read &lquo;do&rquo; with the Qq, but if imperatives, we
should follow the Ff. I think they are imperatives, and I am supported by <SC>Schmidt</SC>
(<I>Zur Textkritik</I>, p. 12). Moreover, <SC>Knight</SC> pronounces <I>do</I> of the Qq feeble, be-
cause it destroys the force of the answer: &lquo;Love, and <I>be silent.</I>&rquo; <SC>White</SC> and <SC>Dyce</SC>,
on the other hand, assert that the answer plainly shows that the Qq are right and the
Ff wrong.</CC>

<CC><P>63. <B>champains]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: Plains. Compare Deut. xi. 30 (ed. 1611): &lquo;the

2, the marginal note to &lquo;valley&rquo; is &lquo;or, champian.&rquo; See <I>Twelfth Night</I>, II, v, 174,

In Florio we find, &lquo;Campagna, a field or a champaine.&rquo;

<P>68. <B>self]</B> Compare &lquo;self mate and mate,&rquo; IV, iii, 34; and for many other in-

<P>69. <B>worth]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC>: Mr. Bishop prescribed the pointing of this passage as
I have regulated it in the text. [See Text-notes.] Regan would say that in the
truth of her heart and affection she equals the worth of her sister. Without this
change in the pointing, she makes a boast of herself without any cause assigned.
<SC>Tyrwhitt</SC> paraphrases his punctuation: &lquo;And <I>so may you</I> prize me at her worth, <I>as</I>
in my true heart I find, <I>that</I> she names,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Mason</SC> (p. 338): I believe we should
read: &lquo;prize <I>you</I> at her worth;&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> set the same high value on you that she does.
<P>70. <B>deed of love]</B> <SC>Eccles</SC>: Describes that kind of agency by which my own
love operates,&mdash;the same effects of which it is productive. <SC>Delius</SC>: The formal,
legal definition of love. <SC>Wright</SC>: That is, exactly describes my love.</CC>

<P>73. <B>square of sense]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC> thinks this refers to the four nobler senses,
<I>sight, hearing, taste</I>, and <I>smell</I>, but <SC>Johnson</SC> thinks it may mean only <I>compass, com-

describe the utmost perfection of sense (alluding to the Pythagorean Tenet, which
held a square to be the most perfect figure). <SC>Capell</SC>: &lquo;Not only the extravagance
of these sisters' professions, but the words they are dress'd in paint their hearts to
perfection. In Regan's we have &ldquo;felicitate,&rdquo; an affected expression, and before it a
line that's all affectation; the governing phrase in it is borrow'd (as thinks the edi-
tor) from some fantastical position of the rosycrucians or cabalists, who use it in the
sense the &ldquo;<I>Canons</I>&rdquo; have put on it, for&mdash;&ldquo;the complement of all the senses.&rdquo;&rquo;
<SC>Mr. Smith</SC> (ap. Grey's <I>Notes</I>, &amp;c., 1754, ii, 102) thinks that &lquo;sense&rquo; should be <I>sense</I>',
because there were two squares referred to by Goneril; &lquo;the first was eye-sight, space,
liberty, and what could be valued rich and rare;&rquo; &lquo;the second square is grace, health,
beauty, honour.&rquo; &lquo;But then Goneril says she loves the king no less than these, and
consequently she loves these as much as she does the king. And this is the point
in which Regan says she falls short of her. The second square is of the superla-
tive kind of joys, and Regan professes herself an enemy to three of the joys, viz.
health, beauty, and honour; which are, of all the other joys, the most precious square
of sense (<I>i. e.</I> sense's joys) possesses; and declares that his dear Highness' love is
the only joy of the <I>square</I> which she values. In this it is plain that she outdoes her
sister Goneril.&rquo; [I think that is worth transcribing as a curiosity.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Collier</SC>
(<I>Notes</I>, &amp;c., p. 449): The (MS.) gives &lquo;<I>sphere</I> of sense,&rquo; which exactly conveys the
meaning of Edward's explanation. Regan loved her father beyond all other joys in
the round, or <I>sphere</I>, of sense. <SC>Singer</SC> reads <I>sphere</I>, and prefixes <I>spacious</I> instead
of &lquo;precious.&rquo; Of both these emendations, <I>Blackwood's Maga.</I> (Oct. 1853) says that
they are good as <I>modernizations</I> of Sh., but that the old text is quite intelligible;
&lquo;square&rquo; means compass, <I>area</I> [by which definition the present editor cannot see
that any progress is gained]. <SC>White</SC> (<I>Sh. Scholar</I>, p. 423), while discarding <I>sphere</I>
for &lquo;square,&rquo; thinks Singer's <I>spacious</I> is more plausible, and proposes, if change be
made, &lquo;<I>spacious</I> square,&rquo; but finds &lquo;the original text comprehensible, with a smack
of Sh. in it.&rquo; But by the time <SC>White</SC> published his ed. in 1861, the original text
had become &lquo;very obscure&rquo; to him, although he was &lquo;by no means confident that it
is corrupt,&rquo; adding that &lquo;it seems to mean the entire domain of sensation.&rquo; As he
does not in his ed..repeat his emendation, &lquo;<I>spacious</I> square,&rquo; it is to be presumed he
withdrew it. <SC>Keightley</SC> estimated it more highly; he adopted it. <SC>Bailey</SC> (ii,
88) has &lquo;not much doubt&rquo; that Sh. wrote &lquo;precious <I>treasure</I> of sense,&rquo; because &lquo;pre-
cious treasure&rquo; occurs in <I>Rom. and Jul.</I>, I, i, 239. Objections to this emendation</CC>

<CC><P>on the score of metre there can be none, says Bailey, because <I>treasure</I> is &lquo;on occa-
sion condensable into a monosyllable.&rquo; <SC>Hudson</SC>: That is, <I>fulness</I> or <I>wealth of sen-
sibility</I> or <I>capacity of joy;</I> so that the meaning seems to be: Which the finest sus-
ceptibility, or the highest capacity of happiness, can grasp or take in. <SC>Wright</SC>:
That is, which the most delicately sensitive part of my nature is capable of enjoy-
ing. <SC>Moberly</SC>: &lquo;The choicest estimate of sense,&rquo; as in <I>Tro. and Cres.</I> V, ii, 132,
&lquo;to square the general sex By Cressid's rule.&rquo; This definition by Moberly, <SC>Schmidt</SC>
(<I>Zur Textkritik</I>, p. 12) thinks is the only one that approaches the truth. He himself
says, the phrase in question means the &lquo;choicest symmetry of reason, the most nor-
mal and intelligent mode of thinking.&rquo; Regan's love is so great that she will know
nothing of all joys, which even a pattern of reason professes to be joys, such as,
&lquo;eye-sight, space, liberty, life, grace, health, beauty, and honour,&rquo; which had just
been extolled by her pattern sister.
<P>73. <B>professes]</B> <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Zur Textkritik</I>, p. 13): To object to a word because
it occurs twice within two lines, appears to be, in the interpretation of Sh., a custom
as ill-grounded as it is widespread, but from which, at all events, the poet himself
was free. [Whatever meaning or no-meaning we may attach to &lquo;square of sense,&rquo; it
seems clear to me that Regan refers to the joys which that &lquo;square&rquo; &lquo;professes&rquo; to
bestow; I therefore follow the Ff.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>74. <B>felicitate]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: That is, made happy. For instances of participles
formed on the model of the Latin participles in -<I>atus</I>, compare &lquo;consecrate&rquo; (<I>Tit.
And.</I> I, i, 14), &lquo;articulate&rquo; (1 <I>Hen. IV:</I> V, i, 72), &lquo;suffocate&rquo; (<I>Tro. and Cres.</I> I, iii,
125), &lquo;create&rquo; (<I>Mid. N. D.</I> V, i, 412). <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 342) calls attention to the fact
that this class of words, being derived directly from the Latin, stands on a different
footing to those verbs ending in -<I>te, -t</I>, and -<I>ed</I>, which because of their already re-
sembling participles in their terminations, do not add -<I>ed</I> in the participle. See
<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 324); <I>Macb.</I> III, vi, 38; <I>Ham.</I> I, ii, 20.
<P>77. <B>ponderous]</B> <SC>White</SC>: &lquo;More ponderous&rquo; of the Ff may possibly be a mis-

moral sense, melancholy, sad; nor is <I>weighty</I> any better; therefore Sh. chose &ldquo;pon-

<P>82. <B>last and least]</B> In his <I>Life of Shakespeare</I> (Var. '21, vol. ii, pp. 276-278),
<SC>Malone</SC> gives many instances to prove that <I>last not least</I> was a <I>formula</I> common in
Shakespeare's time, and is always applied to a person highly valued by the speaker.
<SC>Steevens</SC> refers to King Leir's reply to Mumford in the old ante-Shakespearian
play. [See Appendix, p. 401.] <SC>Malone</SC> adds from <I>The Spanish Tragedy</I>, written
before 1593: &lquo;The third and last, not least, in our account.&rquo; <SC>Dyce</SC> pronounces the
reading of Ff, &lquo;last <I>and</I> least,&rquo; a flagrant error; and <SC>Staunton</SC> says it can scarcely
be doubted that it is a misprint, and to the examples already given and referred to,
adds the following: &lquo;The last, not least, of these brave brethren&rquo;&mdash;Peele's <I>Poly-
hymnia.</I> &lquo;Though I speak last, my lord, I am not least&rquo;&mdash;Middleton's <I>Mayor of
Queenborough</I> I, iii. And &lquo;my last is, and not least,&rquo;&mdash;Beau. &amp; Fl., <I>Monsieur
Thomas</I> III, i. <SC>White</SC> [see Text-notes]: Plainly this passage was rewritten before
the Folio was printed. The last part of line 82, as it appears in the Qq, shows that
the figurative allusion to the king of France and the duke of Burgundy could have
formed no part of the passage when that text was printed. And in the rewriting
there was a happy change made from the commonplace of &lquo;last not least,&rquo; to an
allusion to the personal traits and family position of Cordelia. The impression pro-
duced by all the passages in which she appears or is referred to is, that she was her
father's little pet, while her sisters were big, bold, brazen beauties. Afterwards, in
this very scene, Lear says of her to Burgundy: &lquo;If aught within that <I>little</I> seeming
substance, or all of it, <I>with our displeasure pieced</I>,&rquo; &amp;c. When she is dead, too, her
father, although an infirm old man, &lquo;fourscore and upward,&rquo; carries her body in his
arms. Cordelia was evidently the least, as well as the youngest and best beloved,
of the old king's daughters; and therefore he says to her, &lquo;Now our joy, what can
you say to justify my intention of giving you the richest third of the kingdom,
although you are the youngest born and the least royal in your presence?&rquo; The
poet's every touch upon the figure of Cordelia paints her as, with all her firmness of
character, a creature to nestle in a man's bosom,&mdash;her father's or her husband's,&mdash;
and to be cherished almost like a little child; and this happy afterthought brings the
picture into perfect keeping, and at the very commencement of the drama impresses
upon the mind a characteristic trait of a personage who plays an important part in
it, although she is little seen. <SC>Hudson</SC>: I find it not easy to stand out against
White's argument in favour of the Ff; still, the phrase &lquo;though last, <I>not</I> least,&rquo; ap-
pears to have been so much a favorite with the poet, and withal so good in itself,</CC>

<CC><P>that I feel constrained to read with the majority of the editors. <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Zur
Textkritik des King Lear</I>, p. 13), in following out his theory that in the Qq we
have merely a corrupt text taken down from the stage representation, repudiates the
&lquo;last, not least,&rquo; here, and shrewdly suggests that since the same phrase occurs in <I>Jul.
C&aelig;s.</I> III, i, 189, the actor who took the part of Antony in that play also acted Lear,
and the phrase once learned by heart was repeated by him in <I>Lear</I>, where it does not
belong. &lquo;But let one put himself in the place of Lear, and there will be felt in this
&ldquo;last and least&rdquo; a tender touch of Nature. Our unser Letztes und Kleinstes gives the
meaning certainly, but not quite wholly; &ldquo;least&rdquo; means the youngest child, because
there had been less of formal ado made over her, because in many a f&ecirc;te and state
occasion, in which the elder sisters took part, she had not had any share, and yet
was the joy and &ldquo;object&rdquo; of her father, as the youngest child is always the favorite
of the father, the eldest of the mother.&rquo; [If Hudson finds it not easy to stand out
against White's argument, I find it impossible. White is at his happiest in detecting
subtle, delicate touches, and when, as in this instance, he is in accord with the Folio,
I yield at once, and will merely add that if Malone and Staunton can prove that
&lquo;last, not least,&rquo; was a hackneyed phrase in Shakespeare's time, it is all the more
reason why it should not be used here. Its very opposition to the common use
and wont makes it emphatic.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>83. <B>milk]</B> <SC>Eccles</SC>: The pastures of Burgundy, the effect for the cause. <SC>Mober-
ly</SC>: In ascribing vines to France, and not to Burgundy, Sh. may have thought of
the pastoral countries of Southern Belgium as forming part of Burgundy (as they
did till the death of Charles the Bold, 1477), otherwise we should not understand
the distinction; as in the French Burgundy wine-growing was of very old standing;
the arms of Dijon and Beaune have a vine upon them, and a great insurrection of
vine-dressers took place there in 1630.&mdash;Michelet, <I>Hist. de France</I>, ii, 303.
<P>84. <B>interess'd]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: So in the Preface of Drayton's <I>Polyolbion:</I> &lquo;&mdash;there
is scarce any of the nobilitie or gentry of this land, but he is in some way or other
by his blood interessed therein.&rquo; Again in Jonson's <I>Sejanus</I> III, i: &lquo;The dear re-
public, our sacred laws, and just authority are interess'd therein.&rquo; <SC>Wright</SC>: For
the form of the word, see Cotgrave (Fr. Dict.): &lquo;Interess&eacute; . . . Interessed, or touched
in; dishonoured, hurt, or hindered by,&rquo; &amp;c. See also Massinger, <I>The Duke of Milan</I>,
I, i: &lquo;The wars so long continued between The emperor Charles, and Francis the
French king, Have interess'd in either's cause the most Of the Italian princes.&rquo; And
Florio (Ital. Dict.): &lquo;Interessare, to interesse, to touch or concerne a mans maine
state or fee-simple, to concerne a mans reputation;&rquo; and &lquo;Interessato, interessed,
touched in state, in honour or reputation.&rquo; Again in Minsheu (Span. Dict.): &lquo;In-
teressado, m. interessed, hauing right in.&rquo; For other instances of verbs of which
the participial form has become a new verb, compare &lquo;graff,&rquo; &lquo;hoise,&rquo; which appear
in modern speech as &lquo;graft,&rquo; &lquo;hoist.&rquo; <SC>Schmidt</SC> maintains that &lquo;interest&rquo; of the Ff

<CC><P>86. <B>Nothing]</B> <SC>Coleridge</SC>: There is something of disgust at the ruthless hypoc-
risy of her sisters, and some little faulty admixture of pride and sullenness in Cor-
delia's &lquo;Nothing;&rquo; and her tone is well contrived, indeed, to lessen the glaring
absurdity of Lear's conduct, but answers the yet more important purpose of forcing
away the attention from the nursery-tale the moment it has served its end, that of
supplying the canvas for the picture. This is also materially furthered by Kent's
opposition, which displays Lear's moral incapability of resigning the sovereign power
in the very act of disposing of it. Kent is, perhaps, the nearest to perfect goodness
in all Shakespeare's characters, and yet the most individualized. There is an extra-
ordinary charm in his bluntness, which is that only of a nobleman, arising from a
contempt of overstrained courtesy, and combined with easy placability where good-
ness of heart is apparent. His passionate affection for, and fidelity to, Lear act on
our feelings in Lear's own favour; virtue seems to be in company with him.
<P>91. <B>majesty]</B> A dissyllable. See <I>Macb.</I> III, iv, 2; <SC>Walker</SC>, <I>Vers.</I> 174; <SC>Abbott</SC>,
&sect; 468.
<P>92. W. W. <SC>Lloyd</SC>: The crudity of manners expressed in Lear's solicitation of
flattery has its natural counterpart in the almost sullen and repulsive tone of the
virtue which preserves Cordelia from the degradation he would tempt her to. The
progress of the story required a reply that should provoke the indignation of her
father, and yet not cause her to forfeit our esteem. . . . . Moreover, Sh., it appears
to me, designed to convey, by the very terms and rhythm of the speeches of Cor-
delia, an impression that her speech was usually reserved and low and laconic, and
thus that the very faculty was foreign to her that might have enabled her to effect
the same result for her own dignity with milder method. Certain it is, and it is suf-
ficiently declared in the sequel of the scene, that she took too little thought for the
fact that her disinheriting was a greater misfortune to her father than to herself, and
that to prevent it for his sake were worth incurring some misconstruction; this
thought necessarily arises from the terms in which she commends her father, whose
weakness she had not had the skill to humour honorably, to the sisters, whose natures
she knows too well not to foresee their course, even without the irritation which
the same weakness was sure to give occasion and welcome pretext for. This, then,
is the incongruity of the social state on which the tragic action of the play depends;</CC>

<CC><P>and when Lear enters mad in the last scene, with Cordelia dead in his arms, we have
but the fulfilment for either of the fate they equally provoked; we behold the com-
mon catastrophe of affection too much qualified by unreasonable anger on one side,
and unaccommodating rigour on the other. <SC>Rapp</SC> (<I>Einleitung zur Uebersetzung</I>,
Stuttgart, 1843): The elder sisters are vulgar, selfish natures; Cordelia is not so
vulgar, although possessed of a pride and obstinacy not unusual. When Diogenes
marched up and down in the brilliant rooms of Plato, saying: &lquo;I tread upon the
pride of Plato,&rquo; &lquo;Yes,&rquo; replied Plato, &lquo;with greater pride.&rquo; That is just the case
with Cordelia. She is proud of being in the right, in contrast with her vulgar sis-
ters, and this feeling she opposes to her sisters and to her old father. The weak
old father has a right to a few flattering expressions from a loving child, because
he needs them. She offers him, on the contrary, what he cannot bear, the truth. A
woman, whose nature is love, and who is straitlaced for truth, is a doubly perverted
creature. Truth and Love are completely antipodal; what else is love for an indi-
vidual but the taking of a finite object for an infinite, and worshipping it as such?
Thus, love is essentially a lie, not a truth, and Cordelia misbehaves like her sisters,
only in a different way, by egoism and lovelessness. One for whom she cannot tell
a little lie, she does not love as she should. On this fine ground, which the poet has
laid very close to us, now rests the whole piece.
<P>92. <B>bond]</B> <SC>Eccles</SC>: What I am bound to by duty.
<P>94, <I>et seq.</I> <SC>Moberly</SC>: Sh., with wonderful naturalness, makes the shy and re-
served Cordelia speak, when her false position is forced upon her, with a passion that
will not stop to choose conciliatory expressions, and which makes up by vehemence,
and what sounds like petulance, for the weakness of the argument which she is
driven to use, as she cannot reveal the truth which she knows.

<P>104, <I>et seq.</I> <SC>Seymour</SC> here and in many other places amends the rhythm, which

<P>107. <SC>Bucknill</SC> (p. 176): [This curse] is madness, or it is nothing. Not indeed
raving, incoherent, formed mania, as it subsequently displays itself, but exaggerated
passion, perverted affection, enfeebled judgment, combining to form a state of men-
tal disease&mdash;incipient, indeed, but still disease&mdash;in which man, though he may be
paying for past errors, is during the present irresponsible.
<P>108. <B>sun]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: The oaths given to Lear are admirable for their solemnity,
and are taken from out the creed of his times as fables have given it; he is made
the builder of Leicester (Leir Cestre, <I>Saxonic&eacute;</I>), and a temple of his erection is
talk'd of to <I>Janus Bifrons;</I> so that as well his &lquo;Hecate&rquo; here, as his <I>Apollo</I> and
<I>Jupiter</I> afterwards, are consonant to his imputed religion, whatever comes of his
true; to which, in likelihood, his address before &lquo;Hecate&rquo; has a nearer affinity. <SC>Mo-
berly</SC>: The Druidical gods are, according to C&aelig;sar (<I>Bell. Gall.</I> vi, 17), Apollo,
Mars, Jove, and Minerva. Lear's two oaths, by Apollo and Jupiter, are therefore
historically accurate; so is his swearing by Night, as (c. 18) &lquo;Galli se omnes ab
Dite patre prognatos pr&aelig;dicant,&rquo; and by Hecate, as a temple of Diana once occu-
pied the place of the present St. Paul's in London. (Palgrave's <I>Anglo-Saxons</I>, p. 51.)</CC>

<CC><P>109. <B>Hecate]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: This word is a dissyllable in <I>Mid. N. D.</I> V, i, 391;

only in 1 <I>Hen. VI:</I> III, ii, 64, a significant fact as regards Shakespeare's share in
that play.
<P>110. <B>operation]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: The effect upon the life or death of mortals. <SC>Wright</SC>:
This belief in planetary influence is in keeping with the speech of Edmund in the
next scene.
<P>113. <B>property]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: A stronger expression of the idea contained in &lquo;propin-

<P>115. <B>barbarous]</B> See <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 468, for the contraction of this and similar

<P>115. <B>Scythian]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: Purchas, in his <I>Pilgrimage</I> (ed. 1614, p. 396), says,

<CC><P>121. <B>dragon]</B> <SC>Moberly</SC>: A natural trope for Lear to use, as, like Arthur, he
would wear a helmet (<I>Idylls of the King</I>, p. 256): &lquo;On which for crest the golden
dragon clung For Britain.&rquo; [See <SC>Godwin</SC> on helmets, Appendix, p. 449.]
<P>121. <B>wrath]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: His wrath's object.
<P>122. <B>set my rest]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: A phrase from the game of cards called primero,
used in a double sense. Metaphorically, &lquo;to set one's rest&rquo; is to stake one's all.
Literally in the game of primero it signifies &lquo;to stand upon the cards in one's hand.&rquo;
For an example of the metaphorical sense, see Bacon's <I>Essay</I> xxix, p. 128 (ed.
Wright): &lquo;There be many Examples, where <I>Sea-Fights</I> have beene Finall to the
warre; But this is, when Princes or States, have set up their Rest, vpon Battailes.&rquo;
[See the notes, in this edition, on <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> IV, v, 6. Elsewhere in Sh. the
phrase is uniformly, I think, &lquo;to set up.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>123. <B>Hence,</B> etc.] <SC>Heath</SC>: These words are undoubtedly addressed to Kent;
for in the next words Lear sends for France and Burgundy, in order to tender to
them his youngest daughter. At such a time, therefore, to drive her out of his pres-
ence would be a contradiction to his declared intention. <SC>Jennens</SC> ably maintains
that this is addressed to Cordelia, in so far as she had just raised her father's anger
to the highest pitch, while Kent, the extent of whose opposition was thus far quite
unknown, had been simply warned not to come between the dragon and his wrath.
When Kent interposed a second time, Lear warned him a second time to make from
the shaft. Kent emboldened, then uses rougher language; Lear passionately ad-
jures him, &lquo;on thy life, no more;&rquo; Kent persists, and Lear bids him for the first time
&lquo;out of my sight.&rquo; Kent further entreats, Lear swears; Kent returns the oath, and
then Lear banishes him. This natural gradation in Lear's anger towards Kent, thus
contrasted with his instant rage against Cordelia, whom he loved so deeply and who
had wounded him so bitterly, Jennens thinks is one of the most beautiful in all
Shakespeare. <SC>Malone</SC> thinks that the inconsistency noted by Heath is perfectly
suited to Lear's character, and therefore that this sentence is addressed to Cordelia.
<SC>Delius</SC> adopts Heath's reasons for believing these words were addressed to Kent,
and adds that Cordelia, both before and after them, is spoken of in the third person.
<SC>White</SC>: These words most probably are addressed to Cordelia; yet it may be rea-
sonably urged that Cordelia does not go out, as she would be likely to do upon such
a command; and that although Kent has merely broken in with &lquo;Good, my liege,&mdash;&rquo;
Lear is choleric and unreasonable enough to hound him from his presence upon
such slight provocation. <SC>Hudson</SC>: Perhaps the true explanation is, that Lear an-
ticipates remonstrance from Kent, and, in his excited mood, flares up at any offer of
that kind. <SC>Wright</SC>: After the king, in reply to Kent's interruption, had justified his
conduct, he could scarcely order him from his sight. [If any critic of less weight
than Heath had started this question, I doubt if it would have been ever discussed.&mdash;
<SC>Ed.</SC>]</CC>

<CC><P>125. <B>Who stirs?]</B> <SC>Delius</SC> interprets this as a threat, to terrify into silence any

impending doom, that they stand motionless and forget to move? This is one of
Shakespeare's touches, like old Capulet's calling Juliet &lquo;you tallow-face,&rquo; to be in-

<P>128. <B>marry]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: That is, provide a husband for her.
<P>129, 138. W. W. <SC>Lloyd</SC>: It is apparent that Lear must long have put the sin-
cerest affection to the sorest trials, and tasked the endurance even of sordid self-
interest, and now he manifests undiminished appetite for the coarser luxury of sway
at the very moment he releases unwilling purveyors from their bondage. The re-
served train of one hundred knights, and the alternate visits he proposes, prove that
in a most important respect he contemplates no abdication at all, but expects to ob-
tain still, on the strength of obligation, more than all he had exacted so gallingly by
the force of his regal power and dignity.

<P>148. <B>majesty]</B> A dissyllable. See I, i, 90.
<P>148. <B>Reserve thy state]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: I am inclined to think that <I>Reverse thy doom</I>
was Shakespeare's first reading, as more apposite to the present occasion, and that he
changed it afterwards to &lquo;Reserve thy state,&rquo; which conduces more to the progress of
the action. <SC>Delius</SC> defends the Ff, because Lear's surrender of his royalty proved
subsequently more fatal to him than the unjust doom pronounced on Cordelia.
<SC>White</SC> cannot regard the text of the Ff as other than &lquo;an accidental variation, be-
cause Kent makes no attempt to induce Lear to abandon his design of dividing his
kingdom and abdicating his throne; he simply pleads for Cordelia. Between <I>re-
verse</I> and &ldquo;reserve,&rdquo; the difference is only the transposition of two letters; and that
change once made by accident, the other would naturally follow by design.&rquo; In <I>N.
&amp; Qu.</I> 5th Ser. v, 444, W. A. B. <SC>Coolidge</SC> argues against interpreting &lquo;doom&rquo; by
<I>destiny</I> [which I think no one but the critic himself ever did so interpret. Kent is
such a noble fellow, that we who know Cordelia's truthfulness and honesty, and
have heard her words spoken aside, cannot but think that he is here pleading her
cause. But I am afraid we are too hasty. Kent is pleading not for Cordelia, but
for Lear himself; he has not as yet made the slightest allusion to Cordelia. When
Lear denounces her, Kent, who sees that Lear is crushing the only chance of future
happiness, starts forward with &lquo;Good my liege;&rquo; but before he can utter another word
Lear interrupts him, and interprets his exclamation as an intercession for Cordelia:
and we fall into the same error, so that when Kent speaks again we keep up the
same illusion, whereas all that he now says breathes devotion to the king, and to no
one else. The folly to which majesty falls is not the casting off of a daughter,&mdash;that
is no more foolish in a king than in a subject,&mdash;but it is the surrendering of revenue,
of sway, and of the crown itself,&mdash;this is hideous rashness, this is power bowing to
flattery. Hence, Kent entreats Lear &lquo;to reserve his state.&rquo; And to show still more
conclusively that Lear, and not Cordelia, is chiefly in his thoughts, in his very next
speech he says that the motive for which he now risks his life is the safety of the
king. Furthermore, when Lear has been turned out of doors and his daughters
have usurped all his powers, Gloucester (III, iv, 156) says, &lquo;Ah that good Kent! He
said it would be thus,&rquo; which cannot well refer to any other passage than the present.
Moreover, had Kent been so devoted to Cordelia as to suffer banishment for her
sake, would he not have followed her to France rather than followed as a servant</CC>

<CC><P>son's objection, in a subsequent note, to Shakespeare's making Lear too much a
mythologist.
<P>160. <B>swear'st]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC> (&sect; 200): The preposition is omitted after some verbs
which can easily be regarded as transitive. See also &lquo;smile you my speeches,&rquo; II,
ii, 77. <SC>Wright</SC>: Sh. frequently uses the verb in a transitive sense when it has a
person for its object, as in <I>Jul. C&aelig;s.</I> II, i, 129; but in the sense of appealing to a
deity by an oath, it is not common.
<P>160. <B>miscreant]</B> <SC>Delius</SC> says that Kent is a &lquo;miscreant&rquo; in regard to Apollo and
the gods, whom he has contemptuously termed &lquo;thy gods;&rquo; and that <I>recreant</I>, of the
Qq, he is in regard to Lear. But, as <SC>Schmidt</SC> says, Sh. uses &lquo;miscreant&rquo; very fre-
quently in the sense of moral worthlessness.
<P>164. <B>clamour]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> has a section (<I>Crit.</I> i, 156) devoted to the meaning of
this word, which he seems to think expresses an idea of wailing or lamentation.
The present passage can with difficulty be said to support this theory.
<P>167. <B>That]</B> To <SC>White</SC>, &lquo;That&rquo; of the Ff seems more in keeping with the style
of this play. &lquo;Of old <I>that</I> had, as it still has among our best writers, the sense of
<I>for that, seeing that, assuming.</I>&rquo; So, <SC>Schmidt</SC> also says, that the causative <I>since</I> of
the Qq is less in the tone of suppressed passion which characterizes the speech, and
leads, grammatically, less directly than &lquo;that&rquo; to the main point: &lquo;take thy reward.&rquo;
See I, i, 70.</CC>

<CC><P>169. <B>power]</B> <SC>Edwards</SC>: That is, our power to execute it.
<P>170. <SC>Wright</SC>: This line gives the key to Lear's hasty and impetuous character.
<P>170. <B>nor . . . nor]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: For <I>neither</I> . . . &lquo;nor,&rquo; compare <I>Oth.</I> III, iv, 116, 117.
<P>171. <B>made good,]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: &lquo;As thou hast come with unreasonable pride be-
tween the <I>sentence</I> which I had passed, and the <I>power</I> by which I shall execute it,
<I>take thy reward</I> in another sentence which shall <I>make good</I>, shall establish, shall
maintain, <I>that power.</I>&rquo; Mr. Davies thinks, that &lquo;our potency made good,&rquo; relates only
to <I>our place.</I> Which our nature cannot bear, nor our <I>place</I>, without departure from
the <I>potency</I> of that place. This is easy and clear. Lear, who is characterized
as hot, heady, and violent, is, with very just observation of life, made to entangle
himself with vows, upon any sudden provocation to vow revenge, and then to plead
the obligation of a vow in defence of implacability. <SC>Steevens</SC>: In my opinion,
&lquo;made&rquo; is right. Lear had just delegated his power to Albany and Cornwall, con-
tenting himself with only the name and all the additions of a king. He could, there-
fore, have no <I>power</I> to inflict on Kent the punishment which he thought he deserved.
&lquo;Our potency made good&rquo; seems to me only this: They to whom I have yielded my
power and authority, yielding me the ability to dispense it in this instance, take thy
reward. <SC>Malone</SC>: The meaning, I think is: As a proof that I am not a mere
threatener, that I have power as well as will to punish, take the due reward of thy
demerits; hear thy sentence. The words &lquo;our potency made good&rquo; are in the ab-
solute case. <SC>Wright</SC>: Lear still speaks as king, although he had announced his
intention of abdicating. It is difficult, therefore, to understand why Steevens should
have stumbled at this passage. The reading of Q<SUB>2</SUB> can only mean &lquo;make good or
establish our power by taking thy punishment as an acknowledgement of it.&rquo; <SC>Mo-
berly</SC>: Sh. ingeniously makes Lear forget that he is giving up his power on that
very day, and pronounce a sentence on Kent to take effect in ten days.
<P>173. <B>diseases]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: The alteration of the Ff was made by the printer in
consequence of his not knowing the meaning of the original word. &lquo;Diseases,&rquo; in
old language, meant the slighter <I>inconveniences, troubles</I>, or <I>distresses of the world.</I>
The provision that Kent could make in five days might, in some measure, guard him
against the &lquo;diseases&rquo; of the world, but could not shield him from its <I>disasters.</I> [See
note in <I>Macb.</I> V, iii, 21.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]</CC>

<CC><P>186. <SC>Johnson</SC>: He will follow his old maxims; he will continue to act upon the
same principles. <SC>Steevens</SC> quotes: &lquo;St. George for England! and Ireland now
adieu, For here Tom Stukely shapes his course anew.&rquo;&mdash;Peele's <I>Battle of Alcazar</I>,
1594, p. 117; ed. Dyce. As <SC>You Like It</SC> (<I>Gent. Maga.</I>, lx, p. 402) conjectures

agrees with this anonymous critic as to think that there is &lquo;evidently a play intended
upon the words &ldquo;course&rdquo; and &ldquo;corse.&rdquo;&rquo; [The antithesis is so marked between &lquo;old&rquo;
and &lquo;new&rquo; that, to me, the simpler the interpretation the better: Kent's old age must
be finished in a new country. The jingle between &lquo;course&rquo; and &lquo;corse&rquo; is certainly
Shakespearian, but I cannot see that it is called for here; the situation is not so
tragic that it needs the relief of a smile, and, moreover, &lquo;to shape a corse&rquo; is well-
nigh unintelligible.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<CC><P>195. <B>so]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: Speaking indefinitely, as one unwilling to say how much she
was dear to him; and giving &lquo;so&rquo; the force of &mdash;so and so, or at such and such price,
as men sometimes express themselves. <SC>Eccles, Malone</SC>, and <SC>Moberly</SC> think that
it means &lquo;worthy of that high dowry,&rquo; in which opinion the present Editor agrees,
but <SC>Wright</SC> thinks that it means simply dear.
<P>197. <B>seeming]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Beautiful. <SC>Steevens</SC>: Specious. <SC>Wright</SC>: That
substance which is but little in appearance. <SC>Moberly</SC>: Her nature that seems so
slight and shallow. Lear speaks in the next line of her &lquo;infirmities,&rquo; her want of
established principle as compared with her decided and outspoken sisters. <SC>Schmidt</SC>
thinks that all these definitions fail to take into account Shakespeare's use of the word
&lquo;substance,&rquo; whereby he commonly expresses <I>reality</I> in opposition to <I>shadow;</I> &lquo;seem-
ing substance&rquo; means, therefore, something which pretends to be that which it is not.
Perhaps, he adds, &lquo;seeming&rquo; is to be taken as a gerund, and &lquo;seeming substance&rquo;
may then mean a creature whose reality is mere show or seeming.
<P>198. <B>pieced]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: See III, vi, 2.
<P>199. <B>like]</B> See <I>Ham.</I> II, ii, 80.
<P>201. <B>owes]</B> Owns.

<CC><P>205. <B>makes not up]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: To make up, in familiar language, is neutrally,
to <I>come forward</I>, to <I>make advances</I>, which I think is meant here. <SC>Malone</SC>: Elec-
tion comes not to a decision. <SC>Knight</SC>: The <I>choice</I> of Burgundy refuses to come to
a decision, <I>in</I> such circumstances, or <I>on</I> such terms. <SC>Mason</SC> thinks that &lquo;up&rquo; and
&lquo;on&rquo; should be read as one word, in order to make the sense evident. But <SC>Wright's</SC>
note is conclusive: &lquo;Election makes not its choice, comes to no decision, resolves
not. We still say &ldquo;to make up one's mind,&rdquo; and the phrase is here used elliptically
in the same sense.&rquo;
<P>205. <B>in such conditions]</B> <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Zur Textkritik</I>, &amp;c., p. 14): If &lquo;condi-
tions&rquo; be here taken in its ordinary sense, it requires, even according to Shake-
speare's own mode of speaking, <I>on</I> before it, instead of &lquo;in;&rquo; but it is not &lquo;condi-
tions&rquo; that are spoken of in what precedes: &lquo;Will you, with those infirmities she
owes, Unfriended, new-adopted to our hate, Dower'd with our curse, and stranger'd
with our oath,&rquo; &amp;c. It is qualities that are here enumerated, and it is in just this
sense of <I>quality</I> that Shakespeare very often uses &lquo;condition.&rquo; <I>Meas. for Meas.</I> I, i,
54: &lquo;our haste from hence is of so quick condition that it prefers itself,&rquo; &amp;c. <I>Mer.
of Ven.</I> V, i, 74: &lquo;unhandled colts, fetching mad bounds . . . which is the hot con-
dition of their blood.&rquo; <I>Hen. V:</I> IV, i, 108: &lquo;all his senses have but human condi-
tions.&rquo; <I>Much Ado</I>, III, ii, 68: &lquo;one that knows him, and his ill conditions,&rquo; &amp;c.
That the word in this sense may also have the preposition <I>in</I> before it can be shown
by abundant examples. <I>As You Like it</I>, I, i, 47: &lquo;I know you are my eldest brother,
and in the gentle condition of blood you should so know me.&rquo; <I>Rich. II:</I> II, iii, 107:
&lquo;in conditions of the worst degree, in gross rebellion,&rquo; &amp;c.

<CC><P><I>taint, i. e.</I> his judgement was corrupted, in preferring the extravagant and lying
protestations of his eldest daughters to the sincere and just ones of his youngest.
And if we ruminate a little, this is the only second reason for Lear's rejecting Corde-
lia that can with any probability be supposed to be guessed at by France; for it would
be rude in France to charge Lear with vouching the dearest affections to one he did
not really love; and it is absurd to suppose that so great a love should change to
hate, without she had committed some very great crime, and which France could
not be brought to believe; therefore, this second guess becomes the only one, and the
true one, viz: that Regan and Goneril had, by their superior art in coaxing, won all
Lear's love from Cordelia. <SC>Malone</SC> held to this interpretation until he &lquo;recollected
that France had not heard the extravagant professions made by Regan and Goneril.&rquo;
Then he gives what seems to me the true construction of the passage: &lquo;Either her
offence <I>must be</I> monstrous, or, if she has not committed any such offence, the affection
which you always professed to have for her <I>must be</I> tainted and decayed&rquo; [that
is, &lquo;must be&rquo; is to be understood before &lquo;Fall'n.&rquo; It is easy to see how the text
of the Ff arose. The last syllable of Fall<I>en</I> was absorbed by the first syllable of
&lquo;into,&rquo; so that even were <I>Fall</I> of the Ff to be adopted, I think it should be printed
<I>Fall</I>'.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

France has just before said: &lquo;Sure her offence must be of such <I>unnatural</I> degree

is altogether too general a term to be put in the alternative with &ldquo;foulness,&rdquo; almost
as general, and of like meaning. I do not doubt that Sh. wrote &ldquo;murther.&rdquo;&rquo; [In
his <I>Shakespeare's Scholar</I>, <SC>White</SC> gave in his adherence to Collier's emendation,

<SC>Malone</SC> on &lquo;<I>umber'd</I> face,&rquo; <I>Hen. V:</I> IV, Chorus: &lquo;<I>Umber</I> is a dark yellow earth

titled <I>The Telltale</I>, it appears that <I>umber</I> was used in the stage exhibitions of his
time. In that piece, one of the marginal directions is: &ldquo;He <I>umbers</I> her face.&rdquo;&rquo;
<SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2): Undoubtedly the original reading is a very suspicious one. <SC>Hal-

<CC><P>&lquo;blot&rquo; and &lquo;foulness,&rquo; may there not be opposed that Cordelia's distress might make
her verge on incoherence? As Moberly truly says, &lquo;the gradation from a vicious blot
to murder, and then to foulness, is not happy.&rquo; This alone is so un-Shakespearian that
of itself it would taint the line. Murder may have been a much less heinous crime
in Shakespeare's days than at present, and Lady Capulet may have thought to cheer
Juliet's drooping spirits with the contemplation of Romeo's assassination, but that it
could ever have been of less degree than foulness demands a faith that reason with-
out miracle can never plant in me. Can a parallel instance of anticlimax be found
in Sh.? And mark how admirably the lines are balanced: &lquo;vicious blot or foul-
ness, unchaste action or dishonour'd step.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>229. <B>But . . . richer]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: The construction is imperfect, though the sense
is clear. We should have expected &lquo;even the want,&rquo; as Hanmer reads, but Sh. was
probably guided by what he had written in the line preceding, and mentally supplied

<CC><P>301. <B>hit]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, let us agree. <SC>Hudson</SC>: The meaning of what
follows probably is, if the king continue in the same rash, headstrong, and incon-
stant temper, as he has just shown, in snatching back his authority the moment his
will is crossed, we shall be the worse off for his surrender of the kingdom to us.
<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Zur Textkritik</I>, p. 15) earnestly contends, but I am afraid in vain, for
&lquo;sit&rquo; of the Ff. &lquo;To strike together,&rquo; he says, &lquo;or to act in harmony, as it is expressed
by &ldquo;to hit together,&rdquo; is not a matter of free will, but proceeds directly from the nature
of things, and is not something to which one can be invited. . . . Whereas, the phrase
&ldquo;sit together,&rdquo; has the plain and manifest meaning&mdash;to hold a session, to take counsel
together. Goneril would forthwith see a common plan agreed upon, and to Regan's
dilatory answer: &ldquo;We shall think further of it,&rdquo; replies: &ldquo;We must do something,
and i' th' heat,&rdquo; and for this an agreement is of course essential, and an agreement
she demands in the words &ldquo;let us sit together.&rdquo;&rquo; Schmidt then adduces the fol-
lowing instances in proof: <I>Twelfth Night</I>, I, v, 143; <I>Ham.</I> V, i, 4; <I>Hen. V:</I> V, ii.
80; <I>Rich. III:</I> III, i, 173; <I>Cor.</I> V, ii, 74; <I>Ib.</I> V, iii, 131; <I>Per.</I> II, iii, 92. But in
all these instances, except, perhaps, the last, there is reference to a judicial assembly
or a session more or less formal and solemn, and a meaning is conveyed which I
cannot but think strained when applied to an agreement between two sisters.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>302. <B>disposition]</B> <SC>Dyce</SC>: As to &lquo;dispositions&rquo; or <I>disposition</I>,&mdash;either reading may

<P>305. <B>heat]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, we must strike while the iron is hot.</CC>

<CC><P><SC>Eccles</SC> disapproves of this order of the scenes; in his judgement the accusation
or Edgar by Edmund labours under a weight of improbability, which is increased
the longer that Edgar remains concealed without taking any steps to vindicate him-
self; that he should lie thus quiet, during all the time that passes from the opening
day of the tragedy to Lear's stormy departure for Gloster's castle, is &lquo;an outrage
upon common sense too gross to be admitted,&rquo; thinks Eccles, who, therefore, trans-
poses this scene to the beginning of Act II, bringing it immediately before the scene
where Edmund persuades Edgar to fly, and pretends that he has been wounded.
Thus, the two scenes are &lquo;brought within the compass of the same day, and a few
hours only, or less, may be conceived to intervene between them.&rquo; This consum-
mation, however, is not attained without loss; for Sh. clearly intended that this scene
should be where he put it, as the second of the tragedy: Gloster enters sadly, mut-
tering: &lquo;Kent banished thus, And France in choler parted? And the king gone to-
night? subscribed his power? Confined to exhibition? All this done upon the gad!&rquo;
(lines 23-26). But Eccles says that Sh. was liable to &lquo;unhappy oversights&rquo; of dra-
matic probability, and this must be one; &lquo;these obnoxious lines,&rquo; therefore, he cuts
out and &lquo;degrades&rquo; to the bottom of the page, begging forgiveness for the act, on
the ground that he is &lquo;in pursuit of a favorite object which is essential to the rea-
sonableness and consistency of this admirable drama; more especially as the lines
in themselves are of small importance, and the only ones so treated&rquo; by him.
<P>1. <B>Nature]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: Sh. makes this bastard an atheist. Italian atheism had
much infected the English court. <SC>Steevens</SC>: Edmund speaks of &lquo;nature&rquo; in oppo-
sition to &lquo;custom,&rquo; and not to the existence of a God. Edmund means only, that as
he came not into the world as &lquo;custom&rquo; or law had prescribed, so he had nothing to
do but to follow &lquo;nature&rquo; and her laws, which make no difference between legitimacy
and illegitimacy, between the eldest and the youngest. To contradict Warburton's
assertion yet more strongly, Edmund concludes this very speech by an invocation to
heaven. <SC>Mason</SC>: Edmund calls &lquo;nature&rquo; his &lquo;goddess&rquo; for the same reason that
we call a bastard a <I>natural</I> son,&mdash;one who, according to the law of nature, is the
child of his father, but according to that of civil society is <I>nullius filius.</I> <SC>Cole-
ridge</SC>: In this speech of Edmund you see as soon as a man cannot reconcile him-
self to reason, how his conscience flies off by way of appeal to Nature, who is sure
upon such occasions never to find fault, and also how shame sharpens a predisposi-
tion in the heart to evil. For it is a profound moral, that shame will naturally gene-
rate guilt; the oppressed will be vindictive, like Shylock, and in the anguish of
undeserved ignominy the delusion secretly springs up, of getting over the moral
quality of an action by fixing the mind on the mere physical act alone.</CC>

<CC><P>3. <B>plague]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: An absurd expression. Read <I>plage, i. e.</I> the place, the
country, the boundary of custom. <I>Plage</I> is in common use amongst the old English
writers. <SC>Capell</SC>: The speaker calls &lquo;custom&rquo; a &lquo;plague&rquo; or vexation, and asks why
he should &lquo;stand in it,&rquo; meaning <I>be exposed to it.</I> <SC>Johnson</SC>: I can scarcely think
&lquo;plague&rquo; right. <SC>Staunton</SC>: &lquo;Plague&rquo; may here possibly signify <I>place</I>, or <I>boundary</I>
from <I>plaga;</I> but it is a very suspicious word. <SC>Wright</SC>: I cannot help thinking
that Sh. had in his mind a passage in the Prayer-book Version of Psalm xxxviii, 17,
&lquo;And I truly am set in the plague;&rquo; where &lquo;plague&rquo; is used in a sense for which I
have found no parallel. The version evidently follows the Latin of Jerome's transla-
tion, &lquo;Quia ego ad plagam paratus sum.&rquo; <SC>Halliwell</SC>: Edmund cites for a reason of
the contempt of the world not merely his illegitimacy, but his juniority, so that the
plague is here also the infectious rule of custom, that bids the younger yield to the
elder, a decree he determines wickedly to evade by becoming the only son.
<P>4. <B>curiosity]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC>: This should be <I>curtesie</I>, as in <I>As You Like It</I>, I, i, 49.
Nor must we forget that tenure in our laws, whereby some lands are held by the
&lquo;curtesie of England.&rquo; And I ought to take notice that I had the concurrence of
the ingenious Dr. Thirlby, who hinted to me this very emendation before he knew I
made it. <SC>Heath</SC>: It is not suitable to Edmund's character to term that a <I>curtesy</I>
which he endeavors to expose as a folly, and in virtue of which he was to be him-
self so great a sufferer. <SC>Mason</SC>: By &lquo;curiosity&rquo; Edmund means the <I>nicety</I>, the
<I>strictness</I>, of civil institutions. <SC>White</SC>: &lquo;Curiosity&rquo; is what Johnson would have
called <I>scrupulosity.</I> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 201): The <I>i</I> in -<I>ity</I> is almost uniformly dropt
in pronunciation. I believe that Sh. pronounced <I>curious'ty;</I> for, according to
our common pronunciation, this verse is a verse only in name. <SC>The Bible Word-
book</SC> cites, &lquo;The Scripture then being acknowledged to bee so full and so perfect,
how can wee excuse our selues of negligence, if we doe not studie them, of curiositie,
if we be not content with them.&rquo;&mdash;<I>The Translators to the Reader.</I> Also: &lquo;Now, as
concerning the funerals and enterring of her, I pray you, let the same be performed
without all curiositie and superstition.&rquo;&mdash;Holland's Plutarch, <I>Morals</I>, p. 533. [Cot-
grave: Curiosit&eacute;: <I>daintinesse, nicenesse; affectation.</I> See I, i, 5, and I, iv, 66.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>4. <B>deprive]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Synonymous in Shakespeare's time with <I>disinherit.</I>
<SC>Wright</SC>: Compare Baret's <I>Alvearie</I> [s. v. <I>to deprive</I>]: &lquo;To cast his sonne out
of his house, to depriue or put him from the hope of succession, or inheritance,
for some misdeede: to abastardize him.&rquo;
<P>6. <B>Lag]</B> In <SC>Bell's</SC> <I>Shakespeare's Puck</I>, iii, 94, there is a suggestion, founded on a
misapprehension of the passage, that this word may have been originally the same
as the word <I>law</I> as found in the hunting phrase of &lquo;giving a stag so much law before
the dogs are let loose.&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>6. <B>bastard]</B> <SC>Hanmer</SC>: Edmund inveighs against the tyranny of custom, both in
respect to younger brothers and to bastards. But he must not be understood, in the
former, to mean himself; the argument becomes general by implying more than is
said: &lquo;Wherefore should I or any man,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Boswell</SC>: Why should he not mean
himself in both instances? He <I>was</I> a younger brother. <SC>Moberly</SC>: The word is
from the Celtic &lquo;bas-tardh&rquo; (low birth). The Welsh, however, only learned very
unwillingly in Edward I's time to adopt the English &lquo;curiosity&rquo; as regards illegiti-
mate children. [Can we not infer from this line and line 10 that the pronunciation
in Shakespeare's time was <I>base-tard?</I>]
<P>9. <B>madam's]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: As is frequently the case in Sh. it is here used ironically.
<P>14. <B>the creating]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 93. Although this is a noun, and therefore pre-
ceded by &lquo;the,&rquo; yet it is so far confused with the gerund as to be allowed the privilege
of governing a direct object. See <I>Macb.</I> I, iv, 8.
<P>14. <B>fops]</B> According to <SC>Schmidt</SC> this does not mean fools or dandies, as it does
now, but <I>dupes</I>,&mdash;that is, men who are destined to be duped or deceived by men of
&lquo;more composition and fierce quality.&rquo; Furthermore, this original meaning of the
word is found in all the instances of its use by Sh. Compare &lquo;This is the excellent
foppery of the world,&rquo; line 112; that is, <I>dupery.</I>
<P>15. <B>'tween]</B> <SC>Dodd</SC>: I think the passage originally stood &lquo;<I>atween</I> sleep and wake.&rquo;
The <I>a</I> might very easily have been so transposed.</CC>

<CC><P>21. <B>top]</B> <SC>Hanmer</SC>: As &lquo;the treading upon another's heels&rquo; is an expression used
to signify the being not far behind him, so to <I>toe</I> another means to come up to and
be on even ground with him. <SC>Warburton</SC>: Here the Oxford editor would show
us that he is as good at coining phrases as his author, and so alters the text thus:
&lquo;Shall <I>toe</I> the legitimate,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> says he, &lquo;stand on even ground with him;&rquo; as he would
do with his author. <SC>Edwards</SC> (<I>Canons of Crit.</I>, p. 221, ed. 7): Poor Sir Thomas!
Woe be to you, if you invade Mr. Warburton's prerogative of <I>coining</I> words for Sh.!
One may fairly say here that &lquo;the toe of the <I>peasant</I> comes so near the heel of our
<I>courtier</I> that it galls his kibe.&rquo; But Mr. Warburton ought to have taken notice that
the old reading is &lquo;shall <SC>to</SC> th' legitimate,&rquo; which, though it misled Sir Thomas, may
perhaps direct to the right word: &lquo;Shall <I>top</I> the,&rquo; &amp;c., which he would do if he got
the inheritance from him, though that could not make him <I>be</I> the legitimate. [These
notes are given as instances of the amenities that help to make the early comments
on Sh. so full of &lquo;sweetness and light.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Capell</SC>, referring to this emendation
of Edwards, says, that &lquo;it appear'd in the <I>Canons</I>, into which it was receiv'd from
this editor (together with other communications concerning readings of copies) by
that ingenious work's writer: This emendation will have no impugners or doubters,
if that corruption be look'd upon out of which it arose; if it's opposition to &ldquo;base&rdquo; be
consider'd, and (which is yet a stronger matter than either) it's connection with
&ldquo;grow,&rdquo; which has no natural introduction unless preceded by &ldquo;top.&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Jennens</SC>: If
conjecture be made without any regard to the traces of the letters, <I>out</I> or <I>rout</I> are
better than <I>be.</I> <SC>Malone</SC>: In Devonshire, as Sir Joshua Reynolds informs me, &lquo;to
<I>toe</I> a thing up is to tear it up by the roots; in which sense the word is perhaps used
here, for Edmund immediately adds &ldquo;I <I>grow</I>, I prosper.&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Delius</SC> thus vindicates
Rowe's reading, which he follows: &lquo;The Bastard, if his plan succeed, will to the
legitimate&mdash; What he will inflict upon him he does not say; he is interrupted by the
entrance of his father, at the mere sight of whom he exclaims, in tones of assured
victory, &ldquo;I grow, I prosper.&rdquo;&rquo; [For other instances of the use of this word in the
same sense see <SC>Schmidt's</SC> <I>Lex.</I>] <SC>Nichols</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, &amp;c., No. 2, p. 9) follows the Ff,
and interprets: &lquo;Shall advance to, or take the place of, the legitimate.&rquo;

afterwards III, ii, 18; also <I>Tro. and Cres.</I> IV, v, 105. <SC>White</SC>: That is, <I>yielded.</I>
This seems to be a perversion of the figurative use of &lquo;subscribe&rquo; in the sense of</CC>

<CC><P><I>submit</I>, to which <I>yield</I> is a synonyme, though not in a transitive sense; <I>e. g. Tam.
Shr.</I> I, i, 81. <I>Prescribe</I> of the Folio might be accepted in the sense of <I>limited, cir-
cumscrib'd</I> his power, were it not that the king is manifestly the nominative under-
stood. <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Zur Textkritik</I>, &amp;c., p. 16) prefers <I>prescribed</I>, which he says
means &lquo;his power is restricted, limited, confined in its exercise. The expression is
not exactly what might have been expected from Gloucester; we might wish for a
word a little less tame when applied to an event which so greatly excites him, but
it is perfectly intelligible.&rquo; From the expression &lquo;Prescribe not us our duties,&rquo; I, i,
275, <SC>Schmidt</SC> infers that &lquo;prescribe&rquo; need not of necessity be followed by &lquo;to,&rquo; and
thus Sh. might have used the passive form &lquo;we are prescribed our duties.&rquo; If this
be so, then he conjectures that we might punctuate these lines differently: &lquo;And the
king gone to-night? prescribed? his power Confined to exhibition?&rquo; [Dr. Schmidt
failed to note that the &lquo;to&rquo; is not really absent in &lquo;Prescribe not us our duties,&rquo; but
is simply absorbed in the preceding &lquo;not.&rquo; In his edition of this play he goes even
further, and says that we are nowhere justified (not even in III, vii, 64) in inter-
preting &lquo;to subscribe&rquo; by <I>to yield, to surrender</I>, or <I>to submit.</I> To me Dr. Johnson's
interpretation is satisfactory. Sh. may have intended, by this one word, to convey
the idea that there had been a formal abdication.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>25. <B>exhibition]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: That is, <I>allowance.</I> The term is yet used in the uni-
versities. <SC>Steevens</SC>: So in <I>Two Gent.</I> I, iii, 69. <SC>Nares</SC>: Also Jonson, <I>Silent
Woman</I>, III, i, &lquo;Behave yourself distinctly and with good morality; or, I protest
I'll take away your exhibition.&rquo; <SC>Moberly</SC>: Restricted to a mere maintenance; as
in Roman law, &lquo;si liberi ali desiderent, ut a parente exhibeantur.&rquo; So we have
&lquo;exhibere viam&rquo; for &lquo;to keep up a road.&rquo;
<P>26. <B>gad]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Upon the sudden stimulation of caprice, as cattle run mad-
ding when they are stung by the gadfly. <SC>Ritson</SC>: Done suddenly, or as before,
while &lquo;the iron is hot.&rquo; A &lquo;gad&rquo; is an iron bar. The Statute of 2 and 3 Eliza. 6,
c. 27, is a &lquo;Bill against false forging of iron gadds, instead of gadds of steel.&rquo;
<SC>Collier</SC>: Upon the spur; in <I>Tit. And.</I> IV, 103, the hero wishes to engrave on
brass with &lquo;a gad of steel,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> a <I>point</I> of steel. <SC>Moberly</SC> strangely defines it as
&lquo;at haphazard.&rquo;

<P>44. <B>essay or taste]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Though &lquo;taste&rquo; may stand here, yet I believe we
should read, &lquo;assay or <I>test;</I>&rquo; they are both metallurgical terms and properly joined.
<SC>Steevens</SC>: Both are terms from royal tables. See V, iii, 144. <SC>Singer</SC>: Thus Baret,
<I>Alvearie:</I> &lquo;to Assay or rather Essay of the French woorde <I>Essayer</I>,&rquo; and afterwards:
&lquo;To tast or assay before. <I>Pr&aelig;libo.</I>&rquo; <SC>Wright</SC>: Proof or trial. The two words
&lquo;essay&rquo; and &lquo;assay&rquo; are etymologically the same. In 1 Samuel, xvii, 39, it is said
of David in Saul's armour that he &lquo;assayed to go,&rquo; that is, tried or attempted to go.
&lquo;Taste&rquo; occurs both as a noun and verb as synonymous with &lquo;test.&rquo; Compare 1
<I>Hen. IV:</I> IV, i, 119. Cotgrave has, &lquo;Essay: m. An essay, proofe . . . also, the

<P>45. <B>policy]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: The beginning of Edgar's letter is darken'd by a remov'd

<CC><P>91, 93. <B>Nor . . . earth]</B> <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Zur Textkritik</I>, &amp;c., p. 18) makes a strong
point in favour of omitting these words, as is done in the Ff. &lquo;Were there any
reproach,&rquo; he says, &lquo;against which it would be hard to defend Sh., it would be
the relation between Gloster and Edgar. A father &ldquo;that so tenderly and entirely
loves&rdquo; his son, but, like Gloucester, condemns him unheard, and drives him forth
to misery, is a miscreant in the drama as well as in real life. . . . If there be any sin-
gle trait which is characteristic of this scene, as well as of the similar first scene of
the second Act, it is that not a word of sympathy and warmth for his sons falls from
the lips of Gloucester. His levity, when talking with Kent in the very first scene
of the play, sufficiently betrays the superficial sense of his marital and parental
duties. Only when Edgar is as though dead to him, and the fate of Lear begins to
cast its dark shadow over himself (III, vi), does something of fatherly feeling
awaken at the thought of his son, hunted through the land. Hitherto, he is indif-
ferent and heartless. Evidently his sons have never stood near to his heart; he
knows them not,&mdash;nor what might be expected from either the one or the other.
That Edmund, before the time when the action of the play begins, has been &ldquo;out&rdquo;
nine years in foreign parts is expressly mentioned, and in one way or another Edgar
has been equally a stranger . . . . and is no more to him than Edmund,&mdash;&ldquo;no dearer
in my account,&rdquo; <I>i. e.</I> is of as little account. He has sons and they must be acknow-
ledged, and therein he has done his part. Such and no other is the idea that Sh.
would have us form of Gloucester, and therefore he could never have written the
words: &ldquo;To his father that so tenderly and entirely loves him.&rdquo; They stand in
contradiction to all that precedes and follows. They are doubtless an addition made
by some sensational actor, and they crept into the Qq through some copyist or re-
porter.&rquo;
