<P>112. <SC>Warburton</SC>: In Shakespeare's best plays, besides the vices that arise from
the subject, there is generally some peculiar prevailing folly, principally ridiculed,
that runs through the whole piece. Thus, in <I>The Tempest</I>, the lying disposition of
travellers, and in <I>As You Like It</I>, the fantastick humour of courtiers are exposed and
satirized with infinite pleasantry. In like manner, in this play of <I>Lear</I>, the dotages
of judicial astrology are severely ridiculed. I fancy, was the date of its first per-
formance well considered, it would be found that something or other happened at
that time which gave a more than ordinary run to this deceit, as these words seem to
intimate: &lquo;I am thinking, brother, of a prediction I read this other day, what should
follow these eclipses.&rquo; However this be, an impious cheat, which had so little foun-
dation in nature or reason, so detestable an original, and such fatal consequences on
the manners of the people, who were at that time strangely besotted with it, cer-
tainly deserved the severest lash of satire. It was a fundamental in this noble science,
that whatever seeds of good dispositions the infant unborn might be endowed with,
either from nature, or traductively from its parents, yet if, at the time of its birth,
the delivery was by any casualty so accelerated or retarded as to fall in with the
predominancy of a malignant constellation, that momentary influence would entirely
change its nature, and bias it to all the contrary ill qualities. So wretched and mon-
strous an opinion did it set out with. But the Italians, to whom we owe this, as
well as most other unnatural crimes and follies of these latter ages, fomented its
original impiety to the most detestable height of extravagance. Petrus Aponensis,
an Italian physician of the 13th century, assures us that those prayers which are
made to God when the moon is in conjunction with Jupiter in the Dragon's tail, are
infallibly heard. . . . The great Milton, with a just indignation of this impiety, hath, in
his <I>Paradise Regained</I> (Book IV, 383), satirized it in a very beautiful manner, by</CC>

<CC><P>putting these reveries into the mouth of the devil. . . . Nor could the licentious Rabelais
himself forbear to ridicule this impious dotage, which he does with exquisite address
and humour, where in the fable which he so agreeably tells from &AElig;sop of the man
who applied to Jupiter for the loss of his hatchet, he makes those who, on the poor
man's good success, had projected to trick Jupiter by the same petition, a kind of
astrologic atheists, who ascribed this good fortune that they imagined they were now
all going to partake of, to the influence of some rare conjunction and configuration
of the stars. &lquo;Hen, hen, dirent ilz&mdash;Et doncques telle est au temps present la
revolution des Cieulx, la constellation des Astres, et aspect des Planetes, que qui-
conques coingn&eacute;e perdra soubdain deuiendra ainsi riche?&rquo;&mdash;<I>Nou. Prol. du IV
Livre.</I>&mdash;But to return to Sh. So blasphemous a delusion, therefore, it became the
honesty of our poet to expose. But it was a tender point, and required managing.
For this impious juggle had in his time a kind of religious reverence paid to it. It
was therefore to be done obliquely; and the circumstances of the scene furnished
him as good an opportunity as he could wish. The persons in the drama are all
Pagans, so that as, in compliance to custom, his good characters were not to speak
ill of judicial astrology, they could on account of their religion give no reputation
to it. But in order to expose it the more, he with great judgement makes these
Pagans fatalists, as appears by these words of Lear, &lquo;By all the operations of the
orbs, From whom we do exist and cease to be.&rquo; For the doctrine of fate is the true
foundation of judicial astrology. Having thus discredited it by the very commen-
dations given to it, he was in no danger of having his direct satire against it mis-
taken, by its being put (as he was obliged, both in paying regard to custom and in
following nature) into the mouth of the villain and atheist, especially when he has
added such force of reason to his ridicule, in the words referred to in the beginning
of the note. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: Thus scorn and misanthropy are often the anticipations
and mouthpieces of wisdom in the detection of superstitions. Both individuals and
nations may be free from such prejudices by being below them, as well as by rising
above them.

<CC><P>127. <B>catastrophe]</B> <SC>Heath</SC>: That is, just as the circumstance which decides the
catastrophe of a play intervenes on the very nick of time, when the action is wound
up to its crisis, and the audience are impatiently expecting it.
<P>128. <B>cue]</B> <SC>Bolton Corney</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 5 Aug. 1865) cites the following defini-
tion of this word from Butler's <I>English Grammar</I>, 1634: &lquo;Q. A note of entrance
for actors, because it is the first letter of <I>quando</I>=when, shewing when to enter and
speak.&rquo; <SC>Wedgwood</SC> adopts this definition, but also cites Minsheu: &lquo;A <I>qu</I>, a term
used among stage-players, a Lat. <I>qualis i. e.</I> at what manner of word the actors are
to begin to speak, one after another has done his speech.&rquo; The Fr. term is <I>replique</I>-
<SC>Wright</SC> apparently derives it from Fr. <I>queue</I>, a tail.
<P>129. <B>fa, sol, la, mi]</B> <SC>Dr Burney</SC>: Sh. shows by the context that he was well
acquainted with the property of these syllables in solmization, which imply a series
of sounds so unnatural that ancient musicians prohibited their use. The monkish
writers on music say: <I>mi contra fa est diabolus:</I> the interval <I>fa mi</I>, including a
<I>tritonus</I>, or sharp 4th, consisting of three tones without the intervention of a semi-
tone, expressed in the modern scale by the letters <SC>f g a b</SC>, would form a musical
phrase extremely disagreeable to the ear. Edmund, speaking of eclipses as portents
and prodigies, compares the dislocation of events, the times being out of joint, to
the unnatural and offensive sounds, &lquo;fa sol la mi.&rquo; <SC>White</SC>: According to modern
Italian solmization, fa sol la <I>si; i. e.</I> a progression through the interval of a fourth,
ending upon the seventh or leading note of the scale; which, unless followed by the
tonic, or used for some very special effect, is a most distracting figure, based upon
the most poignant of discords. In Shakespeare's time, and until a comparatively
recent date, the syllables for solmization, instead of <I>do re mi fa sol la si</I>, were <I>fa sol
la fa sol la mi.</I> Sh. often shows that he was a musician as well as a lover of music.
<SC>Wright</SC>: For Dr Burney's note, Mr Chappell assures me, there is not the slightest
foundation. Edmund is merely singing to himself in order not to seem to observe
Edgar's approach. [Just as Mistress Quickly sings &lquo;And down, down, adown-a&rquo; in
<I>Merry Wives</I>, I, iii, 44, when Doctor Caius is approaching.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Moberly</SC>: The
true explanation probably is that the sequence &lquo;fa sol la mi&rquo; (with &lquo;mi&rquo; descending)
is like a deep sigh, as may be easily heard by trial.</CC>

<CC><P>136. <SC>Johnson</SC>: In this speech Edmund, with the common craft of fortune-tellers,

<P>20, 21. <B>Old . . . abused]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC> (Nichols's <I>Lit. Hist.</I> ii, 371) suggests <I>abuses</I>,

use children, with &lquo;checks&rquo; when we find the little &lquo;flatteries&rquo; we employ to quiet
them are &lquo;abus'd&rquo; by their becoming more peevish by indulgence. <SC>Johnson</SC>:

<I>abused.</I> To <I>abuse</I> is, in our author, very frequently the same as to <I>deceive.</I> This
construction is harsh and ungrammatical; Sh. perhaps thought it vicious, and chose
to throw away the lines rather than correct them, nor would now thank the officious-
ness of his editors, who restore what they do not understand. <SC>Tyrwhitt</SC>: Old
fools&mdash;must be used with checks, <I>as well as</I> flatteries, when they (<I>i. e.</I> flatteries) are

liwell</SC>: The rest of the line, after the word &lquo;checks,&rquo; loses its reference to the child,
and merely alludes to the old man as king used to be flattered, which flatteries, being
felt by him, are abused. I have very little doubt, however, but that here there is</CC>

<CC><P>apparently thinks that Kent will <I>disguise</I> his speech by <I>diffusing&mdash;i. e.</I> by spreading
it out. <SC>Hanmer</SC> adopted Theobald's spelling, and gives the true definition: &lquo;to
disguise.&rquo; This interpretation and spelling make <SC>Capell</SC> indignant, and he urges
his emendation <I>deface</I>, thus: &lquo;If I can but deface my speech by a strange accent as
effectually as I have defac'd my person by a strange attire, then my good intent may
do so and so: now for this <I>deface</I> and <I>defac'd</I> substitute <I>diffuse</I> and <I>diffus'd</I>, and see
how you like it; and if <I>diffuse</I> would have suited in this respect, it had not been
given to Kent, whose language is more natural.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>: We must suppose that
Kent advances looking on his disguise. To <I>diffuse</I> speech signifies to <I>disorder</I> it,
and so to <I>disguise</I> it. It may, however, mean to <I>speak broad</I> with a clownish accent.
<SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Rem.</I> 223) cites &lquo;<I>Dyffuse</I> harde to be vnderstande, <I>diffuse.</I>&rquo;&mdash;Palsgrave's
<I>Lesclar. de la Lang. Fr.</I>, 1530. &lquo;But oft by it [logick] a thing playne, bright and
pure, Is made diffuse, vnknowen, harde, and obscure.&rquo;&mdash;Barclay's <I>Ship of Fooles</I>, ed.
1570. &lquo;Kent does not wish to render his speech <I>difficult to be understood</I>, but merely
to disorder it, to disguise it, as he had disguised his person.&rquo; <SC>Wright</SC> cites instances
of the use of &lquo;defuse&rquo; from Lyly's <I>Euphues</I> (ed. Arber), p. 64; and Armin's <I>Nest of
Ninnies</I>, p. 6 (Shaksp. Soc. ed.). For other instances from Sh., see <I>Concordance</I>
or Schmidt's <I>Lex.</I>
<P>6. <B>So . . . come,]</B> To <SC>Capell</SC> this appeared to be a wish and parenthetical.
<P>7. <B>labours]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: His master will find him ready for any hard services, and
any number of them. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 255): Perhaps <I>labour</I> of the Qq is right.
<P>7. <B>Lear]</B> <SC>Coleridge</SC>: In Lear old age is itself a character,&mdash;its natural imper-
fections being increased by lifelong habits of receiving a prompt obedience. Any
addition of individuality would have seen unnecessary and painful; for the relations
of others to him, of wondrous fidelity and of frightful ingratitude, alone sufficiently
distinguish him. Thus Lear becomes the open and ample play-room of nature's
passions.</CC>

<CC><P>11, 13. <B>profess]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: Lear uses this in the sense of <I>trade</I> or <I>calling.</I> Kent
replies in the sense of <I>assertion.</I>

pany</I>, not to <I>discourse</I> or <I>talk.</I>
<P>16. <B>judgement]</B> <SC>Capell</SC> thinks this refers simply to coming before a judge;
<SC>Eccles</SC> and <SC>Moberly</SC> that it refers to the last Judgement.
<P>16. <B>eat no fish.]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: In Queen Elizabeth's time the Papists were
esteemed, and with good reason, enemies to the government. Hence the proverbial
phrase of, &lquo;He's an honest man, and eats no fish,&rquo; to signify he's a friend to the
government and a Protestant. The eating fish, on a religious account, being then
esteemed such a badge of popery, that when it was enjoined for a season by act of
parliament, for the encouragement of the fish-towns, it was thought necessary to
declare the reason; hence it was called &lquo;Cecil's fast.&rquo; To this disgraceful badge
of popery Fletcher alludes in his <I>Woman-Hater</I> [IV, ii], who makes the courtezan
say, when Lazarillo, in search of the umbrana's head, was seized at her house by the
intelligencers for a traitor: &lquo;Gentlemen, I am glad you have discovered him; he
should not have eaten under my roof for twenty pounds; and surely I did not like
him when he called for fish.&rquo; And Marston's <I>Dutch Courtezan</I> [I, ii]: &lquo;I trust I
am none of the wicked that eate fish a Fridaies.&rquo; [<SC>Dyce</SC>, in his ed. of the <I>Woman-
Hater</I>, cites this note by Warburton, and adds: &lquo;<I>Perhaps</I> Warburton is right.&rquo;]
<SC>Capell</SC> thinks that this means simply that Kent was a jolly fellow, and no lover
of such meagre diet as fish.

<P>71. <SC>Hudson</SC>: This aptly touches the key-note of the Fool's character. <SC>Cole-
ridge</SC>: The Fool is no comic buffoon to make the groundlings laugh,&mdash;no forced
condescension of Shakespeare's genius to the taste of his audience. Accordingly,
the poet prepares for his introduction, which he never does with any of his common
clowns and fools, by bringing him into living connection with the pathos of the play.
He is as wonderful a creation as Caliban;&mdash;his wild babblings and inspired idiocy
articulate and gauge the horrors of the scene.

<P>91. <B>Enter Fool.]</B> C. A. <SC>Brown</SC> (<I>Shakespeare's Autobiographical Poems</I>, p. 292,
1838): &lquo;Now, our joy, though last, not least,&rquo; my dearest of all Fools, Lear's Fool!
Ah, what a noble heart, a gentle and a loving one, lies beneath that parti-coloured
jerkin! Thou hast been cruelly treated. Regan and Goneril could but hang thee,
while the unfeeling players did worse; for they tainted thy character, and at last</CC>
<PB N=67>
<HE><SC>act i, sc.</SC> iv.] <I>KING LEAR</I> 67</HE>
<FHL>
<CC><C>[91. <B>Enter Fool.]</B></C>
<P>thrust thee from the stage, as one unfit to appear in their worshipful company. Re-
gardless of that warning voice forbidding them to &lquo;speak more than is set down for
them,&rquo; they have put into thy mouth words so foreign to thy nature, that they might,
with as much propriety, be given to Cardinal Wolsey. But let me take thee, with-
out addition or diminution, from the hands of Sh., and then art thou one of his
perfect creations. Look at him! It may be your eyes see him not as mine do, but he
appears to me of a light delicate frame, every feature expressive of sensibility even
to pain, with eyes lustrously intelligent, a mouth blandly beautiful, and withal a
hectic flush upon his cheek. Oh that I were a painter! Oh that I could describe him
as I knew him in my boyhood, when the Fool made me shed tears, while Lear did
but terrify me! . . . When the Fool enters, throwing his coxcomb at Kent, and
instantly follows it up with allusions to the miserable rashness of Lear, we ought
to understand him from that moment to the last. Throughout this scene his wit,
however varied, still aims at the same point, and in spite of threats, and regardless
how his words may be construed by Goneril's creatures, with the eagerness of a
filial love he prompts the old king to &lquo;resume the shape which he had cast off.&rquo;
&lquo;This is not altogether fool, my lord.&rquo; But, alas! it is too late; and when driven
from the scene by Goneril, he turns upon her with an indignation that knows no fear
of the &lquo;halter&rquo; for himself: &lquo;A fox when one has caught her, And such a daughter,
Should sure to the slaughter, If my cap would buy a halter.&rquo; That such a character
should be distorted by players, printers, and commentators! Observe every word
he speaks; his meaning, one would imagine, could not be misinterpreted; and when
at length, finding his covert reproaches can avail nothing, he changes his discourse
to simple mirth, in order to distract the sorrows of his master. When Lear is in
the storm, who is with him? None&mdash;not even Kent&mdash;&lquo;None but the Fool; who
labours to outjest His heart-struck injuries.&rquo; The tremendous agony of Lear's
mind would be too painful, and even deficient in pathos, without this poor faithful
servant at his side. It is he that touches our hearts with pity, while Lear fills the
imagination to aching. . . . But it is acted otherwise,&mdash;no, it is Tate that is acted.
Let them, if they choose, bring this tragedy on the stage; but, by all means, let us
not be without the Fool. I can imagine an actor in this part, with despair in his
face, and a tongue for ever struggling with a jest, who should thrill every bosom.
What! banish him from the tragedy, when Lear says, &lquo;I have one part in my heart
that's sorry yet for thee;&rquo; and when he so feelingly addresses him with, &lquo;Come on, my
boy; how dost, my boy? Art cold? I am cold myself.&rquo; At that pitch of rage, &lquo;Off!
off, you lendings! Come, unbutton here!&rquo; could we but see the Fool throw himself
into his master's arms, to stay their fury, looking up in his countenance with eyes that
would fain appear as if they wept not, and hear his pathetic entreaty, &lquo;Pr'ythee,
nuncle, be contented;&rquo;&mdash;pshaw! these players know nothing of their trade.
<P>In <SC>Macready's</SC> <I>Diary</I> is the following: 4th [January, 1838].&mdash;Went to the the-
atre, where I went on a first rehearsal of <I>King Lear.</I> My opinion of the introduc-
tion of the Fool is that, like many such terrible contrasts in poetry and painting,
in acting-representation it will fail of effect; it will either weary and annoy or dis-
tract the spectator. I have no hope of it, and think that at the last we shall be
obliged to dispense with it. 5th.&mdash;Speaking to Willmott and Bartley about the part
of the Fool in <I>Lear</I>, and mentioning my apprehensions that, with Meadows, we
should be obliged to omit the part, I described the sort of fragile, hectic, beautiful-</CC>
<PB N=68>
<HE>68 <I>KING LEAR</I> [<SC>act i, sc.</SC> iv.</HE>
<FHL>
<CC><C>[91. <B>Enter Fool.]</B></C>
<P>faced boy that he should be, and stated my belief that it never could be acted. Bart-
ley observed that a woman should play it. I caught at the idea, and instantly ex-
claimed, &lquo;Miss P. Horton is the very person.&rquo; I was delighted at the thought.
<P>C. <SC>Cowden Clarke</SC> (<I>Gent. Mag.</I> No. LVIII, p. 397): Lear's Fool is a youth,
not a grown man; a petted lad, to whom his royal master looks for quaint say-
ings and whimsical sentences when vexed and irritable; a favoured fellow, whose
wayward speeches are tolerated, and even liked, when graver cares press hard on
the old monarch, and to whose playful sallies he turns when desiring to fill a vacant
half hour or beguile a leisure interval. . . . The personal and affectionate interest
taken by Lear in the lad is denoted at the very outset. He not only asks eagerly
and repeatedly for him, but when told that since Cordelia's going into France &lquo;the
Fool hath much pined away,&rquo; Lear answers hurriedly: &lquo;No more of that; <I>I have
noted it well;</I>&rquo; and when the Fool himself appears on the scene, his old master
accosts him with: &lquo;How now, my pretty knave, <I>how dost thou?</I>&rquo; The very expres-
sion, &lquo;My pretty knave,&rquo; serves to paint the Fool's boyish years, and to depict the
fondling regard of Lear for him. . . . This kind of gentle feeling is shown by others
as well as the king towards the stripling fool-jester; for Kent&mdash;who, disguised as
Caius, affects much bluntness of speech&mdash;on more than one occasion speaks favour-
ingly of and to the lad. When the Fool is sportively and keenly rebuking Lear for
having so unwisely cast all power into his unworthy daughter's hands, Kent observes:
&lquo;This is not altogether fool, my lord.&rquo; Afterwards, also, in the storm, when the boy,
scared at finding the Bedlam beggar in the hovel, runs out again, exclaiming: &lquo;Come
not in here, nuncle; here's a spirit. Help me, help me!&rquo; Kent encouragingly says:
&lquo;<I>Give me thy hand.</I> Who's there?&rquo; And still further on, at the close of that wild
night-scene, when the poor old king, worn out, has fallen into weary slumber, Kent,
preparing to bear him away to safer quarters, says to the faithful Fool: &lquo;Come, help
to bear thy master; <I>thou</I> must not stay behind.&rquo; This tenderness with which the boy
is treated partly arises from his delicacy of frame, which is indicated by some slight
but significant side-touches in the course of the play. First, there is his &lquo;pining
away&rquo; on his young mistress's departure from England, above alluded to. Then,
there is his sensitiveness to churlish weather and sharp night air, betokened by his
words during the storm: &lquo;O nuncle, court holy water,&rquo; &amp;c. Again: &lquo;This cold
night will turn us all to fools and madmen.&rquo; Lastly, there is his withdrawal from
the play. It is silently effected, the dramatist giving no express mention of the Fool
after his assisting to bear his old master away to the litter prepared for conveying the
king to Dover; but, to my mind, Sh. evidently meant to infer that the fragile lad&mdash;
weakly in frame, susceptible in temperament, and rendered doubly so by the delicacy
of his nurture in the court household as the petted boy-jester of his royal employer&mdash;
never recovered from the rigours and terrors of that tempestuous night; that he sick-
ened and died soon after, fulfilling actually, as well as poetically, his own last uttered
words: &lquo;And I'll go to bed at noon.&rquo; In this noontide of his youth and fidelity, Lear's
Fool goes to his deathbed, when his old master no longer needs him by his side.

<CC><P>&lquo;labours to outjest his heart-struck injuries.&rquo; [After these long and good notes by
my betters, I wish merely to record humbly but firmly my conviction that the Fool,
one of Shakespeare's most wonderful characters, is not a boy, but a man&mdash;one of the
shrewdest, tenderest of men, whom long life had made shrewd, and whom afflictions
had made tender; his wisdom is too deep for any boy, and could be found only in a
man, removed by not more than a score of years from the king's own age; he had
been Lear's companion from the days of Lear's early manhood. See also White's
note on line 123.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>93. <B>you were best]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 230: The old &lquo;(<I>to</I>) me (<I>it</I>) were better,&rquo; being
misunderstood, was sometimes replaced by &lquo;I were better.&rquo; When the old idiom is
retained, it is generally in instances like the present, where &lquo;you&rquo; may represent
either nominative or dative, but was almost certainly used by Sh. as a nominative.
See III, iv, 99.
<P>93. <B>coxcomb]</B> <SC>Minsheu</SC> (s. v. <I>cockes-combe</I>, ed. 1617): Englishmen use to call
vaine and proud braggers, and men of meane discretion and judgement <I>Coxcombes.</I>
Because naturall Idiots and Fooles haue, and still doe accustome themselues to weare
in their Cappes, cock's feathers, or a hat with a necke and head of a cocke on the
top and a bell thereon, &amp;c., and thinke themselues finely fitted and proudly attired
therewith, so we compare a presumptuous bragging fellow, and wanting all true
Iudgement and discretion, to such an Idiote foole, and call him also Coxecombe.
[Cited in part by <SC>Steevens</SC>.]
<P>94. <B>Why, Fool]</B> <SC>Knight</SC>: The text of the Folio [see Textual Notes] clearly

of serving-man, so soon to begin bandying questions with Lear's favorite. <SC>White</SC>:
The Folio is clearly wrong, as the Fool's reply shows. Lear had taken &lquo;no one's part
that's out of favour,&rquo; but Kent had. The mistake seems to be due to the fact that
both Lear and Kent reply interrogatively to the Fool's remark about his coxcomb.
<SC>Dyce</SC>: The eye of the transcriber or compositor most probably caught the next
speech but one. It is plain that the Fool addresses the king for the first time when
he says: &lquo;How now, nuncle,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Schmidt</SC> silently follows F<SUB>1</SUB>F<SUB>2</SUB>, which are to me

<CC><P>from <I>an</I>, the imperative of <I>unnan</I>, to grant. This plausible but false derivation

<P>96. <B>catch cold]</B> <SC>Farmer</SC>: That is, be turned out of doors and exposed to the
inclemency of the weather.
<P>98. <B>banished]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: This means that he had lost them as daughters, lost
their love and obedience, and by an act of his own. <SC>Eccles</SC> thinks that these
words are spoken in the wanton levity of the character, as being the contrary of
those favours Lear had conferred upon them. <SC>Moberly</SC>: Lear has, by blessing
them, made Goneril and Regan no longer his daughters, and also made Cordelia
queen of France by cursing her.
<P>98. <B>on's]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 182: &lquo;On&rquo; was frequently used for the possessive <I>of</I>, par-
ticularly, in rapid speech, before a contracted pronoun. The explanation of this
change of <I>of</I> to &lquo;on&rquo; appears to be as follows: <I>Of</I> when rapidly pronounced before
a consonant became <I>o</I>'; but when <I>o</I>' came before a vowel it was forced to assume a
euphonic <I>n.</I> See I, v, 19.
<P>98. <B>did]</B> For instances of the transitive use of this word, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 303.
<P>100. <B>nuncle]</B> <SC>Nares</SC>: A familiar contraction of <I>mine uncle.</I> It seems to have
been the customary appellation of the licensed fool to his superiors. In the same
style the fools called each other <I>cousin.</I> In Beaumont and Fletcher's <I>Pilgrim</I>, when
Alinda assumes the character of a fool, she uses the same language. She meets
Alphonso, and calls him <I>nuncle;</I> to which he replies by calling her <I>naunt.</I> <SC>Wright</SC>:
So in Whetstone's <I>Promos and Cassandra</I>, iv, 7, we find &lquo;my nown good harte roote.&rquo;
In Littr&eacute;'s <I>Dict.</I>, under the word &lquo;Tante,&rquo; it is stated that &lquo;nante&rquo; is a form of the
word in Picardy, and in justification of the derivation of <I>tante</I> from <I>ta ante</I>, refer-
ence is made to the Wallon dialect, in which <I>mononk, matante</I>, and similar forms
are used, the possessive pronoun having no force whatever. If the origin of &lquo;nuncle&rquo;
is not analogous, it must be referred to the principle by which Noll, Ned, Nan, Nell,
Numps are formed from Oliver, Edward, Anne, Ellen and Humphrey.</CC>

<CC><P>107. <B>brach]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: A bitch of the hunting kind. Dr Letherland, on the
margin of Warburton's ed., proposed &lquo;<I>lady's</I> brach,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> favoured animal. &lquo;Lady&rquo;
is still a common name for a hound. So Hotspur, in 1 <I>Hen. IV:</I> III, i, 240. <SC>Tol-
let</SC> [Note in III, vi, 67]: The females of all dogs were once called <I>braches.</I> Uli-
tius upon Gratius observes: &lquo;<I>Racha</I> Saxonibus canem significabat unde Scoti hodie
<I>Rache</I> pro cane f&oelig;mina habent, quod Anglis est <I>Brache.</I>&rquo; A[<SC>rchibald</SC>] S[<SC>mith</SC>]
(<I>N. and Qu.</I> 2 Ser., vol. v, p. 202, 1858): Here is a curious opposition between
&lquo;truth&rquo; and &lquo;lady,&rquo; where one would have expected the opposition to be between
&lquo;truth&rquo; and <I>lie.</I> May it not be that Sh. wrote &lquo;lye the brach,&rquo; and that the printers
thought &lquo;lye&rquo; a contraction for &lquo;lady,&rquo; instead of the whole of the opposite of <I>truth?</I>
<SC>Wright</SC>: Florio has, &lquo;Bracca, a brache, or a bitch, a beagle;&rquo; Cotgrave: &lquo;Braque:

gives &lquo;a Brache or biche. Canicula.&rquo; The word is found in German <I>Bracke</I>, and
in Dutch <I>Brak.</I>

<P>118. <B>Set]</B> <SC>Mrs Griffiths</SC>: That is, never set equal to the stake you throw for.
<SC>Schmidt</SC>: The sense varies according to the way in which we understand &lquo;less,&rquo;
whether as an adjective or as an adverb. If it is an adjective, then the meaning is:
&lquo;Set a less sum than thou hast won by thy last throw;&rquo; if an adverb: &lquo;Keep on
throwing, but set nothing.&rquo;
<P>123. <B>Kent]</B> <SC>Knight</SC>: The Ff properly gives this speech to Kent, in reply to the
Fool's address to him, &lquo;Sirrah, I'll teach thee a speech.&rquo; <SC>White</SC> also upholds the
Ff, because: &lquo;it should be observed, that in addressing this poor, faithful follower,
the king never calls him Fool. In speaking <I>of</I> him, he gives him his official title;
but in speaking <I>to</I> him, he always uses some term of familiar and pitiful endear-
ment,&mdash;generally, &ldquo;my boy,&rdquo;&mdash;although the poor fellow had plainly had many years'
sad experience of the world. It seems a deteriorating misapprehension of this phrase
that has led an eminent actor [Macready] to represent the Fool as a boy in years!
I cannot believe that on this solitary occasion Sh. was indifferent to the touching
nature of the relations which he had established between Lear and his humble coun-
sellor; and I accept the evidence of the Folio that this speech is one of Kent's many
characteristic interruptions.&rquo;
<P>124. <B>unfee'd lawyer]</B> <SC>Lord Campbell</SC> (<I>Shakespeare's Legal Acquirements</I>, p.
97, Am. ed.): This seems to show that Sh. had frequently been present at trials in
courts of justice, and now speaks from his own recollection. There is no trace of
such a proverbial saying as &lquo;like the breath of an unfee'd lawyer,&rquo; while all the world
knows the proverb: &lquo;Whosoever is his own counsel has a fool for his client.&rquo; How
unfee'd lawyers may have comported themselves in Shakespeare's time I know not;
but I am bound to say, in vindication of &lquo;my order,&rquo; that in my time there has been
no ground for the Fool's sarcasm upon the bar. The two occasions when &lquo;the breath
of an unfee'd lawyer&rquo; attracts notice in this generation, are when he pleads for a
party suing <I>in form&acirc; pauperis</I>, or when he defends a person prosecuted by the Crown
for high treason. It is contrary to etiquette to take a fee in the one case as in the
other; and on all such occasions counsel, from a regard to their own credit, as well
as from conscientious motives, uniformly exert themselves with extraordinary zeal,
and put forth all their learning and eloquence.</CC>

<P>138. <B>Do]</B> <SC>Jennens</SC> adopts Hanmer's change &lquo;<I>Or</I> do,&rquo; and asserts that the measure
points out that a word is lost here [which is true], and that the sense shows it to be
<I>Or</I> [which is doubtful]. <SC>White</SC> is equally sure that the missing word is <I>And;</I> his
text reads &lquo;<I>And do thou</I>,&rquo; and in his note he says that this <I>And</I> the rhythm so imper-
atively demands that &lquo;it could not possibly have been omitted in a rhyme like this,
even if it were as superfluous as it is appropriate to the sense. It was doubtless
omitted by accident.&rquo; The <SC>Cambridge Editors</SC> suggest an emendation which is,
perhaps, the happiest of any yet offered: &lquo;Do thou <I>there</I> for him stand.&rquo; The an-
tithesis with the preceding line is emphasized, and the similarity of the &lquo;thou&rquo; and
the <I>there</I> in MS might well have been the cause, through oversight, of the omission
of the latter word by the compositor.

<CC><P>179. <B>thee]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 213: &lquo;Thee&rquo; for <I>thou</I> is found after the verb <I>to be</I> not

<P>181. <B>Goneril]</B> <SC>Coleridge</SC>: The monster Goneril prepares what is necessary,
while the character of Albany renders a still more maddening grievance possible&mdash;
namely, Regan and Cornwall in perfect sympathy of monstrosity. Not a sentiment,
not an image, which can give pleasure on its own account, is admitted. Whenever
these creatures are introduced, and they are brought forward as little as possible,
pure horror reigns throughout. In this scene, and in all the early speeches of Lear,
the one general sentiment of filial ingratitude prevails as the main-spring of the
feelings;&mdash;in this early stage the outward object causing the pressure on the mind,
which is not yet sufficiently familiarized with the anguish for the imagination to work
upon it.

where she was solitaryly walking, with her frowning cloth, as sick lately of the
solens,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Staunton</SC>: The very remarkable effect of this band, in the contrac-
tion of the brows, may be observed in some of the monumental effigies of the four-
teenth century, and especially in those small figures usually called &lquo;Weepers&rquo; which
are found standing in tabernacles, on the sides of rich altar-tombs of the same period.
Lear, however, may be supposed to speak metaphorically. <SC>Wright</SC>: Compare
1 <I>Hen. IV:</I> I, iii, 19: &lquo;And majesty might never yet endure The moody frontier
of a servant brow,&rquo; where &lquo;frontier&rquo; is apparently used with some reference to <I>tire</I>
or head-dress.

<P>192. <B>That's . . . peascod]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC> was the first to insert a stage-direction
here, directly referring this sentence to Lear, and he has been followed, I think, by
all edd. except <SC>Delius</SC>. As though the point were not made thereby sufficiently
clear, Warburton changed &lquo;That's&rquo; to <I>Thou art.</I> I cannot help thinking that stage-
directions like these are in general needless, not to say obtrusive. If the action is
so clear that the humblest intellect can perceive it, surely a stage-direction is super-
fluous; for instance, when the Fool says to Kent, &lquo;Here's my coxcomb,&rquo; does any
one require to be told that he here offers Kent his cap? When Lear says &lquo;There's
earnest of thy service,&rquo; may not an editor assume that a reader has some intelligence,
and needs not to be told that Lear here &lquo;gives Kent money&rquo;? In the present in-
stance the application is sufficiently clear without any indication with the finger.&mdash;

<P>210. <B>So . . . darkling]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Farmer concurs with me in supposing that this is
a fragment of some old song. <SC>Malone</SC>: In a very old comedy called <I>The Longer Thou
Livest the more Foole Thou Arte</I>, about 1580, we find the following stage-direction:
&lquo;Entreth Moros, counterfaiting a vaine gesture and a foolish countenance, synging
the foote of many songs, as fools were wont.&rquo; <SC>Sir Joshua Reynolds</SC>: Shakespeare's
fools are certainly copied from the life. The originals whom he copied were no
doubt men of quick parts; lively and sarcastic. Though they were licensed to say
any thing, it was still necessary, to prevent giving offence, that everything they said
should have a playful air; we may suppose, therefore, that they had a custom of
taking off the edge of too sharp a speech by covering it hastily with the end of an
old song, or any glib nonsense that came into the mind. I know no other way of
accounting for the incoherent words with which Sh. often finishes this Fool's speeches.
<SC>Knight</SC> [after quoting this note by Sir Joshua Reynolds, continues]: But the words
before us are not incoherent words. The expression &lquo;so out went the candle,&rquo; &amp;c.,
may have been proverbial to signify the desertion of a man by his mercenary friends
when he is become a &lquo;sheal'd peascod.&rquo; But Sh. found the almost identical image
applied to the story of Lear as related by Spenser: &lquo;But true it is, that, <I>when the oil
is spent, The light goes out</I> and wick is thrown away; So when he had resign'd his
<*>egiment, His daughter 'gan despise his drooping day.&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>of a nightingale. These three meanings yield three interpretations: first, the usual
one, as the refrain of a ballad; second, as the answer to the foregoing question
&lquo;May not an ass know when the cart draws the horse?&rquo; and to be paraphrased:
&lquo;Gee-up, puddle! I love thee!&rquo; and supposed to be addressed by the cart to the

<P>219-228. <B>Does . . . father]</B> Whether it be due to the incoherence of Lear's
passion or to the sophistications of the compositor, these lines have given rise to
much discussion among the early commentators. The later editors have been con-
cerned chiefly with the metrical arrangement, and have little or nothing to say about
the meaning of the passage. <SC>Roderick</SC> (<I>Can. of Crit.</I>, p. 267, 1765, ed. vii) holds
Lear's first speech (lines 219-223) to be ironical. Goneril has told him that he is
transported beyond himself, and he ironically assents to it. To support this view,
Roderick changes &lquo;Ha! waking?&rquo; into &lquo;<I>or</I> waking;&rquo; that is, &lquo;This is not Lear,&mdash;
whether in lethargy or waking&mdash;it is not Lear.&rquo; He would also change &lquo;Who is it
that can tell me?&rquo; into &lquo;Who is it <I>then</I> can tell me?&rquo; Here the irony ceases and
serious resentment begins. &lquo;If I were to be persuaded by the marks of (<I>i. e.</I> the
distinction and respect due to) my sovereignty (as king), my knowledge (as an old
man, of long experience) or my reason (as a man, one of the superior sex) that I
had daughters, it would appear that I was falsely so persuaded. You are therefore
a stranger, and I demand your name.&rquo; This interpretation of Roderick's needs no
refutation. <SC>Heath</SC> denounces it as unnatural to a person in Lear's situation, just</CC>
<PB N=82>
<HE>82 <I>KING LEAR</I> [<SC>act i, sc.</SC> iv.</HE>
<FHL>
<CC><C>[219-228. <B>Does . . . father</B>]</C>
<P>then transported to the highest pitch of astonishment, and not yet sufficiently familiar-
ised to his misfortunes, nor cool enough, to treat the author of them ironically. Heath
himself interprets lines 221, 222: &lquo;Either his apprehension is decayed, his faculty of
discernment is buried under a lethargic sleep, or &mdash;here he was about to go on to the
other alternative&mdash;viz: he is in his sober senses and broad awake, when the sudden
whirl of passion on the bare imagination that what had passed is real, so overwhelms
him that he breaks off: &lquo;Ha! what! that it should be possible that I am now
awake? It cannot be, 'tis impossible.&rquo; <SC>Warburton</SC> aroused the critics by his dog-
matic assertion that we should read &lquo;sovereignty <I>of</I> knowledge&rquo;&mdash;<I>i. e.</I> the under-
standing, like &lquo;sovereignty of reason&rquo; in <I>Ham.</I>, because his sovereignty or kingship
would not enable Lear to judge whether or not these were his daughters. <SC>Heath</SC>
as usual flouts and routs Warburton, but without giving a much better interpretation
of the phrase. He defines &lquo;sovereignty&rquo; as that self-command which distinguishes
the man in his senses from a lunatic or idiot: &lquo;If I should give credit to those
marks I perceive in myself of being in my right senses, and endued with knowledge
and reason, I should be persuaded I had daughters,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Tyrwhitt</SC> says that the
difficulty is &lquo;to conceive how &ldquo;the marks of sovereignty, of knowledge, and of
reason&rdquo; should be of any use to persuade Lear that he had or had not daughters.
No logic could draw such a conclusion from such premises. This difficulty may be
entirely removed by only pointing the passage thus: &ldquo;for by the marks of sovereignty,
knowledge, and reason, I should be false persuaded.&mdash;I had daughters.&mdash;Your name,
fair gentlewoman?&rdquo; The chain of Lear's speech being thus untangled, we can
clearly trace the succession and connection of his ideas. The undutiful behaviour
of his daughter so disconcerts him that he doubts by turns whether she is Goneril
and whether he himself is Lear. Upon her first speech, he only exclaims, &ldquo;Are you
our daughter?&rdquo; Upon her going on in the same style, he begins to question his
own sanity, and even his personal identity. He appeals to the bystanders, &ldquo;Who is
it that can tell me who I am?&rdquo; I should be glad to be told. <I>For</I> (if I was to judge
myself) <I>by the marks of sovereignty, of knowledge, and of reason</I> (which once dis-
tinguished Lear, but which I have now lost), <I>I should be false</I> (against my own
consciousness) <I>persuaded</I> (that I am not Lear). He then slides to the examina-
tion of another distinguishing mark of Lear: &ldquo;I had daughters.&rdquo; But not able,
as it should seem, to dwell upon so tender a subject, he hastily recurs to his first
doubt concerning Goneril: &ldquo;Your name, fair gentlewoman?&rdquo;&rquo; Of this note by
Tyrwhitt, <SC>Johnson</SC> says that it is &lquo;written with confidence disproportionate to the
conviction which it can bring. Lear might as well know by the marks and tokens
arising from sovereignty, knowledge, and reason, that he had or had not daughters,
as he could know by anything else. But, says he, if I judge by these tokens, I find
the persuasion false by which I long thought myself the father of daughters.&rquo; <SC>Mason</SC>
says that by the marks of sovereignty Lear means those tokens of royalty which his
daughters then enjoyed as derived from him. But <SC>Malone</SC> replies: &lquo;Lear had not
parted with all the marks of sovereignty. In the midst of his prodigality to his
children, he reserved to himself the name and all the additions to a king.&rquo; <SC>Staun-
ton</SC> says that this passage is &lquo;certainly obscure. Possibly the meaning may be
restored by simply omitting the comma after &ldquo;sovereignty,&rdquo; &ldquo;&mdash;by the marks of
sovereignty knowledge and reason&rdquo;&mdash;<I>i. e.</I> of <I>supreme</I> or <I>sovereign</I> knowledge, &amp;c.&rquo;
<SC>Knight</SC> puts dashes, to indicate continued speech, after Lear's question, &lquo;Who is it</CC>

<P>228. <B>Which]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: This is used with two deviations from present language:

<CC><P>230. <B>admiration]</B> Astonishment. See <I>Ham.</I> I, ii, 192: &lquo;Season your admiration
for a while.&rquo;
<P>230. <B>savour]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: &lquo;Whether the word of some old editions be <I>favour</I> or
<I>$avour</I> is hard pronouncing; nor is there much choice between them in this place.&rquo;
If <I>favour</I> be adopted, <SC>Steevens</SC> rightly explains it as <I>complexion.</I> <SC>Schmidt</SC> deserts
the Ff and follows Jane Bell's Quarto! Because, as he says, <I>savour</I> bears no other
meaning in Sh. than <I>smell.</I> But this is an assertion which I am afraid it would be
hard to prove, so great is the confusion arising between the long <I>$</I> and <I>f.</I> In all
the passages where the word is used, there is, as Capell says of the present, not
much choice between <I>favour</I> and <I>$avour</I>, and probably a master of fence, like
Schmidt, could successfully uphold either.
<P>233. <B>you should]</B> The omission of &lquo;you&rquo; in the Ff cannot be justified, says
<SC>Schmidt</SC>, by other examples in Sh., but its insertion lames the metre.
<P>235. <B>debosh'd]</B> The old spelling of <I>debauched</I>, of which word, <SC>Wedgwood</SC> says
that the radical idea seems to be to throw out of course, from <I>bauche</I>, a row. rank,
or course of stones, or bricks, in building.
<P>237-238. <B>epicurism . . . lust, . . . tavern . . . brothel]</B> An instance of what
<SC>Corson</SC> calls a <I>respective construction.</I> The first word refers to the third and the
second to the fourth. See <I>Ham.</I> IV, vii, 82.
<P>239. <B>graced]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: A palace graced by the presence of a sovereign.
But <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) interprets it better as &lquo;full of grace, dignified, honourable.&rquo;</CC>

<P>243. <B>depend]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC> interprets &lquo;continue in service;&rquo; or, as <SC>Wright</SC> says,
&lquo;that shall still remain dependents,&rquo; but <SC>Schmidt</SC> denies this meaning, and maintains
with <SC>Delius</SC> that the phrase signifies: &lquo;this shall still be one of the conditions, that
they are men as may besort your age,&rquo; &amp;c. &lquo;Even if <I>dependant</I> means a retainer, a
servant, the verb <I>depend</I>, used absolutely, never means <I>to serve, to be a in a person's
service</I>, but it indicates the opposite of personal freedom, the position of a subject
and bondman. &ldquo;A life so stinkingly depending,&rdquo; in <I>Meas. for Meas.</I> III, ii, 28,
means, a life which is the slave of disgusting coarseness. The remark &ldquo;you depend
upon Lord Paris,&rdquo; in <I>Tro. and Cres.</I>, which, of course, means you are one of the
servants of Lord Paris,&mdash;a simple menial perverts by the reply, &ldquo;I depend upon the
lord.&rdquo; If &ldquo;that,&rdquo; in the present passage, be a relative, the phrase can only mean:
that shall continue to remain servants, not their own masters.&rquo; [Which is exactly
what <SC>Wright</SC> says it means; and is not only the simpler explanation of the two,
but wholly avoids any grammatical difficulty. According to Schmidt's interpreta-
tion the sentence is an anacoluthon,&mdash;there is no verb for &lquo;remainder,&rquo; and he has
to suggest that, grammatically, &lquo;To be such men,&rquo; should be &lquo;On their being such
men.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]</CC>

<CC><P>joy or sorrow. To which, I think, may be added <SC>Singer's</SC> observation that it

<P>269. <SC>Davies</SC> (<I>Dram. Misc.</I> ii, 180): I have heard certain critics complain that, in
pronouncing this denunciation, Garrick was too deliberate, and not so quick in the
emission of his words as he ought to have been; that he did not yield to that im-
petuosity which the situation required. . . . Garrick rendered the curse so terribly
affecting to the audience, that, during his utterance of it, they seemed to shrink
from it as from a blast of lightning. His preparation for it was extremely affecting;
his throwing away his crutch, kneeling on one knee, clasping his hands together, and
lifting his eyes toward heaven, presented a picture worthy the pencil of Raphael.
. . . Dr Franklin [the translator of Sophocles] thinks nothing can exceed the bit-
terness of &OElig;dipus's execration of his two sons, except perhaps this curse of Lear.
<SC>Boaden</SC> (<I>Life of Kemble</I>, i, 378): In January [1788] Kemble acted Lear [in Tate's
version, to the Cordelia of Mrs. Siddons]. I have seen him since in the character,
but he never again achieved the excellence of that night. Subsequently he was too
elaborately aged, and quenched with infirmity the insane fire of the injured father.
The curse, as he then uttered it, harrowed up the soul; the gathering himself together,
with hands convulsively clasped, the increasing fervour and rapidity, and the suffoca-
tion of the concluding words, all evinced consummate skill and original invention.
The countenance, too, was finely made up, and in grandeur approached the <I>most</I>
awful impersonation of Michael Angelo. <SC>Scott</SC> (<I>On Boaden's Life of Kemble,
Quarterly Review</I>, April, 1826): There was visible in Kemble's manner, at times,
a sacrifice of energy of action to grace. We remember this observation being
made by Mrs Siddons herself, who admired her brother in general as much as she
loved him. Nor shall we easily forget the mode in which she illustrated her mean-
ing. She arose and placed herself in the attitude of one of the old Egyptian
statues; the knees joined together, and the feet turned a little inwards. She placed
her elbows close to her sides, folded her hands, and held them upright, with the palms
pressed to each other. Having made us observe that she had assumed one of the
most constrained, and, therefore, most ungraceful positions possible, she proceeded to
recite the curse of King Lear on his undutiful offspring in a manner which made
hair rise and flesh creep, and then called on us to remark the additional effect which
was gained by the concentrated energy which the unusual and ungraceful position
in itself implied. T. R. <SC>Gould</SC> (<I>The Tragedian, an Essay on the Histrionic Genius
of Junius Brutus Booth</I>, p. 142, New York, 1868): It is customary to call this im-
precation on Goneril &lquo;the curse.&rquo; This word roughens the sense of it unnecessarily.
It is in substance a pagan prayer that she may be childless; but &lquo;if she must teem,&rquo;
that her child may be a &lquo;thwart disnatured torment to her;&rquo; that she may suffer the
same kind and quality of anguish which she is now inflicting on her father. The</CC>

<CC><P>principle of the prayer is &lquo;an eye for an eye.&rquo; Putting &lquo;Jehovah&rquo; instead of &lquo;Nature,
a Jew might have uttered it. Booth began it as a solemn adjuration to the unseen
power of Nature. The indignant bitterness in the terms of imprecation seemed as
if it was converted out of sweetest images of what a child should be, that lay in the
core of his fatherly heart. This double action of his mind, in the agony which it
involved, swayed and shook the kneeling figure, and lent his voice a wild vibration
that drew involuntary sympathy and awe. The heart followed him as he arose and
ran out with extended arms. . . . [When he re-enters, on the word &lquo;resume,&rquo; line 303]
he cast the whole energy of his royal will, with a volumed, prolonged, and ringing
intonation. His very figure seemed to dilate with majesty.
<P>269. <B>Nature . . . goddess]</B> <SC>White</SC> thinks that the arrangement in the present
text, in comparison with his (see Textual Notes), loses in freedom, force, and
rhythm.
<P>274. <B>derogate]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: Unnatural. <SC>Heath</SC>: Here, it means whatever

son</SC>: Rather, degraded [Thus, <SC>Dyce</SC>, <I>Gloss.</I>], blasted. <SC>Malone</SC>: Shrunk, wasted.
See Bullokar's <I>Eng. Expositor</I>, 1621, &lquo;<I>Derogate.</I> To empaire, diminish, or take

many adjectives in -<I>ate</I> it stands for <I>derogated.</I> <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>): Depraved, cor-
rupt. <SC>Wright</SC>: Dishonoured, degraded. Todd, in his edition of Johnson's <I>Dic-
tionary</I>, quotes from Sir Thomas Elyot's <I>Governor</I> (1565), fol. 102: &lquo;That he shoulde
obteyne, yf he mought, of the kyng his father his gracious pardon, whereby no lawe
or iustice should be derogate.&rquo; [Bullokar's definition applies to this use of &lquo;derogate&rquo;
in Elyot's <I>Governor.</I>]
<P>277. <B>thwart]</B> <SC>Henderson</SC>: This word is found, as an adjective, in <I>Promos and

to Milton, <I>Par. Lost</I>, viii, 132, and x, 1075, as instances of its use as an adjective.
<SC>Schmidt</SC>: As an adj. nowhere else in Sh.
<P>277. <B>disnatured]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Wanting in natural affection. So Daniel, <I>Hymen's

<I>disfeatur'd.</I>

<P>279. <B>cadent]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Falling. <SC>Moberly</SC>: The effect of an unusual word
formed from the Latin or Greek is often very great in poetry. Thus, Milton speaks
of the &lquo;glassy, cool, translucent wave,&rquo; and Wordsworth of the river, &lquo;diaphanous
because it travels slowly,&rquo; both words being far more effective than the common
word &lquo;transparent.&rquo;
<P>280. <B>her mother's pains and benefits]</B> <SC>Roderick</SC> (<I>Can. of Crit.</I> p. 268, ed. vii)
interprets this as referring to the pains of childbirth, and to the benefits both of
nursing and instruction; and believes that &lquo;a most exquisite stroke of nature&rquo; is lost
unless we perceive, by the use of &lquo;one little syllable,&mdash;<SC>Her</SC>,&rquo; that Sh. talks of the
supposed child as a Daughter, not a son. <SC>Malone</SC> very properly says that &lquo;mother's
pains&rquo; refer to maternal cares, and that &lquo;benefits&rquo; means good offices, her kind and
beneficent attention to the education of her offspring, and that &lquo;her&rquo; refers to Goneril
herself.
<P>282. <B>How sharper, &amp;c.]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: So <I>Psalms</I>, cxl, 3: &lquo;They have sharpened
their tongues like a serpent; adders' poison is under their lips.&rquo; <SC>Moberly</SC>: We
should have to go to the book of Deuteronomy to find a parallel for the concentrated
force of this curse. Can it be Lear who so sternly and simply stabs to the very
inward heart of woman's blessedness, leaving his wicked daughter blasted and
scathed for ever by his withering words?

<CC><P>only of the current month in which Lear has been staying with Albany and Goneril,
and that he may have already taken up his abode many times alternately with both
of his daughters; or else, these words might have reference to a <I>future</I> period, at
the end of which such a number of his knights were to be dismissed. Some such
explanations as these Eccles deems necessary in order to avoid the absurdity of sup-
posing that the news of Lear's brutal treatment could have reached Cordelia, and
that she could have invaded England with a large army within a fortnight after her
dismissal from her father's presence. [See Appendix, Daniel's <I>Time-Analysis</I>, p. 410.]

<CC><P>300. <B>comfortable]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 98): This word, and in like manner <I>uncom-
fortable</I> and <I>discomfortable</I>, are uniformly applied to a person, or to a thing per-
sonified, the idea of will and purpose being always implied in them. [See also
<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 183); <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 3; <I>Ham.</I> I, i, 57; <I>Macb.</I> II, i, 36; <I>Rom. &amp;

Service: &lquo;The most comfortable sacrament of the body and blood of Christ.&rquo;

<I>Ham.</I> I, ii, 242. [See also <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 463.]
<P>305. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: Observe the baffled endeavor of Goneril to act on the fears of
Albany, and yet his passiveness, his <I>inertia;</I> he is not convinced, and yet he is afraid
of looking into the thing. Such characters always yield to those who will take the
trouble of governing them, or for them. Perhaps the influence of a princess, whose
choice of him had royalized his state, may be some little excuse for Albany's
weakness.

occasionally to have used &lquo;more&rquo; as a dissyllable. [See V, iii, 169.]
<P>336. <B>milky gentleness and course]</B> <SC>Schmidt</SC>: That is, this milky gentleness

absence of an unaccented syllable, additional stress being laid on the monosyllable.

have done, including the conservative Dyce?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]</CC>

<CC><P>338. <B>at task]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: It is a common phrase now with parents and gover-
nesses: &lquo;I'll take you to task,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> I will reprehend and correct you. To be &lquo;at
task,&rquo; therefore, is to be liable to reprehension and correction. <SC>Mason</SC>: Frequently
used by Sh. in the sense of <I>tax.</I> <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): May we not speculate that after
all the poet's word was <I>attack'd?</I> <SC>Halliwell</SC>: My copies of Q<SUB>1</SUB> and Q<SUB>2</SUB> both
read <I>alapt. Attask'd</I>, that is, taxed. If the word <I>alapt</I> be correct, it probably
agrees with the context if explained in the same way as <I>attask'd;</I> and the term
<I>alapat</I>, in the following passage, seems used in a similar sense: &lquo;And because the
secret and privy boosome vices of nature are most offensive, and though least seene,
yet most undermining enemies, you must redouble your endeavor, not with a wand
to <I>alapat</I> and strike them, onely as lovers, loath to hurt, so as like a snake they may
growe together, and gette greater strength againe.&rquo;&mdash;Melton's <I>Sixe-fold Politician</I>,
p. 125. [Collier (<I>Poet. Decameron</I>, ii, 305) thinks that this <I>Sixe-fold Politician</I>
was written not by Melton, but by John Milton, the poet's father.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Abbott</SC>,
&sect; 437: <I>At-</I> perhaps represents the Old English intensive prefix &lquo;of,&rquo; which is some-
times changed into &lquo;an-,&rquo; &lquo;on-,&rquo; or &lquo;a-.&rquo; But the word [&lquo;attask'd&rquo; of Q<SUB>1</SUB>] is more
probably a sort of imitation of the similar words, &lquo;attach&rquo; and &lquo;attack.&rquo; <SC>Moberly</SC>:
Both &lquo;task&rquo; and &lquo;tax&rquo; are really the same, as we may see from Wedgwood's quota-
tion: &lquo;Every ploughland was tasked at three shillings.&rquo; <SC>Cambridge Editors</SC>: In
the imperfect copy of Q<SUB>2</SUB> [<I>i. e.</I> Q<SUB>1</SUB>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] in the British Museum, &lquo;attaskt for&rquo; was
the original reading, but the first two letters of the word have been erased. In
II, i, 123, &lquo;lest,&rquo; the original reading, has been altered to &lquo;best.&rquo; [As <SC>Schmidt</SC>
says, there is no reason why <I>attask'd</I> of Q<SUB>1</SUB> should be preferred to the Folio. Dr
Johnson's explanation, if any be needed, is ample.]

Lear is so pathetically remembering; the sisters tell us in their cruellest moments; it
mingles with the midnight storm a sigh of the daughterhood that was repulsed. In
the pining of the Fool we detect it. Through every wail or gust of this awful sym-
phony of madness. ingratitude, and irony, we feel a woman's breath.</CC>

<P>34. <B>seven stars]</B> Both <SC>Delius</SC> and <SC>Wright</SC> refer this phrase to the Pleiades, a
constellation which assuredly is known by the name of The Seven Stars; may it not,
however, refer to the Great Bear, whose seven stars are the most conspicuous group
in the circle of perpetual apparition in the Northern Hemisphere?&mdash;so conspicuous,
indeed, that the Latin word for &lquo;North&rquo; was derived from them. We call this con-
stellation &lquo;The Dipper,&rquo; from its fancied resemblance to the utensil of that name; a
name, I believe, scarcely known in England.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

in the train of thought suggested by Steevens. <SC>Wright</SC> also agrees with Johnson's
interpretation, as more in keeping with what Lear says in line 31: &lquo;I will forget my

<CC><P>43. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: The deepest tragic notes are often struck by a half sense of an
impending blow.
<P>43. <B>mad]</B> <SC>Bucknill</SC> (p. 183): This self-consciousness of gathering madness is
common in various forms of the disease. . . . A most remarkable instance of this was
presented in the case of a patient, whose passionate, but generous, temper became
morbidly exaggerated after a blow upon the head. His constantly expressed fear
was that of impending madness; and when the calamity he so much dreaded had
actually arrived, and he raved incessantly and incoherently, one frequently heard the
very words of Lear proceeding from his lips: &lquo;Oh, let me not be mad!&rquo;
<P>48, 49. <SC>Eccles</SC>: This concluding rhyme seems to intimate that the Fool expects
to return soon, because of the ill treatment which he will probably receive where he
is going. <SC>Steevens</SC>: This idle couplet is apparently addressed to the females present
at the performance of the play; and, not improbably, crept into the playhouse copy
from the mouth of some buffoon actor, who &lquo;spoke more than was set down for him.&rquo;
It should seem, from Shakespeare's speaking in this strong manner, that he suffered
the injury he describes. Indecent jokes, which the applause of the groundlings
might occasion to be repeated, would at last find their way into the prompters' books,
&amp;c. I am aware that such liberties were exercised by the authors of <I>Locrine</I>, &amp;c,
but can such another offensive and extraneous address to the audience be pointed out
among all the dramas of Shakespeare? <SC>Coleridge</SC>: The Fool's conclusion of this
Act, by a grotesque prattling, seems to indicate the dislocation of feeling that has
begun and is to be continued. C. A. <SC>Brown</SC> (p. 292): There are three passages,
foisted in by the players, and adopted by the printers, which ought to be for ever
expunged from the text: The couplet at the end of Act I; the whole of Merlin's
prophecy, III, ii, 79-95, as the Fool should go out with Lear, and those brutal words:
&lquo;And I'll go to bed at noon,&rquo; III, vi, 83, when the old king sinks into sleep. Such
contradictions puzzled me for a long time, till looking among the <I>Annotations</I>, a
profitable task once in a hundred times, I discovered that none of these three pas-
sages are in the Qq, printed eight years before Shakespeare's death. but are intro-</CC>

<CC><P>26. <B>Upon his party]</B> <SC>Delius</SC> was the first to interpret rightly these two ques-
tions of Edmund's. In order to confuse his brother and urge him to a more speedy
flight, by giving him the idea that he is surrounded by perils, Edmund asks Edgar first,
whether he has not spoken 'gainst the Duke of Cornwall, and then, reversing the
question, asks whether he has not said something on the side of Cornwall 'gainst the
Duke of Albany. <SC>Schmidt</SC> gives seven instances, besides the present, where &lquo;upon
the party&rquo; means &lquo;upon the side of.&rquo; Before Delius, <SC>Hanmer's</SC> interpretation ob-
tained, by which line 26 was regarded as only another way of putting the same
question as that in line 23; thus: Have you said nothing upon the party formed
by him against the Duke of Albany? <SC>Capell</SC> added that we must supply the word
&lquo;reflecting&rquo; before &lquo;upon.&rquo; The passage so puzzled <SC>Johnson</SC> that he believed it to
be corrupt, and proposed the reading: <I>Against</I> his party, <I>for</I> the Duke of Albany?
<SC>Eccles</SC> noted how Edmund grasped at every motive, however trivial or insignificant,
that would enforce Edgar's departure. <SC>Moberly</SC> gives an ingenious interpretation
of this second question of Edmund's: the war being only &lquo;toward,&rquo; and having not
yet broken out, &lquo;Albany would be in a position to demand the punishment of any one
who spoke against him, and Cornwall not unlikely to concede it, as Elizabeth might
have done, if his warlike preparations were not sufficiently advanced to make it safe
to throw down the gauntlet.&rquo;
<P>27. <B>Advise]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Consider, recollect yourself. <SC>Wright</SC>: See 1 <I>Chron.</I>
xxi, 12: &lquo;Now, therefore, advise thyself what word I shall bring again to him that
sent me.&rquo;
<P>31. <B>Yield . . . father]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: Edmund speaks these words loud so as to be
heard outside.</CC>

<CC><P>55. <B>gasted]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: Frightened. Steevens quotes from Beau. and Fl. <I>Wit at
Several Weapons</I>, II, iii, but the word there in the original copies is &lquo;gaster'd&rquo;:
&lquo;Either the sight of the Lady has gaster'd him, or else he's drunk.&rquo; This is still an
Essex word. &lquo;Gast&rquo; as a participle occurs in <I>Cursor Mundi</I> (MS Trin. Coll. Cam-
bridge, fol. 31, quoted in Halliwell's <I>Dict.</I>), p. 291 (E. E. Text Soc., ed. Morris):
&lquo;His wille was but to make hem gast.&rquo; The other three printed texts of the poem
have &lquo;agast,&rquo; &lquo;agaste,&rquo; and &lquo;a-gast.&rquo; Sh. uses &lquo;gastness&rquo; in the sense of terror-stricken
look in <I>Oth.</I> V, i, 106: &lquo;Do you perceive the gastness of her eye?&rquo; And Spenser
has &lquo;gastfull&rquo; in the sense of &lquo;awful&rquo; in <I>Shepherd's Calendar</I>, August, 170: &lquo;Here
will I dwell apart In gastfull grove therefore.&rquo; Both these last-mentioned words
appear to have been used as if they were etymologically connected with &lquo;ghost.&rquo;
For this derivation there is no foundation. Cotgrave gives, &lquo;Espoventable: com.
Dreadfull, frightfull, fearefull; horrible, gastfull, horride.&rquo; The form &lquo;gaster&rquo; is
found in Harsnet's <I>Declaration of Popish Imposture</I> (1603), p. 73: &lquo;Did euer the God-
gastring Giants, whom <I>Iupiter</I> overwhelmed with <I>Pelion</I> and <I>Ossa</I>, so complaine
of theyr loade?&rquo; Mr Skeat has pointed out to me an excellent example of &lquo;gast&rquo; in
<I>The Vision of Piers Plowman</I>, Text A, Passus vii, l, 129: &dot; Bo<01>e to sowen and to
setten &dot; and saued his til<01>e, Gaste Crowen from his Corn &dot; and kepen his Beestes.&rquo;

<CC><P>73. <B>suggestion]</B> <SC>Nares</SC>: Temptation, seduction. <SC>Hunter</SC> (Note on <I>Macb.</I> I,
iii, 134): &lquo;Suggestion&rquo; is a theological word, one of the three &lquo;procurators or tempters&rquo;
of sin. <I>Delight</I> and <I>Consent</I> being the others.
<P>73. <B>practice]</B> <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii.): The accent seems to show that <I>pretence</I> of the
Qq is not the right word, unless we read &lquo;<I>damn'd</I> pretence.&rquo; <SC>Wright</SC>: &lquo;Practice&rquo;
is more in keeping with &lquo;plot&rquo; and &lquo;suggestion.&rquo;
<P>75. <B>not thought]</B> For instances of the omission of the auxiliary in negative sen-
tences, or for the transposition of the negative, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 305.
<P>75. <B>death]</B> <SC>Moberly</SC>: This skilful suggestion, that Edmund should be put into
Edgar's place, is acted upon at once by Gloucester; yet it is so indirect that Glou-
cester imagines the thought to have come from himself. Lord Bacon, in his essay
on <I>Cunning</I>, speaks of the trick of &lquo;turning cat in pan;&rquo; that is, making a suggestion
in such a way that the hearer supposes it to be his own. This may be done either
coarsely&mdash;&lquo;as you said, and wisely was it said,&rquo; was Polonius's way of impressing his
own thoughts on the king&mdash;or, in a more skilful way, as here.&rquo;
<P>76. <B>pregnant]</B> In <I>Meas. for Meas.</I> I, i, 12, <SC>Johnson</SC> first defined this word by
&lquo;ready,&rquo; and this definition has been adopted as its general meaning in Sh. down to
the present day; certainly it is generally thus interpreted in the present passage.
<SC>Wright</SC> goes so far as to say that it &lquo;is used by Sh., without any reference to its
literal meaning, in the sense of &ldquo;ready;&rdquo;&rquo; he afterwards defines it as &lquo;manifest,
obvious,&rquo; in certain passages which he cites. <SC>Schmidt</SC> gives no intimation that it is
used in its &lquo;literal meaning;&rquo; the fourteen instances of its use that he cites he divides
under three heads: 1st, expert, clever, ingenious, artful; 2d, disposed, ready, prompt
(under this head the present passage is cited); 3d, probable in the highest degree,
clear, evident. Now, on the other hand, I cannot but think that <SC>Nares</SC> came nearer
the truth when he said that the ruling sense of this word is that of &lquo;being full or pro-
ductive of something.&rquo; Out of Schmidt's fourteen instances eleven appear to me to
come under Nares's definition. Three instances (<I>Lear</I> IV, vi, 222; <I>Wint. Tale</I>, V,
ii, 34; and <I>Ant. and Cleop.</I> II, i, 45) are used in so metaphorical a sense that one
may give to them almost any meaning that his mother wit suggests as applicable to
the passage. My interpretation of the &lquo;pregnant hinges of the knee&rquo; in <I>Ham.</I> III,
ii, 56, is there recorded; the present passage seems to me exactly parallel, and may
be paraphrased thus: &lquo;So great are the profits of my death that the spurs to make
thee seek it are most powerful, and <I>teem with incitements</I> thereto.&rquo; <SC>Schmidt</SC> in
his edition repeats his definitions of &lquo;pregnant,&rquo; and doubts if, thus defined, Sh. ever
could have applied it to &lquo;spurs,&rquo; and, while faithful to the Folio, confesses that <I>spirits</I>
form but a poor predicate to &lquo;profits,&rquo; yet in the sense of <I>evil spirits</I> that it is at least
as probable a reading as &lquo;spurs.&rquo; In my opinion the reading of the Folio is a mis-
print for &lquo;spurs&rquo; of the Quarto. &lquo;Pregnant&rquo; is quite as appropriate to &lquo;spurs&rquo; as to
&lquo;hinges.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC></CC>

<CC><P>89. <B>dost]</B> The fact that Regan at no other time addresses Gloucester in the second
person makes me think that we should here read: &lquo;How does my lord?&rquo; For the
omission of the nominative after &lquo;dost,&rquo; see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect;&sect; 241, 399, 400.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>91. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: Compare Regan's &lquo;did <I>my father's</I> godson seek your life? He
whom <I>my father</I> named?&rquo; with the unfeminine violence of her &lquo;All vengeance
comes too short,&rquo; &amp;c., and yet no reference to the guilt, but only to the accident,
which she uses as an occasion for sneering at her father. Regan is not, in fact, a
greater monster than Goneril, but she has the power of casting more venom.
<P>92. This line <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 478, scans in two ways: First, by pronouncing the last
syllable in it &lquo;with a kind of &ldquo;burr,&rdquo; which produced the effect of an additional
syllable;&rquo; and as he cites &lquo;sirrah&rquo; as an instance of this &lquo;burr,&rquo; the best way, prob-
ably, of conveying his idea in spelling would be &lquo;Ed-garrah.&rquo; Or, secondly, <SC>Abbott</SC>
queries whether it might not be scanned by pronouncing &lquo;your&rquo; <I>dissolut&eacute;</I>, thus:
&lquo;na&verbar;med? you&verbar;r Edgar?&rquo; Of these two methods, the latter seems preferable.
<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 145) suggests, in his chapter on the omission of repeated words,
that Gloucester says: &lquo;O! O lady,&rquo; and that the first &lquo;O!&rquo; which closed this line had
been omitted. <SC>Lettsom</SC>, in a foot-note, queries &lquo;&ldquo;your Edgar, <I>Gloster?</I>&rdquo; <I>Gloster</I>
may have been left out at the end of the line in consequence of <I>Glo.</I> occurring at
the beginning of the next.&rquo; For <SC>Collier's</SC> (MS) emendation, see Textual Notes;
<SC>Moberly</SC>, referring to this emendation, says: &lquo;Probably the intense tone of astonish-
ment would give a prolonging accentuation to several of the syllables as the line
stands, and make it in reality long enough without the addition. If the reading,
however, was invented, its inventor had a good notion of the way in which conso-
nants fall out of the body of a word. There would be the same kind of identity
between &lquo;heir&rquo; and &lquo;Edgar&rquo; as between &lquo;Audrey&rquo; and &lquo;Ethelreda,&rquo; &lquo;Maude&rquo; and
&lquo;Matilda;&rquo; and his theory would be that, from the similarity of the two words, one
had got dropped.&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>early in the scene, calls it still night. Towards the close of it he wishes Gloucester
<I>good morrow</I>, and immediately after calls on the <I>sun</I> to shine that he may read a
letter. <SC>Delius</SC>: It is night, and as, in Sh., that time of day which is approaching
is given by way of greeting, and not that which is then present, Oswald wishes
Kent, whom he does not recognize in the dark, a good dawning.
<P>5. <B>if thou lovest me]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: A conventional phrase before a question or re-
quest, but which Kent here takes literally.
<P>8. <B>Lipsbury pinfold]</B> What <SC>Capell</SC> said a hundred years ago is still true: &lquo;It
is not come to knowledge, where that Lipsbury is,&rquo; but what he adds is question-
able: &lquo;This we may know, and with certainty, that it was some village or other,
fam'd for boxing; that the boxers fought in a ring or enclos'd circle, and that this
ring was call'd&mdash;&ldquo;Lipsbury pinfold.&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Farmer</SC> suggests that it may be a cant
phrase with some corruption, taken from a place where the fines were arbitrary.
<SC>Steevens</SC> surmised that it might import the same as <I>Lob's Pound;</I> with which it
seems to have no more connection than that &lquo;pinfold&rquo; means &lquo;Pound&rquo; and &lquo;Lob&rquo;
and &lquo;Lipsbury&rquo; begin with the same letter. &lquo;Lob's Pound,&rquo; as is well known, means
a place of confinement, whether a prison or the stocks. <SC>Nares's</SC> guess is perhaps
as happy as any: &lquo;It may be,&rquo; he says, &lquo;a coined name, and it is just possible that it
might mean the teeth, as being the pinfold within the <I>lips.</I>&rquo; <SC>Collier's</SC> MS gives <I>Fins-
bury</I>, where, says that editor, there must have been a pinfold, well known to Shake-
speare's audiences; and this word, through mishearing or misprinting, was corrupted
to &lquo;Lipsbury.&rquo; <SC>Halliwell</SC> simply cites Nares; and <SC>Dyce</SC> says merely: &lquo;A <I>pinfold</I>
is a pound; but what the commentators have written about the name <I>Lipsbury</I> is too
unsatisfactory to be cited.&rquo; <SC>Wright</SC> thinks Nares's explanation the most probable
which has yet been given, and adds: Similar names of places, which may or may
not have any local existence, occur in proverbial phrases, such, for instance, as
&lquo;Needham's Shore,&rquo; &lquo;Weeping Cross.&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>14. <B>three-suited]</B> <SC>Farmer</SC>: This should be <I>third-suited</I>, wearing clothes at
third hand. <SC>Steevens</SC>: This might mean, one who had no greater change of rai-
ment than three suits would furnish him with. So in Jonson's <I>Silent Woman</I> [IV, ii,
p. 447, ed. Gifford]: &lquo;thou wert a pitiful poor fellow,. . . and hadst nothing but three
suits of apparel;&rquo; or it may signify a fellow <I>thrice-sued</I> at law, who has <I>three suits</I>
for debt standing out against him. <SC>Delius</SC>: This cannot refer to his poverty, but,
rather, like &lquo;glass-gazing,&rquo; signifies foppishness, changing his suits that many times,
or else wearing them all at the same time. When Edgar describes his former
wealthy state, he says of himself [III, iv, 129], &lquo;who hath had three suits to his
back.&rquo; <SC>Wright</SC>: If the terms of agreement between master and servant in
Shakespeare's time were known, they would probably throw light upon the phrase.
It is probable that three suits of clothes a year were part of a servant's allowance.
In Jonson's <I>Silent Woman</I>, III, i, Mrs Otter, scolding her husband, whom she treats
as a dependant, says, &lquo;Who gives you your maintenance, I pray you? Who allows
you your horse-meat and man's-meat, your three suits of apparel a year? your four
pair of stockings, one silk, three worsted?&rquo; [According to the <SC>Cambridge Editors</SC>,
&lquo;Q<SUB>2</SUB>, Bodl. 1,&rquo; has the misprint <I>snyted</I>, which is corrected in the other Qq to <I>shewted.</I>
From this circumstance, <SC>Wright</SC> inferred not only that the enumeration of the Qq in
the Cam. ed. was wrong, and that what he and his fellow-editor had there called Q<SUB>2</SUB>
was in reality the earliest impression of all, but that &lquo;suit&rquo; in Shakespeare's day was
pronounced <I>shoot.</I> He supposes that while the &lquo;edition was in course of printing the
error, <I>snyted</I>, was discovered, and the correction communicated verbally to the com-
positor, who inserted it according to his own notions of spelling.&rquo;&mdash;Ellis's <I>E. E. Pro-
nunciation</I>, p. 217. This hypothesis (which is certainly as old as Steevens), in regard
to the pronunciation of <I>suit</I>, Wright thinks is strengthened by the puns on <I>suitor</I> and
<I>shooter</I> in <I>Love's Lab. Lost</I>, IV, i, 109, &amp;c., and also in Rowley's <I>Match in the Dark</I>
(1633), II, i; but <SC>Ellis</SC> (p. 217) doubts whether these instances are enough to decide
the point with certainty. &lquo;Hurried corrections, whether of print or manuscript, fre-
quently introduce additional errors, and hence there is no guarantee that the compositor
who substituted <I>shewted</I> for <I>snyted</I> did not himself put <I>shewted</I> when he meant to have
inserted <I>sewted</I>,&rquo; &lquo;which would be a legitimate orthography for <I>suited.</I>&rquo; &lquo;In the present
day we have a joke of an Irish shopman telling his customer to <I>shoot</I> himself, meaning
<I>suit</I> himself. The Irish pronunciation, however, only shows an English pronuncia-
tion of the XVIIth century. In England at the present day, <I>shoot</I> for <I>suit</I> would be
vulgar, but the joke would be readily understood, though few persons use, or have
even heard, the pronunciation. Might not this have been the case in Shakespeare's
time? At any rate, there is no authority for supposing that such a pronunciation
could have been used seriously by Sh. himself.&rquo; In his essay on <I>English Pronun-
ciation in the Elizabethan Era</I> (<I>Sh. Works</I>, xii, p. 430), <SC>White</SC> says: &lquo;<I>S</I> before a
vowel had often the sound of <I>sh</I>, as it now has in <I>sugar</I> and <I>sure.</I> Such was its
sound in <I>sue, suit</I>, and its compounds, and I believe in <I>super</I> and its compounds, and
in <I>supine</I> and <I>supreme. . . . S</I> was also sometimes aspirated before <I>o</I> and <I>i;</I> of which,
and of the <I>o</I> sound of <I>ew</I>, see phonographic evidence in the pronunciation of <I>sewer</I>,</CC>

<P>15. <B>worsted-stocking]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: The stockings in England in the reign of
Queen Elizabeth were remarkably expensive, and scarce any other kind than silk
were worn, even, as says Stubbes in his <I>Anatomie of Abuses</I> [p. 57, ed. Furnivall],
by those who had not above forty shillings a year wages. So in Tailor's <I>The Hog hath
Lost his Pearl</I> [I. i]: &lquo;Good parts, without habiliments of gallantry, are no more set
by in these times than a good leg in a woollen stocking.&rquo; Again in Beau. and Fl.'s
<I>The Captain</I> [III, iii]: &lquo;serving-men with &mdash; woollen stockings.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: See
also Middleton's <I>Ph&oelig;ix</I> [IV, ii, p. 389, ed. Dyce]: &lquo;Metreza Auriola keeps her
love with half the cost I am at: her friend can go a' foot like a good husband, walk
in worsted stockings, and inquire for the six-penny ordinary.&rquo;
<P>15. <B>lily-livered]</B> See <I>Macb.</I> V, iii, 15. <SC>Wright</SC>: Compare 2 <I>Hen. IV:</I> IV,
iii, 111: &lquo;The second property of your excellent sherris is, the warming of the blood;
which, before cold and settled, left the liver white and pale, which is the badge of
pusillanimity and cowardice.&rquo;
<P>15. <B>action-taking]</B> <SC>Mason</SC>: A fellow who, if you beat him, would bring an
action for the assault, instead of resenting it like a man of courage.
<P>16. <B>glass-gazing]</B> <SC>Eccles</SC>: One who wastes his time in gazing at his own person
in a looking-glass.

<P>29. <B>sop o' th' moonshine]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: A ludicrous phrase, importing that he
would lay [Oswald] upon his back on the earth, like a &lquo;sop&rquo; in a dripping-pan, for
the moonbeams to baste him. <SC>Farmer</SC>: Perhaps here an equivoque wa<*> intended.
In <I>The Old Shepherd's Kalendar</I>, among the dishes recommended for Prymetyne,
&lquo;One is egges in moneshine.&rquo; <SC>Nares</SC>: This probably alludes to some dish so called.
There was a way of dressing eggs, called &lquo;eggs in moonshine.&rquo; [Nares here
gives a receipt from May's <I>Accompl. Cook</I>, p. 437, to which I refer the enthusiastic
student. It is sufficient to say that the eggs are fried in &lquo;oyl or butter,&rquo; covered with
slices of onions and seasoned with verjuice, nutmeg and salt; to be eaten with
what appetite you may. A simpler receipt is given in <I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 4th S., xii, 19 July,
1873; and, in the same volume, on p. 84, <SC>Royle Entwisle</SC> says that Nares's
explanation is &lquo;as constrained and shallow as his resort to a cookery-book&rquo; &lquo;is
ridiculous and unnecessary; and it was evidently arrived at without a thought being
expended on Shakespeare's ideal knowledge of the orb of night, as revealed in his
other allusions to it, notably in <I>Macb.</I> III, v, 23, 24.&rquo; &lquo;Plainly, Kent's intention is
to make a &ldquo;sop&rdquo; of him in the sense of <I>steeping</I> him, in his own blood, by the con-
senting light of the moon.&rquo;]
