<P>37. <B>neat]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>, who defines this by &lquo;you mere slave, you very slave,&rquo; comes
nearer to the true meaning, I think, than <SC>Steevens</SC>, although the latter has been fol-
lowed by <SC>Dyce, Schmidt, Wright</SC>, and <SC>Moberly. Steevens</SC> thinks that &lquo;it means
no more than you finical rascal, you are an assemblage of foppery and poverty.&rquo;
Then, by way of proof, Steevens cites Jonson in <I>The Poetaster</I> [IV, i]: &lquo;By thy
leave, my neat scoundrel.&rquo; But we must remember that this is spoken by Tucca, a
blustering captain, whose speech is full of absurd epithets, and that it is addressed
to Gallus, who, we know, is not a &lquo;scoundrel,&rquo; and are not led to suppose that he is
&lquo;neat&rquo; in the sense of finical. On the contrary, it is more likely that Tucca uses
&lquo;neat&rquo; in the sense which <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 352) ascribes to it here, viz: that of
<I>pure, unmixed;</I> still used in the phrase <I>neat wine</I>, &amp;c. <SC>Singer</SC> suggests that it may
mean &lquo;you base cowherd.&rquo; <SC>Staunton</SC> has the following note: &lquo;The sting in this
epithet has been quite misunderstood by the commentators, who suppose it to
mean <I>mere</I> or <I>finical.</I> For the real allusion, see <I>Wint. Tale</I>, I, ii, 123: &ldquo;We
must be neat; not neat, but cleanly, captain, And yet the steer, the heifer, and the calf,
Are all call'd neat.&rdquo; See also Taylor the Water Poet's <I>Epigram on the Husband of
Mrs Parnell:</I> &ldquo;Neate can he talke, and feede, and neatly tread, Neate are his feete, but
most neate is his head.&rdquo;&rquo; But, as <SC>Wright</SC> says, this play on the word &lquo;neat&rquo; would
have no especial point as addressed to Oswald. Walker's interpretation is, I think,
the true one. <SC>Rushton</SC> (<I>Sh. Illust. by Old Authors</I>, p. 63): &lquo;Because Leontes in
<I>Wint. Tale</I> uses the word &lquo;neat&rquo; in a sense implying the uncleanliness which is
common to cattle, or those who tend them, therefore I have thought it probable that</CC>

<P>40. <B>Parting them]</B> <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks</I>, &amp;c. p. 225): <I>Part</I> of the Ff is undoubtedly
a stage-direction. This is clear from its interfering with the dialogue: Edmund
asks &lquo;What's the matter?&rquo; and Kent immediately replies, &lquo;With you [<I>i. e.</I> &lquo;the matter
is with you, I will deal with you&rquo;], goodman boy,&rquo; &amp;c. That such a stage-direction
is common in old plays, hardly perhaps requires to be shown; one instance, however,
may be given: &lquo;<I>Rich.</I> Art thou content to breath? [<I>Fight &amp;</I> part <I>once or twise.</I>&rquo;&mdash;
<I>A Pleasant Commodie, called Looke about you</I>, 1600. <SC>Schmidt</SC> maintains that &lquo;With
you&rquo; in Kent's reply does not refer to &lquo;What's the matter,&rquo; but to <I>Part</I> of the Folio,
which is legitimately a portion of the text and no stage-direction. &lquo;<I>Part</I> in Sh. means
not only to <I>separate</I>, but also to <I>go away, to depart.</I> Edmund means it in the former
sense, and Kent understands in the latter, and asks &ldquo;With you?&rdquo; That Sh., in spite
of a possible misapprehension, uses <I>to part with</I> in the sense of <I>to go away with</I> some-
thing, a passage in <I>Com. of Err.</I> III, i, 66, proves: &ldquo;<I>Ang.</I> Here is neither cheer, sir,
nor welcome: we would fain have either. <I>Bal.</I> In debating which was best we shall
part with neither.&rdquo;&rquo; [This is very ingenious, but, I fear, not convincing.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<CC><P>V, ii, 307, and in Jonson's <I>Cynthia's Revels</I>, V, ii (p. 327, ed. Gifford, 1816), adopted
it here, and, deriving it from the Latin <I>intrinsecus</I>, ingeniously paraphrased it by
&lquo;inward, hidden, perplext, as a knot hard to be unravelled.&rquo; <SC>Upton</SC> (p. 363)
was the first to discover the modern reading under the disguise of the Ff, and,
believing it to be a shorter form of <I>intrinsecate</I>, cited, as a parallel elision, &lquo;reverbs&rquo;
for <I>reverberate</I> in I, i, 145. <SC>Malone</SC> added &lquo;attent&rquo; for <I>attentive</I> in <I>Ham.</I> I, ii, 193,

are Too,&rquo; &amp;c. &lquo;The word &lquo;<I>intrinsicate</I>,&rquo; he adds, &lquo;was but newly introduced into
our language when this play was written. See Marston's <I>Scourge of Villanie</I> [vol.
iii, p. 245, ed. Halliwell]: &ldquo;new-minted epithets (as reall, intrinsecate Delphicke).&rdquo;&rquo;

<P>70. <B>smooth]</B> Flatter; see <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> III, ii, 98, and notes.
<P>71. <B>rebel]</B> This may be either the plural by attraction (by the word &lquo;lords&rquo;), as

<I>Rights</I> reneg'd) Against the <I>Truth</I> and <I>Thee, un-holy Leagu'd.</I>&rquo; [As an additional
proof that the <I>g</I> is pronounced hard, <SC>Dyce</SC> calls attention to the spelling in the Qq.
The word (with <I>g</I> hard) is still common enough among whist-players, in the sense

<P>73. <B>halcyon]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: This is the king-fisher. The vulgar opinion was that
this bird, if hung up, would <I>vary</I> with the wind, and by that means show from what
point it blew. So, in Marlowe's <I>Jew of Malta</I>, I, i: &lquo;But how now stands the
wind? Into what corner peers my halcyon's bill?&rquo; Again, in Storer's <I>Life and
Death of Thomas Wolsey, Cardinall</I>, a poem, 1599: &lquo;Or as a halcyon with her
turning breast, Demonstrates wind from wind, and east from west.&rquo; Again, in <I>The
Tenth Booke of Notable Things</I>, by Thomas Lupton, &lquo;A lytle byrde called the
Kings Fysher, being hanged up in the ayre by the neck, his nebbe or byll wyll be
alwayes dyrect or strayght against ye winde.&rquo; [In Peck's <I>New Memoirs of Milton</I>,
1740, p. 251, an extract is given from Sir Thomas Browne, in which the truth of this
&lquo;conceit&rquo; is disproved by &lquo;<I>reason</I>&rquo; and &lquo;<I>experience.</I>&rquo; By reason, because &lquo;it seemeth
very repugnant that a carcase or body disanimated should be so affected with every
wind as to carry a conformable respect and constant habitude thereto.&rquo; By experience,
because &lquo;if a single kings-fisher be hanged up with untwisted silk in an open roome,</CC>

a &lquo;visage distorted by grinning.&rquo;
<P>77. <B>smile]</B> The reading of all the Qq and Ff (except F<SUB>4</SUB>) is so uniform, that
it is hard not to believe that there is some corruption here, especially since, as
<SC>Wright</SC> says, &lquo;Sh. uses &ldquo;smile&rdquo; more than once with a direct object, but never in
this sense.&rquo; If the word here be really &lquo;smile,&rquo; it is difficult to understand why so
plain a word should have been persistently misspelled. It is spelled correctly in all
the Qq and Ff in the last line of this very scene. <SC>Collier's</SC> (MS) corrects to
&lquo;smile <I>at</I>,&rquo; and <SC>Keightley</SC> reads &lquo;smile you <I>at.</I>&rquo; If the present text be right it
comes under <SC>Abbott's</SC> &sect; 200, where instances are given of the omission of prepo-
sitions after some verbs which can be regarded as transitive, as in &lquo;Thou swear'st
thy gods,&rquo; I, i, 163.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>77. <B>as]</B> Equivalent to <I>as if.</I> For similar instances, see <I>Ham.</I> I, ii, 217; II, i,
91; III, iv, 135; IV, v, 99.

<CC><P>the place where the romances say King Arthur kept his court; so this alludes to
some proverbial speech in those romances. <SC>Steevens</SC>: Thus in Drayton's <I>Polyol-
bion, The Third Song</I> [p. 252, ed. 1748]: &lquo;Like Camelot, what place was ever yet

two places mentioned in this extract from Drayton, Camelot and Caerleon, there was
a third place, Winchester, &lquo;where,&rquo; as <SC>Selden</SC> says in his <I>Illustrations</I> to Drayton's
<I>Fourth Song</I>, p. 259, &lquo;Arthur's table is yet suppos'd to be, but that seems of later

was Winchester, and thence he inferred that the allusion in the text is to a &lquo;Win-

I, iii, 53 and <I>Tro. &amp; Cres.</I> V, x, 55. According to Selden, in another note on
p. 254: &lquo;By South-cadbury is that Camelot; a hill of a mile compass at the top,

different localities of Arthur's Round Table by showing that &lquo;<I>The History of King

finished the printing of the <I>Mort d'Arthur</I> in 1485, he says of the hero: &ldquo;And
yet of record remain, in witness of him in Wales, in the town of Camelot, the great
stones,&rdquo;&rquo; &amp;c. Staunton thinks it unnecessary to imagine with Warburton that there
is any allusion to a proverbial saying in the old romances, but concludes with the
following explanation of the present passage: &lquo;In chapter xlix of Arthur's History
the Quest of the White Hart is undertaken by three knights, at the wedding-feast of
the king with the princess Guenever, which was held at Camelot. This adventure
was encountered by Sir Gawayne, Sir Tor, and King Pellinore, and, whenever they
had overcome the knights whom they engaged, the vanquished combatants were always
sent &ldquo;unto King Arthur, and yielded them unto his grace.&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>) thinks
that there is here perhaps a double allusion, to the geese of Somersetshire, and to
vanquished knights; thus both Hanmer and Staunton are right. <SC>Halliwell</SC> does
not believe that there is in the text &lquo;the slightest allusion to the birds called geese,
excepting of course a metaphorical one.&rquo; It is doubtful whether a knowledge of the
exact location of Camelot, upon which Staunton and others lay stress, would throw
much light on this obscure passage.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]</CC>

<CC><P>92. <B>garb]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Forces his <I>outside</I>, or his <I>appearance</I>, to something totally

<P>118. <B>fleshment]</B> <SC>Henley</SC>: A young soldier is said to <I>flesh</I> his sword the first

to the first act of service, which Kent, in his new capacity, had performed for his
master; and, at the same time, in a sarcastic sense, as though he had esteemed it an
heroic exploit to trip a man behind that was actually falling.</CC>

<CC><P>131. <SC>Cowden Clarke</SC>: Very artfully is this speech thrown in. Not only does
it serve to paint the vindictive disposition of Regan, it also serves to regulate dra-
matic time by making the subsequent scene where Lear arrives before Gloucester's
castle and finds his faithful messenger in the stocks, appear sufficiently advanced in
the morning to allow of that same scene closing with the actual approach of &lquo;night,&rquo;
without disturbing the sense of probability. Sh. makes a whole day pass before our
eyes during a single scene and dialogue, yet all seems consistent and natural in the
course of progression.
<P>135. <B>bring away]</B> <SC>Schmidt</SC>: Sh. frequently uses &lquo;bring away&rquo; and &lquo;come
away&rquo; as equivalent to &lquo;bring here&rquo; and &lquo;come here.&rquo; As in the well-known song,
&lquo;Come away, come away, death.&rquo;
<P>135. <B>Stocks brought out]</B> <SC>Dyce</SC>: In the Folio this stage-direction is placed
two lines earlier, and it no doubt stood so in the prompter's book, that the stocks
might be in readiness. <SC>Farmer</SC>: Formerly in great houses, as still in some col-
leges, there were moveable stocks for the correction of servants.
<P>137. <B>much]</B> For instances of this as an adjective, see <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I> 1.)</CC>

<CC><P>156. <B>common saw, &amp;c.]</B> <SC>Hanmer</SC>: An old proverbial saying applied to those
who are turned out of house and home, deprived of all the comforts of life excepting
the common benefits of the air and sun. <SC>Johnson</SC>: It was perhaps used of men
dismissed from an hospital, or house of charity, such as was erected formerly in many
places for travellers. Those houses had names properly enough alluded to by <I>heaven's
benediction.</I> <SC>Capell</SC>: This saw occurs in one capital passage of Holinshed, and is
there applied to such persons as, going about to make matters better, make them worse,
and that is Kent's application of it:&mdash;Lear, says that speaker, who thinks to mend
his condition by leaving his eldest daughter and coming to Regan, will find himself
in that person's error who foregoes the benediction of heaven for the common and
weak blessing of the warm sun; such opinion had he now entertained of Regan's
superiority in badness. [This &lquo;capital passage&rquo; from Holinshed Capell gives in his
<I>Notes</I>, vol. iii, p. 40: &lquo;This Augustine after his arrivall converted the Saxons indeede
from Paganisme, but as the Proverb sayth, bringing them out of Goddes blessing into
the warme sunne, he also imbued them wyth no lesse hurtfull supersticion then they
did knowe before.&rquo;] <SC>Tyrwhitt</SC>: This &lquo;saw&rquo; is in Heywood's <I>Dialogues on Prov-
erbs</I>, Book ii, chap. v: &lquo;In your rennying from hym to me, ye runne Out of gods
blessing into the warme sunne.&rquo; [This quotation from Heywood is given by Capell
also (<I>Notes</I>, vol. iii, p. 493), whose text I have followed.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Malone</SC>: See
also Howell's <I>Collection of English Proverbs</I>, in his Dictionary, 1660: &lquo;He goes out
of God's blessing to the warm sun, viz. from good to worse.&rquo; <SC>Wright</SC>: Compare
also Lyly's <I>Euphues and his England</I> (ed. Arber, p. 320): &lquo;Thou forsakest Gods
blessing to sit in a warm Sunne.&rquo; The proverb is reversed in the <I>Letters of Euphues</I>
(ibid. p. 196): &lquo;Therefore if thou wilt follow my aduice, and prosecute thine owne
determination, thou shalt come out of a warme Sunne into Gods blessing.&rquo; Both
<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 277) and <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>) note the use of the proverb as late as
Swift. [See <I>Ham.</I> I, ii, 67, where some notes in reference to this &lquo;saw&rquo; will be
found. I think <SC>Hunter's</SC> zeal carries him too far when he proposes the same
origin to this proverb and to Beatrice's &lquo;sunburnt&rquo; in <I>Much Ado</I>, II, i, 331. His
theory is that &lquo;the first and original use of this phrase [&lquo;sunburnt&rquo;] denoted the state
of being unmarried; thus Beatrice uses it. It then expanded so as to include the
state of those who were without family connections of any kind; thus Hamlet uses
it. It expanded still wider and included the state of those who have no home, and
thus it is used in <I>Lear.</I>&rquo; But this is mere theory, ingenious, but unsupported by
proof; no attempt is made to explain, by examples, the change of application from
unchurched women to homeless men. Moreover, Lear is not yet homeless.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]</CC>

<CC><P>161, 162. <B>Nothing . . . misery]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: Kent breaks out into a reflection,
rising from his condition,&mdash;that people born to ill-fortune, like himself,
and living
under her frown, are the only persons almost who can be said to <I>see miracles</I>, so
wonderful are the situations, sometimes, which she is pleased to reduce them to.
<SC>Hudson</SC>: I am very much in the dark as to what the text means. Of course the
literal sense is, &lquo;hardly anything but misery sees miracles;&rquo; but the question is, what
are the particulars referred to, or what are the miraculous things to be seen in this
case? and <I>why</I> is misery said to see them? I suspect that &lquo;see&rquo; is used in the sense
of <I>experience;</I> a sense it often bears. In that case the meaning may be, &lquo;miracles
are hardly ever wrought but in behalf of the wretched.&rquo; And upon this thought
Kent seems to be building a hope of better times, both for himself and the old king;
while, on the other hand, nothing short of a miraculous providence seems able to
turn their course of misfortune. <SC>Delius</SC>: That Cordelia should have thought of
him, or that her letter should have reached him, seems to him such a miracle as only
those in misery experience.

<CC><P>and amplifies Jennens's suggestion (without, however, any acknowledgement of in-
debtedness): I confess I do not understand this passage, unless it may be consid-
ered as divided parts of Cordelia's letter, which he is reading to himself by moon-
light: it certainly conveys the sense of what she would have said. In reading a
letter, it is natural enough to dwell on those circumstances in it that promise the
change in our affairs which we most wish for; and Kent, having read Cordelia's
assurances that she will find a time to free the injured from the enormous misrule of
Regan, is willing to go to sleep with that pleasing reflection uppermost in his mind.
But this is mere conjecture. <SC>Malone</SC> does not think that any part of Cordelia's
letter is, or can be, read by Kent. &lquo;He wishes,&rquo; so Malone continues, &lquo;for the rising
of the sun that he <I>may</I> read it.&rquo; I suspect that two half lines have been lost between
the words &lquo;state&rquo; and &lquo;seeking.&rquo; This &lquo;enormous state&rquo; means, I think, the confu-
sion subsisting in the state in consequence of the discord which had arisen between
the Dukes of Albany and Cornwall; of which Kent hopes Cordelia will avail her-
self. <SC>Mason</SC> thus paraphrases it: &lquo;I know that the letter is from Cordelia, (who
hath been informed of my obscured course,) and shall gain time, by this strange
disguise and situation, which I shall employ in seeking to remedy our present losses.&rquo;
<SC>Tieck</SC> (vol. ix, p. 366) thinks that the poet wishes here only to call Cordelia to
mind, and give us a hint that wholly new events are about to happen. When
Kent says only misery sees miracles, he means that he, disguised as a common man,
has already witnessed the wickedness of Goneril, the unhappy condition of the king,
he himself, a nobleman, has been stocked like a low, common rogue, and yet it is
possible for him to exchange letters with Cordelia. At the word &lquo;remedies,&rquo; sleep
overpowers him, and the sentence is not completed. <SC>Collier</SC>: We are to recollect
that Kent, having a letter from Cordelia in his hand, is endeavoring to make out its
contents by the imperfect light; he is unable to see distinctly, and hence, perhaps,
part of the obscurity of the passage. He can only make out some words, and those
not decisively, but sufficiently to enable the audience to judge of the general tenor
of what he is trying to read. <SC>Singer</SC> says that Kent finds he cannot follow his train
of thought for weariness, and so breaks off and settles himself to sleep. <SC>White</SC>
follows Jennens in thinking that Kent here drowsily reads disjointed fragments of
Cordelia's letter. White also follows the Ff in putting a period after course, line 164.</CC>

<P>169. <SC>Dowden</SC> (p. 271): Kent possesses no vision, like that which gladdens Ed-
gar, of a divine providence. His loyalty to right has something in it of a desperate
instinct, which persists in spite of the appearances presented by the world. Sh.
would have us know that there is not any devotion to truth, to justice, to charity
more intense and real than that of the man who is faithful to them, out of the sheer
spirit of loyalty, unstimulated and unsupported by any faith which can be called
theological. Kent, who has seen the vicissitude of things, knows of no higher
power presiding over the events of the world than fortune. Therefore, all the
more, Kent clings to the passionate instinct of right-doing, and to the hardy temper,
the $ortitude which makes evil, when it happens to come, endurable. The &lquo;mira-
cle&rquo; that Kent sees in his distress is the approaching succour from France, and the
loyalty of Cordelia's spirit. . . . It is Kent who, characteristically making the best of an</CC>

<P>14. <B>Bedlam beggars]</B> Many passages from old authors are cited by modern
editors to show what these &lquo;Bedlam beggars&rquo; were, and many more might be cited;
and yet, after all, none of them contain so good a description of Bedlamites as
that given in these few lines of Edgar's speech. That &lquo;poor Tom&rquo; was their uni-
versal name is shown in the first paragraph of Awdeley's <I>Fraternitye of Vaca-
bondes</I>, 1565: &lquo;An Abraham man is he that walketh bare armed, and bare legged,
and fayneth hym selfe mad, and caryeth a packe of wool, or a stycke with baken
on it, or such lyke toy, and nameth himselfe poore Tom.&rquo;&mdash;ed. Early Eng. Text
Soc. p. 3. The great authority in regard to &lquo;Vagabones&rquo; is Harman's &lquo;<I>Caueat or
Warening for Commen Cvrsetors</I>,&rquo; ed. ii, 1567, also reprinted by the E. E. Text Soc.
Dekker in his <I>Belman of London</I> &lquo;conveyed&rquo; largely from Harman; one passage,
cited by <SC>Steevens</SC>, so strongly corroborates Shakespeare's description that it may
perhaps be worth the while to reprint it here (three editions of this <I>Belman</I> appeared
in 1608, the year in which <I>Lear</I> was first printed): &lquo;Of all the mad rascalls (that
are of this wing) the Abraham-man is the most phantastick: The fellow (quoth the
old Lady of the Lake vnto me) that sat halfe naked (at table to-day) from the
girdle vpward, is the best Abraham-man that euer came to my house, the notablest
villaine: he sweares he hath bin in Bedlam, and will talke frantickly of purpose:
you see pinnes stuck in sundry places of his native flesh, especially in his armes,
which paine hee gladly puts himselfe to (beeing indeede no torment at all, his skin
is either so dead with some fowle disease, or so hardned with weather) onely to
make you beleeue he is out of his wits: he calls himselfe by the name of <I>Poore
Tom</I>, and comming neere any body, cryes out, <I>Poore Tom is a cold.</I> Of these Abra-
ham-men some be exceeding mery, and doe nothing but sing songs, fashioned out
of their owne braines; some will dance, other will do nothing but laugh or weepe;
others are dogged and so sullen both in looke and speech, that spying but small
company in a house, they boldly and bluntly enter, compelling the seruants through
feare to giue them what they demaund, which is commonly bacon, or something that
will yeelde ready mony. The Vpright-man and the Rogue are not terribler ene-
mies to poultry ware than <I>Poore Tom</I> is.&rquo;</CC>

alone called them <I>Turlupins</I>, a name which seems obviously to be connected with

<CC><P>23. <B>upon respect]</B> <SC>Singer</SC> was the first to give the true explanation of this
phrase: &lquo;<I>deliberately</I> or <I>upon consideration.</I>&rquo; <SC>Edwards, Heath</SC>, and <SC>Johnson</SC> all
interpreted it as referring it to the &lquo;respect&rquo; or reverence due to the king's mes-
senger. <SC>Malone</SC> supposed that &lquo;respect&rquo; was personified. <SC>Singer</SC> referred to
<I>Ham.</I> III, i, 68. <SC>Wright</SC> agrees with Singer, and cites a convincing passage from
<I>King John</I>, IV, ii, 214: &lquo;To know the meaning Of dangerous majesty, when per-
chance it frowns More upon humour than advised respect.&rquo; &lquo;That is, rather capri-
ciously than deliberately. Bacon frequently uses &ldquo;upon&rdquo; in similar phrases. See
Glossary to the <I>Essays</I>, ed. Wright.&rquo;

<P>54. <B>mother]</B> <SC>Percy</SC>: Lear here affects to pass off the swelling of his heart, ready
to burst with grief and indignation, for the disease called the <I>Mother</I>, or <I>Hysterica
Passio</I>, which, in our author's time, was not thought peculiar to women only. In
Harsnet's <I>Declaration of Popish Impostures</I>, Richard Mainy, Gent, one of the pre-
tended demoniacs, deposes, p. 263, that the first night that he came to Denham, the
seat of Mr. Peckham, where these impostures were managed, he was somewhat evill
at ease, and he grew worse and worse with an old disease that he had, and which
the priests persuaded him was from the possession of the Devil, viz. &lquo;The disease
I spake of was a spice of the <I>Mother</I>, wherewith I had bene troubled . . . before my
going into Fraunce: whether I doe rightly term it the <I>Mother</I> or no, I know not. . . .
When I was sicke of this disease in Fraunce, a Scottish doctor of physick then in
Paris, called it, as I remember, <I>Vertiginem Capitis.</I> It riseth . . . of a winde in the
bottome of the belly, and proceeding with a great swelling, causeth a very painful
collicke in the stomack, and an extraordinary giddines in the head.&rquo; It is at least
very probable, that Sh. would not have thought of making Lear affect to have the
<I>Hysterick Passion</I>, or <I>Mother</I>, if this passage in Harsnet's pamphlet had not suggested
it to him, when he was selecting the other particulars from it, in order to furnish out his
character of Tom of Bedlam, to whom this demoniacal gibberish is admirably adapted.
<SC>Ritson</SC>: In p. 25 of the above pamphlet it is said, &lquo;Ma: Maynie had a spice of the
<I>Hysterica passio</I>, as seems, from his youth, he himselfe termes it the <I>Moother.</I>&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>61. <B>chance]</B> The conclusion that <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 37, draws from many instances is
that, perhaps, Sh. used &lquo;chance&rquo; as an adverb, but unconsciously retained the order
of words, which shows that, strictly speaking, it is to be considered as a verb.
<P>65. <B>We'll set, &amp;c.]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: &lquo;Go to the ant, thou sluggard,&rquo; says Solomon,
&lquo;consider her ways, and be wise; which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, pro-
videth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest.&rquo; [<I>Proverbs</I>, vi,
6-8.] If, says the Fool, you had been schooled by the ant, you would have known
that the king's train, like that sagacious animal, prefer the summer of prosperity to
the colder season of adversity, from which no profit can be derived. <SC>Schmidt</SC>:
Elsewhere Sh. uses &lquo;to set to school&rquo; in the sense of <I>to teach.</I>
<P>66. <B>All that follow, &amp;c.]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: There is in this sentence no clear series
of thought. If he that follows his nose is led or guided by his eyes, he wants no
information from his nose. I persuade myself, but know not whether I can persuade
others, that Sh. wrote: &lquo;All men are led by their eyes but blind men, and they follow
their noses, and there's not a nose among twenty but can smell him that's stinking.&rquo;
Here is a succession of reasoning. You ask why the king has no more train? Why,
because men who are led by their eyes see that he is ruined, and if there were any
blind among them, who, for want of eyes, followed their noses, they might by their
noses discover that it was no longer fit to follow the king. <SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Twenty&rquo;
refers to the &lquo;noses&rquo; of the &lquo;blind men,&rquo; and not to the men in general. The passage,
thus considered, bears clearly the very sense which the above note endeavors to
establish by alteration. For &lquo;stinking,&rquo; <SC>Mason</SC> maintained that we should read
<I>sinking</I>, because &lquo;it would be nothing extraordinary that a nose should smell out a
person that was &ldquo;stinking.&rdquo; What the Fool wants to describe is the sagacity of
mankind in finding out the man whose fortunes are declining.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>, however,
vindicated the present text by showing that the same simile is applied to fallen for-
tunes in <I>All's Well</I>, V, ii, 5: Mankind, says the Fool, may be divided into those</CC>

<CC><P>who can see and those who are blind. All men, but blind men, though they follow
their noses, are led by their eyes; and this class of mankind, <I>seeing</I> the king ruined,
have all deserted him. With respect to the other class, the blind, who have nothing
but their noses to guide them, they also fly equally from a king whose fortunes are
declining; for, of the noses of twenty blind men, there is not one but can smell him
who, &lquo;being muddied in fortune's mood, smells somewhat strong of her strong dis-
pleasure.&rquo; <SC>Halliwell</SC>: The word &lquo;twenty&rquo; does not, I think, refer solely to the
noses of the blind men. The Fool says Kent deserves to be put in the stocks for his
silly question, for not looking which way the wind blows, for being too simple. He
says that all men who follow their noses are led by their eyes, blind men excepted.
Kent, according to his notion, has not used his eyes, and therefore he deserved the
stocks. Not a nose of any kind but smells him that's stinking; and he infers that
Kent had neither used his eyes to see, nor his nose to smell; in short, had not made
use of his senses.

<CC><P>fool turns knave, that runs away The knave no fool&mdash;.&rquo; That I stay with the
king is a proof that I am a fool, the wise men are deserting him. There is knavery
in this desertion, but there is no folly. <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii) adopted this change by
Johnson (which is also found in his Folio MS), and upholds it thus: &lquo;In the old
editions the very contrary of what Sh. intended is expressed. The reasoning in the
earlier part of the rhyme is that, when it begins to rain, wise men fly to shelter, but
fools stay; and it ought to be followed up by the statement that, if the fool runs
away, he turns knave, and that the knave, being no fool, will not be so silly as to
remain in the wet.&rquo; But Collier, in his Third edition, returns to the old read-
ing. Both <SC>Heath</SC> and <SC>Capell</SC> adopted Johnson's change in the first of these
two lines; and in the second, Heath suggested &lquo;The <I>fool's</I> no knave, perdy.&rquo;
<SC>White</SC>: No transposition is necessary, if, as I believe, &lquo;knave&rquo; in line 80 is used in
the sense of servant, in line 81 of rogue, while &lquo;fool,&rquo; in line 80, has the reproachful
sense it has in the Bible, and in line 81 is but the official title. <SC>Hudson</SC>: The Fool
seems here to be using the trick of suggesting a thing by saying the opposite.
<SC>Clarke</SC>: Sh., in his own noble philosophy, here affirms that the cunning rogue who
deserts his benefactor in the time of reverse, from motives of prudence, shows him-
self fool as well as knave, moral miscalculator as well as moral coward. <SC>Moberly</SC>:
The touching faith of the Fool to his master is one of the most beautiful points of the
play. The history of court-fools does not offer anything quite like it. It, however,
took six strong men to drag away Patch, Cardinal Wolsey's Fool, from his disgraced
master, who wished to send him as a propitiatory offering to Henry VIII. <SC>Wright</SC>:
The text requires no alteration. The Fool points out who the real fools in the world
are. Coleridge said a knave is a fool with a circumbendibus. [I think the meaning
is made clearer by showing the difference, by means of capital letters, as <SC>White</SC>
does, between the generic fool and the specific Fool.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>81. <B>perdy]</B> The corruption of <I>par Dieu.</I> See <I>Ham.</I> III, ii, 282.
<P>83. <B>Not i' th' stocks, fool]</B> <SC>Schmidt</SC> thinks that this &lquo;fool&rquo; is not a mere retort,
but is really meant, according to the song, as a title of respect, which Kent has
earned by his fidelity to the king.

<CC><P>that one Quarto, and probably the oldest [see Q<SUB>2</SUB> (Bodl. 1) in Appendix, p. 374],
reads <I>come and tends service</I>, of course, nonsense, but yet containing nearly the same
letters as the Folio; also that Lear demands service not only from Regan, but also
from Cornwall, and that the circumstances, at least, would require: <I>commands them
service</I>, which would come nearer to the <I>ductus literarum</I> of the true reading. As
concerns this latter, it must be granted that <I>tend</I>, which is elsewhere so often
identical with <I>attend</I>, is used by Sh. nowhere in the sense of <I>await</I>, in which sense
he frequently uses <I>attend</I> (see II, i, 125). But this is of no material weight. Just
as the prefix <I>a</I> is found before numberless verbs without changing their essential
meaning (<I>abate, abide, accursed, advantage, adventure, affright, affront, apper-
tain</I>, &amp;c.), so, on the other hand, in the older language the prefix <I>a</I> (whatever may
be its origin) is o$ten omitted at will. In II, i, 30, we have had &lquo;quit thyself&rquo; as a
hapax legomenon for <I>acquit thyself.</I> So also in IV, i, 49, &lquo;parel&rquo; for <I>apparel.</I> Other
hapax legomena are &lquo;lege&rquo; for <I>allege</I>, &lquo;noyance&rquo; for <I>annoyance</I>, &lquo;paritor&rquo; for
<I>apparitor</I>, &lquo;rest&rquo; (only in <I>Com. of Err.</I>) for <I>arrest</I>, &lquo;say&rquo; for <I>assay</I>, &lquo;stonish&rquo; for
<I>astonish</I>, &lquo;void&rquo; (<I>Cor.</I> IV, v, 88) for <I>avoid.</I> The occurrence of the shortened form
is not therefore conclusive against the use of <I>tend</I> in a sense with which <I>attend</I> does
not seem hitherto to have had anything in common, especially since the meanings
of the two words in other passages coincide in the majority of cases, and also since
<I>tendance</I> is equivalent in Sh. to <I>attendance.</I>

<CC><P>saule ich haue no salt bacon; Nouht a cokeney, by cryst, colhoppes to make&rquo; [Pass.
IX, 309, C. Text, ed. Skeat]. It seems to signify a Cook. And so, perhaps, in
<I>The Turnament of Tottenham</I> [Percy's <I>Reliques</I>, ii, p. 24, ed. 1765]. &lquo;At that
feast were they served in rich aray; Every five and five had a cokeney.&rquo; That is, I
suppose, a <I>cook</I> or <I>scullion</I>, to attend them. In those rhymes ascribed to Hugh
Bigot, which Camden has published: &lquo;Were I in my castle of Bungey upon the
river of Waveney, I would ne care for the King of Cockeney.&rquo; The author, in
calling London Cockeney, might possibly allude to that imaginary country of idle-
ness and luxury which was anciently known by the name of <I>Cokaigne.</I> <SC>Nares</SC> also
believes that it is derived from cookery, and that here in <I>Lear</I> it means a cook, be-
cause she is &lquo;making a pie.&rquo; In the passages cited by Tyrwhitt, <SC>Whalley</SC> and
<SC>Malone</SC> think that it refers to some dish, while <SC>Douce</SC> maintains that it signifies a
little cock. <SC>Halliwell</SC>, in his <I>Archaic Dict.</I>, says that he can find no certain au-
thority for any such interpretation as Tyrwhitt gives it, but in his Folio edition of
<I>Sh.</I> he says that the word &lquo;cockney is used in various senses, amongst others in that
of a cook, which may be its meaning here, although I rather incline to the belief that
the reference is to some absurd tale of a London cockney well known in Shake-
speare's time.&rquo; In which belief <SC>Dyce</SC> agrees with him. <SC>Way</SC> (note on <I>Coknay</I> in
<I>Prompt. Parv.</I>): The term coknay appears in the Promptorium to imply simply a
child spoiled by too much indulgence; thus likewise in the Medulla: &lquo;<I>Mammo-
trophus, qui diu sugit. Mammotrophus mammam longo qui tempore servat</I> Kokenay
<I>dicatur, noster sic sermo notatur.</I>&rquo; There can be little doubt that the word is to be
traced to the imaginary region &lquo;ihote Cokaygne,&rquo; described in the curious poem
given by Hickes, <I>Gramm. A Sax.</I>, p. 231, and apparently translated from the French.
Compare &lquo;<I>le Fabliaus de Coquaigne.</I>&rquo; Fabl. Barbazan et M&eacute;on. iv, 175. Palsgrave
gives the verb &lquo;To bring up lyke a cocknaye, <I>mignotter;</I>&rquo; and Elyot renders &lquo;<I>delicias
facere</I>, to play the cockney.&rquo; &lquo;<I>Dodeliner</I>, to bring vp wantonly as a cockney.&rquo;&mdash;Hol-
lyband's <I>Treasurie.</I> See also Baret's <I>Alvearie.</I> Chaucer uses the word as a term
of contempt, and it occasionally signifies a little cook, <I>coquinator.</I> See Brand's <I>Pop.
Ant.</I>, notes on Shrove Tuesday. <SC>Cotgrave</SC> gives <I>Coquine</I>: A beggar-woman; also
a cockney, simperdecockit, nice thing. <SC>Wedgwood</SC>: The original meaning of
&lquo;cockney&rquo; is a child too tenderly or delicately nurtured, one kept in the house and
not hardened by out-of-doors life; hence applied to citizens, as opposed to the hard-
ier inhabitants of the country, and in modern times confined to the citizens of
London. [Does not this definition lack an allusion to the meaning in which Sh.
here uses it, which is undoubtedly that of a cook? Minsheu's derivation from the
<I>neigh</I> of a <I>cock</I>, is too familiar to be more than referred to.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Badham</SC> (<I>Cam.
Essays</I>, 1856, p. 284): &lquo;Cockney&rquo; is perfectly out of place here in <I>Lear</I>, and must
have supplanted either <I>cook-maid</I> or a similar word.

<CC><P>because the only sense of the verb to &lquo;knap&rquo; is to snap, or break asunder. <SC>Wright</SC>
(who defines &lquo;knapped&rquo; by <I>cracked</I>, and cites <I>Mer. of Ven.</I> III, i, 10; and the
Prayer-Book version of <I>Psalm</I> xlvi, 9: &lquo;He knappeth the spear in sunder&rquo;) replies
to Steevens by saying: &lquo;We use <I>crack</I> in both senses [i. e. <I>rap</I> and <I>snap</I>], and
&ldquo;knap&rdquo; and <I>crack</I> are both imitative words, representing the sound which is made
either by a blow or by breaking anything in halves.&rquo;
<P>128. <B>Sepulchring]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: This word is accented in the same manner [on
the penult] by Milton, <I>Ode on Shakespeare</I>, 15: &lquo;And so sepulcher'd in such pomp

<P>135, 136. <B>You . . . duty]</B> This passage, as <SC>Wright</SC> truly remarks, &lquo;is one of
many passages in Sh. of which the sense is clear, but which it is almost impossible
to paraphrase.&rquo; <SC>Johnson</SC>, on the ground that &lquo;scant&rquo; is directly contrary to the
sense intended, advocated Hanmer's change to <I>scan</I> in the sense of measure or pro-
portion. <SC>Steevens</SC> says, &lquo;Surely no alteration is necessary,&rquo; and then gives what he
says is &lquo;the <I>intended</I> meaning of the passage&rquo;: &lquo;&ldquo;You less know how to value her
desert, than she (knows) to scant her duty,&rdquo; <I>i. e.</I> than she can be capable of being
wanting in her duty.&rquo; <SC>Capell</SC>: Had [line 135] been conceiv'd in these words, &lquo;You
<I>more</I> know how to <I>lessen</I> her desert,&rquo; then had those expressions been proper that suc-
ceed in the next line; as it is, &lquo;scant&rquo; cannot have been the word in that place; and
<I>scan</I> . . . bids fair to be the Poet's intended term in it's room, spoil'd by printers.
<SC>Malone</SC>: The inaccuracy of the expression will clearly appear from inverting the
sentence without changing a word: &lquo;I have hope, says Regan, that she knows <I>more</I>
(or <I>better</I>) how to scant her duty than you know how to value her desert;&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> I have
hope that she is <I>more perfect</I> in the <I>non-performance</I> of her duty than you are perfect,
or accurate, in the estimation of her merit. If Lear is <I>less</I> knowing in the valuation
of Goneril's desert than she is in scanting her duty, then she knows <I>better</I> how to <I>scant</I>
or be deficient in her duty, than he knows how to appreciate her desert. If Sh. had
written &lquo;I have hope that you rather know how to make her <I>desert less</I> than it is, (to
underrate it in your estimation) than that she knows how to scant her duty,&rquo; all would
have been clear, but by placing &lquo;less&rquo; before &lquo;know&rquo; this meaning is destroyed. In
<I>Wint. Tale</I>, III, ii, 55, we meet with a similar inaccuracy: &lquo;&mdash;I ne'er heard yet That
any of these bolder vices wanted Less impudence to gainsay what they did Than to
perform it first,&rquo; where, as Johnson justly observed, &lquo;<I>wanted</I> should be <I>had</I> or <I>less</I> should
be <I>more.</I>&rquo; Again in <I>Macb.</I> III, vi, 8. <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I> p. 1420, 9) gives many similar
instances of what he calls the &lquo;duplication of negative words,&rquo; as here &lquo;less know&rquo;
and &lquo;scant&rquo;; <I>e. g. Mer. of Ven.</I> IV, i, 162: &lquo;Let his lack of years be no impediment
to let him lack a reverend estimation,&rquo; equivalent to either: no motive to let him
lack, or, no impediment to let him have. Again, <I>Tro. and Cres.</I> I, i, 28; <I>Cor.</I> I, iv,
14, &amp;c. &lquo;All such irregularities,&rquo; adds <SC>Schmidt</SC>, &lquo;may be easily accounted for. The
idea of negation was so strong in the poet's mind, that he expressed it in more than</CC>

<P>164. <B>To fall]</B> <SC>Malone</SC> says that this verb is here used actively, meaning to humble
or pull down. &lquo;Infect her beauty so as to fall and blast (<I>i. e.</I> humble and destroy)

[The majority of editors incline to Malone's view that it is here transitive (<SC>Dyce</SC>
enumerates fourteen instances in Sh. of the use of &lquo;fall&rquo; as a transitive verb; this,
however, is not among them), but one of the latest and best, <SC>Wright</SC>, says that,
although in either case it would yield a good sense to this passage, yet it seems pre-
ferable, on the whole, to regard it as intransitive, &lquo;as more in keeping with &ldquo;drawn,&rdquo;
which precedes, and &ldquo;blast,&rdquo; which follows.&rquo; <SC>Schmidt</SC> suggests that &lquo;pride&rquo; has
accidentally been omitted at the end of the line in the Ff, and that the true reading
is &lquo;To fall and blister pride.&rquo; &lquo;To fall&rquo; would be intransitive, and &lquo;pride&rquo; used as
frequently in Sh. in the sense of &lquo;braggart beauty.&rquo; Compare &lquo;a southwest blow
on ye And blister ye all o'er.&rquo; <I>Temp.</I> I, ii, 324; &lquo;Takes off the rose From the fair
forehead of an innocent love, And sets a blister there.&rquo; <I>Ham.</I> III, iv, 42.]

<P>168. <B>tender-hefted]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: <I>Hefted</I> seems to mean the same as <I>heaved.</I>
&lquo;Tender-hefted,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> whose bosom is agitated by tender passions. Sh. uses &lquo;hefts&rquo;
for <I>heavings</I> in <I>Wint. Tale</I>, II, i, 45. The Qq, however, read, &lquo;tender-hested
nature,&rquo; which may mean a nature which is governed by gentle dispositions. &lquo;Hest&rquo;
is an old word, signifying command. <SC>Davies</SC>: I suppose the expression was in-
tended to signify <I>smooth</I>, or <I>soft-handled</I>, consequently put here for <I>gentleness of dis-
position.</I> <SC>Knight</SC>: We doubt Steevens's explanation. <I>Heft,&mdash;haft</I>,&mdash;is that which
is <I>haved,&mdash;held;</I> and thus, &lquo;thy tender-hefted nature&rquo; may be thy nature which may
be held by tenderness. <SC>White</SC>: Although I fail to see the appropriateness of any
sense that may be extracted from either text of the Ff or Qq, I shrink from adopting
the very specious reading of the earlier editors: tender-<I>hearted.</I> <SC>Edinburgh Re-
view</SC> (July, 1869, p. 106): &lquo;Heft&rquo; is a well-known older English word for handle,
that which holds or contains, and &lquo;tender-hefted&rquo; is simply delicately-housed, dain-
tily-bodied, finely-sheathed. &lquo;Heft&rquo; was in this way applied proverbially to the body,
and Howel has a phrase quoted by Halliwell: <I>loose in the heft</I>, to designate an ill
habit of body, a person of dissipated ways. <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) quotes this extract,
and adds: But is <I>haft</I> or <I>heft, i. e.</I> handle, indeed that which holds or contains, or
not rather that by which a thing is held? <I>Loose in the handle</I>, applied to a person,
could not possibly mean any thing else than what <I>loose in the heft</I> is said to have
designated. Perhaps &lquo;tender-hefted,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> tender-handled, is equivalent to tender,
gentle, to touch or to approach; of an easy and winning address, affable. <SC>Wright</SC>:
A heft or haft is a handle, and a nature tender-hefted is one which is set in a tender
handle or delicate bodily frame. Regan was less masculine than Goneril. Cotgrave
has, &lquo;Emmanch&eacute;: m. &eacute;e: f. Helued; set into a haft, or handle. Lasche emmanch&eacute;.
Lazie, idle, slothfull, weake, feeble, loose ioynted, faint-hearted.&rquo; <I>Prompt. Parv.</I>
&lquo;Heftyde, manubriatus.&rquo;

<CC><P>206, 207. <B>To wage . . . howl]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC> (followed by <SC>Hanmer</SC>) transposed
these lines so as to. make &lquo;Necessity's sharp pinch,&rquo; the object of &lquo;wage.&rquo; This
<SC>Jennens</SC> pronounces nonsense, because &lquo;it is that &ldquo;pinch&rdquo; which forces a man to
&ldquo;wage;&rdquo; <I>war</I> is understood, or perhaps it is the very word instead of &ldquo;wage.&rdquo;
&ldquo;Necessity's sharp pinch&rdquo; is in apposition to &ldquo;To be a comrade,&rdquo;&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Capell</SC>:
&lquo;To wage,&rquo; is to wage combat or battle. <SC>Steevens</SC> says, that <I>wage</I> is often used
thus, intransitively, but the only instance that he cites is in I, i, 154, where &lquo;wage&rquo;
means to wager. According to <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>), this is the only instance of its use
in Sh. <SC>Keightly</SC> inserts <I>war</I> in the text.
<P>207. <B>howl]</B> This change from <I>owl</I> of the QqFf to &lquo;howl&rquo; is due to <SC>Collier's</SC>
(MS), and, to my mind, carries conviction. In the old reading, which renders
&lquo;Necessity's sharp pinch&rquo; parenthetical, there is a tameness out of place at the close
of Lear's wild outburst, which is, it seems to me, thoroughly un-Shakespearian. In
the present text there is a climax, terrible in its wildness: roofs are to be abjured,
storms braved, and famine howled forth among wolves. What companionship is
there between wolves and owls, beyond the fact that they are both nocturnal? Yet
what grates me in the old reading is, not so much the association of the wolf and
owl, but the un-Shakespearian feebleness of bringing in &lquo;Necessity's sharp pinch&rquo; as
an explanation of what it is to abjure roofs and to be a comrade with wolves. As if
Lear would stop to explain that people did not usually prefer such houseless poverty
or such companionship, but that it was only the sharp pinch of necessity that drove
them to it. In the old text there is no crest to the wave of Lear's passion; it surges
up wild and threatening, and then when it should &lquo;thunder on the beach&rquo; it subsides
into a gentle apologetic ripple. Theobald's transposition of the lines, or any change
that will avoid putting &lquo;Necessity's sharp pinch&rquo; in apposition with the rest of the
sentence, is better than the old text. <SC>Schmidt</SC> must have felt this, although he does
not say so; he puts a full stop after &lquo;owl,&rquo; and makes &lquo;Necessity's sharp pinch&rquo; an
anacoluthon. Furthermore, <SC>Schmidt</SC> says the circumstances enumerated in lines
205, 206, and 207 are those under which the sharp pinch of necessity is felt, but they</CC>

<CC><P>are not the sharp pinch itself. If it be objected that to howl a pinch is a violent
metaphor, I reply that it is not more violent than to take up arms against a sea. As
far as concerns the addition or the omission of <I>h</I> in Shakespeare's day, I can only
urge the exceeding difficulty, if not impossibility, of deciding what words were as-
pirated and what were not; in the old MSS, especially of the XIIIth century, the use
of the <I>h</I> is very &lquo;uncertain and confused&rquo; (&mdash;Ellis, p. 598). In process of time the
number of words in which it was customary to drop the <I>h</I> diminished, until now, as
Ellis says (p. 221), there are but five: <I>heir, honest, honour, hostler</I>, and <I>hour</I> [qy.
<I>herb?</I>], which it is &lquo;social suicide to aspirate.&rquo; Wherefore the absence of the <I>h</I>, in
the present passage, is not fatal to the emendation; the only instance in the Folio
where &lquo;owlet&rquo; is used, it is spelled <I>Howlet.</I> Note too, as a slight corroboration of the
present reading, that in III, i, 13 occurs the phrase &lquo;the belly-<I>pinched wolf&rquo;;</I> and
the <I>howling</I> of the <I>wolf</I> is again referred to in III, vii, 62. But whether or not the
old pronunciation was <I>owl</I> or <I>howl</I>, and whether or not all the old texts have <I>owl</I>, I
adhere to the maxim of the great Bentley: <I>sana ratio vel centum codicibus potior.</I>
<SC>Dyce's</SC> opinion (<I>Strictures</I>, &amp;c., p. 6) should be recorded here, so emphatic is his
condemnation of the present text: &lquo;the glaring absurdity of &ldquo;the old corrector's
aspirate&rdquo; . . . will inevitably be treated by every future editor with the intense con-
tempt it deserves.&rquo; <SC>Moberly</SC>, although he does not adopt it, pronounces &lquo;howl&rquo;
&lquo;another instance of improvement in the text, suggested&rquo; by Collier's (MS), and
adds that, when thus read, the lines become &lquo;convincingly forcible.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>209. <B>hot-blooded France]</B> For instances of nouns which express the subject of
the thought without any grammatical connection with a verb, see IV, vi, 77: &lquo;That
thing you speak of, I took it for a man;&rquo; <I>Ham.</I> I, v, 53; and <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 417.
<P>211. <B>knee]</B> From the only other use of this word in Sh. as a verb (<I>Cor.</I> V, i, 5),
Schmidt infers, very erroneously I think, that this does not here mean to kneel down
before France's throne, but to travel thither on the knees. The passage in <I>Cor.</I> is
not parallel.

groome).&rquo;
<P>214. <B>groom]</B> For the sake of scansion <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 484, would pronounce this as a

<CC><P>220. <B>boil]</B> <SC>Malone</SC> first changed the spelling of this word, of which the spelling
in the <I>Prompt. Parv.</I>, Cotgrave, QqFf, &amp;c. betokens a uniform pronunciation. Cot-
grave (s. v. <I>Bosse</I>) gives it as a synonym of &lquo;plague-sore.&rquo;
<P>221. <B>embossed]</B> This word is used by Sh. in two different senses, and has conse-
quently given rise to some discussion, chiefly carried on in the pages of <I>Notes &amp;
Queries;</I> (references to all the communications will be found in the Bibliography.)
<SC>Furnivall</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 4th Ser. xi, 507) at last showed that there was here a con-
fusion of two different words. One is from the French <I>embosser</I>, defined by Cot-
grave: &lquo;To swell, or arise in bunches, hulches, knobs; to grow knottie, or knurrie.&rquo;
In this sense it is used here. The other is from the Old French: &lquo;<I>emboser</I>, emboiter,
ench&acirc;sser une chose dans une autre.&mdash;Ducange, v. <I>imbotare.</I>&rquo;&mdash;Hippeau. This is
Cotgrave's &lquo;<I>Emboister:</I> To imbox, inclose, insert, fasten, put, or shut vp, as within
a box,&rquo; and is Shakespeare's word in <I>All's Well</I>, III, vi, 107.</CC>

<CC><P>253, 255. <B>Those . . . praise.]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>, whose punctuation is substantially followed
by <SC>Knight, Delius</SC>, and <SC>Moberly</SC>, puts a stop after &lquo;well-favour'd,&rquo; and a comma
after &lquo;wicked,&rquo; thus preserving, as he claims, &lquo;a natural and just thought full of
dramatic beauty.&rquo; The objection to the present text he finds in &lquo;Those,&rquo; which, he
says, makes the sentence &lquo;particular, confining it to some persons then present, which
are Regan and Goneril.&rquo; His interpretation of line 253 is that &lquo;it is expressive of
the speaker's astonishment that the judgement of heaven is not fallen upon his
daughters for their wickedness; that they are still &ldquo;well-favour'd,&rdquo; and their beauty
not blasted, as he had particularly imprecated upon one of them a few pages before.
The line should be spoken with bitterness, a contracted brow, and surveying them
from head to foot, and a great pause made between that and the next line.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>:
A similar thought appears in <I>Cym.</I> V, v, 215-217, &lquo;It is I that all the abhorred things
of the earth amend By being worse than they.&rquo;
<P>261. <B>Oh, reason, &amp;c.]</B> <SC>Coleridge</SC>: Observe that the tranquillity which follows
the first stunning of the blow permits Lear to reason.
<P>262. <B>superfluous]</B> <SC>Moberly</SC>: Have in their deepest poverty some very poor
thing which may be called superfluous.</CC>

<P>267. <B>need,&mdash;]</B> <SC>Moberly</SC>: To imagine how Shakespeare would have ended this
sentence, one must be a Shakespeare. The poor king stops short in his definition;
it is too plain that his true need is patience.
<P>268. <B>that . . . need!]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: The repetition of &lquo;patience&rquo; is energetical, and
&lquo;that&rquo; a word of great force; importing&mdash;that patience which is seen in you,
&lquo;heavens,&rquo; that patience which none but you can bestow on one in my situation.
<SC>Mason</SC>: The passage should run thus: &lquo;but for true need, You heavens! give me
patience:&mdash;patience I need.&rquo; Nature needs not the gorgeous habits you wear, but
to supply a real need, you heavens! give me patience&mdash;patience I need indeed.
<SC>Hudson</SC> follows Mason's reading of this line. <SC>Jervis</SC> gives what is essentially the
same reading. <SC>Malone</SC>: I believe the word &lquo;patience&rquo; was repeated inadvertently
by the compositor. <SC>White</SC> and <SC>Keightley</SC> adopted this conjecture of Malone's.
<SC>Ritson</SC>: The compositor has repeated the wrong word. Read: &lquo;give me that pa-
tience <I>that</I> I need.&rquo; Or, still better, perhaps: &lquo;give me patience!&mdash;that I need.&rquo;
<SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): Instead of &lquo;that patience&rquo; the (MS) has &lquo;<I>but</I> patience.&rquo; We may
doubt whether the line did not originally run: &lquo;give me but patience that I need.&rquo;
<SC>Dyce</SC>: I would not assert, with Capell, that the old text is uncorrupted. <SC>Walker</SC>
(<I>Crit.</I> iii, 278) prefers either Malone's conj. or Ritson's second suggestion. <SC>Wright</SC>:
If any change be made Mason's seems best. <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 476, would make &lquo;give
. . . need&rquo; a separate line, pronouncing the second &lquo;patience&rquo; as a trisyllable.
<P>271. <B>that stirs]</B> For instances of the relative with a plural antecedent followed

the sound pleas'd him; and he made no scruple of using it, well knowing it could
not be mistaken. <SC>Wright</SC>: Steevens quotes from Bacon's <I>Considerations touching a

technically known as &lquo;the Spanish main,&rquo; but of the landing an army on the coast

<CC><P>was meant by &lquo;the main&rquo; in the former passage. <SC>Delius</SC> doubts that this means the
land; the sense being rather that the curled waters swell above their own especial
domain, the sea, and overflow the land. <SC>Jennens</SC>: Though all the editions have
&lquo;main,&rquo; it is very likely Sh. wrote <I>moon</I>, which is much better, because it more
strongly expresses (according to Shakespeare's custom) the confusion which Lear in
his rage would have introduced into nature; besides, &lquo;main&rquo; is ambiguous, appli-
cable to sea or land. The effect of overflowing the land is not so great nor so certain
confusion; the sea often does that and returns to its usual bounds; whereas the
swelling of the waters above the moon is entirely preternatural, and best answers the
madness of bidding the wind blow the earth into the sea. According to <SC>Schmidt</SC>
(<I>Lex.</I>), Sh. uses &lquo;main&rquo; more frequently for the sea than for the land, but here clearly
for the latter.
<P>8, 9. <B>Which . . . of]</B> <SC>Heath</SC>: Which the impetuous blasts, with undiscerning
rage, catch in their fury, and scatter or disperse to nothing as fast as he tears it off.
<SC>Delius</SC>, more correctly, interprets &lquo;make nothing of&rquo; as meaning to treat with
irreverence; as <SC>Schmidt</SC> says, it is the opposite to &lquo;make much of.&rquo;
<P>10. <B>little world of man]</B> There may be a reference here to the phraseology of
the early astrologers, who were wont to call Man the microcosm, or &lquo;the little world,&rquo;
as containing in miniature the elements of the macrocosm, which is the universe,
terrestrial and heavenly. See Cornelius Agrippa <I>Magische Werke</I>, ii, cap. 27; or
Paracelsus <I>Sagacis Philosophi&aelig;</I>, 1658, Lib. i, p. 532, <I>a.</I> In vol. ix of Dodsley's <I>Old
Plays</I> there is <I>A Morall Maske</I> by Thomas Nabbes, called <I>Microcosmus</I>, 1637; in
the commendatory verses both by Rich. Broome and Will. Cufaude, &lquo;man&rquo; is spoken
of as &lquo;the little world.&rquo; I am not sure that the macrocosm is not referred to by
Gloucester in IV, vi, 133: &lquo;O ruin'd piece of nature! This great world shall so wear
out to nought,&rquo; perhaps alluding to the bond which, as astrologers maintain, exists
between the little world and the great world. In reference to the macrocosm, see
notes on <I>Faust</I>, either in Hayward's or Taylor's translation.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>10. <B>out-scorn]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: I suspect we should read &lquo;out-<I>storm.</I>&rquo; Compare
<I>Lovers' Complaint</I>, 7: &lquo;Storming her world with sorrow's wind and rain.&rquo;
<P>12. <B>cub-drawn]</B> <SC>Pope</SC>: A bear drawn by nature to its young. <SC>Upton</SC> (p. 311,
ed. i): That is, having her cubs drawn from her, being robbed of her cubs. <SC>War-
burton</SC>: That is, a bear whose dugs have been drawn dry by its young. Even
hunger and the support of its young, would not force the bear to leave her den on
such a night. <SC>Steevens</SC> notes the recurrence of the same idea in <I>As You Like it.</I>
IV, ii, 115 and 127.</CC>

<CC><P>15. <B>take all]</B> <SC>Schmidt</SC>: An exclamation of despair, like &lquo;Lucifer take all&rquo;; &lquo;a
shame take all,&rquo; &amp;c.; also, apparently, by players when staking all on a single card.
&lquo;Wouldst thou fight well?&rquo; asks Anthony of Enobarbus, and the latter replies &lquo;I'll
strike, and cry Take all.&rquo; French <I>Va tout!</I>
<P>18. <B>my note]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: My observation. <SC>Capell</SC> (who here followed the Qq)
explains <I>art</I> as the &lquo;art of manners and face-judging, skill in knowledge of men.&rquo;
<SC>Malone</SC> quotes as in favour of the Qq, <I>Macb.</I> I, iv, 11, 12. <SC>Hudson</SC>: But it ap-
pears Kent &lquo;knows&rquo; his man, and therefore has no occasion to use the <I>art</I> or skill
in question.
<P>19. <B>dear]</B> See I, iv, 266.
<P>23. <B>who seem no less]</B> <SC>Capell</SC> supposes that this means servants that seem
as great as themselves, servants in high place. <SC>Delius</SC>, however, interprets it as
servants who seem to be no less, or no other, than what they are&mdash;namely, servants.
<P>24. <B>speculations]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC> (<I>Dict.</I>): Examiner, spy. The word is found no-
where else, and is probably here misprinted for <I>speculators.</I> [This conj. was
adopted by <SC>Singer</SC> (ed. ii), and <SC>Hudson</SC>.] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. ii): <I>Spectators</I> is the
word substituted by the (MS). &lquo;Speculations&rquo; cannot well on any account be right,
while <I>spectators</I> completes both meaning and metre; of course, the emphasis in <I>spec-
tators</I> must not here be placed on the second syllable. See <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>), p. 1421,
for a list of over sixty instances in Sh. of the use of the abstract for the concrete, to
which &lquo;discretion,&rquo; II, iv, 145, may be added.</CC>

<P>25-29. <B>What hat . . . furnishings]</B> <SC>Schmidt</SC>: Whether these incomplete sen-
tences are due to the poet, or to the style in which the scene has been transmitted to
us, cannot be decided; lines 22-29 are lacking in the Qq, and from 30-42 in the
Ff, and it is easily conceivable that between 29 and 30 there were other lines which
have been omitted in both texts.
<P>26. <B>snuffs]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: Quarrels. <SC>Nares</SC>: <I>To take in snuff</I> is to be angry, to
take offence.
<P>26. <B>packings]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Underhand contrivances. [See <I>Ham.</I> III, iv, 211.]
<P>29. <B>furnishings]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: What we now call colours, external pretenses.
<SC>Steevens</SC>: A <I>furnish</I> anciently signified a <I>sample.</I> So in the Epistle before
Greene's <I>Groats-worth of Witte:</I> &lquo;For to lend the world a furnish of witte she layes
her owne to pawne.&rquo; <SC>Staunton</SC>: Steevens's illustration from Greene is not con-
clusive. <SC>Hudson</SC>: That is, whereof these things are but the trimmings or append-
ages, not the thing itself, but only the circumstances or <I>furniture</I> of the thing.
<SC>Wright</SC>: In Scotland the trimmings of a lady's dress are called &lquo;furnishings.&rquo;
<P>31. <B>scatter'd]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Divided, unsettled, disunited. <SC>Schmidt</SC>: Sh. does not
elsewhere use the word in this sense. Perhaps Hanmer's <I>shattered</I> is right.
<P>32. <B>feet]</B> <SC>Upton</SC> (p. 195, ed. ii) suggests <I>seat</I>&mdash;that is, secretly situated, or lodged,
or perhaps <I>see</I> for the Latin <I>sedes</I>, which is used by Douglas in his version of Virgil,
and by Chaucer, and which still survives in &lquo;a Bishop's see.&rquo; <SC>Schmidt</SC>: This ex-
pression is akin to the language of the time, when <I>footed</I> meant the same as
<I>landed.</I>

<P>65. <B>even but now]</B> <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 38: <I>Even now</I> with us is applied to an action that
has been going on for some long time and <I>still</I> continues, the emphasis being laid on
&lquo;now.&rquo; In Sh. the emphasis is often to be laid on &lquo;even,&rquo; and &lquo;<I>even</I> now&rquo; means

<P>65. <B>demanding]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: &lquo;Demand&rquo; and &lquo;require&rquo; are both used formerly in
the simple sense of &lquo;ask,&rquo; without the further idea which the words have now ac-
quired of asking with authority. See <I>Temp.</I> I, ii, 139; <I>Cym.</I> III, vi, 92.
<P>67-73. <SC>Bucknill</SC> (p. 195): The import of this must be weighed with IV, vi,
100-104, when Lear is incoherent and full of delusion. Insanity arising from mental
and moral causes often continues in a certain state of imperfect development; . . . a
state of exaggerated and perverted emotion, accompanied by violent and irregular
conduct, but unconnected with intellectual aberration; until some physical shock is
incurred,&mdash;bodily illness, or accident, or exposure to physical suffering; and then
the imperfect type of mental disease is converted into perfect lunacy, characterised
by more or less profound affection of the intellect, by delusion or incoherence. This
is evidently the case in Lear, and although we have never seen the point referred to
by any writer, and have again and again read the play without perceiving it, we
cannot doubt from these passages, and especially from the second, in which the poor
madman's imperfect memory refers to his suffering in the storm, that Sh. contem-
plated this exposure and physical suffering as the cause of the first crisis in the mal-
ady. Our wonder at his profound knowledge of mental disease increases, the more
carefully we study his works; here and elsewhere he displays with prolific careless-
ness a knowledge of principles, half of which would make the reputation of a mod-
ern psychologist.</CC>

<CC><P>for the passage is one which, if it had been spoken at the time when the copy for that
edition was obtained, whether surreptitiously or not, would hardly have been omitted.
<SC>Cowden Clarke</SC>: This prophecy is clearly a scrap of ribaldry tacked on, by the actor
who played the Fool, to please &lquo;the barren spectators&rquo;; just one of those instances
of irrelevant and extemporaneous jesting to which Sh. himself, through his character
of Hamlet, so strongly objects. The fact of the Fool's present speech occurring
<I>after</I> Lear has left the stage alone serves to condemn it as spurious. <SC>Koppel</SC> (p. 79),
on the other hand, thinks that this speech was added by Sh. after the text which we
have in the Qq was written; &lquo;the poet was generous to this, the most amiable of all
his Fools, and even added somewhat to his part.&rquo; <SC>Warburton</SC> discerned not one,
but two, prophecies here: &lquo;the first, a satyrical description of the present manners as
future; and the second, a satyrical description of future manners, which the corrup-
tion of the present would prevent from ever happening. Each of these prophecies
has its proper inference or deduction; yet by an unaccountable stupidity, the first
editors took the whole to be one prophecy, and so jumbled the two contrary in-
ferences together.&rquo; Accordingly, Warburton transposed lines 93, 94 to follow line
84; that concludes the first prophecy, and Warburton points the allusion to the pres-
ent time by adding parenthetically after them, &lquo;<I>i. e.</I> Now.&rquo; The remaining lines
compose the second prophecy, and at the end of the last line Warburton adds, &lquo;<I>i. e.</I>
Never.&rquo; Warburton's change was followed in the text by <SC>Hanmer, Johnson, Jen-
nens</SC>, and <SC>Eccles. Capell</SC> grants Warburton's conclusions, but denounces the
transposition of the lines as &lquo;destructive of humour, and of the speaker's wild cha-
racter which disclaims regularity.&rquo; Capell's explanation is that Sh. wrote two speeches
for the Fool, &lquo;one comprising the whole of that prophecy which relates to things
<I>present;</I> it's conclusion a waggery [<I>i. e.</I>, I suppose, the line: &lquo;No heretics burn'd,
&amp;c.], at which the speaker might face about and be going, but return to speak the
lines about Merlin, which lines belong with equal propriety to the prophecy about
things that <I>will not be</I> . . . it is conceiv'd, further, that these seperate [<I>sic</I>] prophecies
were at first spoken seperately, or on seperate nights; or one drop'd for the other, and
we judge the drop'd one the first; that both were found in his manuscripts, standing
irregularly; and took their form from the players, who might even present them so
after their author's death&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC> refers to Puttenham's <I>Arte of Poesie</I>, 1589, as
containing these lines. [See p. 232, ed. Arber. &lquo;Sir <I>Geffrey Chaucer</I>, father of our
English Poets, hath these verses following the distributor [a rhetorical term]: When
faith failes in Priestes sawes, And Lords hestes are holden for lawes, And robberie
is tane for purchase, And lechery for solace, Then shall the Realme of Albion Be
brought to great confusion.&rquo; The original, which is called <I>Chaucer's Prophecy</I>, may
be found in vol. vi, p. 307, ed. Morris. See <SC>Brown's</SC> note, I, iv, 91.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<CC><P><B>Scene IV.]</B> <SC>Coleridge</SC>: O, what a world's convention of agonies is here! All
external nature in a storm, all moral nature convulsed,&mdash;the real madness of Lear,
the feigned madness of Edgar, the babbling of the Fool, the desperate fidelity of
Kent,&mdash;surely such a scene was never conceived, before or since! Take it but as a
picture for the eye only, it is more terrific than any which a Michael Angelo, inspired
by a Dante, could have conceived, and which none but a Michael Angelo could have
executed. Or let it have been uttered to the blind, the howlings of nature would
seem converted into the voice of conscious humanity. This scene ends with the first
symptoms of positive derangement; and the intervention of the fifth scene is particu-
larly judicious,&mdash;the interruption allowing an interval for Lear to appear in full mad-
ness in the sixth scene.
<P>2. <B>the open]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 75) suggests that the <I>e</I> in &lquo;the&rquo; be omitted before
&lquo;open.&rquo;
<P>4. <B>heart?]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: I believe that Lear does not address this question to Kent,
but to his own bosom. Perhaps, therefore, we should point the passage thus: &lquo;Wilt
break, my heart?&rquo; The tenderness of Kent, indeed, induces him to reply, as to an
interrogation that seemed to reflect on his own humanity.</CC>

<P>15. <B>as]</B> As if. See V, iii, 202, and <I>Ham.</I> I, ii, 217, with the instances there

that, although the abridged sentence may be explained by the complete form, <I>as if</I>,

<CC><P>26. <B>first]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: This injunction represents that humility, or tenderness, or
neglect of forms, which affliction forces on the mind.
<P>31. <B>loop'd]</B> <SC>Schmidt</SC>: &lquo;Loop&rquo; in Sh. does not mean a loop-hole, but simply a
hole, an opening.
<P>32, 33. <B>O . . . this!]</B> <SC>Vehse</SC> (i, 292) finds in these words the key to the tragedy.
<P>33. <B>Take, &amp;c.]</B> <SC>Jacox</SC> (Colburn's <I>New Monthly Mag.</I>, 1 July, 1867) has gathered an
entertaining collection of passages, parallel to this, from English and French literature.
<P>34. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 292) cites this line with a &lquo;Qu.&rquo; because of the repetition
of the word &lquo;feel.&rquo; But <SC>Dyce</SC> sees no reason for supposing it to be corrupt.
<P>35. <B>superflux]</B> <SC>Schmidt</SC>: A hapax legomenon in Sh.
<P>37. <SC>Coleridge</SC>: Edgar's assumed madness serves the great purpose of taking off
part of the shock which would otherwise be caused by the true madness of Lear,
and further displays the profound difference between the two. In every attempt at
representing madness throughout the whole range of dramatic literature, with the
single exception of Lear, it is mere lightheadedness, as especially in Otway. In
Edgar's ravings, Sh. all the while lets you see a fixed purpose, a practical end in
view;&mdash;in Lear's there is only the brooding of the one anguish, an eddy without
progression.
<P>37. <B>fathom and half]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: These words allude to his being bury'd in straw.</CC>

<P>45, 46. <B>Through . . . winds]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: This has the air of a quotation from
some lost poem. <SC>Schmidt</SC>: The majority of editors prefer the reading of the Qq
because it is more like line 95, and like a line in <I>The Friar of Orders Gray:</I> &lquo;See
through the hawthorn blows the cold wind, and drizzly rain doth fall.&rquo; For a similar
reason they adopt &lquo;go to thy cold bed and warm thee.&rquo;
<P>47. <B>thee]</B> This phrase occurs again in the <I>Ind.</I> to <I>Tam. the Shr.</I>, and in a note
on it there <SC>Theobald</SC> thinks that, because there is just before it a clear allusion to
a phrase in Kyd's <I>Spanish Tragedy</I>, this must also be &lquo;a Banter upon another verse
in that play,&rquo; viz: &lquo;What outcries pluck me from my naked bed?&rquo; But <SC>Capell</SC> is
probably right in thinking this latter allusion more than doubtful, for, as <SC>Staunton</SC>
says, &lquo;to an audience of Shakespeare's age there was nothing risible&rquo; either in this
phrase in <I>Lear</I> or in <I>The Spanish Tragedy.</I> &lquo;The phrase,&rquo; continues Staunton, &lquo;&ldquo;to
go to a cold bed&rdquo; meant only to go cold to bed; &ldquo;to rise from a naked bed&rdquo; sig-
nified to get up naked from bed, and to say one &ldquo;lay on a sick bed&rdquo; (a form of
expression far from uncommon even now) implied merely that he was lying sick
a-bed.&rquo; <SC>Delius</SC> in his first edition conjectured that the omission of &lquo;cold&rquo; in the Ff
was due to Shakespeare's having struck it out in order to avoid the comic effect which
it produced. This conjecture was not repeated in his second edition. But <SC>Dyce</SC>,
commenting on it, says that Sh. &lquo;has studiously made the assumed madness of Edgar</CC>

<P>53. <B>knives under his pillow]</B> To <SC>Theobald</SC> is due the credit of discovering
that here, and throughout Edgar's feigned madness, allusions are made to Harsnet's
<I>Declaration</I>, &amp;c. Thus: &lquo;While the Spaniards were preparing their Armado against
England, the Jesuits were here busily at work to promote the success by making con-
verts. One method they used, to do this, was to dispossess pretended demoniacks of
their own church; by which artifice they made several hundred converts among the
common people, and grew so elate upon their success as to publish an account of
their exploits in this wonderful talent of <I>exorcising.</I> A main scene of their business,
in this seeming-holy discipline, lay in the family of one Mr. Edmund Peckham;
where Marwood, a servant of Antony Babington's, Trayford, an attendant upon Mr.
Peckham, and Sarah and Friswood Williams, and Anne Smith (three chambermaids
in that family), were supposed to be possessed by devils, and came under the hands
of the priests for their cure. The parties either so little liked the discipline, or the
Jesuits behaved with such ill address, that the consequence was, the imposture was
discovered; the demoniacs were examined; and their confessions taken upon oath
before the Privy Council. The whole matter being blown up, the criminals brought
to the stake, and the trick of <I>Devil-hunting</I> brought into ridicule, Dr. Harsnet (who
was chaplain to Archbishop Bancroft, and himself afterwards Archbishop of York)
wrote a smart narrative of this whole proceeding under the following title: &ldquo;A
Declaration of egregious Popish Impostures, to withdraw the harts of her Majesties
Subjects from their allegeance, and from the truth of Christian Religion professed in
England, under the pretence of casting out devils. Practised by Edmunds, alias
Weston a Jesuit, and divers Romish priests his wicked associates. Whereunto are
annexed the Copies of the Confessions, and Examinations of the parties themselves,
which were pretended to be possessed, and dispossessed, taken upon oath before her
Majesties Commissioners for causes Ecclesiasticall. At London Printed by James</CC>

<CC><P>Roberts, dwelling in Barbican 1603.&rdquo; . . . The greatest part of Edgar's dissembled
lunacy, the names of his devils, and the descriptive circumstances he alludes to in
his own case, are all drawn from this pamphlet, and the confessions of the poor
deluded wretches.&rquo; In this mention of &lquo;knives&rquo; and &lquo;halters&rquo; there seems to be an
allusion to the following passage from Harsnet (which is here given as printed by
<SC>Staunton</SC>): &lquo;This examinant further saith, that one Alexander an apothecarie,
having brought with him from London to Denham on a time a new halter, and two
blades of knives, did leave the same upon the gallerie floare in her Maister's house.
The next morning he tooke occasion to goe with this examinant into the said gal-
lerie, where she espying the said halter and blades, asked Ma: Alexander what
they did there: Hee making the matter strange, aunswered, that he saw them not,
though hee looked fully upon them: she her selfe pointing to them with her finger,
where they lay within a yard of them, where they stoode both together. Now (quoth
this examinant) doe you not see them? and so taking them up, said, looke you heere:
Ah (quoth hee) now I see them indeed, but before I could not see them: And there-
fore saith he, I perceave that the devil hath layd them heere, to worke some mischiefe
upon you, that are possessed. Hereupon . . . a great search was made in the house,
to know how the said halter and knife blades came thether: but it could not in any
wise be found out, as it was pretended, till Ma: Mainy in his next fit said, as it was
reported, that the devil layd them in the Gallery, that some of those who were pos-
sessed, might either hang themselves with the halter, or kil themselves with the
blades.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Examination of Friswood Williams</I>, p. 219.

<P>56. <B>five wits]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC> (note on <I>Much Ado</I>, I, i, 66): &lquo;The wits seem to have
been reckoned five, by analogy of the five senses, or the five inlets of ideas.&rquo; In a
note on <I>Twelfth Night</I>, IV, ii, 92, <SC>Malone</SC> quotes from Stephen Hawes's poem
called <I>Graunde Amoure</I>, 1554, to show that the &lquo;five wits&rquo; were: &lquo;common wit,
imagination, fantasy, estimation, and memory.&rquo; That the five wits were confounded
with the five senses, <SC>Collier</SC> shows by a quotation from &lquo;the interlude of <I>The Worlde
and the Chylde</I>, printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1522, and introduced into vol. xii,
p. 334, of Dodsley's <I>Old Plays: &ldquo;Age.</I> Of the .v. wittes I wolde have knowynge.
<I>Perseuerance.</I> Forsoth, syr, herynge, seynge, and smellynge, The remenaunte
tastynge, and felynge: These ben the .v. wittes bodely.&rdquo;&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: Sh., however,
in his 141st <I>Sonnet</I>, considered the &lquo;five wits&rquo; as distinct from the five senses.

<P>83. <B>serving-man]</B> <SC>Knight</SC>: This is not a menial, but a <I>servant</I> in the sense in

<P>84. <B>curled my hair]</B> <SC>Malone</SC> cites from Harsnet: &lquo;Then Ma. Mainy, by the in-
stigation of the first of the seaven [spirits], began to set his hands unto his side,
<I>curled his hair</I>, and used such gestures as Ma. Edmunds [the exorcist] presently
affirmed that that spirit was <I>Pride.</I> Herewith he began to curse and banne, saying,
What a poxe do I here? I will stay no longer amongst a company of rascal priests,
but goe to the court, and brave it amongst my fellows, the noblemen there assem-
bled. . . . Shortly after they [the seven spirits] were all cast forth, and in such man-
ner as Ma. Edmunds directed them, which was, that every devil should depart in
some certaine forme representing either a beast or some other creature, that had the
resemblance of that sinne whereof he was the chief author: whereupon the spirit
of <I>pride</I> departed in the form of a <I>peacock;</I> the spirit of <I>sloth</I> in the likeness of an
<I>asse;</I> the spirit of <I>envie</I> in the similitude of a <I>dog;</I> the spirit of <I>gluttony</I> in the
forme of a <I>wolfe</I>, and the other devils had also in their departure their particular
likenesses agreeable to their natures.&rquo; <SC>Rushton</SC> (<I>Euphuism</I>, p. 47) cites from
Euphues, &lquo;Be not curious to curle thy haire,&rquo; &amp;c. [This may, perhaps, refer to
the &lquo;love-locks&rquo; that were worn by gallants in Shakespeare's day.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>84. <B>gloves]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC> thinks it but justice to mention an emendation which a
learned gentleman suggested to him, viz. that we should read &lquo;wore <I>cloves</I> in my
cap,&rquo; alluding to the fashion then in vogue of quilting spices and perfumes into the
linings of hats. Theobald, of course, dissents, and adds that it was &lquo;the custom to
wear gloves in the hat upon three different motives: as the favour of a mistress; in
honour of some other respected friend; or as a mark to be challeng'd by an adver-
sary where a duel was impending.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>: Portia, in her assumed character,
asks Bassanio for his gloves, which she says she will wear for his sake; and Henry
V gives the pretended glove of Alen&ccedil;on to Fluellen, which afterwards occasions his
quarrel with the English soldier.</CC>

<P>67. <B>lym]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: In Jonson's <I>Bartholomew Fair</I> [I, i]: &lquo;all the lime hounds
o' the city should have drawn after you by the scent.&rquo; A <I>limmer</I> or <I>leamer</I>, a dog
of the chase, was so called from the <I>leam</I> or <I>leash</I> in which he was held till he was
let slip. I have this information from Caius <I>de Canibus Britannicis.</I> So in the book
of <I>Antient Tenures</I> by T. B., 1679, the words &lquo;canes domini regis lesos&rquo; are trans-

<CC><P>72. <B>Sessa!]</B> See III, iv, 96. <SC>Steevens</SC>: It is difficult in this place to say what is

is it impossible but that this may be a part of some old song, and originally stood

into which the words naturally fall adds probability to this conjecture.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>As

nary dog: &lquo;Sessy, or <I>cesse</I>, is still used in some counties to encourage dogs to come
out of kennel,&rquo; &amp;c., &lquo;so here it may mean to encourage a dog to follow him to

probably like &lquo;sa, sa&rquo; below, a word used in following the hunt; being the name
