<P>73. <B>horn]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: I suppose Edgar to speak these words <I>aside.</I> [See Text.

for sustaining the character of Poor Tom are now exhausted; <I>my horn is dry;</I>&rquo; i. e.
has nothing more in it; and accordingly we have no more of his dissembled madness
till he meets his father in the next act, when he resumes it for a speech or two, but
not without expressing the same dislike of it that he expresses here: &lquo;I cannot daub
it further.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: A &lquo;horn&rquo; was usually carried about by every Tom of Bedlam,
to receive such drink as the charitable might afford him, with whatever scraps of food
they might give him. When, therefore, Edgar says <I>his horn is dry</I>, or <I>empty</I>, I con-
ceive he merely means, in the language of the character he assumes, to supplicate that

Persian come here, let him read this and pray for his soul. The Lord receive his
soul; for here lieth Maghmote (Mohammed) Shaughsware, who was born in the
town Noroy in Persia.&rquo; The joke on outlandish dress arises probably from the
presence of these Persians in London.

<CC><P>the Fool has disappeared, and Edgar has left to be the guide of his blind father, that
the king becomes absolutely wild and incoherent. The singular and undoubted fact
is, that few things tranquillize the insane more than the companionship of the insane.
It is a fact not easily explicable, but it is one of which, either by the intuition of
genius, or by the information of experience, Sh. appears to be aware.
<P>83. <B>noon]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: This facetious speech of the Fool is meant as a preparation
for losing him; for 'tis towards &lquo;noon&rquo; with the play (that is, towards the middle
of it) when he takes his leave of us in that speech. <SC>Cowden Clarke</SC>: This speech
is greatly significant, though apparently so trivial. It seems but a playful rejoinder
to his poor old royal master's witless words of exhaustion, but it is, in fact, a dis-
missal of himself from the scene of the tragedy and from his own short day of life.
The dramatist indeed has added one slight passing touch of tender mention (Kent's
saying, &lquo;Come, help to bear thy master; thou must not stay behind&rquo;) ere he withdraws
him from the drama altogether; but he seems by this last speech to let us know that
the gentle-hearted fellow who &lquo;much pined away&rquo; at Cordelia's going into France,
and who has since been subjected to still severer fret at his dear master's miseries,
has sunk beneath the accumulated burden, and has gone to his eternal rest even in
the very &lquo;noon&rquo; of his existence. <SC>Moberly</SC>: The poor creature's fate was sure to
be hard when he was separated from his master, under whose shelter he had offended
so many powerful persons. [See C. A. Brown's note, I, iv, 91.]

<CC><P>In deference to this consensus of authority we have retained it, though, as it seems
to us, internal evidence is conclusive against the supposition that the lines were
written by Sh. <SC>Delius</SC> (<I>New Sh. Soc. Trans.</I> 1875-6, p. 143): If we oppose this
view [of the Cam. Edd.], it is because we cannot comprehend how a spurious passage
appeared in the Qq; for we can hardly ascribe the authorship of the supposed in-
terpolation to the publisher, considering what we know of him and his method of
work. Neither can we suppose that he would attempt to amplify and improve the
MS before him of <I>King Lear</I>, as it was then performed. But even the internal
evidence, from which the Cam. Edd. might be inclined to condemn Edgar's mono-
logue, fails to convince us of its spuriousness. We readily admit that the style is
not that of the rest of the drama; but this difference may be explained in two ways,
partly by the form, and partly by the matter. Sh. is fond of introducing such rhyming
lines, $ormed of a number of pointed, epigrammatic, antithetical sentences. They
stand out from the surrounding blank verse, and point the moral of the preceding
situation, and the actions of the various characters. The second explanation is, that
the poet lays great stress on the parallelism existing between the families of Lear and
Gloucester, and takes this opportunity of impressing it again upon his audience. A
mere interpolator would hardly have known of this peculiar tendency of the poet, or
have carried it out so thoroughly, and in so pregnant a manner, as in the few but
thoroughly Shaksperian words: &lquo;He childed as I father'd.&rquo; For the same reason
it is more than improbable that Sh. should have cut out this passage [Delius is
arguing that the omissions in the Ff were not by Sh., but by the actors], therebv
thwarting his own purpose.

<P>59. <B>hell-black]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: This bold epithet is deriv'd probably from Hakluyt,
who in his third volume, p. 849, has the compound &lquo;hell-darke.&rquo; [Is it not high

<P>59. <B>buoy'd up]</B> <SC>Heath</SC>: Used here as the middle voice in Greek, signifying
to buoy, or lift, itself up. <SC>White</SC> considers &lquo;boil'd&rquo; a very plausible reading.
<SC>Schmidt</SC>: The verb is found in Sh. only here; the noun, in its ordinary significa-
tion, only in IV, vi, 19. The verb is here transitive, and the phrase means: the
sea would have lifted up the fixed fires and extinguished them.
<P>60. <B>stelled]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC>: An adjective coined from <I>stella.</I> In Latin we have
both <I>stellans</I> and <I>stellatus.</I> <SC>Schmidt</SC>: But Sh. uses a verb <I>to stell</I>, i. e. <I>to place, to
six:</I> &lquo;Mine eye hath played the painter, and hath stell'd Thy beauty's form in
table of my heart.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Son.</I> xxiv. [So also &lquo;To this well-painted piece is Lucrece
come, To find a face where all distress is stell'd.&rquo;&mdash;<I>R. of L.</I> 1444.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>62. <B>stern]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: <I>Dearne</I> of the Qq means lonely, solitary, obscure, melan-
choly, &amp;c. See <I>Per.</I> III, i, 15. &lquo;Stern,&rquo; however, is countenanced by a passage
in Chapman's <I>Homer, Iliad</I>, xxiv: &lquo;In this so sterne a time Of night and danger.&rquo;
<SC>Collier</SC> suggests that <I>dearn</I> was Shakespeare's word, but was misheard &lquo;stern.&rquo;

<CC><C>[64. <B>All cruels else subscribe]</B></C>
<P>the sight of his wretchedness. <SC>Capell</SC>: That is, subscrib'd to pity, subscrib'd or
assented to it's being exercis'd here. <SC>Collier, Dyce</SC>, and <SC>Singer</SC> adopt Johnson's
interpretation. <SC>Knight, Staunton</SC>, and <SC>White</SC> are silent. <SC>Cowden Clarke</SC> says
&lquo;cruels&rquo; is used for <I>cruelties</I>, as does also <SC>Wright</SC>, who refers to <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 9,
for adjectives used as nouns. <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 433,: That is, &lquo;All cruel acts to the con-
trary being yielded up, forgiven.&rquo; Compare for the meaning, IV, vii, 36, and For
&lquo;subscribe,&rquo; <I>Tro. and Cress.</I> IV, v, 105. Another explanation is, &lquo;all other cruel
animals being allowed entrance.&rquo; <SC>Jervis</SC> (p. 23) conjectures <I>quarrels.</I> <SC>Moberly</SC>:
All harshness otherwise natural being forborne or yielded from the necessity of the
time. <SC>Schmidt</SC>: &lquo;All cruels&rquo; can mean nothing else but <I>all cruel creatures.</I> In
turning adjectives into nouns, the old language went very far, but in no instance
farther than Sh. went in this phrase. In the singular, &lquo;cruel&rquo; is found in <I>Son.</I>
<*>xlix: &lquo;Canst thou, O cruel, say I love thee not?&rquo; The examples adduced by Abbott
refer also to the singular. At all events it is proved by them (as well as by the
passages cited in the present writer's <I>Lexicon</I>, p. 1415) that <I>the cruel</I>, as a sub-
stantive, can only mean <I>the cruel person</I> or <I>thing</I>, not <I>cruelty;</I> as little can <I>the old</I>
mean old age, or <I>the young</I> mean youth. All interpretations, therefore, which involve
this abstract idea are inadmissible. Even those editors who interpret &lquo;cruels&rquo; cor-
rectly adopt <I>subscribed</I> of the Qq, and hold it to be the imperfect tense. It is far
better to follow the Folio and to interpret the sentence thus: &lquo;Everything, which is at
other times cruel, shows feeling or regard; you alone have not done so.&rquo; Sh. uses
the phrase to <I>subscribe to something</I> in the sense of declaring one's self conquered
by something, of yielding, complying. It is used exactly in the same sense as here,
in <I>Tro. and Cress.</I> IV, v, 105: &lquo;For Hector in his blaze of wrath subscribes To
tender objects,&rquo; that is, Hector yields if he is brought face to face with anything
touching or tender; he is sensible to tender impressions. [This is to me the most
puzzling phrase in this play, more puzzling even than &lquo;runaways&rquo; eyes' or &lquo;the
dram of eale&rquo;; the multitude of emendations proposed for these latter show how easily
the idea of the phrase is grasped; anybody, and everybody, is ready with an emenda-
tion there; here it is different. None of the interpretations are, to my mind, satis-
factory. The latest, Mr <SC>Joseph Crosby's</SC> (<I>Epitome of Lit.</I>, 1 June, 1879), refers
&lquo;cruels&rquo; to <I>feelings</I>, (which is, to me, &lquo;far wide,&rquo;) and emphasizes &lquo;else.&rquo; He thus
paraphrases: &lquo;All thy <I>feelings</I>, no matter how cruel or inhuman &ldquo;else,&rdquo; <I>i. e. at any
other time</I>, or under any other circumstances, having &ldquo;subscribed,&rdquo; <I>i. e. succumbed</I>,
to the terrors of that storm, and <I>yielded</I> to the pity for the old king, thy father.&rquo; In
a case as puzzling as this, anything, as Dr Johnson says elsewhere, may be tried; my
attempt is seen in the text. Not unnaturally, I think it is the true reading; it adheres
to the venerable authority of the First Folio, making &lquo;subscribe&rquo; an imperative like
&lquo;turn.&rquo; The drift of the whole passage is the contrast between the treatment which
Regan's father had received and that which would have been dealt, in that stern time,
to wolves and other animals, howsoever cruel. &lquo;Thou shouldst have said: Good
porter, open the gates, acknowledge the claims of all creatures, however cruel they
may be at other times;&rquo; or, perhaps: &lquo;open the gates; give up all cruel things else,&rquo;
<I>i. e.</I> forget that they are cruel. As in I, ii, 24, Lear &lquo;subscribed&rquo; his powers, so here
the porter should &lquo;subscribe all cruels,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> he should surrender, yield, give up what-
soever was cruel in the poor beasts, and see only their claim to his compassion. An
exactly parallel use of &lquo;subscribe&rquo; cannot perhaps be found in Sh.; and if this be</CC>

<P>66. <SC>Capell</SC>: The barbarity exercis'd upon Gloucester is indeed a part of the story
that was the source of this episode, for that &lquo;Paphlagonian king's&rquo; eyes were put out
by a son; but the putting-out of poor Gloucester's seems to be more immediately
copy'd from <I>Selimus.</I> <SC>Steevens</SC>: In <I>Selimus, Emperor of the Turks</I>, one of the
sons of Bajazet <I>pulls out the eyes</I> of an Aga on the stage, and says: &lquo;Yes thou shalt
live, but never see that day, Wanting the tapers that should give thee light. [<I>Pulls
out his eyes.</I>&rquo; Immediately after, his hands are cut off. I have introduced this
passage to show that Shakespeare's drama was not more sanguinary than that of his
contemporaries. <SC>Malone</SC>: In Marston's <I>Antonio's Revenge</I>, 1602, Piero's tongue is
torn out on the stage. <SC>Davies</SC> (<I>Dram. Misc.</I> ii, 197): After all, Sh. might possibly
contrive not to execute this horrible deed upon the stage, though it is so quoted in
the book. . . . At the present, the sufferer is forced into some adjoining room; and
the ears of the audience are more hurt by his cries than their eyes can be when he
is afterwards led on the stage. The gold-beaters' skin, applied to the sockets, as if to
staunch the bleeding, abates something perhaps of the hideousness of the spectacle.
<SC>Coleridge</SC>: &lquo;What can I say of this scene?&mdash;There is my reluctance to think Shake-
speare wrong, and yet &mdash;.&rquo; Elsewhere Coleridge says: &lquo;I will not disguise my
conviction that in this one point the tragic in this play has been urged beyond the
outermost mark and <I>ne plus ultra</I> of the dramatic.&rquo; <SC>Tieck</SC> (vol. ix, p. 368, ed.
1833): This scene, which is manifestly too horrible, and shocks our very senses, is
rendered still worse by the explanation and the scenery that are intruded. Almost
always when, now-a-days, such a scenic representation is attempted, false methods
are employed, because the architecture and arrangements of the old theatre are not
kept in mind, but confounded with our modern constructions. . . . The chair, in which
Gloster is bound, is the same from which, elevated in the centre of the scene, Lear
first speaks. This lesser stage, in the centre, when not used was hidden by a cur-
tain, that was drawn aside whenever it was necessary. Thus Sh., like all the dra-
matists of the time, often had two scenes at once. The nobles in <I>Henry VIII</I> are
standing in the ante-chamber, the curtain is drawn, and we are directly in the chamber
of the king. So also, when Cranmer has to wait in the ante-chamber, the council
room opens. Thus there was this advantage, that through the pillars, which sep-
arated this little stage in the centre from the proscenium or stage proper, there could
be represented not only a double action, but also at the same time it might be half or
partly hidden, and so two scenes might be represented which were perfectly intelligible,
although not everything on the lesser stage was visible. Thus Gloster sate, probably
out of sight, while Cornwall, near him, was seen, Regan standing in the fore-stage,
lower than Cornwall, but close by him, with the attendants on the stage itself. Corn-
wall, horribly enough, tears out Gloster's eye, but the act is not positively seen; some</CC>

<CC><C>[66. <B>The blinding of Gloucester.]</B></C>
<P>of the servants, holding the chair, stand in the way, and the curtain on one side (for
it was divided into two) was drawn before the spectator. The expression that Corn-
wall uses, &lquo;Upon these eyes of thine I'll set my foot,&rquo; is not to be taken literally; it
certainly is not so intended. During the speech of Cornwall's, one of the servants
rushes up to the higher stage and wounds him; Regan, who is below, snatches a sword
from another attendant and stabs the servant from behind. The groups are all in
motion, and, while attention is distracted, Gloster loses his other eye. His cry is
heard, but he is not seen. He disappears, for there was egress from the lesser stage
also. Cornwall and Regan come forward and retire by the side scene, and the scene
ends with the talk of some of the attendants. It is in this way, which some-
what lessens its horror, that the scene pictures itself to my mind. The Poet
trusted, indeed, to the strong minds of his friends who were to be so much moved by
the general horrors of the representation, as not to linger over the bloody particulars.
<SC>Ulrici</SC> (p. 458): To have the scene where Cornwall puts out Gloster's eyes repre-
sented directly on the stage, can only arouse a feeling of disgust, which has nothing
in common with the idea of beauty, nor with that of grandeur, power, or sublimity,
and which, consequently, can only impair the effect of the tragedy. Whether or not
the nerves of Shakespeare's public may have been of a stronger fibre than those of
the present generation,&mdash;it is not the business of art to consider strong or weak nerves,
but to aim only at the strengthening, the refreshing, and elevating of the mind and
feelings, and such scenes do not effect this even in the case of the strongest nerves.
<SC>Heraud</SC> (<I>Inner Life of Sh.</I> p. 304): In this scene Pity and Terror, the especial
elements of the Tragic, are urged to their utmost limits. Of course there was danger
of excess. But Sh. was on his guard. He might have justified the act by the sup-
posed barbarity of the legendary age whose manners he was tracing, and urged
that their familiarity with such acts prevented the actors in them from recognising
the horrible. No such thing. By inserting in the group a servant who <I>did</I> recognise
its intrinsic horror, and compassionated the sufferer, he converted disgust into pity
The other servants also compassionate the blind old man, and lead him out to help
him, to heal his wounds, and to place him in safe custody. The entire current of
feeling is turned in the direction of pity by the force of sympathy. Thus the horror
in the &lquo;horrid act&rquo; is mitigated, and reduced to the level of terror, which feeling is
enforced by &lquo;the fearful looking-for&rquo; of a coming vengeance, of which an instalment
is secured even in the moment of crime. And this sentiment, too, is expressed by
the servants who act as chorus to the scene. W. W. <SC>Lloyd</SC>: The horrors, like the
indelicacies that are met with in Shakespeare's plays, are never admitted for their
own sakes, never but when absolutely indispensable for his great aim and purpose,
the defining of character, and that complete exhibition of nature with which,&mdash;
recognising in art the same rigour that is challenged by science,&mdash;he allowed nothing
to interfere. The mere convenience of stage-management, it might be said, would
dictate that Gloucester should sit in the chair with his back to the audience, and it
is not even then very apparent why the deed of mutilation should be so much more
shocking than the smothering and the death agonies of Desdemona; it is not worth
denying, however, that if only by usage of theatrical associations it would be so,
and if, as I believe, the painfulness and the horror would not be utterly insupportable,
it must be from a different cause. The cruel act is revolting to think of, and much
more to behold, and yet is the revolting cruelty less heinous than the treatment of</CC>

<CC><P>Lear, though there the physical injury was comparatively slight,&mdash;the exposure of age
and weakness to a pitiless storm,&mdash;and in itself, however well the storm might be
imitated, less harrowing to the feelings. But Sh. evidently relied upon the response
of the sympathies of his audience to the appeal of his art, and he had confidence in
his power to depict the mental anguish, and sufferings, and injuries of the king with
such force that no inferior infliction could supersede it in our interest. If the heart
is touched as it should be by the great scene of the storm, and then by the pitiable
spectacle of the wit-wrecked monarch in the indoors scene, mingling the fantastic
freaks of lunacy with the majesty of sorrow, we shall be aware that the mere narra-
tion of any physical suffering or cruelty whatever must have failed to rouse another
start of indignation. To any other excitement the sensibilities might well seem
lulled or seared, and the exhibition of the act was therefore necessary if it was to
take place at all, and was therefore possible; and the poet daringly and successfully
availed himself of the opportunity to cast the last disgrace upon filial ingratitude, by
exposing its surpassing hatefulness in comparison with the direst crime, acted under
our eyes with every detail of horror.

<CC><P>1. <B>Yet . . . and known]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: The meaning is, &lquo;'Tis better <I>to be</I> thus con-
temned and <I>known</I> to yourself <I>to be contemned.</I>&rquo; Or, perhaps, there is an error,
which may be rectified thus: &lquo;Yet better thus <I>unknown</I> to be contemned.&rquo; When
a man divests himself of his real character he feels no pain from contempt, because
he supposes it incurred only by a voluntary disguise which he can throw off at
pleasure. I do not think any correction necessary. <SC>Sir Joshua Reynolds</SC>: The
meaning seems to be this: &lquo;Yet it is better to be thus in this fixed and acknowledged
contemptible state, than, living in affluence, to be flattered and despised at the same
time.&rquo; He who is placed in the worst and lowest state has this advantage: he lives
in hope, and not in fear, of a reverse of fortune. The lamentable change is from
affluence to beggary. He laughs at the idea of changing for the worse who is
already as low as possible. <SC>Collier</SC>: &lquo;Unknown,&rquo; which is from the (MS), accords
with Johnson's suggestion, and is certainly right. &lquo;Yes&rquo; for <I>Yet</I> may be doubted,
but we feel authorized to insert it by the excellence of the ensuing, and more im-
portant emendation. Edgar enters, giving his assent to some proposition he has
stated to himself before he came upon the stage. <SC>Singer</SC> (in <I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 1 Ser. vi,
6, 1852) expressed his approval of Johnson's emendation, but afterwards, in his ed.
2, withdrew it. <SC>Schmidt</SC>: &lquo;Known to be contemned&rquo; means here conscious of, and
familiar with, contempt.
<P>2. <B>worst]</B> <SC>Tyrwhitt</SC>, adopting Johnson's emendation, thought this line should
read: &lquo;Than still contemned and flatter'd to be <I>worse.</I>&rquo;
<P>3. <B>dejected thing]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: That is, thing dejected by fortune. For this posi-
tion of the participle, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 419a [or <SC>Walker</SC>, <I>Crit.</I> i, 160].</CC>

<CC><P>9. <B>Owes nothing]</B> <SC>Hudson</SC>: They have done their worst upon him, and so
absolved him from all obligations of gratitude.
<P>10, 12. <B>World . . . age]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC> (<I>Sh. Rest.</I> p. 172): My late ingenious friend,
<SC>Dr Sewell</SC>, gave me this conjecture, &lquo;make us <I>bate</I> thee,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> if the many changes
in life did not induce us to <I>abate from</I>, and <I>make</I> allowances for, some of the bad
casualties, we should never endure to live to old age. My explanation is: If the
number of changes and vicissitudes which happen in life did not make us <I>wait</I>, and
hope for some turn of fortune for the better, we could never support the thought of
living to be old on any other terms. [He reads, therefore, &lquo;make us <I>wait</I> thee.&rquo;]
<SC>Capell</SC> [adopting Theobald's <I>wait</I>]: Life has often such evils, and man sees
himself in such situations, that nothing but the hopes of their changing, that
&lquo;esperance&rquo; which Edgar talks of before, prevents his putting an end to, it at any
part of it's course, and before age; he would not stay to see age, age would not be
his finisher. <SC>Malone</SC>: O world! if reverses of fortune and changes such as I now
see and feel, from ease and affluence to poverty and misery, did not show us the
little value of life, we should never submit with any kind of resignation to the
weight of years, and its necessary consequence, infirmity and death.
<P>11. <B>hate]</B> <SC>Nichols</SC> (<I>Notes</I>, &amp;c., No. 2, p. 6) finds here a confirmation of his
belief that &lquo;hatred is a conservative passion, and supplies us with powers of endur-
ance little short of those supplied by piety itself,&rquo; and announces that Shakespeare
herein shows himself &lquo;to have been no mean psychologist.&rquo;
<P>14. <B>tenant]</B> <SC>Cowden Clarke</SC>: We imagine the old man who here speaks to be
the occupant of the farm-house in which Gloucester placed Lear for shelter, and that
the servants who propose to &lquo;get the Bedlam to lead the old earl,&rquo; not finding the
supposed beggar, have left the blind nobleman in charge of his faithful tenant.</CC>

<CC><P>20. <B>means secure us]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: That is, our moderate, mediocre condition.
<SC>Jennens</SC>: &lquo;Means&rquo; may perhaps be understood to be <I>mean things</I> (using the adjec
tive substantively), i. e. <I>advers&aelig; res.</I> <SC>Capell</SC>: <I>Mean</I> is mean or middle condition;
and the maxim seems to arise from this reflection in Gloucester,&mdash;that, had he been
a man in that station, he had 'scap'd these calamities; his &lquo;defects&rquo; (his want of
fortune and title) had screen'd him from the machinations of wickedness, and so
prov'd his commodities. <SC>Knight</SC> [the first, I think, to give the true interpretation]:
&lquo;Means&rquo; is here used only in the common sense of resources, powers, capacities.
The means, such as we possess, are our securities, and further, our mere defects
prove advantages. <SC>Rankin</SC> (<I>Philosophhy of Sh.</I>, 1841, p. 178): Our abilities and
powers make us rash and unwary. <SC>Delius</SC> agrees substantially with Knight. F. W. J.
(<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I>, 1 Ser. viii, 4, 1853) [following Knight's interpretation, paraphrases]:
&lquo;When I had eyes I walked carelessly; when I had the &ldquo;means&rdquo; of seeing and
avoiding stumbling-blocks, I stumbled and fell, because I walked without care and
watchfulness. Our deficiencies, our weaknesses (the sense of them), make us use
such care and exertions as to prove advantages to us.&rquo; As parallel, the following
passages in the Bible are cited: 1 <I>Cor.</I> x, 12; <I>Ps.</I> x, 6; 2 <I>Cor.</I> xii, 9, 10. Also,
&lquo;Secure thy heart.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Timon</I> II, ii, 184. [The following excellent illustration is
given]: &lquo;The <I>means</I> of the hare (<I>i. e.</I> her swiftness) secured her; the defects of the
tortoise (her slowness) proved her commodity.&rquo; To the same effect <SC>Wordsworth</SC>
(<I>Sh. Knowledge of the Bible</I>, 248): &lquo;Means,&rquo; in Gloucester's case, is his sight.
W. R. <SC>Arrowsmith</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I>, 1 Ser. xii, p. 1855) contends that &lquo;means&rquo; here
bears the same meaning that it does in common parlance. &lquo;If man's power were
equal to his will, into what excesses might he not be betrayed, ruinous to himself, as
well as hurtful to others; but happily for him an over-ruling Providence so orders
matters that man's means, his circumscribed and limited means, become his security,
keep him safe.&rquo; <SC>White</SC>: &lquo;Secure&rquo; here means to render careless,&mdash;a radical
sense,&mdash;as it does in <I>Timon</I>, II, ii, 184. <SC>Halliwell</SC>: The term &lquo;means&rquo; is here
used for the <I>want of means</I>, the low state of our means. This usage is not unusual
in writers of the time. <SC>Wright</SC>; Things we think meanly of, our mean or moderate
condition, are our security. Although as an adjective &lquo;secure&rquo; often means &lquo;care-
less,&rquo; I know of no instance of the verb meaning &lquo;to render careless.&rquo; <SC>Moberly</SC>:
&lquo;Secure us&rquo; means &lquo;make us over-secure,&rquo; as we have &lquo;a secure fool,&rquo; &lquo;not jealous
nor secure,&rquo; &amp;c. &amp;c. The antithesis then becomes &lquo;while we are made careless by
the advantages on which we reckoned, we are saved by something which seemed a
weak point.&rquo; The allusion may be to the fable of the stag, endangered by the horns</CC>

<CC><P>which he admired, and saved by the legs which he despised. <SC>Schmidt</SC> gives two
instances of the use of &lquo;secure&rquo; as a verb meaning <I>to render careless;</I> one is the
passage in <I>Tim.</I> II, ii, 184, already cited by F. W. J. and <SC>White</SC>; and the other is
<I>Oth.</I> I, iii, 10: &lquo;I do not so secure me in the error.&rquo; Furthermore, <SC>Schmidt</SC> says
that the signification of &lquo;means&rquo; as &lquo;moderate condition&rquo; is unknown in Sh., and per-
haps in the whole range of the English language. [The various emendations that have
been proposed are as follows:] <SC>Theobald</SC> (<I>Sh. Rest.</I> p. 177) conjectured &lquo;Our means
<I>ensnare</I> us&rquo;; but did not afterwards repeat it in his edition. <SC>Hanmer's</SC> text reads:
&lquo;Meanness secures us.&rquo; <SC>Johnson</SC>: I do not remember that <I>mean</I> is ever used as a
substantive for low fortune, which is the sense here required, nor for mediocrity, except
in the phrase, the &lquo;golden mean.&rquo; I suspect the passage of corruption, and would read:
&lquo;Our means <I>seduce</I> us,&rquo; or &lquo;Our <I>maims</I> secure us.&rquo; That hurt or deprivation which
makes us defenceless proves our safeguard. This is very proper in Gloucester, newly
maimed by the evulsion of his eyes. <SC>Hunter</SC> (<I>New Illust.</I> ii, 272) proposed, without
comment other than that the passage as it now stands cannot be right, &lquo;Our <I>meanness
suc<*>ours</I> us.&rquo; <SC>Anon.</SC> (<I>Gent. Mag.</I>, Aug. 1845, p. 117): Does the exact point of cor-
ruption in the text lie in &lquo;means&rquo; or &lquo;our?&rquo; Can it be &lquo;<I>Poor</I> means secure us,&rquo; &amp;c.?
A. E. B[<SC>rae</SC>] (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 1 Ser. vii, 592, 1853): There are two verbs, one in every-day
use, the other obsolete, which, although of nearly opposite significations, and of very
dissimilar sound, nevertheless differ only in the mutual exchange of place in two
letters: these verbs are <I>secure</I> and <I>recuse</I>; the first implying <I>assurance;</I> the second,
<I>want of assurance</I>, or refusal. Hence any sentence would receive an opposite
meaning from one of these verbs to what it would from the other. In the present
passage one would suppose that the obvious opposition between <I>means</I> and <I>defects</I>
would have preserved these words from being tampered with; and that, on the other
hand, the <I>absence</I> of opposition between <I>secure</I> and <I>commodious</I> would have directed
attention to the real error. But no: all the worritting has been about <I>means.</I> Read,
therefore, &lquo;Our means <I>recuse</I> us,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Singer</SC> (ed. 2): <I>Meanes</I> of the old copy is
possibly a typographical error for <I>needes;</I> the words being easily confounded in old
MSS. The context shows that <I>needs</I> was probably what Sh. wrote. [&lquo;Needs&rquo; is in
Singer's text.] <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. 2): <I>Meanes</I> is corrected to <I>wants</I> in the (MS), and so
we print with confidence; the context shows that the emendation is required, how-
ever much misplaced ingenuity may insist that the old text ought to be preserved.
<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 281): There can be no doubt that Johnson's <I>maims</I> is the right
reading. One of the numberless passages which illustrate the old pronunciation of <I>ea.</I>
<SC>Lettsom</SC> [Foot-note to the foregoing]: Hooker's <I>Ecclesiastical Polity</I>, b. v, sect. lxv:
&lquo;If men of so good experience and insight in the maims of our weak flesh, have
thought,&rquo; &amp;c. b. v, sect. xxiv, 3: &lquo;In a minister, ignorance and disability to teach
is a maim.&rquo; Greene, <I>James the Fourth</I>, Dyce, vol. ii, p. 145: &lquo;But, sir Divine to
you; look on your maims, Divisions, sects, your simonies, and bribes,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Hudson</SC>
adopts <I>maims.</I>
<P>23. <B>see thee in]</B> <SC>Keightley</SC>: The proper word of course is <I>feel</I>, not &lquo;see&rquo;; but
the text may be right. We might also read <I>by</I> for &lquo;in.&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>39. <B>Angering]</B> <SC>Heath</SC>: He at the same time displeases himself and the person
he endeavors to amuse.
<P>46. <B>times']</B> <SC>Dyce</SC> shows by several examples [which Schmidt's <I>Lex.</I> will supply]
that this is the plural. <SC>Moberly</SC>: When enthusiasts madden the ignorant. The ele-
ments were already working in England which produced the Fifth Monarchy and the
Blackfriars' fanatics, Naylor, General Harrison, and the like.
<P>49. <B>'parel]</B> For a long list of words in which the prefix is dropped, see <SC>Abbott</SC>,
&sect; 460. We have &lquo;'filed&rquo; for <I>defiled</I> in <I>Macb.</I> III, i, 65, which is not in Abbott's

<CC><P>63, 64. <B>that . . . happier]</B> <SC>Wordsworth</SC> (p. 216): That is, because my wretch-
edness now teaches me to compassionate those who are in distress.
<P>65. <B>superfluous]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Lear has before uttered the same sentiment, which
indeed cannot be too strongly impressed, though it may be too often repeated.
<SC>Eccles</SC>: Sentiments like these can no more be too often repeated than too strongly
impressed, when recommended by such varied elegance and beauty of expression.
<P>66. <B>slaves]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: Gloucester is speaking of such who by an uninter-
rupted course of prosperity are grown wanton, and callous to the misfortunes of
others; such as those who, fearing no reverse, slight and neglect, and therefore may
be said to <I>brave</I>, the ordinance of heaven. Which is certainly the right reading.
<SC>Heath</SC>: The meaning is, Who, instead of paying the deference and submission due
to your ordinance, treats it as his slave, by making it subservient to his views of
pleasure or interest. <SC>Johnson</SC>: To <I>slave</I> or <I>beslave</I> another is to treat him with
indignity; in a kindred sense, to &lquo;slave the ordinance&rquo; may be to slight or ridicule
it. [In support of Heath's interpretation, which is undoubtedly the true one,]
<SC>Steevens</SC> cites Heywood's <I>Brazen Age:</I> &lquo;none Could slave him like the Lydian
Omphale.&rquo; Massinger's <I>A New Way to Pay Old Debts</I>, IV, iii: &lquo;the smooth brow
Of a pleased sire, that slaves me to his will.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: See Webster's <I>Malcon-
tent</I>, IV, i: &lquo;O powerful blood! how dost thou slave their soul.&rquo; <SC>Wright</SC>: Com-
pare B. and Fl. <I>The False One</I>, V, iv: &lquo;Nay, grant they had slav'd my body, my
free mind,&rquo; &amp;c.; and Middleton, <I>The Roaring Girl</I> (Works, ii, 445, ed. Dyce).
&lquo;Fortune, who slaves men, was my slave.&rquo;
<P>66. <B>ordinance]</B> <SC>Moberly</SC>: The ordinance meant is probably what the parable
of Dives and Lazarus expresses, that ignorance of the sufferings of those near us is
itself a crime. <SC>Schmidt</SC>: Here it must be taken in the sense of the established
order of things, law of nature. <SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 96): &lquo;Read: &ldquo;that <I>slanders</I> your ordi-
nance,&rdquo; <I>i. e.</I> that disparages it, casts reproach or contumely upon it, discredits it.&rquo;
To meet the objection to <I>slander</I> on the score of metre, Bailey cites Walker's <I>Vers.</I> 69,
where this word is given among the dissyllables which Chaucer uses metrically as
monosyllables, and thinks that &lquo;the objection is more than countervailed by the apt-
ness of the term for the place.&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>71. <B>There is, &amp;c.]</B> <SC>Moberly</SC>: It is remarkable that Gloucester goes to Dover,
not, as Regan laughingly says, that he may now do his worst in treason, but simply
that he may throw himself from the cliff in utter despair. The fact is, that this
interpolated part of the plot is one of the many instances of Shakespeare's homage
to Sir Philip Sidney; to pay which he does not hesitate to make a certain sacrifice
of probability. In the <I>Arcadia</I> (p. 160) we have &lquo;a prince of Paphlagonia, who,
being ill-treated by his son, goes to the top of a high rock to cast himself down.&rquo;
(But how slight is the hint in the romance compared with the magnificent use which
Shakespeare makes of it!) So in <I>Pericles</I>, i, 1, we have taken from Sidney's <I>Arcadia</I>
(p. 149) the expression, &lquo;The Senate-house of planets all did sit, To knit in her their
best perfections.&rquo; And in <I>As You Like It</I>, the celebrated passage about &lquo;tongues in
trees,&rquo; &amp;c., is an adaptation from Sidney's <I>Astrophel.</I>
<P>72. <B>Looks fearfully]</B> <SC>Moberly</SC>: The beetling top of the cliff seems to be look-
ing down with alarm over the sea which it hems in. This description seems as if
no particular Dover cliff were meant, as the cliffs there are not really perpendicular.
<P>72. <B>in]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: Sh. considered the sea as a mirrour. To look <I>in</I> a glass is yet
our colloquial phraseology. <SC>Wright</SC> says &lquo;in&rquo; is here equivalent to <I>into</I>, and cites
<I>Rich. III:</I> I, ii, 261: &lquo;But first I'll turn you fellow in his grave.&rquo; [For similar
instances, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 159.] <SC>Schmidt</SC> agrees with Malone.
<P>72. <B>confined]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: Pent in straits.</CC>

<CC><P>29. <B>I . . . whistle]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC> strangely interprets this as an allusion to Edmund's
love: &lquo;though you disregard me thus, I have found one who thinks me worth calling.&rquo;
<SC>Steevens</SC>: This expression is in Heywood's <I>Proverbs:</I> &lquo;A poore dogge that is not
woorth the whystlyng.&rquo;
<P>31. <B>fear]</B> Equivalent to <I>fear for;</I> see <I>Ham.</I> I, iii, 51.
<P>32, 33. <B>That . . . itself]</B> <SC>Heath</SC>: That nature which is arrived to such a pitch
of unnatural degeneracy, as to contemn its origin, cannot from thenceforth be re-
strained within any certain bounds whatever, but is prepared to break out into the
most monstrous excesses every way, as occasion or temptation may offer. <SC>Cowden
Clarke</SC>: &lquo;Cannot be border'd certain in itself&rquo; means, cannot comprise reliable
component substance in itself. <SC>Schmidt</SC>: &lquo;Certain&rquo; is equivalent to <I>fixed, firm.</I>
<P>32. <B>it]</B> See I, iv, 209.
<P>33. <B>border'd]</B> <SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 97): Surely we ought to read here <I>order'd</I> in the sense
of <I>regulated.</I> The blunder seems to have arisen from the preceding &lquo;be.&rquo;
<P>35. <B>material sap]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: That whereby a branch is nourished, and in-
creases in bulk by fresh accession of matter. [After criticising Theobald's suggestion
of &lquo;<I>maternal</I> sap,&rquo; Warburton cites an instance in Theobald's favour, where, in the
title of an old book, &lquo;material&rquo; is apparently equivalent to <I>maternal:</I> &lquo;Sir John
Froissart's Chronicle translated out of Frenche into our material English Tongue
by John Bouchier, printed 1525.&rquo;] <SC>Jennens</SC>: The force of Albany's argument to
prove that a branch torn from a tree must infallibly wither and die, lies in this, that it
is separated from a communication with that which supplies it with the very identical
matter by which it (the branch) lives, and of which it is composed. <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. 2):
Might not <I>natural</I>, in spite of the irregularity of the rhythm, be the word of the poet?
<SC>Schmidt</SC>: From Shakespeare's use of &lquo;material&rquo; elsewhere, in the sense of <I>full of
matter</I>, and hence of <I>importance</I>, it is not easy to explain it here. Theobald's sug-
gestion is appropriate and ingenious, but unfortunately Sh. knows not the word.

<CC><P>54, 55. <B>Fools . . . mischief]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>, as is noted above, refers this to
Gloucester, but <SC>Capell</SC> contends that it could not apply to him, because &lquo;he had
done the harm he was punish'd for, he had reliev'd Lear, and sent him away; but,
horrid as it may seem, her father is the &ldquo;villain,&rdquo; who, according to this lady, is to
be pity'd of none but &ldquo;fools;&rdquo; he, indeed, is &ldquo;punish'd&rdquo; ere any mischief is done by
him.&rquo; <SC>Eccles</SC>: Possibly, she means that persons who harbour evil intentions, but,
through irresolution, or dread of consequences, delay the execution of them till dis-
appointment or punishment overtake them, obtain pity from none but &lquo;fools,&rquo; as men
of sense generally discern the disposition of their hearts. This also serves as an
apology for her own precipitation, and a censure upon the pusillanimity in her hus-
band. It may indeed be objected to this interpretation that she appears thereby to
stamp villainy upon her own conduct, but her words may imply: &lquo;We have mischief
in hand, which it is expedient to effect; if so, the more speedily it is accomplished
the better; for, even if our proceeding merited your imputation, still it is to be con-
sidered that only &ldquo;Fools do these villains pity,&rdquo;&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Malone</SC>: It is not clear
whether this fiend means her father or the King of France. If her words have a
retrospect to Albany's speech, which the word &lquo;pity&rquo; might lead us to suppose, Lear
must be referred to; if they are considered as connected with what follows, &lquo;Where's
thy drum?&rquo; &amp;c., the other interpretation must be adopted. The latter appears to me
the true one, and perhaps the punctuation of the Qq, in which there is only a comma
after &lquo;mischief,&rquo; ought to have been preferred. <SC>Singer</SC>: Surely there cannot be a
doubt that she refers to her father, and to the &lquo;pity&rquo; for his sufferings expressed by
Albany, whom she means indirectly to call a &lquo;fool&rquo; for expressing it. [She cannot
refer to Gloucester, because Albany is ignorant of what had been done to him, and
she herself had left Gloucester's castle before the blinding was accomplished. It is
difficult to believe that she refers to Lear; may it not be that she refers to Albany
himself? She has told him that his preachment about her father was foolish, and</CC>

<CC><P>that he should drop the subject. Is it likely that she would resume it? On the con-
trary, she wishes, as soon as possible, to turn the tables, and put him to his defence,
therefore she launches into bitter railing against his supineness; he is &lquo;milk liver'd,&rquo;
with no sense of honour, &amp;c. &amp;c., and is ignorant that none but fools will have any
pity for villains, like himself, who are punished before they have struck a blow.
Thus interpreted, the taunting question, &lquo;where's thy drum?&rquo; follows keen, like the
lash to a whip. I have not, therefore, put a period after &lquo;mischief,&rquo; as is done in
every other edition since Hanmer's, but have adhered to the Qq, which have merely
a comma.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>57. <B>thy . . . threat]</B> This is <SC>Jennens's</SC> emendation and text, erroneously attributed
in the Cam. ed. to <SC>Eccles</SC>. Through some oversight Jennens's edition seems to have
been somewhat slighted by the Cam. Edd.; many of the readings attributed in their
textual notes to &lquo;Steevens 1778&rquo; should be given to Jennens. In fact Jennens's text,
in this play, owing to a preference for the Qq, which he shares to a certain extent
with the Cam. Edd., agrees, in disputed passages, as closely perhaps as any other,
except Dyce's, in his first edition, with that of the Cambridge edition.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>

<SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) adds, <I>As You Like It</I>, II, vii, 29.
<P>60. <B>Proper deformity]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: Diabolic qualities appear not so horrid in

of Albany's next speech, be-monsters the &lquo;feature&rquo; or peculiar characteristic personal
traits. <SC>Delius</SC>: That is, a deformity which conceals itself under a pleasing, fair
outside, and which appears all the more horrid from its internal contrast. Compare
<I>Twelfth Night</I>, II, ii, 30: &lquo;proper-false,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> externally fair, internally false.

as &lquo;specious&rquo; instead of &lquo;horrid&rquo; in the next line.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Wright</SC> refers to 2 <I>Hen.

<CC><P>62. <B>self-cover'd]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: I cannot but think that this means, thou that hast
<I>disguised</I> nature by wickedness; thou that hast <I>hid</I> the woman under the fiend.
<SC>Henley</SC>: Goneril, having thrown off the convenient seeming of female gentleness,
now no longer played the hypocrite, but exhibited in her face the self-same passions
she had covered in her heart. <SC>Malone</SC>: Thou who hast put a <I>covering on thyself</I>
which nature did not give thee. The covering which Albany means is, the semblance
and appearance of a fiend. <SC>Steevens</SC>: Perhaps there is an allusion to the envelope
which the maggots of some insects furnish to themselves. Voss (iii, 643, Leipzig,
1819) suggests <I>fell</I>-cover'd: &lquo;Albany refers to the expression of satanic unwoman-
liness which covers her face like a dark cloud.&rquo; <SC>Hudson</SC>: An obscure expression,
but probably meaning, thou who hast hid the woman in the fiend, or who hast
changed from what thou rightly art, and covered or lost thy proper self under
an usurped monstrosity. <SC>Cartwright</SC>: Read &lquo;chang'd and <I>discover'd</I> thing,&rquo; &amp;c.
She has just openly exposed her character. <SC>Delius</SC>: That is, a thing whose genuine
self (in this case, therefore, whose fiendish self) is concealed, covered. <SC>Cowden
Clarke</SC>: Thou perverted creature, who hast covered thyself with the hideousness
only proper to a fiend. <SC>Singer</SC> (ed. 2): This is evidently a misprint for <I>false-couer'd.</I>
What follows clearly shows it: &lquo;Howe'er thou art a fiend, <I>A woman's shape</I> doth shield
thee.&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. 2): The (MS) offers no emendation; but we may express our
confidence that Shakespeare's word was &lquo;self-<I>govern'd</I>,&rquo; which was misheard by the
scribe, or by the compositor, &lquo;self-cover'd&rquo;&mdash;a compound out of which it is only just
possible to extract a consistent meaning. Albany complains of the changed and self-
willed disposition of Goneril. J. <SC>Beale</SC> (<I>N. &amp; Qu.</I> 5th Ser. vol. vi, p. 303, 1876)
suggests &lquo;<I>devil</I>-cover'd.&rquo; <SC>John Bulloch</SC> (<I>Ibid.</I>): The proper reading is a term
connected with the law of marriage: &lquo;self-<I>covert.</I>&rquo; <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>): Dressed in one's
native semblance. Goneril must be supposed to have, by changing countenance, be-
trayed all her wickedness. <SC>Wright</SC>: Who hast disguised thyself in this unnatural
and fiendlike shape. <SC>Moberly</SC> [reading, &lquo;self-<I>coloured</I>&rquo;]: A creature whose vile
appearance is self-assumed. It seems allowable to read <I>coloured</I> instead of &lquo;cover'd,&rquo;
in which it is hard to see any sense. <SC>Collier</SC> (ed. 3): Possibly &lquo;self-<I>lower'd</I> thing.&rquo;
<SC>Crosby</SC> (<I>Lit. World</I>, 22 November, Boston, 1879) considers &lquo;changed&rquo; as equivalent
to <I>bewitched</I>, as in <I>Mid. N. D.</I> III, i, 117, and for &lquo;self-cover'd&rquo; proposes <I>sex</I>-cover'd
and urges in proof of its propriety: &lquo;First, it furnishes the ground for Albany's taunt
of shame: Thou be-devilled creature, covered as thou art with all the lineaments
of a woman, and yet guilty of such monstrous, unwomanly cruelty, &ldquo;for shame!&rdquo;
Secondly, the reason why he cannot obey the promptings of his passion, and put her
to instant death, is to be found in the next sentence: &ldquo;Were't,&rdquo; &amp;c., <I>i. e.</I> &ldquo;were it
becoming me, <I>as a man</I>, to lay violent hands upon a woman,&rdquo; and in &ldquo;A woman's
shape doth shield thee,&rdquo; which exactly paraphrases <I>sex-covered.</I> Lastly, it supplies
the antithetic point in Goneril's reply: &ldquo;Marry, your <I>manhood</I>, now!&rdquo;&rquo; Further-
more, Crosby finds in the word &lquo;feature&rquo; another meaning besides its usual one (see

<CC><P><B>Scene III]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: This scene seems to have been left out of the Folio only
to shorten the play. [See Appendix, <I>The Text.</I>]
<P>As will be seen by the Textual Notes, <SC>Eccles</SC> again makes a transposition of
scenes. Between the preceding scene and this present one, he inserts Scene V, call-
ing it Scene III. Wherefore our Scenes III and IV are his Scenes IV and V. The
object of this change is to bring closer together all those scenes which represent the
transactions in the neighborhood of Dover, and to render unnecessary the supposi-
tion that Lear passes a night in the open fields. Eccles says: The distance probably
imagined between the place where Regan has that conference with the Steward,
which makes the subject of the Scene now before us [Eccles's Scene III, our Scene V],
and the vicinity of Dover, seems to be such as requires the notion of a night inter-
vening before he arrives at the latter, and, consequently, the same space of time
must elapse between any scene which precedes that just mentioned and any other
wherein he appears to have arrived near Dover, as he does in the sixth scene. It
follows, then, that between the fourth and sixth, as hitherto numbered, a night must
pass; but the solicitude to find the King, expressed by Cordelia in the former of
these, makes it probable that her efforts were attended with success before the coming
on of night. Let, therefore, scene the fifth of the ancient distribution stand as the
third in this place, and suppose it to pass on the evening of the third day since that,
inclusively taken, on the morning of which Lear, attended by certain of his knights,
began to be conveyed from the castle of Gloucester on his route towards Dover, and
that, in some former part of the same, Edmund had departed from Regan upon the
business which she here mentions as the motive of his expedition. . . . It appears
that the Steward, not finding Edmund as he expected, sets out towards Dover with-
out loss of time in pursuit of him. I suppose the troops of Albany to have begun
their march towards Dover, but in another direction, about the time of the Steward's
departure from home charged with the execution of Goneril's commission. That
might be either some part of the same day on which she had reached her own habi-
tation accompanied by Edmund, or the morning of the succeeding one, so as to
allow time for the Steward to arrive at his destination in the evening, as there is
some reason for supposing he had done by Regan's exhortation in this scene [our
Scene V] to wait the safe conduct of her forces on the morrow, and her hint respect-</CC>

When Eccles comes to this present scene, which he calls Scene IV, he says: Let
the period of this scene be supposed the fourth morning from that (both, however,

is the same who was deputed by him as a messenger to Dover on the night of the
storm. From their conversation we infer that this meeting has but a very little
while before taken place. Kent appears to be but newly arrived. The Gentle-

yet, having travelled with more expedition, may reasonably be thought to have
been long enough arrived to have had an opportunity for the conference with

<P><B>Gentleman]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: The same whom he had sent with letters to Cordelia.
<P>2. <B>reason]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: The King of France being no longer a necessary person-
age, it was fit that some pretext for getting rid of him should be formed before the
play was too near advanced towards a conclusion. Decency required that a monarch
should not be silently shuffled into the pack of insignificant characters; and there
fore his dismission (which could be effected only by a sudden recall to his own
dominions) was to be accounted for before the audience. For this purpose, among
others, the present scene was introduced. It is difficult indeed to say what use could
have been made of the king, had he appeared at the head of his own armament, and
survived the murder of his queen. His conjugal concern on the occasion might have
weakened the effect of Lear's parental sorrow; and, being an object of respect as
well as pity, he would naturally have divided the spectators' attention, and thereby
diminished the consequence of Albany, Edgar, and Kent, whose exemplary virtues
deserved to be ultimately placed in the most conspicuous point of view.

<CC><P>12. <B>trill'd]</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> iii, 282) gives other instances of the use of this word

<P>18. <B>Sunshine and rain]</B> <SC>Moberly</SC>: It is the triumph of a poet thus to make
two feelings work at once in one mind. Thus Homer makes the women's tears for
Patroclus turn to tears for their own bondage (<G>*patro/klou pro/fasin sf<*>n d) au)tw_n
kh/de' e(ka/sth</G>); the dying Dido in Virgil struggles for the light, but hates it when
$ound (qu&aelig;sivit c&aelig;lo lucem ingemuitque reperta). But no poet ever ventures, as Sh.
does here, to imagine a grief, the most powerful of which human nature is capable,
thus controlled by the tranquil graciousness of a calm nature, which cannot do other-
wise than hold its own amid all disturbance, and is incapable of losing its balance;
the inward per$ection thus giving lovely mildness to the accidental and temporary
emotion which still remains entire and undestroyed.
<P>19. <B>like a better way]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC> proposed &lquo;a <I>wetter May</I>, i. e. a spring
season wetter than ordinary;&rquo; and <SC>Theobald</SC> supported the conjecture by citing</CC>
<PB N=252>
<HE>252 <I>KING LEAR</I> [<SC>act iv, sc.</SC> iii.</HE>
<FHL>
<CC><C>[19. <B>like a better way.]</B></C>
<P>Shakespeare's &lquo;May of youth.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Much Ado</I>, V, i, 76; &lquo;sweet May.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Rich. II:</I>
V, i, 79; &lquo;rose of May.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Ham.</I> IV, v, 153; &amp;c. <SC>Heath</SC> proposed &lquo;an <I>April day</I>,&rquo;
because the &lquo;joint appearance of rain and sunshine&rquo; was more characteristic of that
month than of May. In <SC>Theobald's</SC> second edition, although Warburton's change
is still retained in the text, yet the phrase is cited in the note as &lquo;a better <I>day.</I>&rquo; This
emendation was adopted, without credit, by <SC>Steevens</SC> in his edition of 1773; in his
edition of 1778 he says: A <I>better</I> day is the <I>best</I> day, and the <I>best day</I> is a day most
favourable to the productions of the earth. Such are the days in which there is a
due admixture of rain and sunshine. The comparative is used by Milton and others,
instead of the positive and superlative, as well as by Sh. himself in the play before
us: &lquo;The safer sense,&rquo; &amp;c. IV, vi, 81; &lquo;better part of man.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Macb.</I> V, viii, 18.
The thought is taken from Sidney's <I>Arcadia</I>, p. 244: &lquo;Her tears came dropping
down like rain in sunshine.&rquo; Cordelia's behaviour is apparently copied from Philo-
clea's. The same book, in another place, says: &lquo;her tears followed one another like
a precious rope of pearl.&rquo; In this same edition of Steevens in 1778 a note is given
by <SC>Tollet</SC> in which he suggests that &lquo;a better <I>day</I>&rquo; or &lquo;a better <I>May</I>&rquo; is better
than Warburton's alteration, because it implies that sunshine prevails over rain,
whereas Warburton's &lquo;wetter May&rquo; implies that Cordelia's sorrow excelled her
patience. <SC>Malone</SC> adopted Tollet's emendation, without credit, in the following
note: If a <I>better</I> day means either a <I>good</I> day, or the <I>best</I> day, it cannot represent
Cordelia's smiles and tears; for neither the one nor the other necessarily implies <I>rain</I>,
without which there is nothing to correspond with her <I>tears;</I> nor can a <I>rainy day</I>,
occasionally brightened by sunshine, with any propriety be called a <I>good</I> or the <I>best</I>
day. We are compelled, therefore, to make some other change. A <I>better May</I>, on
the other hand, whether we understand by it a good May, or a May better than ordi-
nary, corresponds exactly with the preceding image; for in every May, rain may be
expected, and in a good, or better May than ordinary, the sunshine, like Cordelia's
smiles, will predominate. Mr Steevens has quoted a passage from Sidney's <I>Arcadia.</I>
Perhaps the following passage in the same book, p. 163, ed. 1593, bears a still nearer
resemblance to that before us: &lquo;And with that she prettily <I>smiled</I>, which mingled
with her <I>tears</I>, one could not tell whether it were a mourning pleasure or a delightful
sorrow; but like when a few <I>April</I> drops are scattered by a gentle zephyrus among
fine-coloured flowers.&rquo; [To the citations which he had previously given] <SC>Steevens</SC>
afterwards added the following: Again in <I>A Courtlie Controversie of Cupid's Cautels</I>,
&amp;c., translated from the French, &amp;c. by H. W. [Henry Wotton], 1578, p. 289:
&lquo;Who hath <I>viewed</I> in the spring time, <I>raine and sunne-shine in one moment</I>, might
beholde the troubled countenance of the gentlewoman, after she had read and over-
read the letters of her Floradin with an eye now smyling, then bathed in teares.&rquo;
<SC>Singer</SC>, in his first edition, gives a note, with which he &lquo;had been favoured by Mr
<SC>Boaden</SC>&rquo;: &lquo;&ldquo;Her smiles and tears Were <I>like;</I> a better way.&rdquo; That is, Cordelia's
smiles and tears were <I>like</I> the conjunction of sunshine and rain, in a <I>better way or
manner.</I> Now, in what did this better way consist? Why, simply in the smiles
seeming unconscious of the tears; whereas the sunshine has a <I>watery look</I> through
the falling drops of rain&mdash;&ldquo;Those happy smiles . . . seem'd <I>not to know</I> What guests
were in her eyes.&rdquo; The passages cited by Steevens and Malone prove that the point
of comparison was neither a &ldquo;better day&rdquo; nor a &ldquo;wetter May.&rdquo; I may just observe,</CC>

<CC><P>as perhaps an illustration, that the <I>better way</I> of <SC>charity</SC> is that the right hand should
<I>not know</I> what the left hand giveth.&rquo; Singer adopted this punctuation in both of his
editions. <SC>White</SC>: Here &lquo;better&rquo; is used, not by way of comparing the May of Cor-
delia's smiles and tears in degree to another and inferior encounter of sunshine and
showers, but as an epithet implying eminence (which in its very essence is compara-
tive) to which, in kind, her emotional struggle is likened. This elegant use of the
comparative form is not uncommon with our best writers. <SC>Hudson</SC> [reading &lquo;Were
like: a better way,&mdash;&rquo;]: The sense is clearly completed at &lquo;like,&rquo; and should there
be cut off from what follows: &lquo;You have seen sunshine and rain at once; her smiles
and tears were like;&rquo; that is, were like &lquo;sunshine and rain at once.&rquo; Then begins
another thought, or another mode of illustration: to speak it in a better way, to
express it in a better form of words, &lquo;those happy smilets,&rquo; &amp;c. And I insist upon
it that the passage so read is better poetry, as well as better sense and better logic,
than with &lquo;way&rquo; turned into &lquo;May&rquo; or &lquo;day,&rquo; and made an adjunct or tag to &lquo;like.&rquo;
<SC>Delius</SC> follows Boaden in taking the phrase adverbially, but does not follow Boaden's
punctuation. His text is the same as ours. <SC>Cowden Clarke</SC>: It means that her
mingled &lquo;smiles and tears&rquo; expressed her feelings in &lquo;a better way&rquo; than either
&lquo;patience or sorrow&rquo; could do separately; each of which &lquo;strove who should express
her goodliest.&rquo; The words &lquo;her smiles and tears were like a better way,&rquo; moreover,
include comparison with the opening phrase of the speech, &lquo;Not to a rage;&rquo; showing
that her emotion vented itself in nothing like rage, but (&lquo;a better way&rquo;) in gentle
&lquo;smiles and tears,&rquo; compounded of both &lquo;patience and sorrow.&rquo; <SC>Wright</SC>: It is not
clear what sense can be made of it. The emendations which have been proposed
are none of them perfectly satisfactory. The substitution of <I>May</I> for &lquo;way&rquo; would
be well enough but for the adjective &lquo;better&rquo; which accompanies it. <SC>Moberly</SC>: The
meaning may be &lquo;a better course of nature,&rquo; something better than nature knows.
<SC>Bulloch</SC> (p. 246) proposes &lquo;link'd in bright array.&rquo;
<P>22. <B>dropp'd]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: For the sake of rhythm we might read <I>dropping.</I> This
idea might have been taken from the ornaments of the ancient carcanet or necklace,
which frequently consisted of table <I>diamonds</I> with <I>pearls</I> appended to them, or, in
the jeweler's phrase, <I>dropping</I> from them. Pendants for the ear are still called
<I>drops.</I> A similar thought occurs in Middleton's <I>A Game at Chess</I> [I, i]: &lquo;The holy
dew of prayer lies like pearl Dropt from the opening eye-lids of the morn Upon the
bashful rose.&rquo; Milton has translated this image into his <I>Lycidas:</I> &lquo;Under the open-
ing eye-lids of the morn.&rquo;

<CC><P>sense Sh. frequently uses this word, and not simply as the act of interrogation. Did
she give you to understand her meaning <I>by words</I> as well as by the foregoing external
testimonies of sorrow?
<P>28. <B>Kent!]</B> <SC>Capell</SC> [led by the text of Q<SUB>2</SUB>, supposed that Kent here interrupts
with the exclamation, &lquo;Father! sisters!&rquo; and so printed his text, and was followed
by <SC>Eccles</SC>]: Any mention of Kent, by ejaculation or otherwise, was not probable
to come from Cordelia; and most unfit for this place,&mdash;to rank with &lquo;father&rquo; and
&lquo;sisters&rquo; (indeed, take the lead of them) in the sorrows of that lady; as repetitions,
and in a tone of admiring approaching something to sarcasm, the words have pro-
priety; for this is convey'd by them,&mdash;&lquo;<I>Father indeed; And what sisters!</I>&rquo; they are
heard by the Gentleman, but don't interrupt him; pass with him for an hemistich,
and he goes on in another.

<CC><P>her,&rquo; that is, her outcries were accompanied with tears. <SC>Heath</SC>: The hyphen should
be omitted, and &lquo;clamour moisten'd&rquo; pronounced and considered as two distinct words.
Cordelia had at first broke out into exclamations; then followed the tears, with which,
when she had moistened these exclamations (for the words under consideration are
an ablative absolute), she retired to the farther indulgence of her grief in private.
<SC>Capell</SC>: &lquo;Clamour&rquo; may stand for the exclamations preceding, which Cordelia
&lquo;moistens&rquo; with the tears which followed them instantly; or it may be put with more
boldness for a grief ready to burst out into &lquo;clamour,&rquo; taken strictly and properly;
which she &lquo;moisten'd,&rquo; allayed by moistening, with the tears that then broke from
her, as winds are by rain. <SC>White</SC> [reading &lquo;And, clamour-moisten'd, then&rquo;]: That
is, plainly enough, &lquo;And with her cheeks wet with her outburst of sorrow, away she
started,&rquo; &amp;c. So in this play, V, iii, 205: &lquo;This would have seem'd a period To such
as love not sorrow. . . . Whilst I was big in clamour, came there a man.&rquo; The
reader will not wonder at a Note on this passage, when he sees it in all recent editions
hitherto with this astounding punctuation: &lquo;And clamour moisten'd: then,&rquo; and the
explanation that &lquo;she&rquo; is the nominative to &lquo;moisten'd,&rquo; and that Cordelia moistened
her clamour! <SC>Hudson</SC> [adopting White's text]: I cannot say that the reading here
given altogether satisfies me; but it seems, on the whole, the best both in sense and
in language. The meaning of &lquo;clamour-moisten'd&rquo; is, her voice being smothered with
weeping, or her crying drenched with tears. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> i, 157): Write &lquo;&mdash;her
heavenly eyes, And clamour-moisten'd.&rquo; (<I>luctu madentes.</I>) &lquo;Clamour&rquo; here signifies
<I>wailing.</I> Compare V, iii, 205. [Cited by White.] <SC>Delius</SC>: &lquo;Moisten'd&rquo; is here
used intransitively: clamour became moist. <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>) gives examples of
&lquo;clamour&rquo; bearing the following meanings: outcry, vociferation; loud wailing (the
present passage cited); the sound of bells; of cannon; of the thunder; of trumpets
and drums; of tempests; of the noise of a chase, a battle, &amp;c. <SC>Wright</SC>: The
objection to Walker's interpretation is, that &lquo;clamour&rquo; is the outcry, and not the tears
by which it was accompanied, but perhaps the clamour is the indirect cause of the
tears. [Assuredly.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] For the construction, compare <I>Hen. V:</I> II, ii, 139: &lquo;the
full fraught man and best endued.&rquo; There is probably some corruption. <SC>Moberly</SC>:
Shed tears upon her cry of sorrow. [Of this corrupt phrase in this corrupt scene
(perhaps the most corrupt throughout Shakespeare's plays), I can see but two note-
worthy explanations: Capell's, viz: she moisten'd her clamour; and Walker's, viz:
her eyes that were heavenly and wet with wailing. Of the two I much prefer the
latter.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<CC><P>42. <B>so elbows him]</B> To <SC>Bailey</SC> (ii, 99) the best emendation appears to be &lquo;<I>sole
bars</I> him, <I>i. e.</I> alone prevents him;&rquo; and, furthermore, he thinks that it will be no-
ticed that &lquo;the verbal change is not great: sole bars, so elbows.&rquo; <SC>Badham</SC> (<I>Cam.
Essays</I>, 1856, p. 282): A more incongruous figure of speech than this it would be
difficult to imagine. Sovereigns &lquo;elbow&rquo; no one, and such an expression as &lquo;sov-
ereign shame&rquo; is either beautiful or the reverse, as the epithet is borne out by the
action or effect attributed to &lquo;shame.&rquo; There is also something careless in having two
subjects to the verb &lquo;sting&rquo;; first unkindness, and then the conditions of which the
unkindness was the cause. I therefore propose to read: &lquo;so <I>embows</I> his own unkind-
ness.&rquo; <SC>Wright</SC>: So stands at his elbow and reminds him of the past. Compare
2 <I>Hen. IV:</I> I, ii, 81. <SC>Moberly</SC>: A prevailing shame seems to buffet him. <SC>Schmidt</SC>:
Perhaps it means so pushes him aside.

<P>3. <B>fumiter]</B> <SC>Ellacombe</SC> (p. 75): Of Fumitories we have five species in England,
all of them weeds in cultivated grounds and in hedge-rows. None of them can be
considered garden plants, but they are closely allied to the <I>Corydalis</I>, of which there
are several pretty species, and to the very handsome <I>Dielytras</I>, of which one species,
<I>D. spectabilis</I>, ranks among the very handsomest of our hardy herbaceous plants.
How the plant acquired its name of Fumitory, <I>fumeterre</I>, earth-smoke, is not very
satisfactorily explained, though many explanations have been given; but that the
name was an ancient one, we know from the interesting Stockholm manuscript of
the eleventh century published by Mr J. Pettigrew, and of which a few lines are
worth quoting: &lquo;Fumiter is erbe, I say, Yt spryngyth i April et in May. In feld, in
town, in yard, et gate, Yer lond is fat and good in state, Dun red is his flour Ye erbe
smek lik in colowur.&rquo;
<P>4. <B>burdocks]</B> <SC>Farmer</SC>: <I>Hardocks</I> should be <I>harlocks.</I> Thus Drayton, in one of
his Eclogues: &lquo;The honeysuckle, the harlocke, The lily, and the lady-smocke.&rquo;
<SC>Steevens</SC>: The Qq supply what is perhaps the true reading, though misspelt. The
<I>hoar-dock</I> is the dock with whitish, woolly leaves. <SC>Laertes</SC> (<I>Gent. Mag.</I> lvi, 214):
It is very probable that <I>charlock</I> was the word intended by Sh. It is called <I>charlock</I>
by husbandmen, and grows in great quantity amongst the barley. Corn charlock
(<I>Raphanus Raphanistrum.</I> Linn.). White, or yellow-flowered charlock (<I>Raphanus
sylvestris</I>).&mdash;Gerard, 1597, p. 240. <SC>Wright</SC>: I find &lquo;hardhake&rquo; is given as the
equivalent of <I>Jacea nigra</I> (or knapweed) in a MS herbal in the library of Trinity
College, Cambridge (R. 14, 32); and in John Russell's <I>Boke of Nurture</I> (Early Eng-
lish Text Society, 1868), p. 183, is mentioned &lquo;yardehok,&rquo; which is apparently a kind
of hock or mallow. If the botanists could identify the plants mentioned under these
names, either of them could easily be corrupted into &lquo;Hardokes,&rquo; or &lquo;hor-docks.&rquo;
[It is unfortunate that both <SC>Beisly</SC> and <SC>Ellacombe</SC> suppose Farmer's conjecture
of <I>harlocks</I> to be the original word; they have, therefore, given us nothing new on
the subject, and do not mention &lquo;burdocks.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

Yet the Hemlock adds largely to the beauty of our hedge-rows; its spotted tall stems</CC>

<P>and its finely cut leaves make it a handsome weed, and the dead stems and dried

it has an evil notoriety, as being the poison by which Socrates was put to death,
though this is not quite certain. It is not, however, altogether a useless plant. &lquo;It

<P>4. <B>nettles]</B> <SC>Ellacombe</SC>: The Nettle needs no introduction; we are all too well
acquainted with it, yet it is not altogether a weed to be despised. We have two
native species (<I>Urtica urens</I> and <I>U. dioica</I>), with sufficiently strong qualities, but we
have a third (<I>U. pilulifera</I>), very curious in its manner of bearing its female flowers
in clusters of compact little balls, which is far more virulent than either of our
native species, and is said by Camden to have been introduced by the Romans to
chafe their bodies when frozen by the cold of Britain. The story is probably apocryphal,
but the plant is an alien, and only grows in a few places. Both the Latin and Eng-
lish names of the plant record its qualities. <I>Urtica</I> is from <I>uro</I>, to burn; and Nettle
is etymologically the same word as needle, and the plant is so named, not for its
stinging qualities, but because at one time the Nettle supplied the chief instrument
of sewing; not the instrument which holds the thread, and to which we now confine
the word needle, but the thread itself, and very good linen it made. The poet
Campbell says in one of his letters: &lquo;I have slept in Nettle sheets, and dined off a
Nettle table-cloth, and I have heard my mother say that she thought Nettle cloth
more durable than any other linen.&rquo; It has also been used for making paper, and,
for both these purposes, as well as for rope-making, the Rhea fibre of the Himalaya,
which is simply a gigantic Nettle (<I>Urtica</I> or <I>B&ouml;hmeria nivea</I>), is very largely culti-
vated. Nor is the Nettle to be despised as an article of food. In many parts of
England the young shoots are boiled and much relished. In February, 1661, Pepys
made the entry in his diary: &lquo;We did eat some Nettle porridge which was made on
purpose to-day for some of their coming, and was very good.&rquo; Gipsies are said to
cook it as an excellent vegetable, and M. Soyer tried hard, but almost in vain, to
recommend it as a most dainty dish. Having so many uses, we are not surprised to
find that it has at times been regularly cultivated as a garden crop, so that I have
somewhere seen an account of tithe of Nettles being taken, and in the old church-
wardens' account of St. Michael's, Bath, is the entry in the year 1400: &lquo;Pro urticis
venditis ad Lawrencium Bebbe, 2d.&rquo; In other points the Nettle is a most interesting
plant. Microscopists find in it most beautiful objects for the microscope; entomol-
ogists value it, for it is such a favourite of butterflies and other insects that in Britain
alone upwards of thirty insects feed solely on the Nettle plant, and it is one of those
curious plants which mark the progress of civilization by following man wherever he
goes. But as a garden-plant the only advice to be given is to keep it out of the gar-
den by every means. In good cultivated ground it becomes a sad weed if once
allowed a settlement. The Himalayan <I>B&ouml;hmerias</I>, however, are handsome, but only
for their foliage, and though we cannot, perhaps, admit our roadside Dead Nettles,
which, however, are much handsomer than many foreign flowers which we carefully
tend and prize, yet the Austrian Dead Nettle (<I>Lamium orvala</I>, Bot. Mag. v, 172)
may be well admitted as a handsome garden-plant.

meadow and marsh plant, with rose-coloured flowers and deeply-cut narrow segments;</CC>

<CC><P>it blossoms at the time the cuckoo comes, hence one of its names. <SC>Wright</SC>: Called
also, according to Gerarde, ladies' smocks and wild watercress (<I>Cardamine pratensis</I>).
They &lquo;flower for the most part in Aprill and Maie, when the Cuckowe doth begin to
sing her pleasant notes without stammering.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Herball</I>, p. 203.
<P>5. <B>Darnel]</B> <SC>Ellacombe</SC>: Virgil, in his Fifth Eclogue, says: &lquo;Grandia s&aelig;pe quibus
mandavimus hordea sulcis Infelix lolium et steriles nascuntur aven&aelig;.&rquo; Thus trans-
lated by Thomas Newton, 1587: &lquo;Sometimes there sproutes abundant store Of bag-
gage, noisome weeds, Burres, Brembles, Darnel, Cockle, Dawke, Wild Oates, and
choaking seedes.&rquo; And the same is repeated in the first Georgic, and in both places
<I>lolium</I> is always translated Darnel, and so by common consent Darnel is identified
with the <I>Lolium temulentum</I>, or wild rye grass. But in Shakespeare's time Darnel,
like Cockle, was the general name for any hurtful weed. In the old translation of
the Bible, the Zizania, which is now translated Tares, was sometimes translated
Cockle, and Newton, writing in Shakespeare's time, says: &lquo;Under the name of
Cockle and Darnel is comprehended all vicious, noisom and unprofitable graine, en-
combring and hindring good corne.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Herball to the Bible.</I> The Darnel is not only
injurious from choking the corn, but its seeds become mixed with the true Wheat, and
so in Dorsetshire, and perhaps in other parts, it has the name of &lquo;Cheat&rquo; (Barnes's
<I>Glossary</I>), from its false likeness to Wheat. It was this false likeness that got for it
its bad character. &lquo;Darnell, or Juray,&rquo; says Lyte, <I>Herbal</I>, 1578, &lquo;is a vitious graine
that combereth or anoyeth corne, especially Wheat, and in his knotten straw, blades,
or leaves is like unto Wheate.&rquo;
<P>5. <B>idle]</B> Unproductive, unprofitable, in opposition to &lquo;sustaining corn.&rquo; See &lquo;idle
pebble,&rquo; IV, vi, 21.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>8. <B>can]</B> Compare <I>Ham.</I> IV, vii, 85: &lquo;they can well on horseback.&rquo;
<P>9. <B>the restoring]</B> For instances of the definite article preceding a verbal that is
followed by an object, see <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 93, or <I>Macb.</I> I, iv, 8.
<P>10. <B>helps]</B> For other instances, meaning to <I>cure</I>, see <SC>Schmidt</SC> (<I>Lex.</I>).</CC>

<CC><P>11. <SC>Kellogg</SC> (<I>Sh.'s Delineation of Insanity</I>, p. 26): The reply of the Physician
is significant, and worthy of careful attention, as embracing a brief summary of
almost the only true principles recognized by modern science, and now carried out
by the most eminent physicians in the treatment of the Insane. We find here no
allusion to the scourgings, the charms, the invocation of saints, &amp;c., employed by the
most eminent physicians of the time of Sh.; neither have we any allusion to the
rotary chairs, the vomitings, the purgings by hellebore, the showerings, the bleed-
ings, scalp-shavings, and blisterings, which, even down to our own times, have been
inflicted upon these unfortunates by &lquo;science falsely so called,&rquo; and which stand
recorded as imperishable monuments of medical folly; but in place of all this, Sh.,
speaking through the mouth of the Physician, gives us the principle, simple, truthful,
and universally applicable.
<P>15. <B>anguish]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: Generally used in Sh. of physical pain. See IV, vi, 6.
<P>17. <B>remediate]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: A word of Shakespeare's coinage, which he seems to
have formed on the model of <I>immediate.</I>
<P>19. <B>ungoverned]</B> <SC>Delius</SC>: That is, ungovernable. Adjectives formed from par-
ticiples, with the negative <B><I>un</I>-,</B> not unfrequently admit of this modification of their
original meaning. [See I, iv, 294; IV, vi, 21; or <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 375.]
<P>20. <B>means]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: The reason which should guide it.</CC>

<CC><P>22. <B>rather]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: I know not well why Sh. gives to Oswald, who is a mere

when he is dying, thinks only how it may be safely delivered. <SC>Verplanck</SC>: Sh. has
here incidentally painted, without the formality of a regular moral lesson, one of the
very strange and very common self-contradictions of our enigmatical nature. Zealous,
honourable, even self-sacrificing fidelity,&mdash;sometimes to a chief or leader, sometimes
to a party, a faction, or a gang,&mdash;appears to be so little dependent on any principle
of virtuous duty, that it is often found strongest among those who have thrown off
the common restraints of morality. It would seem that when man's obligations to
his God or his kind are rejected or forgotten, the most abandoned mind still craves
something for the exercise of its natural social sympathies, and as it loses sight of
nobler and truer duties becomes, like the Steward, more and more &lquo;duteous to the
vices&rquo; of its self-chosen masters. This is one of the moral phenomena of artificial</CC>

<CC><P>7. <B>alter'd]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Edgar alters his voice in order to pass afterwards for a
malignant spirit.
<P>11. <B>How fearful, &amp;c.]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: This description has been much admired since
the time of Addison, who has remarked, with a poor attempt at pleasantry, that &lquo;he
who can read it without being giddy has a very good head, or a very bad one.&rquo; The
description is certainly not mean, but I am far from thinking it wrought to the utmost
excellence of poetry. He that looks from a precipice finds himself assailed by one
great and dreadful image of irresistible destruction. But this overwhelming idea is
dissipated and enfeebled from the instant that the mind can restore itself to the obser-
vation of particulars, and diffuse its attention to distinct objects. The enumeration
of the choughs and crows, the samphire-man and the fishers, counteracts the great
effect of the prospect, as it peoples the desert of intermediate vacuity, and stops the
mind in the rapidity of its descent through emptiness and horror. <SC>Mason</SC>: It is to
be considered that Edgar is describing an imaginary precipice, and is not therefore
supposed to be so strongly impressed with the dreadful prospect of inevitable destruc-
tion as a person would be who really found himself on the brink of one. <SC>Eccles</SC>:
The purpose of Edgar was, by a minute and faithful detail of such circumstances, to
give the highest possible air of probability to the imposition which he designed to
practise on his father. <SC>Knight</SC>: In Dr Johnson's criticism we detect much of the
peculiar character of his mind, as well as of the poetical taste of the age in which he
lived. Wordsworth, in the preface to the second edition of his Poems, has shown
clearly upon what false foundations that criticism is built which would prefer high-
sounding words, conveying only indeterminate ideas, and call these the only proper
language of poetry, in opposition to the simple and distinct language, &lquo;however
naturally arranged, and according to the strict laws of metre,&rquo; which by such criti-
cism is denominated prosaic. Johnson was thoroughly consistent in his dislike of
the &lquo;observation of particulars&rquo; and the &lquo;attention to distinct objects.&rquo; In Boswell's
<I>Life</I> we have a more detailed account of his poetical creed, with reference to this
very description of Dover Cliff: &lquo;Johnson said that the description of the temple, in</CC>
