<P>&ldquo;But,&rdquo; said Garrick, all alarmed for the god of his idolatry, &ldquo;we know not the
extent and variety of his powers. We are to suppose there are such passages in his
works; Sh. must not suffer for the badness of our memories.&rdquo; Johnson, diverted by
this enthusiastic jealousy, went on with great ardour&mdash;&ldquo;No, sir; Congreve has <I>nature</I>&rdquo;
(smiling on the tragic eagerness of Garrick); but, composing himself, he added,
&ldquo;Sir, this is not comparing Congreve on the whole with Sh. on the whole, but only
maintaining that Congreve has one finer passage than any that can be found in Sh.
. . . What I mean is, that you can show me no passage where there is simply a
description of material objects, without any intermixture of moral notions, which
produces such an effect.&rdquo; Mr Murphy mentioned Shakespeare's description of the
night before the battle of Agincourt; but it was observed it had men in it. Mr
Davies suggested the speech of Juliet, in which she figures herself awaking in the
tomb of her ancestors. Some one mentioned the description of Dover Cliff. John-
son&mdash;&ldquo;No, sir; it should be all precipice,&mdash;all vacuum. The crows impede your
fall. The diminished appearance of the boats, and other circumstances, are all very
good description, but do not impress the mind at once with the horrible idea of
immense height. The impression is divided; you pass on, by computation, from one
stage of the tremendous space to another. Had the girl in <I>The Mourning Bride</I>
said she could not cast her shoe to the top of one of the pillars in the temple, it
would not have aided the idea, but weakened it.&rdquo;&rquo; Taken as pieces of pure descrip-
tion, there is only one way of testing the different value of the passages in Sh. and
Congreve&mdash;that is, by considering what ideas the mind receives from the different
modes adopted to convey ideas. But the criticism of Johnson, even if it could have
established that the passage of Congreve, taken apart, was &lquo;finer&rquo; than that of Sh.,
utterly overlooks the <I>dramatic</I> propriety of each passage. The &lquo;girl&rquo; in <I>The Mourn-
ing Bride</I> is soliloquizing,&mdash;uttering a piece of versification, harmonious enough,
indeed, but without any dramatic purpose. The mode in which Edgar describes the
cliff is for the special information of the blind Gloucester,&mdash;one who could not look
from a precipice. The crows and choughs, the samphire-gatherer, the fisherman, the
bark, the surge that is seen but not heard,&mdash;each of these, incidental to the place, is
selected as a standard by which Gloucester can measure the altitude of the cliff.
Transpose the description into the generalities of Congreve's description of the
cathedral, and the dramatic propriety at least is utterly destroyed. The height of
the cliff is then only presented as an image to Gloucester's mind upon the vague
assertion of his conductor. Let the description begin, for example, something after
the fashion of Congreve: &lquo;How fearful is the edge of this high cliff!&rquo; and continue
with a proper assortment of chalky crags and gulfs below. Of what worth then
would be Edgar's concluding lines: &lquo;I'll look no more,&rquo; &amp;c.? The mind of</CC>

<P>15. <B>sampire]</B> <SC>Tollet</SC>: &lquo;<I>Samphire</I> grows in great plenty on most of the sea-
cliffs in this country; it is terrible to see how people gather it, hanging by a rope
several fathom from the top of the impending rocks, as it were in the air.&rquo;&mdash;Smith's
<I>History of Waterford</I>, 1774, p. 315. <SC>Malone</SC>: This personage is not a mere crea-
ture of Shakespeare's imagination, for the gathering of samphire was literally a <I>trade</I>
or common occupation in his time, it being carried and cried about the streets, and
much used as a pickle. So, in a song in Heywood's <I>Rape of Lucrece</I>, in which the
cries of London are enumerated under the title of the cries of Rome: &lquo;I ha Rock-
sampier, Rock-sampier; Thus go the cries in Rome faire towne,&rquo; &amp;c. Again, in
Venner's <I>Via Recta</I>, &amp;c. 1622: &lquo;<I>Samphire</I> is in like manner preserved in pickle, and
eaten with meates. It is a very pleasant and familiar sauce, and agreeing with man's
body.&rquo; Dover Cliff was particularly resorted to for this plant. See Drayton's
<I>Polyolbion, The Eighteenth Song:</I> &lquo;Rob Dover's neighbouring cleeves of sampyre,
to excite His dull and sickly taste, and stir up appetite.&rquo; <SC>Wright</SC>: Gerarde gives as
one of its Italian names, &lquo;<I>Herba di San Pietro.</I>&rquo; He says (<I>Herball</I>, p. 428): &lquo;Rocke
Sampier groweth on the rocky cliffes at Douer.&rquo; Cotgrave has &lquo;Herbe de S. Pierre.
Sampire, Crestmarin.&rquo; <SC>Moberly</SC>: This samphire-gatherer is the realizing touch in
the description; it seems a thing that could not be imagined. <SC>Beisly</SC>: <I>Crithmum
maritimum</I>, commonly called St. Peter's Herb and Sea-fennel, is abundant on rocks
by the sea, flowers dull yellow, with long, glaucous, fleshy leaflets. The plant is
aromatic, and the young leaves are gathered, preserved in vinegar, and eaten as a
pickle. It flowers in July, August, and September. Dr W. Turner says of it: &lquo;That
in Italian it is <I>Santi Petri herba</I>, from whence we have the name <I>sampere.</I>&rquo; Evelyn
in his <I>Acetaria</I> has a receipt for pickling sampier, called <I>the Dover receipt.</I> The
plants do not grow on any place which the sea covers; and Sh. noticed this fact in</CC>

<CC><P>27. <B>upright]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: But what danger in leaping &lquo;upright&rquo; or <I>upwards?</I>
He who leaps thus must needs fall again on his feet upon the place whence he rose.
We should read <I>outright</I>, i. e. forward; and then, being on the verge of a precipice,
he must needs fall headlong. <SC>Heath</SC>: The spot is represented as so extremely
near the edge of the precipice, even within a foot of it, that there was the utmost
hazard in leaping even upright upon it. <SC>Mason</SC>: A man's saying on the brink of a
precipice that &lquo;he would not leap forward for all beneath the moon&rquo; conveys no
extraordinary idea of the danger itself, or of the apprehensions it occasioned; it is
merely saying, in other words, that &lquo;he would not for all the world devote himself to
certain destruction.&rquo; But Edgar goes farther, and says he would not &lquo;leap upright,&rquo;
which did not necessarily imply his falling down the precipice. <SC>Malone</SC>: If War-
burton had tried such a leap <I>within a foot</I> of the edge of a precipice, before he
undertook the revision of these plays, the world would, I fear, have been deprived
of his labours.

<CC><P>57. <B>bourn]</B> <SC>Knight</SC>: In a previous passage, &lquo;Come o'er the bourn, Bessy, to me,
&lquo;bourn&rquo; signifies a river; and so in the <I>Faerie Queene</I> (ii, Canto vi, Stanza 10): &lquo;My
little boat can safely pass this perilous bourne.&rquo; In Milton's <I>Comus</I> we have, &lquo;And
every bosky bourn from side to side.&rquo; Here, as Warton well explains the word,
&lquo;bourn&rquo; is a winding, deep, and narrow valley, with a rivulet at the bottom. Such
a spot is a bourn because it is a boundary, a natural division; and this is the sense
in which a river is called a &lquo;bourn.&rquo; The &lquo;chalky bourn&rquo; is, in the same way, the
chalky boundary of England towards France.
<P>58. <B>a-height]</B> See &lquo;a-twain,&rquo; II, ii, 69; &lquo;a-work,&rquo; III, v, 6, or <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 24, who
after this present example adds: &lquo;perhaps.&rquo;
<P>66. <B>strangeness]</B> <SC>Hunter</SC> (ii, 273): The incident of the cliff is so extravagantly
improbable that there is no defending it, and we tolerate it only as having given oc-
casion to Shakespeare's only great attempt at describing a particular piece of scenery.
He had probably been at Dover, and sketched the scene upon the place. He evi-
dently prepares the reader for the passage by several allusions to Dover in the earlier
parts of the play, and, except for the sake of introducing these descriptive lines, one
cannot see why Gloucester should be led so far as Dover, when he might so easily
have executed his purpose elsewhere. There is an obscurity thrown (purposely, I
think) over the topography of this play. Dr Johnson says, that this scene and the
stratagem are wholly borrowed from Sidney's <I>Arcadia;</I> but this is a mistake. It is
true we have a blind king, who seeks the brow of a rock with the intention of throw-
ing himself headlong. He asks his son to conduct him thither. So far the stories
are coincident, but the improbable part is not yet entered upon; and, so far from Sh.
having here followed Sidney, or having any countenance from a more cautious writer</CC>

<P>71. <B>whelk'd]</B> <SC>Hanmer</SC> (<I>Gloss.</I>): A whelk is such a rising tumour upon the skin as
the lash of a switch or whip leaves behind it. <SC>Steevens</SC>: So in <I>Hen. V:</I> III, vi, 108.
Fluellen, speaking of Bardolph, says: &lquo;his face is all bubukles, and whelks, and
knobs,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Malone</SC>: Twisted, convolved. A welk, or whilk, is a small shell fish.
<SC>Wright</SC>: In Sherwood's English-French Dictionary, which forms the supplement to
Cotgrave's second edition, &lquo;whelke&rquo; is given as synonymous with &lquo;wheale,&rquo; a blister
or pustule. In Chaucer (<I>Pardoneres Tale</I>, 14153, ed. T. Wright), we have: &lquo;For
which ful pale and welkid is my face,&rquo; where &lquo;welkid&rquo; is explained by Tyrwhitt as
&lquo;withered,&rquo; but seems to mean swollen with weeping, as in the following passage from
Sackville's Induction, 80: &lquo;Her wealked face with woful teares besprent.&rquo;

as a compound epithet of &lquo;bird.&rquo; <SC>Douce</SC>: Lear certainly refers to falconry. In an
old song on Hawking, set for four voices by Thomas Ravenscroft, &lquo;O well flown&rquo; is
a frequent address to the hawk. <SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Well-flown bird&rquo; was the falconer's
expression when the hawk was successful in her flight, and is so used in <I>A Woman
Killed with Kindness</I> [p. 103, ed. Sh. Soc.].
<P>91. <B>clout]</B> <SC>Nares</SC>: The mark fixed in the centre of the butts, at which archers
shot for practice. <I>Clouette</I>, Fr. Literally, the nail, or pin. The best shot was that
which clove or split the <I>clout</I>, or pin, itself. [See &lquo;pin,&rquo; <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> II, iv, 15, and
notes.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>92. <B>word]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Lear supposes himself in a garrison, and, before he lets
Edgar pass, requires the watch-word.
<P>96. <B>beard]</B> <SC>Halliwell</SC>: It is hardly requisite to fill up the context of a dis-
jointed raving. Ha! Goneril!&mdash;to be so unfilial to a father with a white beard, to
an aged father, the age of the parent aggravating the crime of the daughter. In a
former part of the tragedy he says to Goneril: &lquo;art not ashamed to look upon this
beard,&rquo; meaning his venerable white beard. <SC>Moberly</SC>: I suppose you are Goneril,
though your white beard seems against it.
<P>98. <B>black ones]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: He was told he had the wisdom of age before he had
reach'd to that of a youth.
<P>99. <B>&lquo;Ay&rquo; and &lquo;no&rquo; too]</B> <SC>Pye</SC> (p. 295): It does not appear how it could be flattery
to dissent from, as well as to assent to, every thing he said. The following reading
was suggested to me by an ingenious friend, by only a change in the pointing and
the omission of a single letter: &lquo;To say <I>ay</I> and <I>no</I> to every thing I said <I>ay</I>
and <I>no</I> to, was no good divinity.&rquo; [<SC>White</SC> adopted this reading.] <SC>Singer</SC>: It
may, however, mean that they said &lquo;ay&rquo; or &lquo;no&rquo; as he said &lquo;ay&rquo; or &lquo;no,&rquo; but more
probably that they had double thoughts, and said &lquo;ay&rquo; to flatter him, when they said
&lquo;no&rquo; to themselves, and vice vers&acirc;. <SC>Delius</SC>: That is, in contradiction to the Biblica
injunction to &lquo;let your speech be yea, yea and nay, nay.&rquo; <SC>Cowden Clarke</SC>: Lea
first exclaims indignantly: &lquo;To say &ldquo;ay and &ldquo;no&rdquo; to every thing I said!&rquo; recollect

varying moods, just as Osric does to Hamlet; and then he goes on to say that this</CC>

<CC><P>136. <B>squiny]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: To look asquint. The word is used by Armin, Shake-

<P>139. <B>report]</B> <SC>Staunton</SC>: There is some obscurity here. What is it Edgar would
not take from report? He must have been aware of his father's deprivation of sight;
because it is mentioned in the previous scene. We are, perhaps, to suppose that the
poor king exhibits the proclamation for the killing of Gloucester. <SC>Cowden Clarke</SC>:
That which Edgar would not <I>believe without witnessing</I> is the extremity of pathos in
the meeting between his blind father and the distracted king. <SC>Delius</SC> thinks it
refers to Lear's condition.

<P>142. <B>the case]</B> <SC>Jennens</SC>: Having lost my eyes, would you have me read with

V, ii, 14: &lquo;tear the cases of their eyes.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: Also in <I>Per.</I> V, i, 112: &lquo;her
eyes as jewel-like and cased as richly,&rquo; and <I>Ib.</I> III, ii, 99: &lquo;her eyelids, cases to
those heavenly jewels.&rquo; &lquo;<I>This</I> case of eyes&rquo; could not have been Shakespeare's
phrase, because, in the language of that day, it would mean &lquo;this pair of eyes,&rquo; a
sense directly opposite to that intended to be conveyed. <SC>White</SC>: But still I must
regard Rowe's reading (<I>i. e.</I> with such a pair of eyes as this, <I>i. e.</I> none at all) as
being the true text.

<CC><P>147. <B>feelingly]</B> <SC>Moberly</SC>: In an inward and heartfelt way. Lear takes the
word to mean &lquo;only by feeling as I have no eyes.&rquo; &lquo;What do you want with <I>eyes</I>,&rquo;

<P>151. <B>handy-dandy]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: This is a play among children, in which some-
thing is shaken between the hands, and then a guess is made in which hand it is
retained. See Florio: &lquo;<I>Bazzicchiare.</I> To shake betweene two hands, to play handy-
dandy.&rquo; Coles (<I>Latin Dict.</I>, 1679) renders &lquo;to play handy-dandy,&rquo; by <I>digitis micare;</I>
and he is followed by Ainsworth; but they appear to have been mistaken, as is Dr
Johnson in his definition, in his <I>Dictionary</I>, which seems to have been formed on the
passage before us, misunderstood. He says, Handy-dandy is &lquo;a play in which chil-
dren <I>change</I> hands and places.&rquo; <SC>Douce</SC>: This explanation is confirmed by the fol-
lowing extract from <I>A free discourse touching the murmurers of the tymes</I>, MS:
&lquo;They . . . play with your majestie as men play with little children at handye dandye,
which hand will you have, when they are disposed to keep any thinge from them.&rquo;
<SC>Halliwell</SC> says this is one of the oldest games in existence, not only alluded to by
Piers Plowman, but, according to Pope in his <I>Memoirs of Martinus Scriblerus</I>, by
Plato. &lquo;Sometimes the game is played by a sort of sleight of hand, changing the
article rapidly from one hand to another. . . . This is what Sh. alludes to by changing
places.&rquo;

<CC><P>172. <B>impertinency]</B> <SC>Douce</SC>: That is, something not belonging to the subject.
Thus an old collection of domestic recipes, &amp;c., entitled <I>The treasurie of com-
modious conceits</I>, 1594, is said to be &lquo;not impertinent for every good huswife to use
in her house amongst her own familie.&rquo; This word does not seem to have been used
in the sense of <I>rude</I> or <I>unmannerly</I> till the middle of the seventeenth century, nor
in that of <I>saucy</I> till a considerable time afterwards.
<P>178. <B>wawl]</B> <SC>Wright</SC>: Cotgrave has: &lquo;Ho&uuml;aller. To yawle, wawle, or cry out aloud.&rquo;
<P>181. <B>This']</B> <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 80): <I>This is</I> is not unfrequently,&mdash;like <I>that is</I>, &amp;c.&mdash;
contracted into a monosyllable. See <I>Lear</I>, V, iii, 283; <I>Tam. Shr.</I> I, ii, 45, &lquo;Why
this' a heavy chance 'twixt him and you.&rquo; <SC>Wright</SC>: See <I>Meas. for Meas.</I> V, i, 131,
&lquo;this' a good Fryer belike.&rquo; See <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 461; also II, ii, 116, of this play.
<SC>Ritson</SC> needlessly suggested &lquo;'Tis.&rquo;
<P>181. <B>block]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC> would read &lquo;a good <I>flock</I>,&rquo; that is, a flock of wool. &lquo;Lear
picks up a <I>flock</I>, and immediately thinks to surprise his enemies by a troop of horse
shod with <I>flocks</I> or <I>felt.</I> Yet &lquo;block&rquo; may stand, if we suppose that the sight of a
block put him in mind of mounting his horse. <SC>Capell</SC>: The mode of Lear's mad-
ness is chang'd; it is calm, and shews some sparks of reason; he knows Gloucester,
and his condition; tells him he must be patient; . . . says he will &lquo;preach&rquo; to him;
upon this he puts himself in posture of one who would preach, and pulls off his hat:
Scarce has he utter'd a few words when some fumes of a wilder nature fly up; the
<I>hat</I> catches his eye, and sets fire to another train of ideas; the words &lquo;This a good
block?&rquo; are spoke looking upon the hat; and this is follow'd by a second conceit,
which has it's rise from the same circumstance, about &lquo;felt,&rquo; and the use it might
be put to. <SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;Block&rquo; anciently signified the head part of the hat, or the
thing on which a hat is formed, and sometimes the hat itself. Thus <I>Much Ado</I>, I, i,</CC>

&ldquo;kill, kill.&rdquo;&rquo; Again, in <I>The Mirrour for Magistrates</I>, 1610, p. 315: &lquo;Our English-
men came boldly forth at night, Crying Saint <I>George, Salisbury</I>, kill, kill.&rquo;
<P>189. <B>fool of fortune]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: Compare &lquo;I am fortune's fool,&rquo; <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I>
III, i, 129. <SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Crit.</I> ii, 309): Here &lquo;natural fool&rquo; means one <I>born</I> to be the
sport of fortune. Bacon speaks of &lquo;<I>natural</I> Spaniards,&rquo; <B><I>i. e.</I></B> native. Massinger, in

<P>191. <B>cut to th' brains]</B> <SC>Cowden Clarke</SC>: This, one of the most powerfully, yet
briefly expressed, utterances of mingled bodily pain and consciousness of mental in-
firmity ever penned, is not the only subtle indication in this scene that Lear not
merely feels himself to be insane, but also feels acute physical suffering. &lquo;I am not
ague-proof&rquo; tells how severely shaken his poor old frame has been by exposure through-
out that tempestuous night; &lquo;pull off my boots; harder, harder,&rquo; gives evidence of a
sensation of pressure and impeded circulation in the feet, so closely connected
with injury to the brain; and &lquo;I am cut to the brains&rquo; conveys the impression of
wounded writhing within the head, that touches us with deepest sympathy. Yet, at
the same time, there are the gay irrationality and the incoherency that mark this
stage of mania.</CC>

<CC><P>221. <B>known and feeling]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: Sorrows past and present. <SC>Malone</SC>:
I doubt whether <I>feeling</I> is not used for <I>felt.</I> Sorrows known, not by relation, but
by experience. <SC>Eccles</SC>: &lquo;Feeling sorrows&rquo; are such as, by awakening sympathy,
make us feel for others. <SC>Cowden Clarke</SC>: &lquo;Feeling&rquo; is here used in both senses
of &lquo;personally felt&rquo; and &lquo;deeply moving.&rquo; Compare <I>Wint. Tale</I>, IV, ii, 8: &lquo;To
whose feeling sorrows I might be some allay.&rquo; <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 372, seems to adopt
Malone's view; he explains &lquo;Feeling&rquo; as &lquo;known,&rquo; passively, &lquo;known and realized
sorrows.&rquo; <SC>Schmidt</SC>: &lquo;Feeling&rquo; is here not a participle but a gerund, and &lquo;feeling
sorrows&rquo; is equivalent to <I>heartfelt sorrows.</I> It is essentially the same gerund as in
<I>dying speech, writing book, washing tub</I>, &amp;c.
<P>222. <B>pregnant]</B> <SC>Schmidt</SC>: Disposed, prompt, ready. [See II, i, 76.]
<P>228. <B>remember]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: Recollect the past offences of thy life and recom-
mend thyself to heaven.
<P>229, 230. <B>Now . . . to 't]</B> <SC>Cowden Clarke</SC> understands this as a call to Edgar
to defend him. With all deference I cannot but think that it is addressed to Oswald,
begging him to put strength enough to his destroying sword to make sure work
with it.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC></CC>

<CC><P>234. <B>Chill, &amp;c.]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: When our ancient writers introduce a rustic they
commonly allot him this Somersetshire dialect. Mercury, in the second book of
Ovid's <I>Metamorphoses</I>, assumes the appearance of a clown, and Golding has made
him speak with the provinciality of Shakespeare's Edgar [p. 26, &lquo;And I chill gethee
vor thy paine an Hecfar an hir match.&rquo; The pleonastic &lquo;I chill&rquo; is probably an over-
sight on Golding's part; a line or two farther on there is no &lquo;I&rquo; before &lquo;Cham zure.&rquo;
Capell's spelling <I>ch'ill</I>, and <I>ch'ud</I> in line 237, is probably the most correct, but, in a
matter so trifling and so vague, we might as well follow the Ff, even in their mis-
spellings. I have, therefore, printed &lquo;bin&rquo; and &lquo;whither,&rquo; which may be, in reality,
indications of the pronunciation.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Ellis</SC> (<I>E. E. Pronunciation</I>, p. 293):
The contractions <I>cham, chas, chil</I> (tsham, tshas, tsh<I>i</I>l) for ich am, ich was, ich will,
are mentioned by Gill (<I>Logonomia</I>, p. 17) as a Southern pronunciation, in Rev. W.
Barnes's edition of the <I>Glossary of the Dialect of Forth and Bargy</I>, and in the
Glossary to his Poems in the Dorset dialect, 1858, p. 150. The dialectic pronun-
ciations <I>Ise, 'ch</I> are preserved [here in <I>Lear</I>]. About thirty years ago <I>utchy</I> was
in use for <I>I</I> in the eastern border of Devonshire and in Dorset, and examples of
<I>cham, chould</I> = I am, I would, occur in the <I>Exmoor Scolding</I>, which dates from
the beginning of the last century. <SC>Wright</SC>: I will, contracted from &lquo;ich will,&rquo; just
as &lquo;chud&rquo; is for &lquo;ich would&rquo; or &lquo;ich should.&rquo; In Grose's <I>Provincial Glossary</I> &lquo;chell&rquo;
is said to be used for &lquo;I shall&rquo; in Somerset and Devon, and &lquo;cham&rquo; for &lquo;I am&rquo; in
Somerset. In Whetstone's <I>Promos and Cassandra</I> we find &lquo;cham,&rquo; &lquo;chy,&rquo; &lquo;chaue,&rquo;
&lquo;chul.&rquo;
<P>236. <B>gait]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: In the last rebellion, when the Scotch soldiers had finished
their exercise, instead of our term of dismission, their phrase was &lquo;gang your gaits.&rquo;</CC>

<P>240. <B>costard]</B> The name of an apple, and hence, according to <SC>Gifford</SC> (Note on

a corruption of the true word, as it is in the Folio.

<P>247. <B>letters]</B> Here, and in line 255, <SC>Mr Smith</SC> thinks we should read <I>letter</I>, be-

the audience no doubt should have heard it as well as Goneril's.&rquo; See IV, v, 33.
[<SC>Eccles, Malone</SC>, and <SC>The Cambridge Editors</SC> attribute this note to &lquo;Mr Smith;&rquo;
it is found in Grey's <I>Notes</I>, &amp;c., vol. ii, p. 114, and, although it is not always perfectly
clear where Grey's own notes end, and &lquo;Mr Smith's&rquo; notes, that he quotes, begin, yet
I think that they are correct in this instance. When I compiled the note on IV, v,
33. I thought that to &lquo;Mr Smith&rquo; belonged only the note on &lquo;undistinguish'd space
of woman's will,&rquo; and that what I have quoted above was Grey's. &lquo;Mr Smith of
Harleston in Norfolk&rquo; Grey pronounces &lquo;the most friendly and communicative man
living,&rquo; and adds, that he was &lquo;greatly assistant to Sir Thomas Hanmer in his edition
of Shakespeare.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Malone</SC> shows that &lquo;letters&rquo; was used like <I>epistol&aelig;</I>, when
only one was intended. In I, v, 1, Lear tells Kent to go before with these &lquo;letters,&rquo;
and Kent replies that he would deliver the &lquo;letter.&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>249. <B>English]</B> See III, iv, 176. <SC>Knight</SC>: This slight difference between the Qq
and Ff proves one of two things: Either that upon the publication of the Folio the
distinction between British and English, which was meant as a mark of compliment
to James, had ceased to be regarded; or that the passage, having been written before
his accession, had not been changed in the copy from which the Folio was printed,
as it was changed in the copy of the play acted before the king in 1606. <SC>White</SC>:
&lquo;English&rquo; is a sophistication doubtless. Sh. must have known well enough that in
Lear's time there were no more Englishmen in Britain than in America. [See Ap-
pendix, p. 379.]

<P>269. <B>space]</B> <SC>Theobald</SC> in his correspondence with <SC>Warburton</SC> (Nichols's <I>Illus.</I>

woman's wit.&rdquo;&rquo; Whereupon <SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. i) remarks: &lquo;Mr Singer offers a brace of
conjectures, which I must take the liberty of saying he ought to have suppressed.&rquo;
The &lquo;brace&rquo; failed to appear in Singer's subsequent edition. Voss conjectures <I>pace</I>,
that is, &lquo;How trifling, insignificant, is the step between a woman's different wills!&rquo;
<SC>Bailey</SC> (i, 110) thinks &lquo;we have only to reflect on what a man in Edgar's position
would be likely to say in order to arrive at the right reading.&rquo; This simple process
leads Bailey to the belief that <I>maze</I> is the true word here.
<P>269. <SC>Theobald</SC>: The reading [of the Ff: &lquo;will,&rquo; instead of <I>wit</I> of the Qq] gives
us, as Mr Warburton observes to me, a most elegant Expression and most satirical
Thought; more delicate than the &lquo;varium et mutabile semper femina&rquo; of Virgil. 'Tis
not the Extravagance, but the Mutability, of a Woman's Will that is here satiriz'd.
The Change of which (our Author would be understood to say,) is so speedy, that
there is no Space of time, no Distance, between the present Will and the next; but
it is an undistinguish'd Space. This Sentiment may not be ill explain'd further from
what honest <I>Sancho</I>, in <I>Don Quixote</I>, with infinite Humour says upon the subject.</CC>

Betwixt a Woman's <I>Yea</I>, and <I>No</I>, I would not undertake to thrust a Pin's Point.
<SC>Davies</SC>: A vicious woman sets no bounds to her appetites. <SC>Steevens</SC>: O undis-
tinguishing licentiousness of a woman's inclinations! <SC>Collier</SC>: Here, according to
the (MS), we have a remarkable proof of mishearing. . . . The fact is that &lquo;undis-
tinguish'd&rquo; ought to be <I>unextinguish'd</I>, and &lquo;space&rquo; <I>blaze;</I> thus taking &lquo;will&rquo; for
<I>disposition</I>, the clear intention of the poet is to make Edgar exclaim against the
unextinguishable fire or <I>blaze</I> of the appetite of woman, as illustrated by the letter
and conduct of Goneril. <SC>Dyce</SC>: &lquo;Undistinguish'd space&rquo; means <I>space whose limits
are not to be distinguished.</I> <SC>White</SC>: That is, O, unmarked, boundless reach of
woman's will! <SC>Hudson</SC>: &lquo;Undistinguish'd&rquo; for <I>undistinguishable</I>, like &lquo;unnum-
bered&rquo; for <I>innumerable.</I> Woman's will has no distinguishable bounds or no assign-
able limits; there is no telling what she will do or where she will stop. <SC>Staunton</SC>:
Whatever may have been the original lection, it was plainly an exclamation against
the indiscriminate caprice of woman as exhibited by Goneril in plotting against a
virtuous husband's life merely to gain a villain like Edmund. We should perhaps
read: &lquo;<I>undistinguishable sense</I> of woman's will.&rquo; <SC>Wright</SC>: So wide-reaching [is
a woman's will] that its workings cannot be discovered. . . . Without calling in ques-
tion the absolute truth of Sancho's profound observation [as quoted by Theobald], it
is at least allowable to doubt the propriety of applying it in the present case. Edgar's
astonishment is not at the fickleness and caprice of Goneril, but at the enormous
wickedness of the plot which her letter revealed. <SC>Moberly</SC>: The passage may be
a reminiscence of Horace's: &lquo;Cum fas atque nefas exiguo fine libidinum Discernunt
avidi&rquo; (<I>Odes</I>, I, xviii), which Mr Wickham renders: &lquo;While in their greedy haste they
divide right and wrong by the slender line of their own appetite;&rquo; <I>i.e.</I> &lquo;when the
only distinction which they place between right and wrong is, that they desire the
thing or not.&rquo; So here Shakespeare's idea seems to be that a woman's will knows
<I>no</I> limits between good and evil. <SC>Schmidt</SC>: That is, &lquo;Oh undistinguishable range
of the female appetite!&rquo; Edgar is astonished that a woman can be found to prefer
Edmund to the noble Albany.

<CC><P>9. <B>made intent]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: There is a dissonancy in terms in &lquo;made intent&rquo;;

&lquo;<I>laid</I> intent,&rquo; <I>i.e.</I> projected. [Thus Warburton's text.] <SC>Johnson</SC>: An intent <I>made</I>

change his dress, since he must, in that case, be known, which would defeat his chief

<P>17. <B>child-changed]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: That is, changed to a child by his years and his

<CC><P>20. <B>Is he array'd?]</B> From this question <SC>Delius</SC> infers that the stage-direction of
the Ff is correct, and that Lear is not on the stage at the opening of the scene. [But,

<P>21. <B>of'sleep]</B> I think this is, probably, an instance of the absorption of <I>his.</I>&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>
<P>25. <B>Louder . . . there!]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: A noble thought of the poet's in this editor's
judgement [<I>i. e.</I> Capell's]; what he gathers [from these words] is this: that a soft
&lquo;music&rquo; should be heard at the scene's opening, and behind the bed, which is dis-
tant; that this music had been Lear's composer, and (together with his composure)
his cure; that it is now call'd-to by the Doctor for the purpose of waking him, by
such strains as were proper, rising gradually; which is not a noble thought only, but
just, and of good effect on the scene.
<P>25. <B>music]</B> <SC>Bucknill</SC> (p. 222): This seems a bold experiment, and one not un-
fraught with danger. The idea that the insane mind is beneficially influenced by
music is, indeed, an ancient and general one; but that the medicated sleep of insanity
should be interrupted by it, and that the first object presented to the consciousness
should be the very person most likely to excite profound emotion, appear to be ex-
pedients little calculated to promote that tranquillity of the mental functions which is,
undoubtedly, the safest state to induce, after the excitement of mania. A suspicion
of this may have crossed Shakespeare's mind, for he represents Lear in imminent
danger of passing into a new form of delusion. The earliest note of the employ-
ment of music in the treatment of the insane is in the Bible (1 <I>Sam.</I> xvi) where
David calmed Saul. . . . Modern physicians appear to have little faith in its effects
when simply listened to. Esquirol says, &lquo;I have often employed music, but very
rarely obtained any success thereby. It calms and composes the mind, but does not</CC>

<P>35. <B>perdu]</B> <SC>Reed</SC>: In Polemon's <I>Collection of Battels</I>, bl. l. p. 98, an account of
the battle of Marignano is translated from Jovius, in which is the following passage:
&lquo;They were very chosen fellowes taken out of all the Cantons, men in the prime of
youth, and of singular forwardenesse: who by a very auntient order of that country, that
by dooyng some deede of passyng prowesse they may obtaine rare honour of warrefare
before they be growen in yeares, doe of themselves request all perillous and harde
pieces of service, and often use with deadlye praise to runne unto proposed death.
These men do they call, of their immoderate fortitude and stoutnesse, the desperats
forlorne hopen, and the Frenchmen <I>enfans perdus:</I> and it is lawfull for them, by the
prerogative of their prowesse, to beare an ensigne, to have conducte and double wages
all their life long. Neyther, are the forlorne knowen from the rest by anye other
marke and cognisance than the plumes of white feathers, the which, after the manner
of captaines, they doe tourn behinde, waveryng over theyr shoulder with a brave kynde
of riot.&rquo; Again, in Bacon's <I>Apology touching the late Earl of Essex</I>, 1651, p. 105:
&lquo;&mdash;you have put me like one of those that the Frenchmen call <I>Enfans perdus</I> that
serve on foot before horsemen.&rquo; <SC>Whalley</SC>: Amongst other desperate services in
which the forlorn hope, or <I>enfans perdus</I>, were engaged, the night-watches seem to
have been a common one. So in Beau. and Fl.: &lquo;These are trim things. I am set
here like a <I>perdu</I>, To <I>watch</I> a fellow that has wrong'd my mistress.&rquo;&mdash;<I>Little French
Lawyer</I>, II, iii. <SC>Wright</SC>: Cotgrave says, &lquo;Enfans perdus. Perdus; or the forlorne
hope, of a campe (are commonly Gentlemen of Companies).&rquo; <SC>Moberly</SC>: The mean-
ing may be simply &lquo;poor lost one.&rquo; [The <SC>Cambridge Edition</SC> records <I>pour perdu</I>
as a conjecture by <SC>Pye</SC>, but I think it is merely a misprint in the latter's volume.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>36. <B>dog]</B> <SC>Collier</SC>: The misprint of the Qq: <I>injurious</I> for &lquo;enemy's&rquo; is quite as
extraordinary as that of &lquo;runaways&rquo; for <I>enemies</I> in <I>Rom. &amp; Jul.</I> <SC>Mitford</SC> (<I>Gent.
Mag.</I> p. 469, 1844) conjectures that the Qq lead to the word that will supply the
line, &lquo;Mine enemy's <I>furious</I> dog.&rquo; <SC>Verplanck</SC>: The late J. W. Jarvis, the artist,
used often to quote these lines as accumulating in the shortest compass the greatest
causes of dislike to be overcome by good-natured pity. It is not merely the personal
enemy, for whom there might be human sympathy, that is admitted to the family
fireside, but his dog, and that a dog who had himself inflicted his own share of
personal injury, and that too upon a gentle being from whom it was not possible that
he could have received any provocation.

<P>47. <B>fire]</B> <SC>Moberly</SC>: It would almost seem as if Sh. had borrowed the description
of Lear's reviving senses from what he had seen or known of in some one recov-
ered from drowning. At any rate, the feelings of one thus returning to life, as
described by Sir F. Beaufort, have striking points of resemblance: &lquo;A helpless
anxiety seemed to press on every sense, and to prevent the formation of any dis-
tinct thought; and it was with difficulty that I became convinced I was really
alive. Again, instead of being free from bodily pain, as in my drowning state, I
was now tortured with pain all over me; and though I have often been wounded,
and had to submit to severe surgical discipline, yet my sufferings at that time were
far greater, at least in general distress.&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Martineau</SC>, <I>Biog. Sketches.</I> p. 221. [Does
Lear refer to physical pain?&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<CC><P>79. <B>kill'd]</B> <SC>Collier</SC>: <I>Quell'd</I> was perhaps the poet's word, and <I>quell'd</I> and &lquo;kill'd,&rquo;

<P>80. <B>even o'er]</B> <SC>Warburton</SC>: That is, to reconcile it to his apprehension. <SC>Stee-
vens</SC>: I believe Warburton's explanation is just. The poor old king had nothing to
tell, though he had much to hear. The speaker's meaning, therefore, I conceive to
be&mdash;it is dangerous to render all that passed during the interval of his insanity, <I>even</I>
(<I>i. e.</I> plain or level) to his understanding, while it continues in its present state of
uncertainty. <SC>Collier</SC>: We may suspect some corruption, but the meaning is evi-
dent, and no alteration absolutely required. <SC>Hudson</SC>: This means, <I>try to account for</I>
the time, or to make the last day of his remembering tally or fit with the present.
<SC>Delius</SC> prefers to consider &lquo;even&rquo; as an adjective rather than as a verb. <SC>Schmidt</SC>
(<I>Lex.</I> s. v. <I>even</I>, adj. 7): That is, to give a full insight into, a clear perception of.
<SC>Wright</SC>: To smooth over, render what had passed unbroken in his recollection.
The sense is the same [whether it be taken as an adj. or as a verb], but it seems pre-
ferable to consider it as a verb. The danger consisted rather in allowing Lear's
mind to exert itself in recalling the past than in telling him what had happened.
<SC>Schmidt</SC>: A verb <I>to even</I> equivalent to <I>to smooth</I> is not to be found in Sh.

<CC><P><I>heavy causes make</I>, or compel, as it were, to <I>oppose</I> us, I esteem it unjust to engage
against them. <SC>Capell</SC> thus paraphrases: &lquo;As for this business,&mdash;it toucheth us as
France invades our kingdom, not <I>as he</I> holds for the king, <I>in conjunction</I> with <I>the</I>
others whom,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Steevens</SC>: This business touches us as France invades our
land, not <I>as it</I> &lquo;bolds the king,&rquo; <I>i. e.</I> emboldens him to assert his former title. Thus
in the ancient interlude of Hycke Scorner: &lquo;Alas, that I had not one to <I>bold</I> me!&rquo;
Again, in Hall's trans. of the <I>Fourth Iliad</I>, 1581: &lquo;And Pallas bolds the Greeks,&rquo; &amp;c.
[As <SC>Wright</SC> observes, Steevens is wrong here; it is not &lquo;this business&rquo; that &lquo;bolds
the king,&rquo; but &lquo;France,&rquo; as Warburton and Capell have justly interpreted it. For a
long list of verbs like &lquo;bolds&rquo; formed from nouns and adjectives, see <SC>Abbott</SC>,
&sect; 290.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] <SC>Cambridge Editors</SC>: &lquo;Not bolds the king&rquo; is usually interpreted as
an elliptical phrase for &lquo;Not as it emboldens the king.&rquo; This is, however, a very
harsh construction, and the word &lquo;bolds&rquo; occurs nowhere else in Sh. with this
meaning, though we have, according to the most probable reading, &lquo;dear'd&rquo; for
&lquo;endear'd&rquo; in <I>Ant. &amp; Cleop.</I> I, iv, 44. Possibly these words are corrupt and a line
has dropped out before them. Albany ought to say something of this kind: &lquo;I
should be ready to resist any mere invader, but the presence in the invader's camp
of the king and other Britons, who have a just cause of enmity to us, dashes my
courage.&rquo;
<P>28. <B>nobly]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: Edmund's reply is irony, and his &lquo;nobly&rquo; a trisyllable.
<SC>Walker</SC> (<I>Vers.</I> 12) says that &lquo;nobly&rquo; is not a fair instance of the expansion of a
dissyllable into a trisyllable, like &lquo;angry,&rquo; &lquo;children,&rquo; &amp;c., because &lquo;nobly&rquo; is con-
tracted from <I>noblely.</I> <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 477, cites it under that head.
<P>30. <B>particular]</B> <SC>Malone</SC>: <I>Doore</I> or <I>dore</I> of the Qq was probably a misprint for
<I>dear</I>, i. e. important. <SC>Steevens</SC>: &lquo;<I>Door</I> particulars&rquo; signify, I believe, particulars
at our very doors, close to us, and consequently fitter to be settled at home. <SC>Collier</SC>:
The text of the Qq is impossible to strain to a meaning unless we suppose <I>door</I> mis-
printed for <I>poor.</I> <SC>Mitford</SC> (<I>Gent. Maga.</I> p. 469, 1844): In &lquo;doore particulars&rquo; of
the Qq the <I>d</I> is only a <I>p</I> reversed. Read then, &lquo;these domestic <I>poore</I> particulars.&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>167. <B>charity]</B> <SC>Johnson</SC>: Our author, by negligence, gives his heathens the senti-
ments and practices of Christianity. In <I>Hamlet</I> there is the same solemn act of final
reconciliation, but with exact propriety, for the personages are Christians: &lquo;Exchange
forgiveness with me, noble Hamlet,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Cowden Clarke</SC>: Can we believe that
the most careful dramatist that ever wrote set down anything &lquo;by negligence&rquo;? Is
not the virtue of a magnanimous generosity proper to human nature in all ages and
in all creeds?
<P>169. <B>the more]</B> According to <SC>Abbott</SC>, &sect; 480, the emphasis on this &lquo;more&rquo; causes
it, in scansion, to be prolonged. Abbott thus quotes and divides the line: &lquo;If
m&oacute;re &verbar; the <I>m&oacute; &verbar; re</I> h&aacute;st &verbar; thou wr&oacute;ng'd &verbar; (&egrave;d) m&eacute;.&rquo; See I, iv, 334. <SC>White</SC>: I am
inclined to think that this imper$ect line is corrupted, and that it was written: &lquo;If
more, the more thou <I>then</I> hast <I>wronged</I> me.&rquo; [I have preferred to print the line
exactly as it stands in the Ff.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]
<P>171. <SC>Wordsworth</SC> (p. 113): The same sentiment is in the Apocryphal <I>Book
of Wisdom</I>, xi, 16: &lquo;wherewithal a man sinneth, by the same also shall he be
punished.&rquo;</CC>

<CC><P>the passage I transcribe for the benefit of the reader, who is doubtless quite as com-
petent as I am, &lquo;to endow its purposes with words&rquo;: &lquo;The verses&rquo; form was most
easy; the change of &ldquo;would&rdquo; into &ldquo;to&rdquo; presented sense, and points follow'd the
sense. &ldquo;much&rdquo; and &ldquo;too much&rdquo; are put substantively; and &ldquo;another&rdquo; is&mdash;<I>take
another</I>, indicated by the tone and the pause: by which tone too, we may conceive
of what is put in parenthesis the sense following;&mdash;<I>since you will put me upon
amplifying what is already too much, upon making much more, and topping ex-
tremity</I>, take another relation: The period contains a proper reproof of Edmund's
unfeelingness.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC> thus paraphrases: &lquo;This would have seemed a period to
such as love not sorrow; but&mdash;another, <I>i. e.</I> but I must add another, <I>i. e.</I> another
period, another kind of conclusion to my story, such as will increase the horrors of
what has been already told.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC> inclines to Dodd's view: &lquo;This, says Edgar,
would have seemed the utmost completion of woe, to such as do not delight in
sorrow; but <I>another</I>, of a different disposition, to amplify misery, would &ldquo;give more
strength to that which hath too much.&rdquo; Edgar's words, however, may have no refer-
ence to what Edmund has said, and he may only allude to the relation he is about
to give of Kent's adding a new sorrow to what Edgar already suffered, by recounting
the miseries which the old king and his faithful follower had endured. <SC>Steevens</SC>:
Malone's explanation may be just; and yet it is probable that we are struggling with
a passage, the obscurity of which is derived from its corruption. <SC>Collier</SC>: The
disputed meaning seems to be: &lquo;but I have yet another misfortune to relate, which
will make the rest too much,&rquo; &amp;c. <SC>Mitford</SC> (<I>Gent. Mag.</I>, p. 469, 1844) thinks that
a slight transposition will cure line 207, and proposes: &lquo;To amplify, <I>would make
much more too much.</I>&rquo; [All commentators, whether they understand &lquo;another&rquo; as
referring to <I>man</I> or to <I>misfortune</I>, have taken &lquo;but&rquo; in an adversative sense; but
<SC>Wright</SC> gives what seems the true explanation; he says:] &lquo;It seems better to take
it as qualifying &ldquo;another,&rdquo; as if [Edgar] said &ldquo;one more such circumstance only, by
amplifying what is already too much, would add to it, and so exceed what seemed
to be the limit of sorrow.&rdquo; For this gerundial use of the infinitive, see III, v, 8.&rquo;
[The unaided Qq text is synonymous with obscurity in almost every sentence.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<CC><P>214. <B>him]</B> (See Textual Notes.) <SC>Steevens</SC>: There is tragic propriety in Kent's
throwing himself on the body of a deceased friend; but this propriety is lost in the
act of clumsily tumbling a son over the lifeless remains of his father. <SC>Malone</SC>:
Kent, in his transport of joy at meeting Edgar, embraced him with such violence as
to throw him on the dead body of Gloucester. <SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Remarks</I>, p. 232): Kent's
tumbling down Edgar on the dead body of his father is an incident more suited to a
comic pantomime than to a serious narrative in a tragedy. The progress of the error
here is plain: &lquo;<I>him</I>&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;'<I>em</I>&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;me.&rquo; Other corruptions may be traced in the same way;
for instance, we sometimes find &lquo;thou&rquo; where the sense positively requires &lquo;yon,&rquo;&mdash;
the progress of that error having been&mdash;&lquo;<I>yon</I>&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;you&rquo;&mdash;&lquo;thou.&rquo; <SC>White</SC>: Does
Edgar mean, &lquo;Threw himself on my father&rquo;? the expression being like &lquo;Ascends
me into the brain.&rquo;

<P>264, 265. <B>Is . . . horror?]</B> <SC>Capell</SC> was the first to point out that &lquo;the &ldquo;horror&rdquo;
of which this sight was the image, according to Edgar, is&mdash;the horror of the last day,
or day of judgement, call'd emphatically&mdash;<I>that</I> horror.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC> at first thought
that Kent meant to ask: Is this conclusion such as the present turn of affairs seemed
to promise? Or is it only, as Edgar replied, a representation of that horror which
we suppose to be real? but Steevens afterwards acknowledged the excellence of the
following explanation by <SC>Mason</SC>: By the &lquo;promised end&rquo; Kent does not mean
that conclusion which the state of their affairs seemed to promise, but the end of
the world. In <I>St. Mark's Gospel</I>, when Christ foretells to his disciples the end of
the world, and is describing to them the signs that were to precede, and mark the
approach of, our final dissolution, he says: &lquo;For in those days shall be affliction such
as was not from the beginning of the creation which God created, unto this time,
neither shall be;&rquo; and afterwards he says, &lquo;Now the brother shall betray the brother
to death, and the father the son; and the children shall rise up against their parents,
and shall cause them to be put to death.&rquo; Kent, in contemplating the unexampled
scene of exquisite affliction which was then before him, and the unnatural attempt
of Goneril and Regan against their father's life, recollects these passages, and asks,
whether that was the end of the world that had been foretold to us. To which
Edgar adds, Or only a representation or resemblance of that horror? So Macbeth,
when he calls upon Banquo, Malcolm, &amp;c. to view Duncan murdered, says: &lquo;&mdash;up,
up, and see The great doom's image!&rquo; There is evidently an allusion to the same
passage in Scripture in a speech of Gloster's which he makes, I, ii, 98, &amp;c. If any
critick should urge it as an objection to this explanation, that the persons of the drama
are pagans, and, of consequence, unacquainted with the Scriptures, they give Sh.
credit for more accuracy than I fear he possessed. <SC>Steevens</SC>: This note de-
serves the highest praise, and is inserted with the utmost degree of gratitude to its
author. [Although Mason's view, for which a hint may have been supplied by
Capell, is probably correct, yet the following note by <SC>Henley</SC> deserves consideration:]
Does not this exclamation refer to the confidence expressed in her letter to himself,
&lquo;that&mdash;seeking to give losses their remedies&mdash;she should find time amidst the enor-
mities of the state, to obtain the full effect of her purpose?&rquo; As these words (sup-
posing this to be their reference in the mouth of Kent) were not addressed to Edgar,
there is no necessity for considering them as understood by him in their proper sense;
his resumption, therefore, or rather adaptation of them, may not only admit, but
even require, a different interpretation. Mason's is an ingenious, and may be the true
one; for, though the passage of <I>St. Mark</I>, which he cites, does not refer to the &lquo;end
of the world&rquo; (as he might have learned from the 30th verse of the same chapter),
but to the destruction of Jerusalem and the Jewish state, yet the prediction itself is
vulgarly received in the sense in which he applies it. <SC>Halliwell</SC>: The reference</CC>

<P>265. <B>Fall and cease]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: These words were made very intelligible by the
action accompanying; the wide display of his hands, and the lifting-up of his eye,
both directed towards the heavens, would shew plain enough that it is they who are
call'd upon to <I>fall</I>, and crush a world that is such a scene of calamity . . . [The
words mean] Fall, heaven! and let things cease!&rquo; <SC>Jennens</SC> tells us, &lquo;till a better
emendation is proposed,&rquo; to read as in his text: &lquo;<I>Edg.</I> O image of true honour!
<I>Alb.</I> Fair and chaste.&rquo; &lquo;Which,&rquo; adds Jennens, &lquo;is a very natural exclamation on
the murder of so amiable a creature.&rquo; <SC>Steevens</SC>: Albany is looking with attention
on the pains employed by Lear to recover his child, and knows to what miseries he
must survive when he finds them to be ineffectual. Having these images present to
his eyes and imagination, he cries out: &lquo;Rather fall, and cease to be at once, than
continue in existence only to be wretched.&rquo; So in <I>All's Well</I>, to <I>cease</I> is used for to
<I>die;</I> and in <I>Ham.</I> the death of Majesty is called &ldquo;the <I>cease</I> of majesty.&rdquo; See III,
i, 7. <SC>Malone</SC>: I doubt whether this speech is addressed to Lear. <SC>Mason</SC>: Pos-
sibly this might be an allusion to the theatre, and Albany may mean to say, &lquo;Let
fall the curtain, and end the horrid scene.&rquo; <SC>Davies</SC> (<I>Dram. Misc.</I> ii, 212): Perhaps
Albany means, &lquo;Lower your voice, and cease all exclamation, lest you interrupt the
dying king.&rquo; This is not unlike to the word &lquo;quietness&rquo; in <I>Ant. &amp; Cleop.:</I> Char-
mian, on the Queen's fainting, whispers to Iras, &lquo;O quietness!&rquo; <SC>Delius</SC> supposes
that Edgar and Albany continue Kent's train of thought. Kent asks: Is this the
promised end of the world? Or the image of that horror? asks Edgar. Of that
fall and cease? continues Albany. &lquo;Fall and cease&rquo; are, therefore, to be considered
substantives, and in apposition to &lquo;that horror.&rquo; In his text Delius puts an interroga-
tion-mark after &lquo;cease.&rquo; <SC>Moberly</SC> seems to adopt Delius's view: &lquo;&ldquo;Yes,&rdquo; replies
Albany, &ldquo;of the general fall and cessation of all things.&rdquo;&rquo; [Would not the gaze of
every spectator be riveted horrorstruck upon Lear and Cordelia? and is it likely that
Albany's attention would be so far diverted from the sight as to reply to Edgar's
question, which really needed no answer? If &lquo;Fall and cease&rquo; be addressed to Lear,
there is a curt harshness in the words which is scarcely in keeping with Albany's
character. I have tried in vain to find authority for interpreting &lquo;Fall&rquo; in the sense
of &lquo;Fall back,&rquo; &lquo;Give way.&rquo; Then the sentence might be addressed to Kent and
Edgar, and equivalent to &lquo;Make room, and hush.&rquo; After all, Capell's interpretation
may be the true one; and yet, an address to the Heavens, unaccompanied by any
invocation, is unusual, to say the least.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<P>271. <B>I might have,</B> &amp;c.] <SC>Schmidt</SC> adopts in his text an emendation, which, he

<P>273. <B>voice]</B> <SC>Moberly</SC>: This wonderfully quiet touch seems to complete the per-
fection of Cordelia's character, evidently the poet's best loved creation, his type of
the ideal Englishwoman. Her voice was the outward signature of her graciously-
tempered nature. Burke's description of his wife is a master's variation on Shake-
speare's theme: &lquo;Her eyes have a mild light, but they awe you when she pleases;
they command, like a good man out of office, not by authority, but by virtue. Her
smiles are inexpressible. Her voice is a soft, low music, not formed to rule in public
assemblies, but to charm those who can distinguish a company from a crowd. It has
this advantage, you must be close to her to hear it.&rquo;

<CC><P>281, 282. <B>If . . . behold]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: In Kent's speech the two objects of fortune's
love and her hate are,&mdash;himself, and his master; they had both felt them, and both

display of her power: of these two, says the speaker, you (the person spoke to)
&lquo;behold&rquo; one, and I another. <SC>Eccles</SC>: I think Kent speaks of the object of her
&lquo;love&rquo; indefinitely, without intending any particular person, but considers <I>himself</I> as
the object of her &lquo;hate.&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC>: Kent may be only thinking of Lear, the object
of her hate. <SC>Mason</SC> is non-committal, and tells us that &lquo;the latter,&rquo; whom we now
behold, is the object of fortune's hate, but he does not tell us whether &lquo;the latter&rquo; is
Lear or Kent. <SC>Delius</SC> thinks it refers to Lear, as does also <SC>Moberly</SC>, &lquo;if the reading
is correct.&rquo; [Justice has scarcely been done, I think, to Jennens's reading here;
which might be improved, perhaps, by changing, as more in accordance with the
<I>ductus literarum, you</I> to <I>ye.</I> Thus read, Kent refers to himself, in answer to Lear's
question, &lquo;Who are you?&rquo;&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>]

<CC><P>305. <B>Oh, see, see!]</B> <SC>Capell</SC>: These words are occasion'd by seeing Lear exert
himself to embrace the body he lay upon once more, and pour his agonies over it.
<P>306. <B>my poor fool]</B> <SC>Steevens</SC>: This is an expression of tenderness for his dead
Cordelia (not his Fool, as some have thought), on whose lips he is still intent, and
dies away while he is searching there for indications of life. &lquo;Poor fool,&rquo; in the age
of Sh., was an expression of endearment. I may add, that the Fool of Lear was
long ago forgotten. Having filled the space allotted him in the arrangement of the
play, he appears to have been silently withdrawn, III, vi. That the thoughts of a
father, in the bitterest of all moments, while his favourite child lay dead in his arms,
should recur to the antick who had formerly diverted him, has somewhat in it that I
cannot reconcile to the idea of genuine sorrow and despair. Besides this, Cordelia
was recently hanged; but we know not that the Fool had suffered in the same man-
ner, nor can imagine why he should. The party adverse to Lear was little interested
in the fate of his jester. The only use of him was to contrast and alleviate the sor-
rows of his master; and, that purpose being fully answered, the poet's solicitude about
him was at an end. The term &lquo;poor fool&rquo; might indeed have misbecome the mouth
of a vassal commiserating the untimely end of a princess, but has no impropriety
when used by a weak, old, distracted king, in whose mind the distinctions of nature
only survive, while he is uttering his last frantic exclamations over a murdered
daughter. <SC>Sir Joshua Reynolds</SC>: I confess I am one of those who <I>have thought</I>
that Lear means his Fool, and not Cordelia. If he means Cordelia, then what I
have always considered as a beauty, is of the same kind as the accidental stroke of
the pencil that produced the foam. Lear's affectionate remembrance of the Fool, in
this place, I used to think, was one of those strokes of genius, or of nature, which
are so often found in Sh., and in him only. Lear appears to have a particular affec-
tion for this Fool, whose fidelity in attending him, and endeavouring to divert him
in his distress, seems to deserve all his kindness. &lquo;Poor fool and knave,&rquo; says he, in
the midst of the thunder-storm, &lquo;I have one part in my heart that's sorry yet for
thee.&rquo; It does not, therefore, appear to me, to be allowing too much consequence to
the Fool, in making Lear bestow a thought on him, even when in still greater distress.
Lear is represented as a good-natured, passionate, and rather weak, old man; it is the
old age of a cockered spoilt boy. There is no impropriety in giving to such a cha-
racter those tender domestic affections which would ill become a more heroic cha-
racter, such as Othello, Macbeth, or Richard III. The words, &lquo;No, no, no life,&rquo; I
suppose to be spoken, not tenderly, but with passion: Let nothing now live;&mdash;let
there be universal destruction;&mdash;&lquo;Why should a dog, a horse, a rat, have life, and</CC>
<PB N=346>
<HE>346 <I>KING LEAR</I> [<SC>act v, sc.</SC> iii.</HE>
<FHL>
<CC><C>[306. <B>my poor fool.]</B></C>
<P>thou no breath at all?&rquo; It may be observed, that as there was a necessity, the neces-
sity of propriety at least, that this Fool, the favourite of the author, of Lear, and
consequently of the audience, should not be lost or forgot, it ought to be known what
became of him. However, it must be acknowledged, that we cannot infer much
from thence; Sh. is not always attentive to finish the figures of his groups. I have
only to add, that if an actor, by adopting the interpretation mentioned above, should
apply the words &lquo;poor fool&rquo; to Cordelia, the audience would, I should imagine, think
it a strange mode of expressing the grief and affection of a father for his dead daugh-
ter, and that daughter a queen. The words &lquo;poor fool&rquo; are undoubtedly expressive
of endearment, and Sh. himself, in another place, speaking of a dying animal, calls
it &lquo;poor dappled fool,&rquo; but it never is, nor never can be, used with any degree of
propriety, but to commiserate some very inferior object, which may be loved, without
much esteem or respect. <SC>Malone</SC>: I have not the smallest doubt that Mr Steevens's
interpretation of these words is the true one. The passage, indeed, before us appears
to me so clear, and so inapplicable to any person but Cordelia, that I fear the reader
may think any further comment on it altogether superfluous. It is observable that
Lear, from the time of his entrance in this scene to his uttering these words, and
from thence to his death, is wholly occupied by the loss of his daughter. He is
diverted, indeed, from it for a moment by the intrusion of Kent, who forces himself
on his notice; but he instantly returns to his beloved Cordelia, over whose dead body
he continues to hang. He is now himself in the agony of death; and surely at such
a time, when his heart is just breaking, it would be highly unnatural that he should
think of his Fool. But the great and decisive objection to such a supposition is that
which Mr Steevens has mentioned&mdash;that Lear had just seen his daughter <I>hanged</I>,
having unfortunately been admitted too late to preserve her life, though time enough to
punish the perpetrator of the act; but we have no authority whatsoever for supposing
his Fool hanged also. Whether the expression &lquo;poor fool&rquo; can be applied with pro-
priety only to &lquo;inferior objects, for whom we have not much respect or esteem,&rquo; is
not, I conceive, the question. Sh. does not always use his terms with strict propriety,
but he is always the best commentator on himself, and he certainly <I>has</I> applied this
term in another place to the <I>young</I>, the <I>beautiful</I>, and <I>innocent</I> Adonis, the object
of somewhat more than the esteem of a goddess: &lquo;For pity now she can no more
detain him; The <I>poor fool</I> prays her that he may depart.&rquo; In Old English a <I>fool</I>
and an <I>innocent</I> were synonymous terms. Hence, probably, the peculiar use of the
expression &lquo;poor fool.&rquo; In the passage before us Lear, I conceive, means by it <I>dear,
tender, helpless innocence!</I> <SC>Rann</SC>: My hapless, innocent Cordelia. <SC>As You Like
It</SC> (<I>Gent. Mag.</I> lx, 402) imagines &lquo;poor soul&rquo; to be the original phrase. <SC>Knight</SC>:
&lquo;Poor fool&rquo; might indeed be here employed something like the &lquo;excellent wretch&rquo;
of Othello; but we cannot avoid thinking that Sh., in this place, meant to express
a peculiar tenderness, derived from Lear's confused recollection of his regard for his
poor follower, the Fool. In the depth of his distress during the storm Lear says:
&lquo;Poor fool and knave, I have one part in my heart that's sorry yet for thee.&rquo; And
now, when the last and deepest calamity has fallen upon him, his expressions shape
themselves out of the indistinctness with which he views the present and the past,
and Cordelia is his &lquo;poor fool.&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC>: It may be urged that, as Cordelia had
