<C>THE TEXT</C>
<P><SC>In</SC> the Registers of the Stationers Company,<SUP>*</SUP> for the year 1594, we find the fol-
lowing entry:
<C>riiijto die Maij.</C>
<P><SP><B>Adam Islip.</B></SP>&verbar; Entred al$oe for his Copie vnder th andes of bothe the wardens
<B>Edward White.</B>&verbar;. a booke entituled &verbar; <I>The mo$te famous Chronicle hi$torye of</I> <SC>Leir<*></SC>
<I>kinge of England and his Three Daughters</I> . . . vj<SUP>d</SUP> C.&verbar;.
<P>Of this book no copy is known to be extant; this is the only trace we have of
it. Possibly but few copies were issued; Edward White was not, at that time, a
prominent stationer. If we were certain that this &lquo;booke&rquo; was a drama we should
be at liberty to conjecture that it is the original on which Shakespeare founded his
tragedy, and that it has eluded our search out of the sheer perversity of that &lquo;nature
of things&rquo; which Porson was wont to damn, and which seems to envelope in a thick
mist everything pertaining to Shakespeare. But we know nothing more about it
than is contained in the foregoing entry, and in this ignorance we get what comfort
we may from the supposition that it is not really lost, but re-appears in the follow
ing entries:&dagger;
<C>8 maij [1605]</C>
<P><B>Simon Stafford</B> Entred for his Copie vnder th andes of the Wardens A booke
called &lquo;<I>the Tragecall hi$torie of kinge <SC>leir</SC> and his Three
Daughiers &amp;c.&rquo; As it was latelie Acted</I> . . . . . . vj<SUP>d</SUP>
<P><B>John Wright</B> &verbar; Entred for his Copie by a$$ignement from <B>Simon Stafford</B> and
by con$ent of Ma$ter <B>Leake</B>, <I>The Tragicall hi$tory of kinge
<SC>leire</SC> and his Three Daughters</I> &verbar; <SC>Provided</SC> that <B>Simon Staf-
ford</B> $hall haue the printinge of this booke &verbar;&verbar; . . . . vj<SUP>d</SUP>
<P>[It is evident that <I>King Lear</I> was printed by S. Stafford before
the 8th May, 1605, though not entered until it was assigned on
that date.&mdash;<SC>Arber</SC>.]
<P>A $ew copies of this &lquo;booke&rquo; are extant. It is perhaps worth noting that the
title which they now bear does not correspond exactly with that in the registered
entry. The present title, as given by <SC>Capell</SC> (vol. i, p. 55), is as follows: &lquo;The &verbar;
True Chronicle Hi- &verbar; $tory of King <SC>Leir</SC>, and his three &verbar; <I>daughters</I>, Gonorill, Ra-
gan, &verbar; and Cordella. &verbar; As it hath bene divers and $undry &verbar; times lately acted. &verbar; <SC>Lon-
don</SC>, &verbar; Printed by Simon Stafford for John &verbar; Wright, and are to bee $old at his $hop
at &verbar; Chri$tes Church dore, next Newgate- &verbar; Market, 1605.&rquo;
<FHL>
<NOTE><SC>Arber's</SC> <I>Transcript</I>, ii, 649.</NOTE>
<NOTE><I>Ibid.</I>, iii, 289.</NOTE>
<PB N=354>
<HE>354 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>In the Stationers' Registers it is styled &lquo;The Tragicall hi$tory;&rquo; on its published
title-page, it is called &lquo;The True Chronicle Hi$tory.&rquo; Now although the entries in
the Register do not assume to give complete or exact titles (enough merely of the
titles was recorded to identify the source whence came the various sums of money
which were received by the Wardens), yet the use of the word &lquo;Tragicall&rquo; seems
not altogether purposeless, especially when the assertion is added: &lquo;As it was lately
&lquo;acted.&rquo; It may be that Stafford looked more to the body of the drama than to
the mere ending, in which case he was certainly justified in calling it a &lquo;tragicall
hiftory,&rquo; and as he was under no obligation to adhere afterward to the description
given to the Warden, he may have described it, at the moment, according to its
most characteristic feature. Still Malone and others scent fraud here, and Stafford
has been accused of double-dealing, in that he called his &lquo;booke&rquo; one thing on the
eighth of May, and another thing when it was actually presented to the public; in
other words, as though his first intention were to deceive the public by calling that
a tragedy which was no tragedy, but a comedy of a rarely felicitous ending, and
that afterward that deception was abandoned as too palpable. Now if at this very
time, the eighth of May, 1605, another play was acting, whose hero was Lear, one
which was highly popular and at the same time a genuine tragedy, a desire on the
part of Stafford to beguile purchasers into the belief that his &lquo;booke&rquo; was the
popular tragedy would perhaps explain his use of the word &lquo;tragical&rquo; and the refer-
ence to its being &lquo;lately acted.&rquo; If this conjecture, hardly more than &lquo;gracious fool-
&lquo;ing&rquo; at the best, be worth anything, we may get a hint from it of the date of the
composition of Shakespeare's <I>Lear.</I>
<P>Two years and a half after the date of this entry of <I>King Leir</I>, we find the follow-
ing in the Stationers' Registers:<SUP>*</SUP>
<C>26 Novembris [1607]</C>
<P><B>Nathaniel Butter</B> Entred for their copie vnder th andes of Sir <SC>George Buck</SC>
<B>John Busby</B> knight and Th wardens A booke called. Ma$ter <SC>William
Shakespeare</SC> <I>his &lquo;hi$torye of Kinge <SC>lear</SC>&rquo; as yt was played
before the kinges maie$tie at Whitehall vppon Sainct Stephens
night</I> [26 December] <I>at Chri$tmas La$t by his maie$ties $er-
vantes playinge v$ually at the &lquo;Globe&rquo; on the Bank$yde.</I> vj<SUP>d</SUP>
<P>Here, then, we have our first genuine Quarto edition of <I>King Lear.</I> In passing,
it may be remarked that this entry, like the generality of entries at about this same
time, is fuller in its description than those during Queen Elizabeth's reign, an indi-
cation, according to <SC>Arber</SC>, of the stricter censorship of the press; in confirmation
whereof, we see that it was necessary to cite the authority for the license not only of
the Wardens, but also of Sir George Buck, the Master of the Revels.
<P>When the Quarto was published, in the next year, it bore the following title:
<P>M. William Shak-$peare: &verbar; <I>HIS</I> &verbar; True Chronicle Hi$torie of the life and &verbar; death
of King <SC>lear</SC> and his three &verbar; Daughters. &verbar; <I>With the vnfortunate life of</I> Edgar,
<I>$onne</I> &verbar; and heire to the Earle of Glo$ter, and his &verbar; $ullen and a$$umed humor
of &verbar; <SC>Tom</SC> of Bedlam: &verbar; <I>As it was played before the Kings Maie$tie at Whitehall
vpon</I> &verbar; <I>S.</I> Stephans <I>night in Chri$tmas Hollidayes.</I> &verbar; By his Maie$ties $eruants
playing v$ually at the Gloabe &verbar; on the Bancke-$ide. &verbar; <I>LONDON.</I> &verbar; Printed for
<I>Nathaniel Butter</I>, and are to be $old at his $hop in <I>Pauls</I> &verbar; Church-yard at the
$igne of the Pide Bull neere &verbar; S<SUP>t</SUP>. <I>Au$tins</I> Gate. 1608. &verbar;
<FHL>
<NOTE><SC>Arber's</SC> <I>Transcript</I>, iii, 366.</NOTE>
<PB N=355>
<HE><I>THE TEXT</I> 355</HE>
<P>In the original title-page &lquo;M. William Shak-$peare&rquo; is in much larger type than
any other words on the page; &lquo;moreover,&rquo; says <SC>Collier</SC>, &lquo;we have it again at the
&lquo;head of the leaf on which the tragedy commences, &ldquo;M. William Shake-$peare, his
&lquo;hi$tory of King Lear.&rdquo; This peculiarity has never attracted sufficient attention,
&lquo;and it belongs not only to no other of Shakespeare's plays, but to no other pro-
&lquo;duction of any kind of that period which we recollect. It was clearly intended to
&lquo;enable purchasers to make sure that they were buying the drama which &ldquo;M. Wil-
&lquo;liam Shake-$peare&rdquo; had written upon the popular story of King Lear.&rquo;
<P>Were it not for the entry in the Stationers' Registers we should be unable to fix
the date of &lquo;S. Stephans night in Chri$tmas Hollidayes;&rquo; as it is, however, we know
that it was the twenty-sixth of December, 1606,&mdash;a date which should be borne
in mind.
<P>This, however, is not the only edition published by N. Butter. In this very same
year, 1608, he issued a second edition, with the following title:
<P>M. William Shake-$peare, &verbar; <I>HIS</I> &verbar; True Chronicle Hi$tory of the life &verbar; and death
of King <I>Lear</I>, and his &verbar; <I>three Daughters.</I> &verbar; <I>With the vnfortunate life of</I> <SC>Ed-
gar</SC>, &verbar; $onne and heire to the Earle of <I>Gloce$ter</I>, and &verbar; <I>his $ullen and a$$umed
humour of</I> TOM &verbar; of Bedlam. &verbar; <I>As it was plaid before the Kings Maie$ty at
White-Hall, vp-</I> &verbar; <I>pon S. Stephens night, in Chri$tmas Hollidaies.</I> &verbar; By his Mai-
e$ties Seruants, playing v$ually at the &verbar; <I>Globe</I> on the <I>Banck-$ide.</I> &verbar; Printed for
<I>Nathaniel Butter.</I> &verbar; 1608. &verbar;
<P>As will be seen, the titles of these two editions are almost identical; the only differ-
ence, omitting varieties in type, lies in the imprint. In the second edition there is
no allusion to the shop at the sign of the &lquo;Pide Bull.&rquo;
<P>When we turn to the contents, we find that it is not alone on the title-pages that
these two editions vary. There are throughout such differences of spelling, punc-
tuation, pagination, and of text, as su$$ice to make them two distinct editions.
<P>For the sake of convenience I shall refer to the former as the <I>Pide Bull edition</I>,
or Q<SUB>1</SUB>; to the latter, as the <I>N. Butter edition</I>, or Q<SUB>2</SUB>. And yet the precedence of one
over the other, in point of time, is inferential merely; the evidence is only circum-
stantial, direct evidence there is none; and so shifting are the grounds on which we
have to decide, that those keen and practised critics, Messrs <SC>Clark</SC> and <SC>Wright</SC>,
at the conclusion of the collation of the two texts, as recorded in the <I>Cambridge
Edition</I>, confess, in their Preface, that they believe, after all, that edition to be
the later, which throughout their foot-notes they had cited as the earlier. In fact,
I think it would be difficult to find in all Bibliography a puzzle greater than that
which Nathaniel Butter has bequeathed to us. What complicates the puzzle and
makes it almost &lquo;too intrinse to unloose,&rquo; is that we have to choose not between two
well-defined and separate editions, but between all the copies of the two editions.
Mr <SC>Halliwell-Phillipps</SC> says, that no two of the twelve copies of the <I>Pide Bull</I>
edition that survive are exactly alike! Two copies of the same edition will be found
to vary, errors in one will be corrected in the other, and errors in the latter corrected
in the former. This confusion is well illustrated in the following extract from the
Preface of the <I>Cambridge Edition.</I> Be it remembered that &lquo;Q<SUB>1</SUB>&rquo; of the Cambridge
Editors is what I have called Q<SUB>2</SUB>, or the N. Butter edition; their &lquo;Q<SUB>2</SUB>&rquo; is my Q<SUB>1</SUB>, or
Pide Bull edition.
<P>&lquo;The differences in various copies of Q<SUB>2</SUB> are accounted for by supposing that the
&lquo;corrections were made before the sheets were all worked off, and that the corrected
<PB N=356>
<HE>356 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
&lquo;and uncorrected sheets were bound up indiscriminately. It will be observed that
&lquo;the readings of the uncorrected sheets of Q<SUB>2</SUB> agree for the most part with those of
&lquo;Q<SUB>1</SUB>, and this led us to the conclusion which had previously been arrived at by Ca-
&lquo;pell and also by J. P. Kemble, that the edition which we have called Q<SUB>1</SUB> was the
&lquo;earlier of the two printed in the same year. But upon collating a copy of Q<SUB>2</SUB> in
&lquo;the Bodleian, which we have called Q<SUB>2</SUB> (Bodl. 1), we found evidence which points
&lquo;to an opposite conclusion. In Kent's soliloquy (II, ii, 160) that copy, as will be
&lquo;seen in our notes, reads,
<BQ>nothing almost sees <I>my rackles</I><LB REND=RIGHT>
But miserie, &amp;c.<LB></BQ>
<P>&lquo;which of course is an accidental corruption, by displacement of the type, of &ldquo;my-
&lquo;rackles&rdquo; (<I>i.e.</I> &ldquo;miracles&rdquo;), the true reading. In the corrected copies of Q<SUB>2</SUB> this is
&lquo;altered, apparently by the printer's conjecture, to &ldquo;my wracke,&rdquo; which is also the
&lquo;reading of Q<SUB>1</SUB>. Throughout the sheet in which this occurs the readings of Q<SUB>1</SUB>
&lquo;agree with the corrected copies of Q<SUB>2</SUB>, and had it not been for the instance quoted,
&lquo;we might have supposed that the corrections in the latter were made from Q<SUB>1</SUB>.
&lquo;But the corruption &ldquo;my rackles&rdquo; for &ldquo;miracles&rdquo; must have come from the orig-
&lquo;inal MS, and &ldquo;my wracke&rdquo; is only a conjectural emendation, so that the order of
&lquo;succession in this sheet, at least, appears to be the following: First the uncorrected
&lquo;copy o$ Q<SUB>2</SUB>, then the same corrected, and lastly Q<SUB>1</SUB>. On the other hand it is re-
&lquo;markable that Q<SUB>1</SUB>, if printed from Q<SUB>2</SUB> at all, must have been printed from a copy
&lquo;made up, with the exception just mentioned from II, i, 128 to II, iv, 133, and an-
&lquo;other containing from IV, vi, 224 to V, iii, 64, of uncorrected sheets. Another
&lquo;hypothesis which might be made, is that Q<SUB>1</SUB> and Q<SUB>2</SUB> were printed from the same
&lquo;manuscript, and that the printer of Q<SUB>1</SUB> corrupted &ldquo;miracles&rdquo; into &ldquo;my wracke,&rdquo;
&lquo;while the printer of Q<SUB>2</SUB> made it &ldquo;my rackles,&rdquo; which was afterwards altered by a
&lquo;reference to Q<SUB>1</SUB>.&rquo;
<P>In <SC>Ellis's</SC> <I>Early English Pronunciation</I> (i, 217, foot-note), a communication from
Mr <SC>Aldis Wright</SC> is quoted, which states quite as conclusively the conviction of the
Cambridge Editors, that they had been misled in their chronological order of the
Qq: &lquo;We are now convinced that this edition [the Pide Bull edition, which is cited
&lquo;as Q<SUB>2</SUB> in the foot-notes of the Cam. ed.] was earlier than the one in the same year,
&lquo;which we have called Q<SUB>1</SUB>. These copies of Q<SUB>2</SUB> (so-called) differ from each other in
&lquo;having some of them been corrected while passing through the press. The earliest
&lquo;of these which we have met with is one of the two copies in the Bodleian, and we
&lquo;call it for distinction sake Q<SUB>2</SUB> (Bodl. 1). This has the reading <I>three snyted:</I> but
&lquo;<I>all</I> the other copies of the <I>same</I> edition read <I>three shewted.</I> I suppose, therefore,
&lquo;that while the edition was in course of printing the error was discovered, and the
&lquo;correction communicated verbally to the compositor, who inserted it according to
&lquo;his own notions of spelling. It is not a question between the readings of two <I>dif-
&lquo;ferent</I> editions, but between an uncorrected copy and a corrected copy of the <I>same</I>
&lquo;edition. The later Quartos follow the corrected copy, but their testimony is of no
&lquo;value, because their reading is merely a reprint.&rquo; [See also II, ii, 14.]
<P>I am inclined to think that the true solution of the puzzle is to be found, as has
been suggested, in the blunders not of the printer but of the binder. The text of
these Quarto editions was evidently set up piecemeal. For some reason or other
&lquo;Master N. Butter&rquo; was in a hurry to publish his &lquo;booke,&rquo; and he, therefore, sent
out the &lquo;copy,&rquo; divided into several parts to several compositors, and these different
parts, when printed, were dispatched to a binder to be stitched (it is not probable that
<PB N=357>
<HE><I>THE TEXT</I> 357</HE>
<P>any of the Shakespearian Quartos were more than merely stitched, or had other than
paper covers). We learn from <SC>Arber's</SC> invaluable <I>Transcript</I>, ii, 881-2, that the
binding was not done by the printers, and as there were nearly fifty freemen binders
at that time in London, there must have been among them various degrees of excel-
lence; as ill-luck would have it, the several portions of this tragedy of <I>Lear</I> fell to
the charge of a careless binder, and the signatures, corrected and uncorrected, from
the different printers, were mixed up, to the confusing extent in which the few copies
that survive have come down to us.
<P>That these Quartos were set up piecemeal is, I think, clear. On the forty-sixth
page of what I have called Q<SUB>2</SUB>, or the N. Butter edition, the lines do not &lquo;run on;&rquo;
the sentence stops in the middle and the rest of the line is left blank, thus<*>
<BQ>toade pold, the wall-wort, and the water, that in the fruite of his<LB>
heart, when the foule fiend rages,<LB>
Eates cowdung for $allets, $wallowes the old rat, and the ditch-<LB></BQ>
<P>And as though the compositor were careless at the close of his task, some of the
grossest misprints occur in these closing lines of his stint: not to mention <I>fruite</I> in
the foregoing lines for &lquo;fury,&rquo; or <I>wall-wort</I> for &lquo;wall-newt,&rquo; we have &lquo;<I>pinqueuer the
&lquo;eye,&rquo; &lquo;hart lip,&rquo; &lquo;olde anelthu night Moore</I>,&rquo; &amp;c.
<P>Another similar break occurs on the fifty-first page of this same Quarto.
<P>An indication that the Pide Bull edition was also set up by piecework is found
at V, iii, 236, where <I>Alb.</I> is changed to <I>Duke</I>, and <I>Duke</I> it continues throughout the
rest of the play.
<P>It may be that the mere announcement on the title-page that the book is &lquo;printed
&lquo;for&rquo; Nathaniel Butter, indicates that it was done by more than one printer; had it
been the work of one sole printer it would perhaps have been so stated, as is not
unfrequently the case in other Quartos.
<P>The Cambridge Editors say that &lquo;the printer's device&rquo; on Q<SUB>2</SUB>, or the N. Butter
edition, &lquo;is that of J. Roberts.&rquo; It is a matter of small moment, but I must confess
that I mistrust any inferences drawn from the devices on the title-pages of the Shake-
spearian Quartos. Undoubtedly, at times, these vignettes were the devices of the
printers: Thomas Creede, for instance, has his initials inserted in his device. But
different printers sometimes used the same device, as, for instance, John Danter in
<I>Romeo and Juliet</I>, 1597, and S[imon] S[tafford] in <I>Henry IV</I>, 1599. Sometimes
the device is clearly that of the stationer, and not that of the printer at all; Nicholas
Ling in <I>Hamlet</I>, 1604, displays a <I>fish</I>, and Thomas Fisher in <I>Midsummer Night's
Dream</I> has a <I>King-fisher. If</I>, however, any conclusion may be drawn from these
vignettes or devices, then, perhaps, N[icholas] O[akes], whose vignette in <I>Othello</I>,
1622, is repeated on the title-page of the Pide Bull edition, was the printer of the
latter also.
<P>The different readings in the different copies of the same Quarto gave rise to the
assertion that there was a Third Quarto, also published in 1608. This assertion,
instead of being a proof of the diligence and thoroughness with which the work of
collation had been executed, unfortunately proves the opposite. Had the editors,
who asserted this, been only a little more thorough, they would have been led prob-
ably to maintain not that there were three editions merely, but three times three.
<P>It was reserved for the Cambridge Editors to disprove the existence of this Third
Quarto. In their Preface they say:
<P>&lquo;It has been supposed, in consequence of statements made by Malone and Bos-

<P>&lquo;well, that a third edition of <I>King Lear</I> was published in 1608. We shall show
&lquo;that there is no evidence for this. In the <I>Variorum Shakespeare</I> (ii, 652), edited
&lquo;by Boswell in 1821, three Quartos are described, which are distinguished in the
&lquo;notes to the play by the letters A, B, C, respectively. The first of these is a copy
&lquo;of Q<SUB>2</SUB>,<SUP>*</SUP> quoted by us as Q<SUB>2</SUB> (Bodl. 1); the second is a copy of Q<SUB>1</SUB>; and the third,
&lquo;which is in reality another copy of Q<SUB>2</SUB> and is quoted by us as Q<SUB>2</SUB> (Bodl. 2), is de-
&lquo;scribed as follows:
<P>&ldquo;Title the same as the two former, except that like the first it begins at signature
B: and like the second, has no reference to the place of sale.&rdquo;
<P>&lquo;This statement of Boswell's is taken from a note in Malone's handwriting pre-
&lquo;fixed to the copy in question, which we transcribe.
<P>&ldquo;This copy of King Lear differs in some particulars from the two others in
Vol. IV.
<P>&ldquo;The title-page of it is the same as the second of those copies, that is, it has no
direction to the place of sale, and the first signat. is B,&mdash;notwithstanding which
there are minute diversities; thus, in this copy in H<SUB>3</SUB> verso, we have &lquo;A <I>foole</I>
vsurps my <I>bed</I>&rquo;; in the other, whose first signature is also B, we find&mdash;&lquo;My <I>foote</I>
usurps my <I>body</I>&rquo;, and in the copy without any direction to the place of sale (whose
first signature is A) &lquo;My <I>foote</I> usurps my <I>head</I>&rquo;.&rdquo;
<P>&lquo;Now it is a little remarkable that at present the copy has no title-page at all, and
&lquo;there is no trace of the title-page having been removed since the volume has been
&lquo;in its present condition. The probability is that the title was originally wanting,
&lquo;and that one had been supplied from a copy of Q<SUB>1</SUB> before it came into Malone's
&lquo;hands, and that while it was in this condition he wrote the above note upon it. It
&lquo;was then sent to be bound in a volume with other quartos, and the title may have
&lquo;been lost at the binder's, or may have been intentionally removed as not belonging
&lquo;to the book. That alterations were made by the binder is evident from the fact
&lquo;that the copy to which Malone refers as the <I>second</I> of those in Vol. IV is in reality
&lquo;the <I>first.</I> Malone, writing his note when Vol. IV was arranged for binding, de-
&lquo;scribed the then order of the plays, which must afterwards have been altered. In
&lquo;any case, however Malone's statement is to be accounted for, it is quite clear that
&lquo;Boswell must have described the Quarto after it was bound, when the title could
&lquo;not have existed.
<P>&lquo;We have said that Boswell quotes the three Quartos of Lear, now in the Bod-
&lquo;leian, by the letters A, B, C, respectively. In doing so, however, he is not con-
&lquo;sistent. We record his mistakes, that others may not be misled by them. Bearing
&lquo;in mind, therefore, that A=Q<SUB>2</SUB> (Bodl. 1), B=Q<SUB>1</SUB>, and C=Q<SUB>2</SUB> (Bodl. 2), we find in
&lquo;Act <SC>ii</SC>, Scene 2 (vol. x, p. 97) &ldquo;Quarto B, <I>ausrent;</I> Quarto A, reads <I>unreverent.</I>&rdquo;
&lquo;Here B and A should change places. In Act <SC>iii</SC>, Scene 7 (p. 188), &ldquo;Quarto A
&lquo;omits <I>roguish:</I>&rdquo; for A read C. In Act <SC>iv</SC>, Scene 2 (p. 199), for &ldquo;Quartos B and
&lquo;C, <I>the whistling</I>,&rdquo; read &ldquo;Quarto C&rdquo; alone. In Act <SC>iv</SC>, Scene 6 (p. 220), B and A
&lquo;should again be interchanged. In Act <SC>v</SC>, Scene 3 (p. 277), &ldquo;Quarto A omits this
&lquo;line&rdquo;; for A read B. It will be seen from these instances, that A has been in turn
&lquo;made to represent three different copies.&rquo;

<P>lable of praise. It is a reprint, page for page, of Q<SUB>2</SUB>, and has almost reached the
limit of incorrect typography. Here and there, in the earlier scenes, I have re-
corded in the foot-notes, some of its grossest misprints; but, generally I have

<P>As <SC>Rowe's</SC> ill-luck put the Fourth and poorest Folio under his pillow, so here, I
think, the same ill-luck may, perhaps, have put Jane Bell's Quarto in his pew, and
led him to peep into it now and then. See III, iv, 108, or III, vii, 60.
<P><SC>Davies</SC> (<I>Dramatic Misc.</I> ii, p. 167) &lquo;cannot help suspecting&rquo; that <I>Lear</I> was not
popular, because only two Quarto editions appeared before it was reprinted in the
Folio. <SC>Knight</SC> pronounces Davies's &lquo;argument worthless,&rquo; &lquo;for it must be remem-
&lquo;bered that other of Shakspere's most perfect efforts, such as <I>Macbeth</I>, were not pub-
&lquo;lished at all till they were collected in the Folio.&rquo; &lquo;In all likelihood, the Quarto
&lquo;editions were piratical and were probably suppressed. . . . Butter was undoubtedly
&lquo;not a publisher authorised by Shakspere, for he printed, in 1605, <I>The London
&lquo;Prodigal</I>, one of the plays fraudulently ascribed to our poet.&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC>, on the
other hand, thinks that <I>Lear</I> was extremely popular, because it required more than
one edition in one year to satisfy the public demand. &lquo;Why, however,&rquo; he says, &lquo;it
&lquo;was never republished in quarto in the interval [between 1608 and 1623] must be
&lquo;matter of speculation; but such was not an unusual occurrence with the works of
&lquo;our great dramatist; his <I>Midsummer Night's Dream, Merchant of Venice</I>, and
&lquo;<I>Troilus and Cressida</I>, were each twice printed, the first two in 1600, and the last
&lquo;in 1609, and they were not again seen in type until they were inserted in the
&lquo;Folio; there was also no second quarto of <I>Much Ado about Nothing</I>, nor of <I>Love's
&lquo;Labour's Lost.</I>&rquo;
<P>So much for the Quartos, with their puzzling, interlaced texts. It is comforting
to reflect that to decide upon the precedence, in point of time, of these editions, or,
in other words, which is Q<SUB>1</SUB> and which is Q<SUB>2</SUB>, belongs wholly to the province of
Bibliography; it has no bearing whatever on the elucidation of the text of this
tragedy.
<P>In the Folio, <I>King Lear</I> appears in the division of Tragedies, and among them
shares with <I>Macbeth, Othello</I>, and <I>Cymbeline</I>, the distinction of being divided into
Acts and Scenes. I believe there is no dissenting voice to the opinion, that we
have here a text much superior, in general, to that of the Quartos, and one that was
printed from an independent manuscript. And yet in spite of this superiority, there
are, as <SC>Collier</SC> says, few of Shakespeare's plays which are more indebted than this,
to the Quartos, for the completeness of their text. This arises from the remarkable
difference in length between the Folios and the Quartos. The Quartos exceed the
Folios by about a hundred and seventy-five lines. There are about two hundred
and twenty lines in the Quartos that are not in the Folios, and the Folios contain
fifty lines not to be found in the Quartos. This discrepancy, with its abridgement
on the one hand and its amplification on the other, presents a highly interesting
field of investigation. By whom were these excisions made when the text of the
Folio came to be printed, amounting in one instance to the omission of an entire
scene? By the master himself, or by the actors? Are they made in accordance
with a plan, or at hap-hazard? Was the object to shorten the play, or to emphasise
dramatic effects? Such are some of the questions which this very important fact
suggests, and their answers have received more attention from German than from
English scholars.
<PB N=360>
<HE>360 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P><SC>Dr Johnson</SC> expressed the belief that the Folio was printed from Shakespeare's
last revision, carelessly and hastily performed, with more thought of shortening the
scenes than of continuing the action. See note on III, vi, 100-113.
<P><SC>Tieck</SC> (ix, 370) suggests that some of these omissions in the Folio may be due
to a deference to the censorship of the press, which after the death of James became
more strict; or again some of them may be due to the obscurity which speedily falls
on local allusions, or allusions to passing events, of which no play of Shakespeare
contains more; or again the Third Scene of Act Fourth may have been omitted, be-
cause of the lack of an actor who could adequately represent it; or its omission may
have been due to a desire to simplify the plot, and to avoid complications which,
as it stands, it unquestionably creates.
<P><SC>Knight</SC>, who appears to have bestowed more thought upon the subject than other
English editors, says: &lquo;Speech after speech, and scene after scene, which in the
&lquo;genuine copy of the Folio are metrically correct, are, in the Quarto, either printed
&lquo;as prose, or the lines are so mixed together, without any apparent knowledge in
&lquo;the editor of the metrical laws by which they were constructed, that it would
&lquo;have been almost impossible, from this text alone, to have reduced them to any-
&lquo;thing like the form in which they were written by the author. This circumstance
&lquo;appears to us conclusive, that these copies could not have been printed from the
&lquo;author's manuscript; and yet they might have been printed from a genuine play-
&lquo;house copy.&rquo;
<P>After mentioning the large omissions in the Folio of passages to be found in the
Quarto, <SC>Knight</SC> goes on to say, that it would be very easy to assume that these omis-
sions were made by the editors of the Folio for the purpose of cutting the play down
for representation; but this theory requires us to assume that the additions also, in the
Folio, were made by the editors, and these comprise several such minute touches as
none but the hand of the master could have added. He then examines the sub-
ject more in detail: &lquo;In the First and Second Acts the omissions are very slight.
&lquo;In the opening of Act III we lose a spirited description of Lear in the storm&mdash;
&lquo;&ldquo;tears his white hair,&rdquo; etc. But mark&mdash;it is <I>description;</I> and the judgement of
&lquo;Shakespeare in omitting it is unquestionable, for he subsequently shows Lear in
&lquo;<I>action</I> under precisely the same circumstances. In the sixth scene of the same
&lquo;act is omitted the imaginary trial of Regan and Goneril, &ldquo;I will arraign them
&lquo;straight.&rdquo; Was this a passage that an author would have thrust out carelessly
&lquo;and hastily? It is impossible, as it would be presumptuous were it possible, un-
&lquo;hesitatingly to assign a motive for this omission. The physical exertion that would
&lquo;be necessary for any actor (even for Burbage, who we know played Lear) to carry
&lquo;through the whole of the third act might have been so extreme as to render it ex-
&lquo;pedient to make this abridgement; or, what is more probable, as Kent previous to
&lquo;this passage had said, &ldquo;All power of his wits has given way to his impatience,&rdquo;
&lquo;the imaginary arraignment might have been rejected by the poet, as exhibiting too
&lquo;much method in the madness. The rhyming soliloquy of Edgar, with which this
&lquo;scene closes, might have been spared by the poet without much compunction. The
&lquo;second scene of the fourth act, in which Albany so bitterly reproaches Goneril, is
&lquo;greatly abridged. In its amplified state it does not advance the progress of the
&lquo;action, nor contribute to the developement of the characters. The whole of the
&lquo;third scene of that act is also omitted. It is one of the most beautifully written
&lquo;of the play; and we should indeed regret had it not been preserved to us in the
&lquo;Quartos. But let it be borne in mind, that the greater part of the scene is purely
<PB N=361>
<HE><I>THE TEXT</I> 361</HE>
<P>&lquo;descriptive; and, exquisite as the description is, particularly in those parts which
&lquo;make us better understand the surpassing loveliness of Cordelia's character, we
&lquo;cannot avoid believing that the poet sternly resolved to let the effect of this won-
&lquo;der$ul drama entirely depend upon its action. . . . The subsequent omissions, to the
&lquo;end of the drama, are few and unimportant.&rquo;
<P><SC>Staunton</SC> says, that a &lquo;careful comparison of the Quarto and Folio texts con-
&lquo;vinces us that, unlike that of <I>Richard III</I>, the text of <I>Lear</I> in the Folio is taken
&lquo;from a later and revised copy of the play. Whether the curtailment is the work
&lquo;of the author, it is impossible now to determine; it is not always judicious, and
&lquo;some of the substitutions are inferior to the language they displace; yet, on the
&lquo;other hand, the additions that we meet with in the Folio bear the undoubted mark
&lquo;of Shakespeare's mint; and while the metrical arrangement of the speeches in that
&lquo;edition has been carefully regarded, the text of the Quartos is printed in parts
&lquo;without any observance of prosodial construction.&rquo;
<P>Hitherto, as we have seen, the omissions in the Folio have been supposed to be
abridgements made by Shakespeare himself.
<P><SC>Dr Delius</SC>,<SUP>*</SUP> however, denies this, not only with regard to the omissions in the
Folio, but to the omissions in the Quartos also.
<P>Before entering on the discussion, the learned German premises that the texts of
the two Quartos are to be considered as practically identical. There are, in effect,
but two texts, that of the Folios and that of the Quartos; and the question is, are the
variations in them due to the hand of Shakespeare? To answer this, Delius sub-
jects the two texts to a minute comparison, and begins with a list of the <I>vari&aelig; lec-
tiones</I> in the Quartos, which may be considered as errors either of the copyist or of
the compositor, either of the pen or of the eye; according, as we think that they
were to be found in the original MS, or were wrongly read by the printer&mdash;a dilem-
ma hard to determine. This list, which I here reprint as a proof, if any were needed,
that the conclusions at which Delius has arrived, were not reached without great care,
contains several instances of what I cannot but think are not mere misprints, but
words or phrases, which, making sense with the context, rise to the dignity of
&lquo;readings;&rquo; these I have marked with an asterisk. The text of the Quartos is in
Italic; that of the Folios in Roman.

<P>The conclusion which Delius draws from an examination of this list of misprints,
&lquo;which could be readily increased,&rquo; is, &lquo;that the hand of the poet could have had
&lquo;nothing to do with them. In other words, Sh. wrote only what stands in the
&lquo;Folio.&rquo; A similar conclusion, he thinks, is also to be drawn from another class of
readings in the Quartos, where evident misprints in one copy are corrected in an-
other, such as II, ii, 121, where for the genuine &lquo;ancient&rquo; we have <I>ausrent</I>, changed
to <I>miscreant;</I> also II, ii, 160, &lquo;miracles&rquo;; II, i, 100, &lquo;To have th' expence,&rquo; where,
&lquo;instead of &ldquo;th' expence&rdquo; which cannot have been very clearly written in the MS,
&lquo;the compositor of the Quarto first substituted &ldquo;these &mdash;;&rdquo; which, in some
&lquo;copies, was afterwards filled up from pure conjecture, as &ldquo;wast and spoyle&rdquo;&rquo;,
&lquo;III, iv, &lquo;Contentious&rquo;; III, vi, 94, 95, &lquo;Take up&rquo;; IV, ii, 56, 57, France-
&lquo;threats.&rquo; [For all these instances reference to the Textual Notes will supply
the various changes to be found in the Quartos.] Delius then examines a third
class of errors, where the changes seem to be purely arbitrary, such as <I>will</I> for
&lquo;shall,&rquo; <I>space or liberty</I> for &lquo;space and liberty,&rdquo; <I>That</I> for &lquo;Which,&rquo; &amp;c. &amp;c. Then
again there are certain differences where synonymous words are used&mdash;<I>e. g.</I>, I, i,
<I>stoops to folly</I> for &lquo;falls to folly&rquo;; Ib. <I>respects</I> for &lquo;regards&rquo;; I, iii, <I>dislike</I> for &lquo;dis-
&lquo;taste&rquo;; II, i, <I>caitiff</I> for &lquo;coward,&rquo; &amp;c. In view of all these different readings, De-
lius makes the following strong point: &lquo;Is it at all probable, that Shakespeare, even
<PB N=363>
<HE><I>THE TEXT</I> 363</HE>
<P>&lquo;granting that he revised the text, would have undertaken such superfluous trouble,
&lquo;as, we cannot say to improve, but merely to change the text in these innumerable,
&lquo;and minute, and insignificant particulars; and for no conceivable reason withal, in-
&lquo;stead of taking in hand some real incisive improvement? Or is it not more likely
&lquo;that a simple transcriber, attaching but slight importance to Shakespeare's words as
&lquo;such, in the hurry of his work substituted heedlessly or purposely, any phrase that
&lquo;occurred to him for another, one particle for another, one mood or number for
&lquo;another?&rquo;
<P>In the substitution of prose for verse, of verse for prose, and in the omissions of
words, phrases, and lines, in the Quartos, <SC>Delius</SC> sees the proof also that no trace
of Shakespeare's revising hand can be detected. He then returns to the text of
the Folio, with its note-worthy omission of &lquo;220 lines,&rquo; that are in the Quartos. All
these omissions, he concludes, were made by the players, for the purpose of short-
ening the time of representation, not by Shakespeare. In the Quartos we have the
play as it was originally performed before King James, and before the audience at
the Globe, but sadly marred by misprints, printers' sophistications, and omissions,
perhaps due to an imperfect and illegible MS. In the Folio we have a later MS,
belonging to the Theatre, and more nearly identical with what Shakespeare wrote.
The omissions of the Quartos are the blunders of the printers; the omissions of the
Folios are the abridgements of the actors. &lquo;From the very nature of the case,&rquo; says
Delius, &lquo;it seems far more natural that the Poet, who was also an actor, should have
&lquo;been himself the one to mark the omissions in his own drama. But on the other
&lquo;hand, if we remember with what careless indifference Shakespeare committed his
&lquo;plays to the care of the Theatre for which he wrote them, without troubling himself
&lquo;about their fate or literary future; it will seem highly probable, that in the present
&lquo;instance he gave himself no further personal care about its representation, but left
&lquo;all that to those whom it most concerned&mdash;the actors of the Globe, the owners of
&lquo;the MS.&rquo; Moreover, in 1608, when the Quartos were published, and the unabridged
play may be presumed to have held the stage, Shakespeare was living at Stratford.
&lquo;Is it to be supposed then,&rquo; asks Delius, &lquo;that at that time or later&mdash;for the play may
&lquo;have been abridged later&mdash;the actors would have applied to the absent, far-distant
&lquo;poet, to modify his drama for the stage, when such a task would seem to them, ac-
&lquo;customed as they were to matters of routine, an affair of such every-day occurrence,
&lquo;that they themselves could just as easily do it for themselves?&rquo; Furthermore, De-
lius thinks, that if Shakespeare himself had really revised this drama, we should
have found more emphatic traces of his revision than mere omissions of certain pas-
sages. In the general character of these omissions, Delius sees a desire to spare to
the utmost, and to strike out such passages only, which contain amplified descrip-
tions; or which, at least, are not essential to the developement of the dramatic treat-
ment or of the characters. This point is emphasised, because in his Introduction to
the play Delius had been led by these very considerations to an opposite conclusion
&mdash;viz., that none but Shakespeare could have discriminated between the needful
and the useless. Delius then proceeds to examine these omissions of the Folio, in
detail. Some of his remarks I have incorporated in the commentary under the pas-
sages in the text where they apply; for the others, it may be said, that in any drama
by Shakespeare, it is much more easy to say why a certain passage should not be
omitted, than to give a reason why it should. The presence of any passage in a
play of Shakespeare's, is presumptive evidence that it is required; and to prove that
it is not, lies upon those who approve of its excision. So perfect and so unerring a
<PB N=364>
<HE>364 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>master was Shakespeare, that any abridgement of his plays is likely to be clumsy;
it is easier to maintain, that a piece of clumsy work was done by any one rather
than by Shakespeare. As Delius, in this very Essay (p. 67), truly says: &lquo;assuredly,
&lquo;Shakespeare did not himsel$ think any passage in his <I>King Lear</I> superfluous, other-
&lquo;wise he would scarcely have inserted that which his editors might deem needless.&rquo;
<P>Delius sums up as follows: &lquo;Having traced the variations between the Quarto
&lquo;and the Folio to their true source, we are led to the conclusion:&mdash;That there is <I>no</I>
&lquo;evidence for the supposition that Shakspere himself revised this drama.&rquo;
<P>Dr <SC>Koppel</SC> (<I>Textkritische Studien &udblac;ber Shakespeare's Richard III and King
Lear</I>, Dresden, 1877) comes to a conclusion directly opposed to Delius, and main-
tains that it was Shakespeare's own hand that cut out many of the passages both in
the Quarto text and the Folio text. The larger portion of his Essay is devoted to
attacking Delius's position, and as destructive criticism does not come within my
scope, I simply allude to his opposition without repeating his arguments. Koppel has
evidently studied the notes in the Cambridge edition most thoroughly, and comes to
the same conclusion as that to which the Cambridge Editors themselves had arrived
before him&mdash;namely, that the N. Butter edition has been erroneously supposed to be
Q<SUB>1</SUB>; that the real Q<SUB>1</SUB> is that which in the notes to the Cambridge edition is called Q<SUB>2</SUB>.
He maintains with vigor and plausibility, that there are many corrected passages in
Q<SUB>1</SUB> (<I>i. e.</I> the Pide Bull), in &lquo;some of which it is clear beyond a peradventure, and
&lquo;in others it is highly probable, that resort was had to the original MS. For in-
&lquo;stance, in I, iv, 294 <I>untender</I> becomes &ldquo;untented,&rdquo; <I>peruse</I>, in the next line, be-
&lquo;comes &ldquo;pierce;&rdquo; in line 336 <I>mildie gentleness</I> is corrected to &ldquo;milkie gentleness.&rdquo;
&lquo;Such corrections as these would never have been made by a compositor out of
&lquo;hand; with &ldquo;mildie gentleness&rdquo; before him a compositor would never have
&lquo;thought of changing it to the poetic form of &ldquo;milkie gentleness,&rdquo; but would have
&lquo;corrected it simply to &ldquo;mild gentleness;&rdquo; moreover, to suppose that in every case
&lquo;the compositor could have hit upon the correct word or phrase as we find them in
&lquo;the Folio, is simply incredible.&rquo; In those instances where some copies of the Pide
Bull edition have one reading, and other copies of the same edition have different
ones (such as <I>ausrent, my rackles, crulentious</I> in some copies, and <I>miscreant, my
wrack, tempestious</I> in others), Koppel infers that the MS must have been illegible.
<P>But, as has been before remarked, however interesting the discussion may be of
the succession in time of these different Quartos, the question in reality is merely
bibliographical; and Koppel acknowledges that all this collation is unimportant in
comparison with the variation between the Quartos and Folios: according to the
enumeration of the lines in the Cambridge edition, he finds two hundred and eighty-
seven more lines in the Quarto than in the Folio, and one hundred and ten lines in
the Folio which are wanting in the Quarto. As to whether the omissions in the
Folio were due to Shakespeare or not, Koppel says, that however indifferent the
poet may have been to the <I>literary</I> fate of his dramas, it is inconceivable that Shake-
speare, the Actor, Manager, Dramatist, and Theatre-poet, should have taken no care
for the representation of his pieces, or for their adaptation to the stage, or for their
needful abbreviations or amplifications. &lquo;Is it to be inferred that he took no per-
&lquo;sonal interest in the reproduction on the stage of his pieces, because he took no
&lquo;thought for their <I>publication in print?</I> Far more likely is it that the literary future
&lquo;of his dramas pressed lightly on him, because the present practical interest in their
&lquo;representation, their scenic success, pressed upon him so heavily.&rquo; No inference,
Koppel thinks, as to the state of the text can be drawn from the date of the Quartos,
<PB N=365>
<HE><I>THE TEXT</I> 365</HE>
<P>nor from the statement on their title-pages, &lquo;as it was plaid . . . at Whitehall,&rquo; which
was merely a bookseller's puff, and designed to show the difference between this edi-
tion and the older play of <I>King Leir</I>, with no intention of more accurately specifying
the very text which was given before his Majesty. &lquo;It is very possible that, when the
&lquo;First Quarto (Q<SUB>2</SUB> of the Cambridge edition) appeared, the version which is the basis
&lquo;of the Folio text had existed long before, and was used in public, notwithstanding
&lquo;that the MS which the publisher of the Quartos managed to procure, contained the
&lquo;earlier and discarded text; and perhaps it was for this very reason, because it was
&lquo;discarded, that it could be handed over to the publisher merely, perhaps, for the
&lquo;preparation of a transcript&rquo; (p. 72). Wherefore, the mere publication alone of the
Quartos in 1608 does not hinder us from supposing that the version which the Folio
follows belongs to an earlier year, when Shakespeare was in London and not in Strat-
ford. In view of all the circumstances of the case, if we cannot regard the additions
of the Folio as original portions of the text, Dr Koppel thinks that the following may
be supposed as possible: &lquo;The <I>original</I> form was, essentially, that of the Quarto, then
&lquo;followed a <I>longer</I> form, <I>with the additions in the Folio</I>, as substantially <I>our modern
&lquo;editions have again restored them;</I> then the shortest form, as it is preserved for us
&lquo;in the Folio&rquo; (p. 74).
<P>&lquo;Although in general the omissions in the Quarto may be attributed to Shakespeare,
&lquo;yet we must be prepared to find several of them unworthy of the Poet; such for
&lquo;instance is I, i, 38-43. The next omission in the Quartos, I, i, 47, 48, may very
&lquo;possibly be a later addition in the Folio. But it is not essential, its gist has been
&lquo;already given in lines 35-38, and it may be considered as a skilful abridgement in
&lquo;the Quartos.&rquo; [Space will not permit me to follow Dr Koppel in his criticisms and
explanations of all the omissions or additions of the Quartos and Folios; to a student
interested in such matters of collation, it will not be a tedious task to examine this
subject thoroughly for himself at first hand; it will cost him but little more trouble
to do so than to look up all the references to act, scene, and line, which would be
all that I could possibly give him here, were I to reproduce all of Dr Koppel's essay,
of which, however, I will give those passages that seem to me the most striking,
wherein he assumes the task of proving that Shakespeare himself, with cause, added
or omitted certain passages. The italics are Dr Koppel's.]
<P>At the conclusion of his examination of all the important passages omitted in the
Quartos, Dr Koppel finds (p. 82), &lquo;with the trifling exception of only two passages, I,
&lquo;i, 38-43 and III, vi, 12-15, that <I>nothing forbids their being regarded as later addi-
&lquo;tions by the Poet.</I> That they really are so, it is obviously impossible <I>to prove.</I> It
&lquo;would have to be assumed that these additions to the text of the tragedy, made
&lquo;perhaps, not all at the same time, gradually so increased that at last a reduction
&lquo;proved to be necessary. The <I>abridged</I> form, <I>rendered essentially shorter than the
&lquo;piece originally was</I>, would then be necessarily regarded as transmitted to us in <I>the
&lquo;Folio.</I> If we have thus shown that the passages wanting in the Quartos did not
&lquo;necessarily form a part of the original text, it is, on the other hand, at the same
&lquo;time shown, that these omissions <I>were made at fitting places</I>, and <I>had the same
&lquo;practical design of abridgement</I> as in the later form of the piece, which was <I>pre-
&lquo;pared for the stage</I>, and which is the basis of the Folio.&rquo; . . . [P. 87.] Of the pas-
sage, III, i, 7-15, omitted in the Folios, it may be &lquo;said that Shakespeare, after-
&lquo;wards, and partly before, partly in this scene, partly in what precedes, and in what
&lquo;follows, has enlarged sufficiently upon these things, the white uncovered head, the
&lquo;rain, the storm, the fearful night, and Lear's mad defiance, and could when abridge-

<P>&lquo;ment were the object, very well dispense with this passage. . . . Besides we may
&lquo;see here the artist's hand in the choice of passages to be erased, expunging a grand
&lquo;description of the King in the stormy night, which might weaken the impression
&lquo;of his actual appearance when he comes before us in the next scene.&rquo; . . . [P. 88.]
The notable omission in the Folios of III, i, 30-42, Koppel justifies: &lquo;The suffer-
&lquo;ings of Lear being known in France (in the Quartos, merely the quarrel between
&lquo;the British Dukes, of which advantage was to be taken by the enemy, appears as
&lquo;the occasion for the French invasion), the sending of the nobleman to Dover to
&lquo;Cordelia is rendered superfluous, aimless. Hence, from the text of the Folio, we
&lquo;gather from this mission merely a <I>cheering assurance</I> of the approaching deliver-
&lquo;ance of Lear, which Kent gives to the nobleman, although only by hints. For he
&lquo;tells him only that from France, where Lear's sufferings are known, war is com-
&lquo;ing, and that he will soon get to see Cordelia. The declaration, that French troops
&lquo;have already landed at Dover, is stricken out. This cheering intimation, which,
&lquo;as well as the material compensation (Kent's purse and ring), was well earned by
&lquo;the good faith of the knight, fits well into this preparatory scene, which thus pos-
&lquo;sesses the effect of a soothing pause in the rapid progress of the tragic action.&rquo;
Koppel's hardest task lies in justifying the omission of the entire Third Scene of
Act IV; while granting the justice of the general opinion that this scene is necessary
for the reawakening of interest in Cordelia, who has not been seen since the intro-
ductory scene, &lquo;yet,&rquo; he urges, &lquo;perhaps, for the expunging of this full <I>poetic descrip-
&lquo;tion</I>, preceding the personal appearance of Cordelia, there was the same reason as
&lquo;for the omission, mentioned above, of the description of Lear before he himself
&lquo;appears in the stormy night.
<P>&lquo;When then, with this scene, the necessary reason for the non-appearance of the
&lquo;French King in the subsequent warlike scenes is also left out, it does not prove
&lquo;the impossibility of Shakespeare's having made these erasures. How often Shake-
&lquo;speare was careless in regard to secondary incidents, how often he even con-
&lquo;tradicts himself in such matters, is sufficiently known. Instances, more or less
&lquo;striking, may be found everywhere. For example, in this very scene in the orig-
&lquo;inal longer form of the tragedy, the Gentleman and Kent speak of a letter of
&lquo;Kent's (&lquo;Did your letters pierce,&rquo; &amp;c. &amp;c.), which the former was to hand to Cor-
&lquo;delia; while, according, to an earlier scene of the Third Act, only an oral mes-
&lquo;sage had been entrusted to the Gentleman. So likewise in that scene, Kent and
&lquo;the Gentleman are to seek the King in different directions, and he who first lights
&lquo;on him was to holla the other; the Poet causes this arrangement to be made in de-
&lquo;tail, without any mention being made afterwards of i&tdot;s having been carried out, in
&lquo;the tragic scene where Lear is found by Kent. Kent does not trouble himself about
&lquo;his $ellow-seeker, and consequently as little do <I>we</I> know where he has gone. Only
&lquo;in Dover do we find him again. Just so, in that scene, Kent gives to the same
&lquo;gentleman a ring which he is to show to Cordelia, and learn from her who &lquo;your
&lquo;$ellow is That yet you do not know.&rquo; Notwithstanding, we find that when the
&lquo;gentleman has delivered his message to Cordelia and reports the fact to Kent, he

&lquo;aright, you shall not grieve Lending me this acquaintance;&rquo; and when the gentle-
&lquo;man is speaking again (IV, vii, 91) with Kent, he tells him, as a report which he
&lquo;himself believes, that Kent is in Germany with Edgar.&rquo; [It is only an inference
of Koppel's, that the &lquo;gentleman&rquo; in this scene is same as Kent's messenger in the

<P>former scene. The stage directions give simply &lquo;gentleman,&rquo; and it may well have
been two different men.&mdash;<SC>Ed.</SC>] &lquo;Finally, a similar instance of carelessness is to be
&lquo;found in IV, iii, where it is said, that the French king must for urgent reasons re-
&lquo;turn to France, and that he has left Monsieur La Far &lquo;behind him, general&rquo;. And
&lquo;yet the Poet forgot this entirely. This La Far is never afterwards alluded to. Cor-
&lquo;delia alone represents the French military power. It may well be supposed, that
&lquo;if it were the Poet who struck out this scene, the opportunity of getting rid of the

&lquo;tion of the king of France, closely connected therewith, together with the whole
