&lquo;sible, that, by the insertion of some brief passage, the hiatus thus made was filled
&lquo;up, and this passage was afterward forgotten in the MS of the Folio, or in the
&lquo;printed edition.&rquo;
<P>&lquo;[P. 93.] The last eight lines of Act III, which are omitted in the Folio, contain,
&lquo;in the Quartos, a contradiction between them and the opening scene of the next act;
&lquo;which, of itself, would lead us to suspect the genuineness of the Quartos. The
&lquo;Second Servant says: &lquo;Let's follow the old earl, and get the Bedlam To lead him,&rquo;
&lquo;&amp;c. But in the next scene, Gloucester is led by an &lquo;Old Man,&rquo; and apparently
&lquo;meets the Bedlam by accident, and it is Gloucester himself who asks the Bedlam to
&lquo;lead him. This is, after all, only one of the many little things in Shakespeare in
&lquo;which, as we have shown above, especially in <I>King Lear</I>, inconsistencies and con-
&lquo;tradictions may be discovered, that do not authorise any hap-hazard assumption,
&lquo;that the passage in the Quartos is not genuine. But, on the other hand, this causes
&lquo;the omission in the Folio to appear all the more explicable and fitting.
<P>&lquo;[P. 94.] In IV, i, the passage in Edgar's speech about &lquo;Obidicut,&rquo; &lquo;Hobbidi-
&lquo;&lquo;dance,&rquo; and &lquo;Mahu,&rquo; is omitted. The reference to Harsnet's book, in this Tragedy,
&lquo;was desirable only so long as the book was fresh in men's memories.&rquo;
<P>On page 96 Dr Koppel sums up his conclusion: &lquo;Thus it appears that these
&lquo;omissions, <I>with some exceptions quite immaterial, are of such a kind that they might
&lquo;very well have been made by the poet himself;</I> in many cases, this possibility has
&lquo;more probability, in others less; and, furthermore, it is also <I>possible</I>, that different
&lquo;passages were stricken out at different times, and in part also by different hands.&rquo;
<P>Dr <SC>Schmidt</SC>, at whose hands we have all received that valuable gift, <I>The Shake-
speare Lexicon</I>, has written an Essay on the <I>Text of King Lear</I>, of which only a
portion, at this date, has appeared in type; and even of this portion, I can give only
an abridgement.
<P>In all cases, where two texts exist, the Quartos and the Folios, the first thing to be
done, according to Dr Schmidt, is to decide which of the two is authentic. &lquo;May we
&lquo;assume, that Shakespeare had such an interest in the publication of the Quartos as
&lquo;to give them an authority higher than that of the Folio, which appeared after his
&lquo;death? Or, on the other hand, shall we pin our faith exclusively to that form of
&lquo;the text whose lawful origin is undoubted? Are the different texts different remod-
&lquo;ellings, and if so, are the changes in the later, due to the hand of the Poet, or to
&lquo;that of another? To these questions there can be but one true answer, and until
&lquo;that answer be found, all genuine textual criticism is merely a groping in the dark.
&lquo;In England, it is customary to accord &lquo;equivalent validity&rquo; to the Quartos and Folios;
&lquo;and to decide at one time for one, and at another time for another, according to indi-
&lquo;vidual bias; and the result is an eclectic text. When the editor is a man of taste, the
<PB N=368>
<HE>368 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>&lquo;reader, perhaps, does not fare so badly; but such dealing cannot be termed critical.
&lquo;Even in the case where we have to deal with two different versions from the hand
&lquo;of a Poet himself, one of the two must be laid aside; no matter, whether we prefer
&lquo;that version which gives us the first hurried sketch, or that which has received the
&lquo;improvements of maturer judgement. To weld both into one, yields a result, which
&lquo;never had any existence for the Poet himself even . . . . The universal acknowledge-
&lquo;ment, that the <I>Romeo and Juliet</I> of 1597, the <I>Hamlet</I> of 1603, and the Quartos of
&lquo;<I>Henry V</I>, and the 2d and 3d Parts of <I>Henry VI</I>, and of <I>The Merry Wives</I>, are mere
&lquo;compilations, hastily made up from copies taken down from performances on the stage,
&lquo;and from untrustworthy recollections,&mdash;this acknowledgement can be but a question
&lquo;of time. . . . Shakespeare's indifference to the fate of his dramas, has been praised by
&lquo;some and blamed by others, and all have perceived in it, the poet's unconsciousness
&lquo;of his own greatness; whereas it may have been the natural result of the highest
&lquo;intellectual power, which finds in the joy of creating its fullest and completest
&lquo;reward, and in the prospect of the future loses all interest in the present and the
&lquo;past. . . . Every doubt as to the unlawful character of these Quartos ought to be
&lquo;reasonably laid, when we have in the Preface to the Folio, such a decided, unam-
&lquo;biguous proof. &lquo;Where before you were abused,&rquo; so we read there, &lquo;with divers
&lquo;&lquo;stolen and surreptitious copies, maimed and deformed by the frauds and stealths
&lquo;&lquo;of injurious imposters that exposed them, even those are now offered to your view
&lquo;&lquo;cured and perfect of their limbs,&rquo; &amp;c. It is remarkable, how completely this famil-
&lquo;iar announcement has been lost sight of, and discarded, by almost every Shakespeare
&lquo;student. Perhaps, it is thought, that editor against editor and publisher against pub-
&lquo;lisher, are not competent witnesses. And, moreover, the judge is not uncorrupted.
&lquo;The short-comings of the Folio, the sole authorised edition, give to the Quartos,
&lquo;spite of their lack of authenticity, such a disproportionate importance, that the mod-
&lquo;ern critic is in duty bound to thank them at every step; and cannot refrain from hold-
&lquo;ing them in high honour. Their present relative importance, induces a very natural
&lquo;delusion as to their absolute worth. It has been thought, that the foregoing sentence
&lquo;from the Preface in the Folio referred only to the six Quartos mentioned above, and
&lquo;that we were, therefore, justified in dividing the Quartos into authentic and spurious
&lquo;Quartos. In fact, several of them afford a text essentially complete and worthy of
&lquo;the poet, nay, some even appear to be set forth with greater care than the Folio.
&lquo;But this, by no means, proves that there is no difference between a lawful and an
&lquo;unlawful edition; but at best only between more adroit and less adroit sophistications,
&lquo;and gives us no right to restrict, just as we please, the general assertion of the Folio,
&lquo;and to draw the line at a boundary which our own needs have set up. When this
&lquo;or that Quarto is termed authentic, it is not absolutely meant, that it must have been
&lquo;published in an authorised manner by the direct or indirect means of the lawful
&lquo;owner of the MS. But this expression implies rather, that authentic copies, by
&lquo;some means or other, must have come into the possession of the publisher. Of
&lquo;course, this would not be impossible, but it would be very difficult. . . . The com-
&lquo;plete MS, be it remembered, was in the possession of the managers alone, among
&lquo;whom it is not likely that a traitor to their own monopoly would be found; the indi-
&lquo;vidual actors knew nothing more than their own parts, and it would, therefore, require
&lquo;an organised complicity of all of them, in a plot to place their collected r&ocirc;les in the
&lquo;hands of an outside purchaser. On the other hand, it could not have been difficult,
&lquo;where neither pains nor cost were spared, to procure by copyists in the Theatre a
&lquo;passable, nay, even a complete and correct printer's copy. If it proved too much for
<PB N=369>
<HE><I>THE TEXT</I> 369</HE>
<P>&lquo;one short-hand writer, two or three could accomplish it, by relieving each other; and
&lquo;if it could not be finished at the first performance, it could certainly be done at the
&lquo;second or third. Here is hypothesis against hypothesis, possibility against possi-
&lquo;bility, and it will need a series of minute investigations to turn the scale. The fol-
&lquo;lowing pages will be devoted to the task of proving, that one of the so-called authentic
&lquo;Quartos could have had its origin only in copies made at a performance on the stage,
&lquo;and that its various readings merit no regard in comparison with the text of the Folio,
&lquo;which has, at least, an indirect connection with the handwriting of the poet; and
&lquo;when, moreover, the Folio is not marred by manifest misprints. . . .
<P>&lquo;[P. 5.] The omissions in the Folio are not of vital importance, owing to the firm
&lquo;structure of the drama, which does not permit much to be removed without danger
&lquo;to the whole; and they have been made by no unskilful hand. We may, therefore,
&lquo;assume, that we have here the piece in that shape in which it was presented on the
&lquo;Shakespearian stage in the years just preceding its appearance in type, and it is
&lquo;manifest that it has suffered no material injury by its abridgements. These abridge-
&lquo;ments might have occurred all the more easily, if we suppose that the original MS
&lquo;had been neglected, mislaid, and finally lost. The greater completeness of the
&lquo;Quartos, however, by no means proves, that they represent a more complete MS
&lquo;than the Folio; but only that they appeared, or were prepared, at a time, when the
&lquo;drama was acted in its unabridged form, owing to a lack of sufficient experience of
&lquo;the needs of the stage.
<P>&lquo;[P. 6.] It would be unfair to deny that a number of Quarto readings correct some
&lquo;unmistakeable misprints of the Folio. Thus I, i, 173, &lquo;diseases&rquo; for <I>disasters;</I> II, i,
&lquo;89, &lquo;strange news&rquo; for <I>strangeness;</I> II, ii, 130, &lquo;dread&rquo; for <I>dead;</I> II, iv, 34, &lquo;whose&rquo;
&lquo;for <I>those;</I> II, iv, 170, &lquo;blast her pride&rquo; for <I>blister;</I> 183, &lquo;fickle&rquo; for <I>fickly;</I> III, iv,
&lquo;53, &lquo;ford&rquo; for <I>sword;</I> III, vi, 73, &lquo;tike&rquo; for <I>tight;</I> IV, ii, 75, &lquo;thereat&rquo; for <I>threat;</I>
&lquo;IV, iv, 18, &lquo;distress&rquo; for <I>desires;</I> IV, vi, 17, &lquo;walk&rquo; for <I>walked;</I> 83, &lquo;coining&rquo; for
&lquo;<I>crying;</I> 265, &lquo;we'ld&rquo; for <I>we.</I> But from all these we are not to conclude that the
&lquo;Quartos were genuine, that is, that they were derived from authentic MSS; but the
&lquo;inference to be drawn, with the greater assurance from such separate instances, is
&lquo;that the actors during a performance pronounced these words or phrases rightly and
&lquo;clearly, which the compositor of the Folio read wrongly.
<P>&lquo;These thirteen, or at most fifteen, instances in which the Folio is corrected by the
&lquo;Quartos, are offset by numberless, utterly senseless, readings in the latter. When they
&lquo;read I, i, 39, <I>first</I> for &lquo;fast&rquo;; 37, <I>of our state</I> for &lquo;from our age&rquo;; 38, <I>confirming</I> for
&lquo;&lquo;con$erring&rquo;, &amp;c. &amp;c; it has never occurred to any modern editor to allow his previous
&lquo;preference for the Quartos to have sway here. Nevertheless, it must be conceded,
&lquo;that such instances of carelessness as these have no bearing on the main question.
<P>&lquo;More remarkable and significant is a third class of discrepancies, which give
&lquo;editors the most embarrassment&mdash;<I>e. g.</I>, in the Quartos, I, i, 33, &lquo;my liege&rquo; for <I>my
&lquo;lord;</I> 34, &lquo;we shall&rquo; for <I>we will;</I> 38, <I>years</I> for &lquo;strengths;&rquo; 51, <I>merit doth most chal-
&lquo;lenge it</I> for &lquo;nature doth with merit challenge;&rquo; 147, &lquo;stoops to folly&rquo; for <I>falls to
&lquo;folly;</I> 181, <I>protection</I> for &lquo;dear shelter&rquo;; II, ii, 84, <I>What's his offence</I> for &lquo;What is
&lquo;&lquo;his $ault&rquo;; II, iv, 297, <I>bleak winds</I> for &lquo;high winds&rquo;, &amp;c. &amp;c; and when we find in
&lquo;round numbers, a hundred more similar variations, it is obvious enough, that the
&lquo;fault is not to be laid to illegible MS, or to mere typographical errors.
<P>&lquo;The prevailing opinion is, that there are two different versions of the tragedy, that
&lquo;the Quartos contain the earlier and original, and the Folio the second and revised
version. We cannot find the least historical support for a theory, that Shakespeare
<PB N=370>
<HE>370 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>&lquo;himself had any hand in such a revision. The editors of the Folio mention, as his
&lquo;characteristic, that &lquo;we have scarce received from him a blot in his papers,&rquo; and
&lquo;Ben Jonson quotes the same from the mouth of his fellow-actors. It may be granted
&lquo;that genuine changes, such as Schiller introduced into his <I>Robbers</I>, or Goethe into
&lquo;his <I>G&odblac;tz</I>, would not preclude in consequence thereof, the complete re-writing of his
&lquo;pieces, if, on other grounds, we had reason to believe that such changes there were.
&lquo;But absolutely excluded are all trifling corrections, changes in words and phrases
&lquo;that change nothing, which are utterly unimportant to the piece as a whole, and
&lquo;even to the impression in detail. It would be impossible to recognize in such trifles
&lquo;the hand of the poet, even if we knew nothing of his &lquo;unblotted papers;&rquo; especially
of a poet, who was by profession an actor.
<P>&lquo;The only result from such a revision would have been vexation and confusion to
the actors, who having once stamped upon their memories a certain phrase, would
have to unlearn all their r&ocirc;les for such bagatelles as these. It is very doubtful, if
&lquo;Ben Jonson would have had the chance to report Shakespeare's praise in the mouth
of his fellow-players, if he had ever set them such a task as this. . . . Everything
&lquo;becomes clear, as soon as we suppose that the MS for the Quartos was prepared by
&lquo;taking it down during a performance on the stage. Actors have now and then an
&lquo;unsure memory, or perhaps, they are not conscientious enough to use the precise
&lquo;word of the poet. It makes little difference to them, whether they say &lquo;stoops to
&lquo;&lquo;folly&rquo; or &lquo;falls to folly&rquo;, &lquo;protection&rquo; or &lquo;dear shelter&rquo;, &amp;c. &amp;c. Copyists writing
&lquo;rapidly use abbreviations (<I>e. g. my l.</I> for &lquo;my lord&rquo;, but which the compositor makes
&lquo;&lquo;my liege&rquo;); and they leave gaps which they afterwards fill out erroneously from
&lquo;memory (<I>e. g.</I> &lquo;bleak winds&rquo; for &lquo;high winds&rquo;), they mis-hear much and mis-write
much. A complete and exhaustive explanation, of all the changes in the Quarto
&lquo;Text, is to be found in the broad path, at every fresh station exposed to fresh dan-
&lquo;gers, which the words of the poet travel, through the mouth of the actor, the ear of
&lquo;the spectator, the hand of the copyist, and the eye of the compositor.&rquo; [Dr <SC>Schmidt</SC>
brings forward certain classes of errors, to prove his position. I can give only the
headings:] &lquo;1. The Quartos make no distinction between verse and prose; not even
&lquo;where the lines rhyme at the end of a scene. 2. Many errors of the Quartos are
&lquo;mistakes of the ear, not of the eye. 3. Capriciousness of the actors&rquo; diction is
&lquo;noticeable in the use of expletives, like &lquo;come,&rquo; &lquo;do,&rquo; &lquo;go to,&rquo; &lquo;how,&rquo; &lquo;sir,&rquo; &amp;c. In
&lquo;common life Englishmen are fond of beginning their sentences with such little words,
&lquo;which, like tuning-forks, give the key in which they intend to speak. 4. The omissions
&lquo;in the Quartos are evidently due to the actors, occurring as they do in the middle of
&lquo;speeches, where care is taken merely to preserve the cue, &amp;c. &amp;c.&rquo; [Dr <SC>Schmidt</SC>
sums up as follows:] &lquo;Such are the reasons in general and in particular, which prove
&lquo;that the Quarto-Text of <I>King Lear</I> lacks authority, and that its various readings are to
&lquo;be expunged for our editions; excepting, in those few instances, where they serve to
&lquo;correct indubitable errors in the Folio. At how early, or at how late, a day this con-
&lquo;viction will take root and bear fruit, cannot from past experience be approximately
&lquo;reckoned. It is not every-one's business to let himself be convinced, and it is not
&lquo;every-one's business to follow his convictions.&rquo; [Nearly all the remainder of Dr
Schmidt's remarks will be found in the commentary to the text. Unfortunately, his
essay is only a fragment. It does not extend beyond the second Scene of the first Act.
<P>Since the foregoing was written an article has appeared in <I>Robinson's Epitome o$
Literature</I>, 1 August, 1879, by the Rev. Mr <SC>Fleay</SC>, on <I>The Date and The Text</I> of
<PB N=371>
<HE><I>THE TEXT</I> 371</HE>
<P>this play. The portion that relates to the Text is substantially as follows:] &lquo;In the
&lquo;Quarto we have the version of the play as it was performed on the 26th of Decem-
&lquo;ber, 1606, before the King. I am unable to trace any revivals of it, but the fact that
&lquo;the Folio is divided into Acts and Scenes, and the numerous omissions in it, prove
&lquo;that version to be an abridgement for stage purposes, most likely made after Shake-
&lquo;speare's retirement, and probably <I>circa</I> 1616-22.
<P>&lquo;I will now proceed to examine some peculiarities in the versions. We must re-
&lquo;member that in 1605, when the original version (which we call &lquo;O&rquo;) was produced,
&lquo;the Queen had recently (in October, 1604) been consulting astrologers and firmly
&lquo;believed in them; that James I. was popularly supposed to be on anything but good
&lquo;terms with Prince Henry; that his wholesale creation of knights had been satirised
&lquo;abundantly on the boards; and that England and Scotland had been merged in
&lquo;Great Britain by proclamation (October 20, 1604). Again, in 1606, December 26,
&lquo;when the revival took place, the Gunpowder Plot had disturbed the Court and people.
<P>&lquo;Now turn to I, ii, 103, <I>seq.</I>, it is clear that a passage, innocent perhaps originally,
&lquo;but liable to misconstruction by the Court, has been carefully left out in the Quarto.
&lquo;&lquo;This villain of mine comes under the prediction; there's son against father: <I>the
&lquo;King falls from bias of nature, there's father against child.</I> We have seen the best
&lquo;of our time,&rquo; &amp;c.
<P>&lquo;On the other hand, l. 91 <I>seq.</I>, 137 <I>seq.</I>, which were inserted in the Quarto in place
&lquo;of this, speak of a &lquo;father that so tenderly and entirely loves him;&rquo; &lquo;menaces and
&lquo;maledictions against king and nobles;&rquo; (Gunpowder Plot;) &lquo;nuptial breaches;&rquo;
&lquo;(Lady Essex;) and the like, none of which allusions would be disagreeable to the
&lquo;King.
<P>&lquo;Again, in I, iv, 345, <I>seq.</I>, this passage was omitted:
<BQ>&lquo;&lquo;This man hath had good counsel: a hundred knights,<LB>
&lquo;&lquo;Tis politic and safe to let him keep<LB>
&lquo;At point a hundred knights; yes, that, on every dream<LB>
&lquo;Each buzz, each fancy, each complaint, dislike,<LB>
&lquo;<I>He may enguard his dotage with their powers</I>,<LB>
&lquo;<I>And hold our lives in mercy.</I>&rquo;<LB></BQ>
<P>&lquo;But the strongest instance of this kind is in III, i, 22-42, where 22-29 (from the
&lquo;Folio) are clearly alternative with 30-42 (from the Quarto). In the Folio we read:
<BQ>&lquo;&lquo;Who have, as who have not, that their great stars<LB>
&lquo;Throned and set high? servants, who seem no less,<LB>
&lquo;Which are to France the spies and speculations<LB>
&lquo;Intelligent of our state; what hath been seen,<LB>
&lquo;* * * * in * * * * something deeper,<LB>
&lquo;Whereof, perchance, these are but furnishings.&rquo;<LB></BQ>
<P>&lquo;But in the Quarto we are only told of &lquo;secret $eet in some of our best ports.&rquo;
&lquo;Is it not clear that the former passage would, in the winter of 1604-5, when the
&lquo;peace with Spain was not six months old&mdash;a peace procured by the bribery of Suf-
&lquo;folk, Northampton, Pembroke, Southampton, Dirleton, &amp;c., &amp;c.&mdash;be taken by the
&lquo;populace as a direct allusion to this scandalous corruption, and is it not also clear
&lquo;that the Court could not allow the play to be acted before them without the clever
&lquo;reformations introduced by Shakespeare in this Quarto version?
<P>&lquo;Another omission of the same kind is that of the Merlin prophecy at the end of
&lquo;III, ii. James would not have tolerated even so distant a prospect of a time when
&lquo;the realm of Albion should come to great confusion, and any allusion to the cut-
<PB N=372>
<HE>372 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>&lquo;purse who &lquo;came to the throng&rquo; during his first progress is known to have been
&lquo;very obnoxious to him.
<P>&lquo;It is clear then that the Quarto is, as stated on the title-page, the version &lquo;played
&lquo;before the King's Majesty.&rquo; It is, however, a scandalously incorrect and surrepti-
&lquo;tious copy of that version, taken from a wretchedly written MS.
<P>&lquo;Taking it then that the Quarto is a somewhat altered version of &lquo;O&rquo; for Court
&lquo;performance, but very carelessly copied and erroneously printed, we have yet to
&lquo;examine the Folio. In this case, fortunately, as in the corresponding cases of
&lquo;<I>Othello</I> and <I>Hamlet</I>, we have two versions, one abridged considerably. It is not
&lquo;then possible for ingenuous editors to sneer at the very notion of abridgement as
&lquo;they do when it is suggested that <I>The Tempest</I> or <I>Julius C&aelig;sar</I> have been curtailed
&lquo;for theatrical purposes. But they all agree that in this instance the alteration was
&lquo;made by Shakespeare himself. In spite of the recorded facts that Shirley, Massin-
&lquo;ger, &amp;c. did rewrite great portions of Beaumont and Fletcher (who were then,
&lquo;1616-40, esteemed above Shakespeare); in spite of the probability that portions,
&lquo;if not all, of his MSS were burnt with the Globe Theatre; in spite of the palpable
&lquo;fact that <I>Timon</I> was so remodelled before 1623, and <I>Macbeth, The Tempest</I>, &amp;c.
&lquo;afterwards, by D'Avenant and Dryden; in spite of the persistence to our own time
&lquo;of managers in playing <I>Richard III, Macbeth</I>, &amp;c. in their altered forms, we are
&lquo;required to believe that Shakespeare, who left his plays to take care of themselves,
&lquo;and did not collect them like Jonson, was regarded as too sacred to be remodelled
&lquo;until his plays were published in 1623, but after that they were open to any one to
&lquo;refashion as he pleased; in other words, the very thing which preserved Jonson's
&lquo;plays from being altered was the beginning of the corruption of Shakespeare's. I
&lquo;believe, on the contrary, that this process began immediately after his death, and
&lquo;that nearly every play revived was, at the revival, revised also; abridged, &lquo;re-
&lquo;formed&rquo; of oaths, &amp;c., corrected by alteration of obsolete words, and &lquo;emended&rquo;
&lquo;in metre as well as diction. In some cases I believe also interpolations were intro-
&lquo;duced,&mdash;not, however, in this play of <I>Lear</I>, to which I return.
<P>&lquo;Besides the <I>alterations</I> I have noted from &lquo;O&rquo; to the Quarto, there are omissions
&lquo;in the Folio, especially in the later part of the play. Besides shorter ones of a line
&lquo;or so, which may be due to the careless copy, or of single words, which may be
&lquo;due to the printer, I may notice the following: I, iii, 16-23; I, iv, 154-169; I, iv,
&lquo;252-257; II, ii, 148-152 (clearly a purposed omission, not accidental, the metre
&lquo;being set right by inserting, &lquo;need&rquo;); III, vi, 18-59; III, vi, 109-122 (omitted
&lquo;because, as Heywood tells us, rhyme had become unfashionable); III, vii, 98-107;
&lquo;IV, i, 60-66; IV, i, 31-50; IV, i, 53-58; IV, i, 62-69. The whole of IV, iii
&lquo;(intentional, for the scenes are renumbered <I>Tertia</I> for <I>Quarta</I>, etc., up to <I>Septima</I>,
&lquo;which remains unaltered); IV, vii, 86-97; V, i, 23-28; V, iii, 54-59; V, iii, 203-221.
<P>&lquo;Now I cannot believe that these omissions were made by Shakespeare; the last
&lquo;one, for instance, narrating the meeting of Edgar and Kent, is <I>necessary</I> to the plot.
&lquo;See how abrupt line 229 (&lquo;Here comes Kent&rquo;) becomes without it. But on this
&lquo;point, and on the incorrectness of the Quarto I need not enlarge. Four years since
&lquo;Prof. Delius, in an able paper, displayed his views on them, with which I entirely
&lquo;coincide. The portions of this article which I claim as original are the fixing the
&lquo;date of production in 1605, not 1606 [see <I>Date of the Composition</I>, p. 381], and the
&lquo;hypothesis that the Quarto version was one altered by Shakespeare from &lquo;O&rquo; for
&lquo;production at Court.
<P>&lquo;While the very numerous irregularities of metre in the Quarto are due entirely to
<PB N=373>
<HE><I>THE TEXT</I> 373</HE>
<P>&lquo;the misreading of the badly written MS by a careless printer, the many broken lines
&lquo;of less than five feet in the Folio are due to the omission of passages cut out to
&lquo;shorten the representation. I pointed this out in the case of <I>Julius C&aelig;sar</I>, in 1875.
&lquo;I now say that it applies to all the shortened plays of Shakespeare, and that in re-
&lquo;gard to his works, and Fletcher's, or to any of the great dramatists, we can always
&lquo;tell if any play has been abridged by examination of this one peculiarity.&rquo;

<P>A LIST OF VARIOUS READINGS IN CERTAIN QUARTOS, COLLATED

THE FOOT-NOTES OF THEIR EDITION.
<P>The following collation is wholly the work of Messrs <SC>Clark</SC> and <SC>Wright</SC>. I
have not incorporated it in my own collation, as recorded in the foregoing Textual
notes. The discrepancies hardly rise to the dignity of <I>vari&aelig; lectiones</I>, in the strict
sense in which the phrase is used among schoolmen; they are little else than gross
typographical blunders, and are interesting mainly for bibliographical purposes, in
deciding the priority in printing among several copies, or even portions of copies,
of Quartos of the same date. Interest too may be found in deciding whether the
various readings are errors of the eye or of the ear.
<P>It is to be borne in mind, that I have here reprinted the collation exactly as it is
recorded in the Cambridge Edition, except in some cases where the reading is iden-
tical with the received text, there it seemed superfluous; and that &lquo;Q<SUB>2</SUB>&rquo; of the Cam-
bridge Edition is Q<SUB>1</SUB> of this, viz: the <I>Pide Bull</I> edition.

<C>DATE OF THE COMPOSITION</C>
<P><SC>The</SC> Date of the Composition of this play can be ascertained with an unusual degree
of accuracy. We have one limit fixed by external evidence, and another by internal,
and the term between the two consists of merely three years: from 1603 to 1606.
<P>The external evidence is supplied by the Stationers' Registers, which give us the
Christmas holidays in 1606 as the earliest date before which the play must of course
have been written. To the internal evidence we must look for the latest date after
which it must have been written.
<P>There are three items of internal evidence, viz: first, the references to Dr Hars-
net's book, noted by <SC>Theobald</SC>; secondly, the use by Edgar of &lquo;British man&rquo; instead
of <I>Englishman</I> in the popular rhyme; this was noted by <SC>Malone</SC>; and thirdly,
the reference by Gloucester to the &lquo;late eclipses,&rquo; to which attention was called by
Mr <SC>Aldis Wright</SC>.
<P>First, Dr Harsnet's book. This was published in 1603. See III, iv, 53. Of the
three items, this is really the only one that is sure beyond a peradventure. Concern-
ing the other two, there may be more or less difference of opinion.
<P>Of the Second, <SC>Malone</SC> (vol. i, p. 352, 1790) says: &lquo;This play is ascertained to
&lquo;have been written after October, 1604, by a minute change which Shakespeare made
&lquo;in a traditional line put into the mouth of Edgar: &ldquo;Fie, foh, fum, I smell the blood
&lquo;of a <I>British</I> man.&rdquo; [See III, iv, 175.] The old metrical saying, which is found
&lquo;in one of Nashe's pamphlets, printed in 1596, and in other books, was: &ldquo;Fy, fa,
&lquo;fum, I smell the blood of an <I>Englishman.</I>&rdquo; Though a complete union of Eng-
&lquo;land and Scotland, which was projected in the first parliament that met after James's
&lquo;accession to the English throne, was not carried into effect till a century afterwards,
&lquo;the two kingdoms were united in <I>name</I>, and he was proclaimed King of <I>Great
&lquo;Britain</I>, 24 October, 1604.&rquo;
<P><SC>Malone</SC> therefore assigns the composition to 1605, and thinks it &lquo;extremely prob-
able&rquo; that it was performed for the first time in March or April of that year, &lquo;in which
&lquo;year the old play of <I>King Leir</I>, that had been entered at Stationers' Hall in 1594,
&lquo;was printed by Simon Stafford for John Wright, who, we may presume, finding
&lquo;Shakespeare's play successful, hoped to palm the spurious one on the public for his.&rquo;
See p. 353. It is to be regretted that Malone did not furnish the proofs of his asser-
tion that the old play of 1594 is identical with that which was afterwards printed in
1605. I am strongly inclined to believe that it is a fact, but I think it can only be
conjecture when we assert that it is so. After imputing to Simon Stafford an intention
to deceive the public, Malone is obliged to put the date of the performance as far
back as March or April, 1605. It was on the eighth of May in that year that Stafford
entered his book at Stationers' Hall, and if Shakespeare's <I>Lear</I> was then on the
stage, or had been lately, it must have been written some months before. If, as
Malone supposes, it was performed in March, it must have been written in January
or February, in order to keep it within the year 1605. I do not remember that
Malone anywhere expresses himself quite as explicitly as this, but if he had he would
have carried <SC>Chalmers</SC> completely with him; and if he had extended the compo-
sition over a little longer space than two months, and stretched it into December or
<PB N=378>
<HE>378 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>November, 1604, he would have taken with him <SC>Drake</SC> also, and probably all others
who profess to detect sharp practice between the lines of Simon Stafford's title-page;
but, as I said when speaking of the entry of Stafford's book in the Stationers' Regis-
ters, these arguments, founded on a printer's chance phrase, are to me only &lquo;gracious
fooling.&rquo; Simon Stafford, in all likelihood, tells the truth when he says his <I>King
Leir</I> was &lquo;latelie acted.&rquo; I dare say it was a popular play; it is quite a good speci-
men of the third-rate class of comedies, and its success was sufficiently marked
to suggest to Shakespeare a tragedy on the same subject. And as to Stafford's
calling it a tragedy,&mdash;I really think that he was to a certain extent justified in retain-
ing the impression which the whole drift of the play except the last two or three
scenes left upon his mind. If the spectacle of a respectable elderly king, reduced
to such an extremity of hunger as to induce his faithful attendant to offer him his
bare and living arm as an article of diet, be not tragic, it is difficult to say what
tragedy is. Moreover, <SC>Dryden</SC> in his Preface to <I>The Spanish Friar</I> speaks of a
&lquo;<I>Tragedy ending happily.</I>&rquo; The half-title of <SC>Tate's</SC> version of this very play reads,
&lquo;The tragedy of King Lear,&rquo; and we all know that the declared purpose of that
version was to turn it into a comedy; and when we find even <SC>Campbell</SC>, the poet,
in his <I>Remarks</I> on this play, speaking of this same <I>King Leir</I> as &lquo;a tragedy,&rquo; I
think we ought not to be too severe on an Elizabethan printer for applying to it the
same title. In these days, when Henry VIII, Nero, and Judas Iscariot find vindi-
cators, I really think a faint murmur might be raised for humble Simon Stafford.
<P>As I have said, <SC>Chalmers</SC> (<I>Supplemental Apology</I>, p. 413) concurs generally with
Malone in the belief that <I>Lear</I> was written early in 1605, but he thinks Malone is
mistaken in some of his premises. For instance, he says that the argument, derived
from the change of <I>English</I> to &lquo;British,&rquo; that the play was written after October,
1604, is not absolutely conclusive, for &lquo;the fact is that there was issued from Green-
&lquo;wich a royal proclamation, on the 13th of May, 1603, declaring that, until a com-
&lquo;plete union, the king held, and esteemed, the two realms, as <I>presently</I> united, and as
&lquo;one kingdom; and the two poets, Daniel, and Drayton, who wrote gratulatory verses
&lquo;on his accession, spoke of the two kingdoms as united, thereby, into one realm, by
&lquo;the name of Britain; and of the inhabitants of England and Scotland, as one
&lquo;people, by the denomination of British. Before King James arrived at London,
&lquo;Daniel offered tc him: &lquo;<I>A Panegyrike Congratulatory, delivered to the King's most
&lquo;excellent Majesty at Burleigh-Harrington in Rutlandshire</I>,&rquo; which was printed in
1603, for Blount, with a Defence of Rhime:
<BQ>&lquo;Lo here the glory of a greater day<LB>
Than <I>England</I> ever heretofore could see<LB>
In all her days. . . .<LB>
And now she is, and now in peace therefore<LB>
<I>Shake hands with union</I>, O thou mightie state,<LB>
Now thou art all <I>great Britain</I>, and no more,<LB>
<I>No Scot</I>, no <I>English</I> now, nor no debate.&rquo;<LB></BQ>
<P>&lquo;This very rare publication of Daniel confutes, by the fact, the Commentator's rea<*>
&lquo;soning, from the proclamation; for we see how a poet did write before any procla-
&lquo;mation issued upon the point.&rquo;
<P><SC>Drake</SC> (<I>Shakespeare and his Times</I>, ii, 457) thinks it &lquo;more probable that its pro-
duction is to be attributed to the close of 1604,&rquo; for three reasons: First, if the change
from English to British were made out of compliment to the king, the compliment
would be all the greater if the change were made between the declaratory proclama-
tion of May, 1603, and the definitive proclamation of October, 1604. Secondly, the
<PB N=379>
<HE><I>DATE OF THE COMPOSITION</I> 379</HE>
<P>old play of <I>King Leir</I> was entered on the Stationers' books on the 8th of May, 1605,
&lquo;as it was <I>lately</I> acted.&rquo; Now, as the publisher hoped to impose on the public this
old tragedy for Shakespeare's successful drama, it was evidently intended that the
word &lquo;<I>lately</I>&rquo; should be referred by the reader to Shakespeare's play; hence, it fol-
lows that <I>Lear</I> had been acted some months before, and was not then actually per-
forming. This inference harmonises with the supposition that <I>Lear</I> was written about
the end of 1604, but does not agree with Malone's theory that it appeared in April,
1605. Thirdly, &lquo;<I>Cymbeline</I> is assigned to 1605, and, in consequence of the removal
of <I>The Winter's Tale</I> to 1613,&rquo; the year 1604 is left vacant for the admission of <I>Lear.</I>
<P><SC>Knight</SC> observes that &lquo;Malone and Drake are at issue on a question of merely three
months, when the facts, which we really have, give us a range of three years.&rquo; &lquo;It is
&lquo;sufficient,&rquo; adds Knight, &lquo;for us to be confirmed in the belief, derived from internal
&lquo;evidence, that <I>Lear</I> was produced at that period when the genius of Shakespeare
&lquo;was &ldquo;at its very point of culmination.&rdquo;&rquo; He also points out that the Folio has
&lquo;English&rquo; in IV, vi, 249 [see his note <I>ad loc.</I>], despite the fact that the Quartos
changed it to <I>British</I>, not only here, but in Edgar's &lquo;Fee, fa, fum.&rquo;
<P>Mr <SC>Wright</SC> thinks it well not to lay too much stress upon the change from
&lquo;English&rquo; of the Folio to <I>British</I> of the Quarto, and to infer therefrom that the line in
the Folio was written before the royal proclamation in October, 1604, and corrected
before the Quartos were printed in 1608. &lquo;It is as likely,&rquo; says the Editor of the Clar-
endon Edition, &lquo;that Shakespeare, writing not long after 1604, while the change was
&lquo;still fresh, and before the word &lquo;British&rquo; had become familiar in men's mouths, may
&lquo;have inadvertently written &lquo;English,&rquo; and subsequently changed it to &lquo;British.&rquo;&rquo;
<P>The Third item of indirect internal evidence is thus set forth by Mr <SC>Aldis Wright</SC>:
&lquo;We are helped forward another step in determining the date by a passage in Glou-
&lquo;cester's speech (I, ii, 98, <I>et seq.</I>): &lquo;These late eclipses in the sun and moon portend
&lquo;&lquo;no good to us.&rquo; By those who observed the signs in the air and sky the great
&lquo;eclipse of the sun, which took place in October, 1605, had been looked forward to
&lquo;with apprehension as the precursor of evil, especially as it was preceded by an
&lquo;eclipse of the moon within the space of a month. In arguing against such appre-
&lquo;hensions, John Harvey, of King's Lynn, who reasoned with the &lquo;wisdom of nature,&rquo;
&lquo;in his book called <I>A Discoursive Probleme Concerning Prophesies</I>, printed in 1588,
&lquo;wrote as follows (p. 119):
<P>&lquo;&ldquo;Moreouer, the like concourse of two Eclipses in one, and the same month, shal
&ldquo;hereafter more euidently in shew, and more effectually in deed, appeere, <I>Anno</I>
&ldquo;1590. the 7. and 21. daies of Iuly: and <I>Anno</I> 1598. the 11. and 25. daies of Feb-
&ldquo;ruary; and <I>Anno</I> 1601. the 29. day of Nouember, and 14. of December: but espe-
&ldquo;cially, and most notably <I>Anno</I> 1605. the second day of October, when the sunne
&ldquo;shall be obscured aboue 11. digits, and darknes appeere euen at midday, the Moone
&ldquo;at the very next full immediately preceding hauing likewise beene Eclipsed. Wher-
&ldquo;fore as two Eclipses in the space of one month, are no great strange nouities, so if
&ldquo;either they, or an huge fearefull Eclipse of the Sunne were to iustifie or confirme
&ldquo;this oracle: the author thereof should haue staied his wisedome vntill after the
&ldquo;foresaid yeere of Christ, 1605. when so rare a spectacle shall be seene, or the yeeres
&ldquo;1606. 1607. or 1608. immediately following, when so mightie an Eclipse shall so
&ldquo;perlously rage.&rdquo;
<P>&lquo;Reading this in connection with the speech of Gloucester, which has been re-
&lquo;ferred to, and with what Edmund, the sceptic of the time, subsequently (I, ii, 120,
<PB N=380>
<HE>380 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>&lquo;124, 125) says, &lquo;O, these eclipses portend these divisions,&rquo; and, &lquo;I am thinking,
&lquo;&lquo;brother, of a prediction I read this other day, what should follow these eclipses,&rquo;
&lquo;it can scarcely be doubted that Shakespeare had in his mind the great eclipse, and
&lquo;that <I>Lear</I> was written while the recollection of it was still fresh, and while the
&lquo;ephemeral literature of the day abounded with pamphlets foreboding the conse-
&lquo;quences that were to follow. If we imagine further that, in Gloucester's words,
&lquo;&lquo;machinations, hollowness, treachery, and all ruinous disorders follow us disquietly
&lquo;&lquo;to our graves,&rquo; there is a reference to the Gunpowder Plot of Nov. 5, 1605, we
&lquo;have another approximation to the date. But, without insisting too much upon this,
&lquo;it is, I think, highly probable that Shakespeare did not begin to write <I>King Lear</I>
&lquo;till towards the end of the year 1605, and that his attention may have been directed
&lquo;to the story as a subject for tragedy by the revival of the older play above men-
&lquo;tioned, which was published in the same year.
<P>&lquo;Having now reduced the period of composition to the narrow limits between the
&lquo;end of 1605 and Christmas, 1606, any attempt to assign the date more exactly must
&lquo;be purely conjectural and derived from internal evidence. It would be difficult to
&lquo;fix the precise season to which the storm in the third Act is appropriate. Various
&lquo;indications in the previous Act seem to point to the winter; such as the Fool's
&lquo;speech (II, iv, 45), &lquo;Winter's not gone yet, if the wild geese fly that way,&rquo; though
&lquo;of course this had also another meaning. Again, the signs of the gathering storm
&lquo;are wintry, &lquo;the bleak winds do sorely ruffle,&rquo; &lquo;'tis a wild night&rquo;; but Lear's apos-
&lquo;trophe is addressed to a violent summer tempest, and so Kent describes it. And in
&lquo;accordance with this all the colouring of the fourth Act is of the summer. Lear
&lquo;is seen
<BQ>Crown'd with rank fumiter and furrow-weeds,<LB>
With hor-docks, hemlocks, nettles, cuckow-flowers,<LB>
Darnel, and all the idle weeds that grow<LB>
In our sustaining corn.<*><LB></BQ>
<P>&lquo;&lquo;Search every acre in the high-grown field,&rquo; points to July, and we must not insist
&lquo;too much upon strict botanical accuracy, for this would be late for cuckoo-flowers, as
&lquo;well as for the samphire-gathering in a subsequent scene, which generally takes place
&lquo;in May. Perhaps Shakespeare began the play in the winter of 1605, and finished it
&lquo;in the summer of 1606, while the fields were still covered with the unharvested corn,
&lquo;and the great storm of March was still fresh in his recollection.&rquo;
<P>Mr <SC>Moberly</SC> thinks that the play must have been written in 1605-6, &lquo;in the midst
&lquo;of the stirring events connected with the Gunpowder Plot; and the absence of
&lquo;allusion to them is a striking instance of the way in which Shakespeare's mind, like
&lquo;that of Goethe in after-time, could keep aloof from subjects of absorbing public
&lquo;interest, and live simply among its own creations.&rquo;
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> adopts <SC>Malone's</SC> view (which, however, he erroneously attributes to <SC>Stee-
vens</SC>), that its date is March or April, 1605.
<P>Dr <SC>Delius</SC> thinks that it must have been written in 1604 or 1605, in Shakespeare's
fortieth or forty-first year.
<P>Mr <SC>Fleay</SC> (<I>Shakespeare Manual</I>, p. 47) says that it was probably produced early in
1605, as the old play was then reprinted, and entered on the eighth of May as &lquo;lately
acted&rquo; in order to deceive the public.
<P>I think we must remain content with the term of three years; no date more pre-
cise than this will probably ever gain general acceptance. I am afraid we are con-
<PB N=381>
<HE><I>DATE OF THE COMPOSITION</I> 381</HE>
<P>sidering too curiously in attempting to ascertain the precise year or time of the year.
To suppose that when Shakespeare alludes to winter there must be actually icicles
hanging by the wall, or that when he mentions flowers the meadows must be painted
with delight before his very eyes, is to put a narrow limitation to his imagination.
His allusions to contemporary events are not always so defined as to be at once
manifest to close students or accomplished scholars. As we have seen, one editor
discovers in this play a possible allusion to the Gunpowder Plot, while another dis-
cerns none. To a certain extent this same vagueness holds true in regard to eclipses
and other natural phenomena. I cannot but think we deal unworthily with Shake-
speare's genius when we suppose that he needed, or that he himself felt that he
needed, to resort to such allusions in order to produce dramatic effects. While we
all agree in believing that he throws around his dramas the atmosphere of the times
in which the scenes are laid, it can scarcely be but that his auditors, and assuredly
Shakespeare himself, would have felt the jar that an allusion to an event of yester-
day would have instantly occasioned. At the same time, so truly did Shakespeare
write for the hour then present that it is presumptuous to say what he would not do
for that hour's success. There are instances, undoubtedly, in his plays where he
alludes to recent local events; but I do not think the number as large as is generally
supposed.
<P>Since the foregoing was written the article by Mr <SC>Fleay</SC> appeared, from which
extracts were made at the close of the preceding article on <I>The Text.</I> Mr Fleay is
so eminent in all that pertains to metrical tests, and has devoted so much learning to
the discovery of the dates of these plays, that it is with reluctance that I acknow-
ledge my inability to follow him to his exact conclusion. As will be seen, he follows
the popular tide in reading fraud in Simon Stafford's entry on the Stationers'
Registers. The following extract from Mr <SC>Fleay's</SC> article bears upon the present
subject:
<P>&lquo;The date had long since been determined by Malone, as between October, 1604,
&lquo;and the 8th of May, 1605, on satisfactory grounds; but Mr Aldis Wright has shifted
&lquo;it forward to the summer of 1606, in the plausible introduction to his edition of the
&lquo;play. Now, the whole theory of metrical tests depends on the date of this play.
&lquo;Shakespeare wrote <I>Pericles</I> (or his share of it), in 1606; and <I>Pericles</I> is as certainly
&lquo;in his fourth manner as <I>Lear</I> is in his third; if the periods overlap my theories are
&lquo;worthless; and <I>Lear</I> and <I>Pericles</I> written within a few months would bring them
&lquo;dangerously near. Hence I have examined this question with special minuteness,
&lquo;and, I am glad to add, have been rewarded by a positive result. The play <I>was</I>
&lquo;written before May 8, 1605. For the old play of <I>Leir</I> (written for the Queen's
&lquo;men, <I>circa</I> 1588, played by the Queen's and Sussex's men at the Rose, 1593, April
&lquo;6; entered for E. White, 1594, May 14; entered for S. Stafford, and printed by him
&lquo;for J. Wright, to whom he assigned it, 1605, May 8) was put on the Stationers'
&lquo;books as <I>The</I> <SC>Tragical History</SC> <I>of King Leir and his three daughters, &amp;c.</I>, <SC>as
&lquo;it was lately acted</SC>. Now Mr Aldis Wright himself noticed that no writer
&lquo;(historical or theatrical) had given a tragic ending to this story till Shakespeare
&lquo;made his play; &lquo;Cordelia's <I>fate</I> and character are all his own,&rquo; says he. Hence the
&lquo;old &lquo;Chronicle History&rquo; could not have been described as &lquo;<I>Tragical</I>&rquo; in 1605 had
&lquo;not a <I>tragedy</I> on the subject been &lquo;lately acted,&rquo; nor could the <I>tragedy</I> have been
&lquo;any other than Shakespeare's. Hence Malone was right in his date and in his in-
&lquo;ference that Stafford (who had to do with the surreptitious editions of <I>Pericles</I> and
&lquo;<I>Edward III</I>) wished to pass the old play off as Shakespeare's. Wright, however,
<PB N=382>
<HE>382 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>&lquo;had not the impudence to put Stafford's &lquo;Tragical History&rquo; on his title-page, though
&lquo;he kept the &lquo;lately acted,&rquo; which was probably, as far as the older play is concerned,
&lquo;not true. Accordingly, when the real &lquo;tragedy&rquo; was issued in 1608, Butter marks
&lquo;his edition as the genuine &lquo;Dirty Dick,&rquo; by putting &lquo;Chronicle History&rquo; on its fore-
&lquo;head; only in the Folio does the real name of &lquo;Tragedy&rquo; appear. The date, then,
&lquo;is early in 1605.&rquo;
<P>Again &lquo;the wheel has come full circle&rquo;; the same is true of <SC>Wright</SC> and <SC>Fleay</SC>
as of <SC>Malone</SC> and <SC>Chalmers</SC>: they differ only by a few months. Wright supposes
that Shakespeare began the play, and Fleay that he ended it, in 1605.
<P>For me it is sufficient that we have the play; and all these discussions as to the
time when it was written, even if they could give us the very day of the week and
the very hour of the day, would still remain among the extrinsic facts which, it
seems fated, are to be all that we shall ever learn about Shakespeare. While I am
reading such delightful books as <I>Shakspere, His Mind and Art</I>, I yield to the glamour
and confess the charm; and, kindled by the enthusiasm of the Director of the <I>New
Shakspere Society</I>, and of his fellow-workers, I am persuaded that naught's had,
all's spent, when our researches are not devoted to the discovery of the order of the
plays; but I turn to the plays themselves, and, lost in their grandeur and their beau-
ties, find that I am indifferent as to when they were written, where they were written,
or even by whom they were written. Standards for measuring them we have none;
they stand by themselves, written by no mortal hand. Well is it for him, and for us,
that the man Shakespeare has faded, and left not a wrack behind. No outward
life could rise to the grandeur of these plays.
<P>Shall we ever outgrow the wisdom of <SC>Lessing</SC>? In one of his Hamburg criti-
cisms, speaking of the pitiful spectacle made by Voltaire when suffering himself to
be shown to the theatre after the performance of one of his plays, Lessing says:
&lquo;I know not which strikes me as the more pitiful, the childish curiosity of the public,
&lquo;or the conceited complaisance of the poet. How then do people think a poet looks?
&lquo;Not like other men? And how weak must be the impression which the work has
&lquo;made when, in the same moment, the only curiosity is to hold up the figure of the
&lquo;master alongside of it! The true masterpiece, it seems to me, fills us so wholly
&lquo;with itself that we forget the author, and look upon it, not as the production of an
&lquo;individual, but of universal nature. . . . I suppose the true reason why we know so
&lquo;little that is certain about the person and life of Homer is the excellence of his
&lquo;poems. We stand full of astonishment by the broad, rushing river, without thinking
&lquo;of its source in the mountains. We care not to know, we find our account in for-
&lquo;getting, that Homer, the schoolmaster in Smyrna, the blind beggar, is the very
&lquo;Homer who so enraptures us in his works. He leads us into the presence of the
&lquo;gods and heroes; the company must be very tedious, we must be greatly ennuied
&lquo;by it, if we are so very curious to know all about the doorkeeper who let us in.
&lquo;The illusion must be very weak, one must be little natural, but all the more sophis-
&lquo;ticated, when one is so anxious about the artist.&rquo;
<PB N=383>
<C>THE SOURCE OF THE PLOT</C>
<P><SC>Of</SC> the two tragic stories in <I>Lear</I>, the source from which Shakespeare derived the
subordinate one, that of Gloucester, is well known. The extract from Sidney's <I>Arcadia</I>,
containing the story of &lquo;the Paphlagonian unkind king,&rquo; will be found on p. 386; it was
pointed out, as similar to Gloucester's, by our countrywoman, Mrs <SC>Lennox</SC>, in 1754,
and I know of only one commentator, <SC>Hunter</SC> (see IV, vi, 66), who has questioned,
since then, the general belief that it was the original of Shakespeare's secondary plot.
<P>There is some doubt, however, as to the source from which the main plot of <I>Lear</I>
is directly derived. The story itself, in its broad outlines of doting paternal kind-
ness repaid with filial ingratitude, and paternal harshness requited with devoted love,
is as old as almost any story in English literature. It is told by Geoffrey of Mon-
mouth in his <I>Historia Britonum</I>, by Layamon in his <I>Brut</I>, by Robert of Gloucester,
by Fabyan in his <I>Chronicle</I>, by Spenser in his <I>Faery Queene</I>, by Holinshed, by
Camden, and it is found in the <I>Mirour for Magistrates</I>, the <I>Gesta Romanorum</I>,
in Warner's <I>Albion's England</I>, and, I dare say, elsewhere. It is not, however,
likely that Shakespeare went to any of the older of these authorities for his ma-
terials; we know how fond he was of Holinshed, and unless there were a drama
ready to his hand to be remodelled, we should look to Holinshed; and there, indeed,
some of the best of modern editors do find the immediate source of Shakespeare's
<I>Lear.</I> But I am afraid I cannot agree with them. Holinshed, I think, furnished
merely the indirect source of <I>Lear.</I> I think we can approach one step nearer and
discern the direct source in the ante-Shakespearian drama of the <I>Chronicle History of
King Leir</I>, which <SC>Halliwell</SC>, following <SC>Malone</SC>, says was dramatized as early as
1593 or 1594, and is probably the same that Edward White entered in the Stationers'
Registers in the latter of these years, and which reappeared as the &lquo;tragecall historie&rquo;
printed by Simon Stafford in 1605. The author of this old comedy of <I>King Leir</I>
undoubtedly drew from the old chroniclers, probably Holinshed; and Shakespeare,
I think, drew from him. But what false impressions are conveyed in the phrases
which we have to use to express the process whereby Shakespeare converted the
stocks and stones of the old dramas and chronicles into living, breathing men and
women! We say he &lquo;drew his original&rquo; from this source, or he &lquo;found his materials&rquo;
in that source. But how much did he &lquo;draw,&rquo; or what did he &lquo;find&rquo;? Granting
that he drew from Holinshed, or from the old comedy, or whence you please, where
did he find Lear's madness, or the pudder of the elements, or the inspired babblings
of the Fool? Of whatsoever makes his tragedies sublime and heaven-high above
all other human compositions,&mdash;of that we find never a trace. And this minds me
to say that of all departments of Shakespearian study none seems to me more profit-
less than this search for the sources whence Shakespeare gathered his dramas; the
distance is always immeasurable between the hint and the fulfilment; what to our
purblind eyes is a bare, naked rock becomes, when gilded by Shakespeare's heavenly
alchemy, encrusted thick all over with jewels. When, after reading one of his
tragedies, we turn to what we are pleased to call the &lquo;original of his plot,&rquo; I am
reminded of those glittering gems, of which Heine speaks, that we see at night in
lovely gardens, and think must have been left there by kings' children at play, but
when we look for these jewels by day we see only wretched little worms which
crawl painfully away, and which the foot forbears to crush only out of strange pity.
<PB N=384>
<HE>384 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>If we must find an original for <I>Lear</I>, I think it is in the old drama, and not in
Holinshed; and I mean by this, that, in reading this old drama, every now and then
there comes across us an incident, or a line, or a phrase, that reminds us of Shake-
speare's <I>Lear</I>, and that this cannot be said of Holinshed's story. For instance, in
<I>Leir</I> we find a faithful courtier who defends Cordella to her father, and the old
king replies, &lquo;Urge this no more, and if thou love thy life.&rquo; And this same courtier
afterwards accompanies the old king in his exile as his faithful companion and ser-
vant. Again, in the trial-scene Cordella murmurs aside her abhorrence at the hypoc-
risy of her sisters' asseverations of affection. Again, Leir alludes to Gonorill's &lquo;young
bones.&rquo; Again, Perillus says of Leir, &lquo;But he the myrrour of mild patience, Puts up
&lquo;all wrongs and never gives reply.&rquo; Shakespeare's Lear says: &lquo;No I will be the
&lquo;pattern of all patience, I will say nothing.&rquo; Again, when Leir recognises Cordella
after their estrangement he kneels to her. But it is needless to multiply instances. I
have given on p. 393 <I>et seq.</I> an abstract of the old drama, much too long and tiresome
to be reprinted entire, and the reader can judge for himself, if he take any interest in a
question which is, I repeat, to me a barren one. No one, I think, has done fuller justice
to the old drama, which, by the way, <SC>Capell</SC> called a &lquo;silly old play,&rquo; than <SC>Campbell</SC>,
the poet, who, in his <I>Remarks</I> on Shakespeare's <I>Lear</I>, says: &lquo;The elder tragedy of
&lquo;<I>King Leir</I> is simple and touching. There is one entire scene in it, the meeting of
&lquo;Cordelia with her father in a lonely forest, which, with Shakespeare's <I>Lear</I> in my
&lquo;memory and heart, I could scarcely read with dry eyes. This <I>Leir</I> is a pleasing
&lquo;tragedy, and, though it precedes our poet's <I>Lear</I>, is not its prototype, and its mild
&lquo;merits only show us the wide expanse of difference between respectable talent and
&lquo;commanding inspiration. The two Lears have nothing in common but their aged
&lquo;weakness, their general goodness of heart, their royal rank, and their misfortunes.
&lquo;The ante-Shakespearian Lear is a patient, simple old man, who bears his sorrows
&lquo;very meekly, till Cordelia arrives with her husband, the King of France, and his
&lquo;victorious army, and restores her father to the throne of Britain. . . . In the old
&lquo;play, Leir has a friend Perillus, who moves our interest, though not so deeply as
&lquo;Kent in the later and grander drama. But, independently of Shakespeare's having
&lquo;created a new Lear, he has sublimated the old tragedy into a new one by an entire
&lquo;originality in the spiritual portraiture of its personages. . . . In fine, wherever Shake-
&lquo;speare works on old materials you will find him not wiping dusted gold, but extract-
&lquo;ing gold from dust, where none but himself could have made the golden extraction.&rquo;
<P>The story of Leir, as told by <SC>Holinshed</SC> (<I>The second Booke of the historie of Eng-
land</I>, chaps. v, vi, ed. 1574) is as follows:
<P>&lquo;Leir the sonne of Baldud, was admitted ruler ouer the Britaines, in the yeere of
&lquo;the world 3105, at what time Ioas raigned as yet in Iuda. This Leir was a prince
&lquo;of right noble demeanor, gouerning his land and subiects in great wealth. He made
&lquo;the towne of Caerlier nowe called Leicester, which standeth vpon the riuer of Sore.
&lquo;It is written that he had by his wife three daughters without other issue, whose
&lquo;names were Gonorilla, Regan, and Cordeilla, which daughters he greatly loued, but
&lquo;specially Cordeilla the yoongest farre aboue the two elder. When this Leir therefore
&lquo;was come to great yeeres, &amp; began to waxe vnweldie through age, he thought to
&lquo;vnderstand the affections of his daughters towards him, and preferre hir whome
&lquo;he best loued, to the succession ouer the kingdome. Whervpon he first asked
&lquo;Gonorilla the eldest, how well shee loued him: who calling hir gods to record,
&lquo;protested, that she loued him more than hir owne life, which by right and reason

&lquo;turned to the second, and demanded of hir how well she loued him: who answered
&lquo;(confirming hir saiengs with great othes) that she loued him more than toung could
&lquo;expresse, and farre aboue all other creatures of the world.
<P>&lquo;Then called he his yoongest daughter Cordeilla before him, and asked of hir what
&lquo;account she made of him: vnto whome she made this answer as followeth: Know-
&lquo;ing the great loue and fatherlie zeale that you haue always borne towards me, (for
&lquo;the which I maie not answere you otherwise than I thinke, and as my conscience

&lquo;(while I liue) loue you as my naturall father And if you would more vnderstand
&lquo;of the loue that I beare you, assertaine your selfe, that so much as you haue, so
&lquo;much you are worth, and so much I loue you, and no more. The father being

&lquo;Henninus, the Duke of Cornewal, and the other vnto Maglanus, the Duke of

&lquo;after his death, and the one halfe thereof immediatelie should be assigned to them
&lquo;in hand: but for the third daughter Cordeilla he reserued nothing.

&lquo;France) whose name was Aganippus, hearing of the beautie, womanhood, and good
&lquo;conditions of the said Cordeilla, desired to haue hir in mariage, and sent ouer to

&lquo;eldest daughters, thinking long yer the gouernment of the land did come to their
&lquo;hands, arose against him in armour, and reft from him the gouernance of the
&lquo;land, vpon conditions to be continued for terme of life: by the which he was put

<P>&lquo;In the end, such was the vnkindnesse, or (as I maie saie) the vnnaturalnesse

<P>&lquo;Now when he had informed his son in law and his daughter in what sort he had

&lquo;of Britaine, in the yeere of the world 3155, before the bylding of Rome 54, Uzia
&lquo;was then reigning in Juda, and Jeroboam ouer Israell. This Cordeilla after hir
&lquo;father's deceasse ruled the land of Britaine right worthilie during the space of fiue
&lquo;yeeres, in which meane time hir husband died, and then about the end of those
&lquo;fiue yeeres, hir two nephewes Margan and Cunedag, sonnes to hir aforesaid sisters,
&lquo;disdaining to be vnder the gouernment of a woman, leuied warre against hir, and
&ldquo;destroied a great part of the land, and finallie tooke hir prisoner, and laid hir fast in
&ldquo;ward, wherewith she tooke suche griefe, being a woman of a manlie courage, and
&ldquo;despairing to recouer libertie, there she slue hirselfe.&rquo;
<P>The following extract from <SC>Sir Philip Sidney's</SC> <I>Arcadia</I> (lib. ii, pp. 133-138, ed.
1598, as quoted in the Clarendon ed.) contains the story out of which Shakespeare
moulded Gloucester's tragic fate. It is called, in ed. 1590, &lquo;The pitifull state, and
&lquo;story of the Paphlagonian vnkinde king, and his kind sonne, first related by the son,
&lquo;then by the blind father&rquo;:
<P>&lquo;It was in the kingdome of <I>Galacia</I>, the season being (as in the depth of winter)
&lquo;verie cold, and as then sodainlie growne to so extreame and foule a storme, that
&lquo;neuer any winter (I thinke) brought forth a fowler child: so that the Princes were
&lquo;euen c&omacr;pelled by the haile, that the pride of the winde blew into their faces, to seeke
&lquo;some shrowding place which a certain hollow rocke offering vnto them, they made
&lquo;it their shield against the tempests furie. And so staying there, till the violence
&lquo;thereof was passed, they heard the speach of a couple, who not perceiuing them,
&lquo;being hid within that rude canapie, held a straunge and pitifull disputation, which
&lquo;made them step out, yet in such sort, as they might see vnseene. There they per-
&lquo;ceiued an aged man, and a young, scarcelie come to the age of a man, both poorely
&lquo;arrayed, extreamely weather-beaten; the olde man blind, the young man leading
&lquo;him: and yet through all those miseries, in both there seemed to appeare a kind
&lquo;of noblenesse, not sutable to that affliction. But the first words they heard, were
&lquo;these of the old man. Well <I>Leonatus</I> (said he) since I cannot perswade thee to
&lquo;leade me to that which should end my griefe, and thy trouble, let me now intreat
thee to leaue me: feare not, my miserie cannot be greater then it is, and nothing
<PB N=387>
<HE><I>THE SOURCE OF THE PLOT</I> 387</HE>
<P>doth become me but miserie: feare not the daunger of my blind steps, I cannot
&lquo;fall worse then I am: and do not I pray thee, do not obstinately continue to infect
&lquo;thee with my wretchednesse: but flie, flie from this region only worthie of me.
&lquo;Deare father (answered he) do not take away from me the only remnant of my
&lquo;happinesse: while I haue power to do you seruice, I am not whollie miserable.
&lquo;Ah my sonne (said he, and with that he groned, as if sorrow straue to breake his
&lquo;heart) how euill fits it me to haue such a sonne, and how much doth thy kindnesse
&lquo;vpbraid my wickednesse? These dolefull speeches, and some others to like pur-
&lquo;pose (well shewing they had not bene borne to the fortune they were in,) moued the
&lquo;Princes to go out vnto them, and aske the younger what they were? Sirs (answered
&lquo;he with a good grace, and made the more agreeable by a certaine noble kind of
&lquo;piteousnesse) I see well you are straungers, that know not our miserie, so well here
&lquo;knowne, that no man dare know, but that we must be miserable. Indeed our state
&lquo;is such, as though nothing is so needfull vnto vs as pitie, yet nothing is more dan-
&lquo;gerous vnto vs, then to make our selues so knowne as may stirre pitie; but your
&lquo;presence promiseth that crueltie shall not ouer-runne hate: and if it did, in truth
&lquo;our state is sunke below the degree of feare.
<P>&lquo;This old man (whom I leade) was lately rightfull Prince of this countrie of
&lquo;<I>Paphlagonia</I>, by the hard-hearted vngratefulnesse of a sonne of his, depriued, not
&lquo;onely of his kingdome (whereof no forraine forces were euer able to spoyle him)
&lquo;but of his sight, the riches which Nature graunts to the poorest creatures. Whereby,
&lquo;and by other his vnnaturall dealings, he hath bene driuen to such griefe, as euen
&lquo;now he would haue had me to haue led him to the top of this rocke, thence to cast
&lquo;himselfe headlong to death: and so would haue made me, who receiued my life
&lquo;of him, to be the worker of his destruction. But noble Gentlemen, said he, if
&lquo;either of you haue a father, and feele what dutifull affection is engraffed in a sonnes
&lquo;heart, let me intreat you to conueigh this afflicted Prince to some place of rest and
&lquo;securitie: amongst your worthie acts it shall be none of the least, that a king of such
&lquo;might and fame, &amp; so vniustlie oppressed, is in any sort by you relieued.
<P>&lquo;But before they could make him answere, his father beganne to speake. Ah my
&lquo;sonne, said he, how euill an Historian are you, that leaue out the chiefe knot of all
&lquo;the discourse? my wickednesse, my wickednesse: and if thou doest it to spare my
&lquo;eares, (the only sense now left me proper for knowledge) assure thy selfe thou doest
&lquo;mistake me: and I take witnesse of that Sunne which you see (with that he cast vp
&lquo;his blind eyes, as if he would hunt for light) and wish my selfe in worse case then
&lquo;I do wish my selfe, which is as euill as may be, if I speake vntrulie, that nothing
&lquo;is so welcome to my thoughts, as the publishing of my shame. Therefore know
&lquo;you Gentlemen (to whom from my heart I wish that it may not proue some ominous
&lquo;foretoken of misfortune to haue met with such a miser as I am) that whatsoeuer my
&lquo;son (&ocirc; God, that truth binds me to reproch him with the name of my son) hath said
&lquo;is true. But besides those truthes, this also is true, that hauing had in lawfull mar-
&lquo;iage, of a mother fit to beare royall children, this sonne (such a one as partly you
&lquo;see, and better shall know by my short declaration) and so enioyed the expectations
&lquo;in the world of him, till he was growne to iustifie their expectations (so as I needed
&lquo;enuie no father for the chiefe comfort of mortalitie, to leaue another ones-selfe after
&lquo;me) I was caried by a bastard sonne of mine (if at least I be bound to beleeue the
&lquo;words of that base woman my concubine, his mother) first to mislike, then to hate,
&lquo;lastlie to destroy, or to do my best to destroy this sonne (I thinke you thinke) vnde-
&lquo;seruing destruction. What wayes he vsed to bring me to it, if I should tell you, I

<P>&lquo;should tediouslie trouble you with as much poisonous hypocrisie, desperate fraud,
&lquo;smooth malice, hidden ambition, and smiling enuie, as in anie liuing person could
&lquo;be harboured: but I list it not; no remembrance of naughtinesse delights me but
&lquo;mine owne; and me thinks, the accusing his traps might in some maner excuse
&lquo;my fault, which certainlie I lothe to do. But the conclusion is, that I gaue orders
&lquo;to some seruants of mine, whom I thought as apt for such charities as my selfe, to
&lquo;leade him out into a forrest, and there to kill him.
<P>&lquo;But those theeues (better natured to my sonne then myselfe) spared his life, let-
&lquo;ting him go to learne to liue poorely: which he did, giuing himselfe to be a priuate
&lquo;souldier in a countrey here by: but as he was ready to be greatly aduanced for
&lquo;some noble peeces of seruice which he did, he heard newes of me: who (drunke
&lquo;in my affection to that vnlawfull and vnnaturall sonne of mine) suffered my selfe so
&lquo;to be gouerned by him, that all fauours and punishments passed by him, all offices,
&lquo;and places of importance distributed to his fauorites; so that ere I was aware, I had
&lquo;left my selfe nothing but the name of a King: which he shortly wearie of too, with
&lquo;many indignities (if any thing may be called an indignitie, which was laid vpon me)
&lquo;threw me out of my seat, and put out my eyes; and then (proud in his tyrannie)
&lquo;let me go, neither imprisoning, nor killing me; but rather delighting to make me
&lquo;feele my miserie; miserie indeed, if euer there were anie; full of wretchednesse,
&lquo;fuller of disgrace, and fullest of guiltinesse. And as he came to the crowne by so
&lquo;vniust means, as vniustlie he kept it, by force of straunger souldiers in <I>Cittadels</I>, the
&lquo;neasts of tyrannie, and murderers of libertie; disarming all his owne countrimen,
&lquo;that no man durst shew himself a wel-willer of mine: to say the truth (I thinke)
&lquo;few of them being so (considering my cruell follie to my good sonne, and foolish
&lquo;kindnesse to my vnkind bastard:) but if there were any who felt a pitie of so great
&lquo;a fall, and had yet any sparkes of vnslaine dutie left in them towards me; yet durst
&lquo;they not shew it, scarcelie with giuing me almes at their doores; which yet was the
&lquo;onlie sustenance of my distressed life, no bodie daring to shew so much charitie, as
&lquo;to lend me a hand to guide my darke steps: till this sonne of mine (God knowes,
&lquo;worthy of a more vertuous, and more fortunate father) forgetting my abhominable
&lquo;wrongs, not recking daunger, and neglecting the present good way hee was in of
&lquo;doing himselfe good, came hither to do this kind office you see him performe to-
&lquo;wards me, to my vnspeakeable griefe; not onlie because his kindnesse is a glasse
&lquo;euen to my blind eyes of my naughtinesse, but that aboue all griefes, it grieues me
&lquo;he should desperatelie aduenture the losse of his well-deseruing life for mine, that
&lquo;yet owe more to Fortune for my deserts, as if he would carie mudde in a chest of
&lquo;Chrystall: for well I know, he that now raigneth, how much so euer (and with
&lquo;good reason) he despiseth me, of all men despised; yet he will not let slip any ad-
&lquo;uantage to make away him, whose iust title (ennobled by courage &amp; goodnesse)
&lquo;may one day shake the seat of a neuer secure tyrannie. And for this cause I craued
&lquo;of him to leade me to the top of this rocke, indeed I must confesse, with meaning
&lquo;to free him from so serpentine a companion as I am. But he finding what I pur-
&lquo;posed, onely therein since he was borne, shewed himselfe disobedient vnto me.
&lquo;And now Gentlemen, you haue the true storie, which I pray you publish to the
&lquo;world, that my mischieuous proceedings may be the glorie of his filiall pietie, the
&lquo;onlie reward now left for so great a merite. And if it may be, let me obtaine that
&lquo;of you, which my sonne denies me: for neuer was there more pity in sauing any,
&lquo;then in ending me, both because therin my agonie shall end, &amp; so you shal preserue
&lquo;this excellent young man, who else wilfully followes his owne ruine.&rquo;

<P><SC>Malone</SC> quotes, from Camden's <I>Remaines</I>, 1674, Cordelia's answer to her father,
and thinks it &lquo;more probable that Shakespeare had it in his thoughts than <I>The Mirour
&lquo;for Magistrates</I>, as Camden's book was published recently before he appears to have
&lquo;composed this play, and that portion of it which is entitled <I>Wise Speeches</I>, where
&lquo;[the answer] is found, furnished him with a hint in <I>Coriolanus.</I>&rquo; The answer is as
follows: &lquo;that albeit she did love, honour, and reverence him, and so would whilst
&lquo;she lived, as much as nature and daughterlie dutie at the uttermost could expect,
&lquo;yet she did think that one day it would come to passe that she should affect another

<P>We now come to the ante-Shakespearian drama of <I>King Leir</I>, the exact title whereof
is given on p. 353. While giving an abstract of each Scene, I have endeavored to
retain all words or phrases that the ingenuity of an ardent partisan could convert or
pervert into a suggestion of Shakespeare's <I>Lear.</I> <SC>Skottowe</SC> is the most zealous ad-
vocate that I know, of the claims of <I>King Leir;</I> I am afraid his zeal outruns his wisdom.
I believe I have incorporated in the abstract every passage to which he appeals for con-
firmation of his theory. I have followed the text given in <I>Six Old Plays</I>, &amp;c., 1779.
<P>In the opening scene Leir announces to his assembled court that, the obsequies of
his &lquo;deceast and dearest queen&rquo; having been duly performed, his care now is to see
his daughters befittingly married. As for himself, &lquo;One foot already hangeth in the
&lquo;grave,&rquo;&mdash;
<BQ>And I would faine resigne these earthly cares,<LB>
And thinke upon the welfare of my soule;<LB>
Which by no better means may be effected,<LB>
Then by resigning up the crown from me<LB>
In equal dowry to my daughters three.&rquo;<LB></BQ>
<P>A courtier, Skalliger by name, then proposes that, since his majesty knows well
&lquo;What several suters [the] princely daughters have,&rquo; he should &lquo;make them eche a
&lquo;jointer more or lesse, As is their worth, to them that love professe.&rquo; To which Leir
replies, &lquo;No more, nor lesse, but even all alike, My zeale is fixt, all fashioned in one
&lquo;mould.&rquo; Cornwall and Cambria, &lquo;two neere neighbouring kings,&rquo; &lquo;motion love to
&lquo;Gonorill and Ragan,&rquo; but Cordella, it appears, has more than one lover; Leir says:
<BQ>&lquo;My youngest daughter, faire <I>Cordella</I>, vowes<LB>
No liking to a monarch, unlesse love allowes.<LB>
She is sollicited by divers peeres;<LB>
But none of them her partial fancy heares.<LB>
Yet, if my policy may her beguile,<LB>
Ile match her to some king within this ile,<LB>
And so establish such a perfit peace,<LB>
As fortunes force shall ne'er prevaile to cease.&rdquo;<LB></BQ>
<P>Perillus, another noble courtier, begs his majesty not to &lquo;force love, where fancy
cannot dwell,&rquo; and Leir replies:
<BQ>&lquo;I am resolv'd, and even now my mind<LB>
Doth meditate a sudden strategem,<LB>
To try which of my daughters loves me best:<LB>

<P>(Justice has never been done, I think, to the unaffected loveliness, at times, of Cor-

<P>In the mean time Cordella's distress is so great that her husband promises to send

<P>At the appointed hour Ragan meets the messenger that had come to her from
Gonorill, and hires him to kill Leir and Perillus in a thicket some two miles from
the court, whither she will send them on some pretext or other on the morrow.
<P>The scene then changes to Cornwall, where Gonorill and her husband receive the
ambassador from the Gallian king, who comes with a message to Leir; but as Leir
is absent, Gonorill and Cornwall persuade the ambassador to tarry at their court for
a few days until Leir's return.
<P>We now go back to Leir and Perillus, whom we find at the thicket some two miles
from the court. The assassin appears before them and announces his design of
killing them. Leir thinks that he must have been sent by Cordella, and is willing to
submit to what he cannot but consider the justice of Heaven. He is undeceived by
Gonorill's letter which the assassin shows him. While the two old men are praying
for their lives, some highly opportune claps of thunder so terrify the assassin that he
drops his daggers and departs, after calling them the &lquo;parlosest old men that ere he
heard.&rquo; Perillus then persuades Leir to try his fortune with Cordella; and while
they are crossing over to Brittany we find that the Gallian king, Cordella, and Mum-
ford devise a pleasant little excursion to the seaside for recreation, and that the
Gallian ambassador, giving up all hope of finding Leir at Gonorill's court, comes
to Ragan's; there he finds Ragan trying to persuade her husband that her father's
absence is due to Cordella's machinations, and that Cordella has undoubtedly killed
Leir. This accusation she repeats to the ambassador, and falls into a great rage with
him for attempting to defend his mistress, and strikes him.
<P>When Leir and Perillus land on the coast of Brittany, they are obliged to pay for

Perillus calls Gonorill a &lquo;monster,&rquo; and Ragan says she never heard a fouler-spoken
man than Perillus. Leir interrupts these amenities, and adds to them, by addressing

<BQ>&lquo;Out on thee, viper, scum, filthy parricide,<LB>

<P>After some further conversation in the same style, they proceed to business. Corn-
