<HE>466 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>autant que l'histoire peut-&ecirc;tre, mais a un autre point de vue, une v&eacute;rit&eacute;. Shakespeare
est d'accord avec Walter Mapes, archidiacre d'Oxford, c'est bien quelque chose; il
admet, depuis Brutus jusqu'a Cadvalla, les quatre-vingt-dix-neuf rois celtes qui ont
pr&eacute;c&eacute;d&eacute; le scandinave Hengist et le saxon Horsa; et puisqu'il croit &agrave; Mulmutius, &agrave;
Cinigisil, &agrave; C&eacute;olulfe, &agrave; Cassibelan, &agrave; Cymbeline, &agrave; Cynulphus, &agrave; Arviragus, &agrave; Gui-
derius, &agrave; Escuin, &agrave; Cudred, &agrave; Vortigerne, &agrave; Arthur, &agrave; Uther Pendragon, il a bien le droit
de croire au roi Lear, et de cr&eacute;er Cordelia. Ce terrain adopt&eacute;, ce lieu de sc&egrave;ne d&eacute;-
sign&eacute;, cette fondation creus&eacute;e, il prend tout, et il b&acirc;tit son &oelig;uvre. Construction inou&iuml;e.
Il prend la tyrannie, dont il fera plus tard la faiblesse, Lear; il prend la trahison,
Edmund; il prend le d&eacute;vouement, Kent; il prend l'ingratitude qui commence par
une caresse, et il donne &agrave; ce monstre deux t&ecirc;tes, Goneril, que la l&eacute;gende appelle
Gornerille, et Regane, que la l&eacute;gende appelle Raga&uuml;; il prend la paternit&eacute;; il prend
la royaut&eacute;; il prend la f&eacute;odalit&eacute;; il prend l'ambition; il prend la d&eacute;mence qu'il
partage en trois, et il met en pr&eacute;sence trois fous, le bouffon du roi, fou par m&eacute;tier,
Edgar de Glocester, fou par prudence, le roi, fou par mis&egrave;re. C'est au sommet de cet
entassement tragique qu'il dresse et penche Cordelia.
<P>Il y a de formidables tours de cath&eacute;drales, comme, par exemple, la giralda de
S&eacute;ville, qui semblent faites tout enti&egrave;res, avec leurs spirales, leurs escaliers, leurs
sculptures, leurs caves, leurs c&oelig;cums, leurs cellules a&eacute;riennes, leurs chambres sonores,
leurs cloches, leur plainte, et leur masse, et leur fl&egrave;che, et toute leur &eacute;normit&eacute;, pour
porter un ange ouvrant sur leur cime ses ailes dor&eacute;es. Tel est ce drame, <I>le Roi Lear.</I>
<P>Le p&egrave;re est le pr&eacute;texte de la fille. Cette admirable cr&eacute;ation humaine, Lear, sert
de support &agrave; cette ineffable cr&eacute;ation divine, Cordelia. Tout ce chaos de crimes, de
vices, de d&eacute;mences et de mis&egrave;res, a pour raison d'&ecirc;tre l'apparition splendide de la
vertu. Shakespeare, portant Cordelia dans sa pens&eacute;e, a cr&eacute;&eacute; cette trag&eacute;die comme
un dieu qui, ayant une aurore &agrave; placer, ferait tout expr&egrave;s un monde pour l'y mettre.
<P>Et quelle figure que le p&egrave;re! quelle caryatide! C'est l'homme courb&eacute;. Il ne fait
que changer de fardeaux, toujours plus lourds. Plus le vieillard faiblit, plus le poids
augmente. Il vit sous la surcharge. Il porte d'abord l'empire, puis l'ingratitude,
puis l'isolement, puis le d&eacute;sespoir, puis la faim, et la soif, puis la folie puis toute la
nature. Les nu&eacute;es viennent sur sa t&ecirc;te, les for&ecirc;ts l'accablent d'ombre, l'ouragan s'abat
sur sa nuque, l'orage plombe son manteau, la pluie p&egrave;se sur ses &eacute;paules, il marche
pli&eacute; et hagard, comme s'il avait les deux genoux de la nuit sur son dos. &Eacute;perdu et
immense, il jette aux bourrasques et aux gr&ecirc;les ce cri &eacute;pique: Pourquoi me ha&iuml;ssez-
vous, temp&ecirc;tes? pourquoi me pers&eacute;cutez-vous? <I>Vous n'&ecirc;tes pas mes filles.</I> Et alors,
c'est fini, la lueur s'&eacute;teint, la raison se d&eacute;courage et s'en va, Lear est en enfance.
Ah! il est enfant, ce vieillard. Eh bien! il lui faut une m&egrave;re. Sa fille para<*>t. Son
unique fille, Cordelia. Car les deux autres, Regane et Goneril, ne sont plus ses
filles que de la quantit&eacute; n&eacute;cessaire pour avoir droit au nom de parricides.
<P>Cordelia approche.&mdash;<I>Me reconnaissez-vous, sire?&mdash;Vous &ecirc;tes un esprit, je le sais</I>,
r&eacute;pond le vieillard, avec la clairvoyance sublime de l'&eacute;garement. A partir de ce
moment, l'adorable allaitement commence. Cordelia se met &agrave; nourrir cette vielle
&acirc;me d&eacute;sesp&eacute;r&eacute;e qui se mourait d'inanition dans la haine. Cordelia nourrit Lear
d'amour, et le courage revient; elle le nourrit de respect, et le sourire revient; elle le
nourrit d'esp&eacute;rance, et la confiance revient; elle le nourrit de sagesse, et la raison re-
vient. Lear, convalescent, remonte, et, de degr&eacute; en degr&eacute;, retrouve la vie. L'enfant
redevient un vieillard, le vieillard redevient un homme. Et le voil&agrave; heureux, ce
mis&eacute;rable. C'est sur cet &eacute;panouissement que fond la catastrophe. H&eacute;las, il y a des
traitres, il y a des parjures, il y a des meurtriers. Cordelia meurt. Rien de plus

<HE><I>TATE'S VERSION</I> 467</HE>
<P>navrant. Le vieillard s'&eacute;tonne, il ne comprend plus, et, embrassant ce cadavre, il
expire. Il meurt sur cette morte. Ce d&eacute;sespoir supr&ecirc;me lui est &eacute;pargn&eacute; de rester
derri&egrave;re elle parmi les vivants, pauvre ombre, t&acirc;tant la place de son c&oelig;ur vid&eacute; et
cherchant son &acirc;me emport&eacute;e par ce doux &ecirc;tre qui est parti. O Dieu, ceux que vous
aimez, vous ne les laissez pas survivre.
<P>Demeurer apr&egrave;s l'envolement de l'ange, &ecirc;tre le p&egrave;re orphelin de son enfant, &ecirc;tre

c'est une sombre destin&eacute;e. Tu as bien fait, po&euml;te, de tuer ce vieillard.

<C>NAHUM TATE'S VERSION</C>
<P><SC>An</SC> edition like the present would be incomplete without some notice of the version
of <I>King Lear</I> which held the stage for a hundred and sixty years, and in which all
our greatest actors, Garrick, Kemble, Kean, and others, won applause, and which
was discarded only about forty years ago. It is so much easier to blame than to
praise that we echo very readily the anathemas that are now heaped on the name
of Tate. But really Tate was little to blame; he was merely the exponent of the age
in which he lived, and no genius. &lquo;You must think of this, look you, the worm will
&lquo;do his kind.&rquo; We must remember, too, that <I>Lear</I> is the sublimest tragedy ever
written, so awful in its grandeur that it almost passes into a realm by itself. Charles
Lamb avers that it ought not to be acted at all, and in thus saying he exonerates Tate,
to a certain extent, in the very breath with which he condemns him. Tate's Version
is better than none; if we had not Shakespeare's play to read, surely it were better
to listen to Tate than not to know the play at all. There is more of Shakespeare in
Tate's Version than there is of Tate.
<P>At any rate, I cannot but think that others, however hard they may be upon Tate for
his laughable attempts to be Shakespearian in his changes, will, like myself, be a little
softened towards him after reading his Dedication; a tone of reverence for Shake-
speare runs through it that quite took me by surprise. It is as follows: To my Esteemed
Friend <I>Thomas Boteler</I>, Esq; Sir, You have a natural Right to this Piece, since by
your Advice I attempted the Revival of it with Alterations. Nothing but the Power of
your Persuasions, and my Zeal for all the Remains of <I>Shakespear</I> cou'd have wrought
me to so bold an Undertaking. I found that the New-modelling of this Story wou'd
force me sometimes on the difficult Task of making the chiefest Persons speak some-
thing like their Character, on Matter whereof I had no Ground in my Author. <I>Lear's</I>
real and <I>Edgar's</I> pretended Madness have so much of <I>extravagant Nature</I> (I know
not how else to express it), as cou'd never have started but from our <I>Shakespear's</I>
Creating Fancy. The Images and Language are so odd and surprizing, and yet so
agreeable and proper, that whilst we grant that none but <I>Shakespear</I> could have
form'd such Conceptions; yet we are satisfied that they were the only Things in the
World that ought to be said on those Occasions. I found the whole to answer your
<PB N=468>
<HE>468 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>account of it, a Heap of Jewels, unstrung, and unpolisht; yet so dazling in their
Disorder, that I soon perceiv'd I had seiz'd a Treasure. 'Twas my good Fortune to
light on one Expedient to rectify what was wanting in the Regularity and Probability
of the Tale, which was to run through the whole, as <I>Love</I> betwixt <I>Edgar</I> and <I>Cor-
delia;</I> that never chang'd a Word with each other in the Original. This renders
<I>Cordelia's</I> Indifference, and her Father's Passion in the first Scene, probable. It
likewise gives Countenance to <I>Edgar's</I> Disguise, making that a generous Design that
was before a poor Shift to save his Life. The Distress of the Story is evidently
heightened by it; and it particularly gave Occasion of a New Scene or Two, of more
Success (perhaps) than Merit. This method necessarily threw me on making the
Tale conclude in a Success to the innocent distrest Persons: Otherwise I must have
incumbred the Stage with dead Bodies, which Conduct makes many Tragedies con-
clude with unseasonable Jests. Yet was I wract with no small Fears for so bold a
Change, till I found it well receiv'd by my Audience; and if this will not satisfy
the Reader, I can produce an Authority that questionless will.
<I>Neither is it of so Trivial an Undertaking to make a Tragedy end</I>
<marg><I>Mr.</I> Dryd. <I>Pre<*>
to the</I> Spanish
Fryer.</marg>
<I>happily, for 'tis more difficult to save than 'tis to Kill: The Dagger
and Cup of Poison are always in Readiness; but to bring the Action
to the last Extremity, and then by probable means to recover All, will require the
Art and Judgment of a Writer, and cost him many a Pang in the Performance.</I>
<P>I have one thing more to apologize for, which is that I have us'd less Quaintness
of Expression even in the Newest Parts of this Play. I confess, 'twas Design in me,
partly to comply with my Author's Style, to make the Scenes of a Piece, and partly
to give it some Resemblance of the Time and Persons here Represented. This, Sir,
I submit wholly to you, who are both a Judg and Master of Style. Nature had
exempted you before you went Abroad from the Morose Saturnine Humour of our
Country, and you brought home the Refinedness of Travel without the Affectation.
Many faults I see in the following Pages, and question not but you will discover
more; yet I will presume so far on your Friendship as to make the whole a Present
to you, and Subscribe myself <I>Your obliged Friend and humble Servant</I>, N. <SC>Tate</SC>.

<P>When the play opens Gloucester is already convinced of Edgar's treachery, and
Edmund is in high favour.
<P>As the royal procession is entering, before the division of the kingdom, Edgar,
&lquo;speaking to Cordelia at Entrance,&rquo; declares his love for her, and is assured by her
that his love is returned, so ardently, indeed, that Cordelia's blunt replies to her
father are prompted, not so much by detestation of her sisters' hypocrisy, as by a de-
sire to avoid marriage with Burgundy:
<BQ>&lquo;<S>Cordelia.</S> [<I>Aside</I>] Now comes my trial, How am I distrest,<LB>

Rather to leave me Dowerless; then condemn me<LB>
To loath'd embraces.&rquo;<LB></BQ>
<P>Cordelia is cast off, and Burgundy refuses her; of the King of France there is no
mention throughout the play. Kent is banished.
<P>Now that Cordelia is in disgrace Edgar renews his suit, but Cordelia, true to the

must test Edgar's love by coldness, and alleges that she is now no longer &lquo;the darling
&lquo;of a king.&rquo; Whereupon Edgar:

<P>The next Act opens with a short scene between Goneril and her &lquo;Poisoner,&rquo;

sisters. In the next scene, after Edgar has left Gloucester in the shadow of a tree

<SHL>
<P><SC>Addison</SC>, in <I>The Spectator</I> (No. 40, April 16, 1711), says, &lquo;<I>King Lear</I> is an admir-
able tragedy . . . as Shakespeare wrote it; but as it is reformed according to the
chimerical notion of poetical justice, in my humble opinion it has lost half its beauty.&rquo;
<P><SC>Davies</SC> (<I>Dram. Misc.</I>, ii, 212): Though Tate's alterations are, in many places,
mean and unworthy to be placed so near the composition of the best dramatic author,
it must be confessed, that in the conduct of some Scenes, whether contrived by him-
self or hinted to him by his friend Dryden, he is not unhappy. One situation of his
is particularly affecting; where the Scene opens and discovers Lear, with his head
on Cordelia's lap, and the king in his sleep, attacking the forces of his enemies. The
bringing that action forward to the audience, which is only related in the old play,
of Lear's killing the two soldiers employed to murder him and Cordelia, is a circum-
stance that gives pleasure and exultation to the spectators. The half-breathing and
panting of Garrick, with a look and action which confessed the infirmity of old age,
greatly heightened the picture. To speak in Shakespeare's phrase, this incident will
be <I>locked in the memvry</I> of those who have the pleasure to remember it. Barry, in
this Scene, was a lively copy of Garrick's manner, and had the superior advantage
of a more important figure. Who could possibly think of depriving an audience,
almost exhausted with the feelings of so many terrible Scenes, of the inexpressible
delight which they enjoyed, when the old king in rapture cried out,&mdash;
<BQ>&lquo;Old Lear shall be a King again&rquo;?<LB REND=RIGHT></BQ>
<PB N=478>
<HE>478 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P><SC>Arthur Murphy</SC>, whom <SC>Dr Johnson</SC> pronounced a very judicious critic, thus
speaks of Tate's Version (<I>Gray's-Inn Journal</I>, ii, 222, 1754): The close of this
Tragedy is full of Terror and Commiseration, and our great Poet has here given us
a Death, which is not often to be found in the Play-house Bill of Mortality, <I>viz.</I>,
the Death of Lear without the Dagger or the Bowl. But, perhaps, after all the
Heart-piercing Sensations which we have before endured through the whole Piece,
it would be too much to see this actually performed on the Stage; from the actor
whom I have already named [Garrick] I am sure it would, though I should be glad
to see the Experiment made, convinced at the same Time that the Play, as it is altered,
will always be most agreeable to an Audience, as the Circumstances of Lear's Res-
toration, and the virtuous Edgar's Alliance with the amiable Cordelia, must always
call forth those gushing Tears which are swelled and ennobled by a virtuous Joy.
<P><SC>Macready</SC> in his <I>Reminiscences</I> (p. 697, New York, 1875) says that &lquo;Tate's
&lquo;<I>King Lear</I> was the only acting copy from the date of its production until the res-
&lquo;toration of Shakespeare's tragedy at Covent Garden in 1838. Previously to that,
&lquo;I think, in the year 1823, or a little later, the play, Tate's, was acted by Kean, with
&lquo;the last Scene of the original restored. I believe the elder Colman put out an
&lquo;alteration, but I question whether it was acted; certainly it did not hold its place
&lquo;on the stage.&rquo;

<P>The Agreement of the Folios is indicated by the symbol Ff; that of Q<SUB>1</SUB> and Q.
by Qq.
<P>The sign + after Ff, or F<SUB>4</SUB>, indicates the agreement of <SC>Rowe, Pope, Theobald.
Hanmer, Warburton</SC>, and <SC>Johnson</SC>.
<P>The same sign after Glo. indicates the agreement of the <I>Globe Edition</I>, the <I>Cam-
bridge Edition</I>, and <SC>Wright's</SC> (<I>Clarendon</I>) Edition.
<P>The abbreviation (subs.) indicates that the reading is substantially given, and that
immaterial variations in spelling, punctuation, or stage-directions are disregarded
<P>When <SC>Warburton</SC> precedes <SC>Hanmer</SC>, in the Textual Notes, it indicates that
<SC>Hanmer</SC> has adopted a suggestion of <SC>Warburton's</SC>.
<P>When the <SC>Variorum of</SC> 1821 follows <SC>Malone's</SC> edition of 1790, <I>Var.</I> stands for
both; when they disagree, <I>Bos.</I>, i. e., Boswell, stands for the former only.
<P><I>Coll.</I> (<I>MS</I>) refers to Mr <SC>Collier's</SC> annotated F<SUB>2</SUB>.
<P><I>Quincy</I> (<I>MS</I>) refers to Mr Quincy's annotated F<SUB>4</SUB>.
<P>The words <I>et cet.</I> after any reading indicate that it is the reading of <I>all other</I>
editions.
<P>The frequent omission of the apostrophe in the F<SUB>2</SUB>, a peculiarity of that edition, is
not generally noted.
<P>An Emendation or Conjecture which is discussed in the Commentary is not repeated
in the Textual Notes; nor is &lquo;conj.&rquo; added to any name in the Textual Notes unless
it happens to be that of an editor, in which case its omission would be misleading.
<P>In the matter of punctuation the colon is used as it is in German, as equivalent
to &lquo;namely.&rquo;
<P>A dash at the close of a sentence, in the Text, indicates that the speaker changes
his address from one person to another.
<P>All citations of Acts, Scenes, and lines in <I>Romeo and Juliet, Macbeth</I>, and
<I>Hamlet</I> refer to this edition of those plays; in citations from other plays the <I>Globe
Edition</I> is followed.
